## The State Buddha Sāsana
## Mahābuddhavaṃsa
## Introduction
**********
## Namo Buddhāya
## (Siddhaṃ)
Kīdiso te mahāvīra,
abhinīhāro naruttama.
kamhi kāle tayā dhīra,
patthitā bodhimuttamā.

O Great Hero (Mahāvīra), who possesses great energy and exertion through the fourfold Right Efforts (Sammappadhāna)! O Supreme among Men (Naruttama), the Lord of the Three Worlds, who excels above humans, devas, and Brahmas! How should your initial resolve (abhinīhāra) be understood—that great aspiration to become a Buddha, which shook the ten thousand world systems from the lowest hell to the highest heaven? O Wise One (Dhīra), Master of Omniscient Knowledge, Lord of the Three Worlds! In which era and at what time did you incline your mind and make the aspiration for the supreme and noble Sammāsambodhi (Supreme Enlightenment), which is superior to Paccekabodhi and Sāvakabodhi?
2:
(b)
This question and problem arose 2,548 years ago, on the 1st waning day of Kason in the year 104 of the Great Era (Maha Sakkarit), at the end of the spring season, as a sound emerging from the sky above the royal city of Kapilavatthu. I shall briefly describe how this question came to be.

The Lord Buddha, known as the Omniscient One (Sabbaññū), the Supreme of the Three Worlds, spent his first rainy season (vassa) after enlightenment in the year 103 of the Great Era at the Isipatana Deer Park near Bārāṇasī. During that rainy season, he established the five monks of the group of five (Pañcavaggiya) and fifty-four friends led by the merchant's son Yasa in the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). When the rainy season ended, he sent the sixty Arahants to missionary work, instructing each to travel a different path alone to preach the Dhamma, which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end. The Buddha himself traveled alone toward the entrance of the Uruvelā forest to convert the one thousand hermit brothers led by Uruvelā Kassapa.

On his way to the Uruvelā forest, the Buddha arrived at the Kappāsika grove. There, he preached to the thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes who were searching for a missing woman, established them in the lower Paths and Fruits, and ordained them as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. Continuing alone to the Uruvelā forest, he performed over 3,500 types of miracles for the great hermit teacher Uruvelā Kassapa and his five hundred followers, leading them to liberation from wrong views and ordaining them as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. Thereafter, along with the three hundred followers...
3:
(c)
...of the teacher Nadī Kassapa and the two hundred followers of the teacher Gayā Kassapa, he successively liberated them from wrong views and ordained them as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. Having established those one thousand hermit-monks in the Fruit of Arahantship through the discourse of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta at the Gayāsīsa rock, he traveled to the city of Rājagaha accompanied by those one thousand Arahants.

On the very day he arrived at Rājagaha, he established King Bimbisāra and 110,000 brahmins and householders in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala), and 10,000 brahmins and householders as lay followers (upāsaka) who took refuge in the Triple Gem. On the following day, he accepted the donation of the great Veluvana monastery from King Bimbisāra—the first such donation in the Buddha's Dispensation, which caused the earth to tremble. From that time on, while he was bestowing the medicine of the Deathless Dhamma upon the Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka), Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka), and ordinary disciples (Pakatisāvaka) who were ready for liberation...

His father, King Suddhodana, sent nine ministers, each with a retinue of one thousand men, on nine separate occasions to invite the Buddha, but none returned with news as they all became Arahants. On the tenth occasion, the King sent the internal minister Kāḷudāyī, who was born on the same day as the Buddha. Like the others, Kāḷudāyī and his one thousand followers became Arahants. After spending time in the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti), when the winter had passed and spring arrived, he invited the Buddha to the royal city using sixty-four verses of gentle and pleasant persuasion.
4:
(d)
Because of this invitation, starting from the 1st waning day of Tabaung, the Buddha traveled one yojana per day, accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants. Moving with the 'unhurried' (aturita) pace of a Buddha, like the full moon surrounded by stars, he arrived at the royal city of Kapilavatthu on the 1st waning day of Kason in the year 104 of the Great Era.

On that very day, all the Sakyan princes, according to their prior consultation and plan, escorted the Saṅgha led by the Buddha to the Nigrodhārāma monastery with great ceremony. Upon reaching the monastery, the Buddha sat peacefully upon the Buddha-seat (buddhāsana) surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants. However, the Sakyan princes, being stiff with pride in their lineage (jātimāna), thought: "Prince Siddhattha is younger than us; he is only our younger brother, nephew, or grandson." With such thoughts, they spoke to one another with arrogance, saying, "You younger ones, pay homage; we shall sit behind you."

The Buddha, perceiving the intense pride and inner thoughts of the Sakyan princes, reflected: "These relatives of mine, full of pride, do not realize they are aging in vain without achieving their own benefit. They do not know at all the nature of a Buddha or the power of the Buddhas. Now, I shall demonstrate the power of a Buddha and perform the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) of fire and water. In the sky, I shall create a great jeweled walkway (ratana-caṅkama) as wide as the ten thousand world systems..."
5:
(e)
"...and after creating it, I shall walk back and forth upon that jeweled walkway. Observing the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of all the beings who have gathered, I shall rain down the rain of the Dhamma." As soon as he made this resolution, the devas and Brahmas from the ten thousand world systems shouted in acclaim and uttered "Sādhu."

Then, immediately after his reflection, the Buddha entered the meditative attainment of the fourth jhana using the white kasina (odātakasiṇa) as the object. Emerging from that attainment, he made the firm resolution: "Let the light spread throughout the ten thousand world systems." Simultaneously with his resolution, the light enveloped the ten thousand world systems. While many humans, devas, and Brahmas were rejoicing, he ascended into the sky through the fourth jhana of direct knowledge (abhiññā). From twelve locations—(1) upper and lower body, (2) front and back, (3) both eyes, (4) ears, (5) nostrils, (6) shoulders, (7) hands, (8) sides, (9) feet, (10) fingers and toes and their intervals, (11) each single hair, and (12) each single pore—he emitted jets of fire and streams of water alternately. As the colors changed with every view, he performed the Twin Miracle beautifully in the midst of the assembly of humans and devas, as if scattering the dust of his feet upon the heads of the Sakyan princes who were filled with wonder and ceaseless praise.

Having created a magnificent jeweled walkway that extended across the ten thousand world systems from east to west, he walked back and forth upon it, and according to the wishes and inclinations of humans and devas...
6:
(f)
...he rained down the rain of the Dhamma copiously. While this was happening, the Venerable Mahāthera Sāriputta, residing at Gijjhakūṭa Hill in Rājagaha, clearly saw these events. He thought, "I shall now approach the Buddha and request him to preach the Buddhavaṃsa Dhamma—the lineage and history of the Bodhisattas." He immediately assembled five hundred Arahants who lived with him and urged them, saying, "Etha sabbe gamissāma = Come, let us all go! Let us go to the presence of the Buddha, pay homage, and ask about the past practices and conduct of the Buddhas."

Traveling through the sky with the psychic power of Iddhividha-abhiññā, which is swifter than a storm, they arrived in the Buddha's presence in an instant. After paying homage with joined palms, Sāriputta requested the Buddha to preach in detail about how he made his aspiration and received the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa) from previous Buddhas, and how he fulfilled the thirty perfections (pāramīs), using the verses mentioned at the beginning: "Kīdiso te mahāvīra, abhinīhāro naruttama..."

Then, while still residing on the jeweled walkway, the Buddha spoke two verses beginning with "Pītipāmojjajananaṃ, sokasallavinodanaṃ...", saying: "Listen respectfully to the Buddhavaṃsa discourse, which generates joy and delight, removes the thorn of sorrow, and brings the three types of prosperity—human, celestial, and Nibbāna. Having heard it, you should strive to follow the path of my practice as found in the Buddhavaṃsa, which removes pride and sorrow..."
7:
(g)
"...which leads to liberation from saṃsāra and brings about the end of all suffering." Having thus encouraged the humans, devas, and Brahmas with compassion, he preached the Buddhavaṃsa discourse (including the introduction) consisting of 1,070 verses, equivalent to four bhāṇavāras (the amount recited in four sittings during the Council).

## The Buddhavaṃsa Commentary
The commentary (Atthakathā) on this Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi—which was included in the Khuddaka Nikāya of the Suttanta Piṭaka by the Arahants led by Venerable Mahākassapa during the First, Second, and Third Councils—is twenty-six bhāṇavāras in length. It was composed under the title "Madhuratthavilāsinī" by the Venerable Mahāthera Buddhadatta, who resided at the monastery of the port of Kāveripaṭṭana in the Coḷa country, east of Anurādhapura in the island of Sri Lanka.

## The Great Chronicle of Buddhas (Buddhavaṃsa Vatthu-daw-gyi)
During the reign of King Bagyidaw, the founder of the fourth city and palace of Ratanapura, the first Ngakhun Sayadaw—who received the title "Ādiccavansābhidhaja Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru" and was a native of Ngakhun village—desired for the noble sons and daughters of Myanmar who follow the Buddha's teachings to obtain the benefits of joy, delight, and the cooling of sorrow mentioned before. Since there were already well-known ancient Nissayas (word-for-word translations), he did not write in the Nissaya style but instead synthesized the Pāḷi and the Commentary, including the important Pāḷi verses and their translations...
8:
(h) ...interspersed with the prose narrative of the Buddhavamsa.

This great prose work of the Buddhavamsa was printed about 25 years ago (in the Burmese Era 1297, 1935 CE) by the Jambumait-swe Pitaka Press in Yangon under the title "Maha Buddhavamsa Vatthu-daw-gyi" (The Great Narrative of the Chronicle of Buddhas), consisting of three volumes (Volume I, II, and III).

## The Sudhammavati Buddhavamsa Text

Not long after the publication of the Maha Buddhavamsa Vatthu-daw-gyi by the Jambumait-swe Press, the "Sudhammavati Maha Buddhavamsa Vatthu-daw-gyi," written in rhythmic prose by the Chief Editor Saya Gyi U Tun Sein in a single volume, was also published by the Sudhammavati Pitaka Press in Yangon.

## The State Buddha Sasana Maha Buddhavamsa Text

When the Union of Myanmar was established and reached the era of the Sixth Buddhist Council (Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana), the Prime Minister of Myanmar, U Nu, deeply reflected on the fact that both monastics and laypeople were diligently performing their respective preliminary duties (pubbabhāga-parikamma) for the Great Council. With a sincere intention to see a new, most comprehensive Buddhavamsa text emerge during the Sixth Council era—one based primarily on the Pali Canon and Commentaries—he made a formal request to me. This request was made during the ceremony of the consecration (anekajā) of Buddha images at the opening of the new Buddha-vut-yon Monastery within his residence in the year 1313 ME.
9:
(i) At that time, I declined the request to write the Maha Buddhavamsa, explaining, "I still have the responsibility to participate as a Tipiṭakadhara in the upcoming Sixth Buddhist Council and must strive to achieve the Tipiṭakadhara title in time for the Council." Indeed, at that time, I had only completed and passed the examinations for the Vinaya Piṭaka and was about to sit for the Abhidhamma Piṭaka examinations.

## Succession of Teachers

Due to the Prime Minister's unwavering aspiration and persistent effort to bring this Maha Buddhavamsa into existence, the project was first led by the Great Teacher U Saing (Medhavī). He worked on it for a few months but could not complete it. From him, the leadership passed to the Great Teacher U Kyi Pe (Maha Panna Bala Pathama Kyaw). Following him, the responsibility was transferred to the Great Teacher U Lin (MA, Agga Maha Pandita). Under his leadership, after about a year and a half of writing (from the Sumedha-kathā to the end of the Kassapa Buddhavamsa), enough for the first volume was completed. However, the sun that was Saya Gyi U Lin set, leaving only his reputation behind, a loss to be deeply mourned...

Sakiñce asamatteva, sañjahanti bahū janā.
Yathāladdhaṃ bhavaṃ sāyaṃ, puthujjanāna dhammatā.

## The Responsibility Falls Upon Me

On the 11th waxing day of Nat-taw, 1316 ME (December 6, 1954 CE), four days after the passing of the sun-like Saya Gyi U Lin, the Prime Minister's...
10: (j) ...at the urging and request of the Prime Minister, my lay supporter and spiritual father, Sir U Thwin (Thado Thiri Thudhamma), Chairman of the Union Buddha Sāsana Council and leader of the Sixth Council, personally came to me. He requested that I should not refuse if the Prime Minister came to ask me to lead the writing of the great Buddhavaṃsa. Later, on the full moon day of Pyatho, 1316 ME (January 8, 1955), the Prime Minister himself came to the Dhamma Yeiktha within the Sāsana Yeiktha where I was temporarily residing and requested: (1) To lead the writing of the great Buddhavaṃsa text. In doing so, to write it so comprehensively that not a single detail of the Buddha's history is omitted. Even if it takes one, two, four, or eight volumes, please prioritize completeness of content. (2) To write it in a way that is understandable and interesting to adults, youths, and children, as well as to those of other faiths. (3) That if I were to write it, it would be acceptable to both the Sangha and the laity. Having been urged once in 1313 ME, once in 1315 ME, and now again in 1316 ME—both through my lay supporter and by his own personal visit—it was no longer appropriate to refuse. Thus, at 8:00 AM on the full moon day of Pyatho, I replied, "Very well, Dayaka-gyi. After the work of the Pali Council (Saṅgāyana) is finished..."
11:
(k) ..."Once the Council duties are finished, I will lead the writing with all my ability and without reservation," I firmly promised. After the Prime Minister departed...

Yaṃ hi kayirā taṃ hi vade,
yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade.
Akaroṃtaṃ bhāsamānaṃ,
parijānanti paṇḍitā.

(One should say only what one will do; one should not say what one will not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks but does not act.)

I gave myself this cautionary note: "Do not speak without doing; speak only when doing; this is the nature of the pure. To merely expand on speech without action is to not escape blame."

## Request from the Buddha Sasana Council

Not long after promising the Prime Minister, the Union Buddha Sasana Council also formally requested me to serve as the Chief Patron (Nāyaka) for the Buddhavamsa project. I replied that I would accept if the Council agreed to three points: (1) I would serve only as a volunteer (out of faith), (2) I would not be involved in any administrative or office matters, and (3) I would have sole authority over the literary and scholarly aspects. Within a few days, the responsible officials from the Council—Chief Editor Saya U Ba Hmi, Buddhavamsa Editor Saya Tun, and Buddhavamsa Editor Saya U Ba Than—arrived and informed me that the Council agreed to my three conditions. I then told Saya Tun and Saya U Ba Than: "Anāyakā vinassanti, nassanti bahunāyakā = Works without a leader perish; works with too many leaders also perish."
12:
(l) "Therefore, to ensure the work of writing the Buddhavamsa does not fail, I accept the role of Patron. You two should continue writing as you did during Saya Gyi U Lin's time, following the assigned outline. Once the Council is over, I will finalize and refine the work." Thus, I accepted the role of Patron and began.

## Letter of Request

I, your disciple, respectfully and humbly request the Most Venerable Sayadaw Ashin Vicittasārābhivaṃsa, recipient of the titles "Buddha Sasana Visidha Tipiṭakadhara Maha Tipiṭaka Kovida" and "Vicittasārābhivaṃsa Tipiṭakadhara Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika."
13: (m) The great commentator Venerable Mahā Buddhaghosa, in expressing praise and special veneration for the attributes and grace of the Buddha, stated: "Buddho Buddho'ti ghoso atidullabhataro" (The sound 'Buddha, Buddha' is extremely rare). Thus, we know that in this world, even to hear the sound "Buddha, Buddha" is very difficult, and to be able to utter "Buddha, Buddha" with one's mouth is also very difficult. In this regard, although non-Buddhists may easily hear the sound "Buddha, Buddha" uttered by Buddhists, they cannot be said to have truly heard it because they do not understand the attributes and grace of the Buddha. For example, among those who see the great mind-made ruby (Manomaya Padamya), which is fit only for Universal Monarchs, those who do not know its unique and noble qualities will regard it as an ordinary stone. However, those who fully know its unique and noble qualities will gaze at it with great satisfaction and be filled with deep joy. Similarly, the Omniscient Buddha is the Lord of infinite glory, merit, wisdom, and power, an incomparable Jewel far superior to that mind-made ruby.
14: (n) I believe that if people understand the history of the Omniscient Buddha, the Lord of infinite glory, merit, wisdom, and power, it will inspire faith in those who do not yet have it and greatly increase the faith of those who already do. Therefore, because we wish to know and understand, and wish for others to know and understand, the life story and history of the Omniscient Buddha, who is peerless and supreme in the three worlds, I respectfully request you to create and compile the best, most complete, and most detailed Buddhavaṃsa text. In this Buddhavaṃsa text, our primary requirements are as follows: (1) To include everything as it appears in the Pali, Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), Sub-commentaries (Ṭīkā), Anudīpanī, Madhu, Yojanā, Gaṇṭhi, and various scholarly decisions (Vinicchaya), without omitting anything regardless of whether it is minor, obscure, profound, or difficult. (2) To include a complete and comprehensive summary of each of the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya Piṭaka teachings that the Lord Buddha preached throughout his forty-five years of ministry. (3) To make it a Buddhavaṃsa text that is superior, more complete, and more detailed than all previous Buddhavaṃsa texts, such that one never tires of reading it and is filled with faith and satisfaction.
15: (o) (4) Since this is the Mahā Buddhavaṃsa text compiled by a Tipiṭakadhara Dhamma-Bhaṇḍāgārika at the time when the Buddha's Sāsana reaches the 2500th year, I wish for it to be established as a monumental pillar and record of the Sāsana for the next 2500 years of the future Sāsana, for the benefit of the present life, the future lives, and the attainment of Nibbāna for all people. Out of compassion for the benefit of future generations, I respectfully request the Most Venerable Sayadaw to use your supreme wisdom to open, reveal, and compile this noble and extraordinary Mahā Buddhavaṃsa text, which is endowed with these great qualities.

## The Intellectual Brilliance of Saya Gyi U Lin
According to the Prime Minister's request and my own acknowledgment, when I began finalizing the Maha Buddhavamsa after the 1318 ME Pali Sixth Council and the 2500th Sasana Anniversary, I found that the manuscripts of over 700 pages for the first volume, written under the leadership of Saya Gyi U Lin during his lifetime, were like the final hoisting of a banner of wisdom in his life. They contained profound meanings that were "extremely extensive, full of noteworthy points, and difficult for ordinary people to understand."
Indeed... when Saya Gyi U Lin first prepared this Maha Buddhavamsa, he wrote it briefly, focusing only on the text of the Buddha's life. However, the Prime Minister, who was the requester (abhiyācaka), requested again: "Saya Gyi, let it be as extensive as it needs to be... Please write as much as possible for future generations, without leaving out even a needle's point of everything we should know about the Buddha." Thus, Saya Gyi discarded all the brief text he had prepared and spent all his time in the four postures with his mind only on the Buddha's life. When he arrived at the office and started working, he would rest both elbows on the desk, sometimes clicking his tongue (tock), clenching his fists with satisfaction, closing his eyes, and gritting his teeth. He spoke with great heart and soul, not giving the shorthand writer any rest. This was well known from the report of Saya Tun, the current editor of the Buddhavamsa, who was Saya Gyi's personal assistant at that time.

## Exhortation
O virtuous readers of the Buddha's life... the introduction to how this Maha Buddhavamsa came to be has been presented. This Great Chronicle of Buddhas is identical in meaning and essence to the Buddhavamsa Pali and Commentaries, differing only in language (Pali and Burmese).
Since it can certainly provide the virtuous readers of the Buddha's life with (1) the benefit of joy and delight, (2) the benefit of the calming of grief, and (3) the benefit of the three types of prosperity—human, celestial, and Nibbana—I shall conclude this introduction to the Maha Buddhavamsa by exhorting you with a verse (uyyojana gāthā) to enjoy and partake in these benefits individually now...

## 1. Homage and Aspiration
Among the Brahmas, Devas, and humans in the three worlds, there is no one equal to the Buddha. He is the one to whom all Brahmas, Devas, humans, and all beings bow their heads in refuge and worship. Among the Buddhas themselves, there is no difference in any of their glory, power, grace, or attributes; they are identical and no different from the previous Buddhas, following the same path (except for these eight things: lifespan, stature, lineage, duration of austerities, rays, the vehicle used for renunciation, the Bodhi tree, and the size of the throne/seat).
21:

...appearing only with extreme difficulty. I pay homage to that Buddha... to the Dhamma which that Buddha himself taught well for the sake of beings with a very clear Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and very intense Great Compassion (Mahā-karuṇā), and which he himself highly respected... and to the Noble Sangha (Ariya Saṅgha) who are the true sons of the Buddha by practicing well and uprightly according to the practice (paṭipatti) of that noble Dhamma. I pay my respects.
Having paid homage, I shall compose the Maha Buddhavamsa, the sequence of the appearance of the twenty-five Buddhas, starting from Dīpaṅkara Buddha, from whom the Bodhisatta Sumedha the hermit received the Definite Prophecy (niyata-byādika), among the Buddhas who have appeared in the past, more numerous than the grains of sand in the Ganges. I shall do so by taking the Buddhavamsa Pali and Commentaries as the basis, and by bringing in as much as possible the noteworthy matters from other Pali and Commentaries, using a medium style of language that is neither too brief nor too detailed, neither too difficult nor too easy.
May all virtuous people who desire to seek merit and knowledge make firm their foundation in the Buddha-saraṇagam (refuge in the Buddha), Dhamma-saraṇagam (refuge in the Dhamma), and Sangha-saraṇagam (refuge in the Sangha), which are like the jewel-pinnacle of the three worlds. And by practicing well and uprightly the three trainings (sikkhā) of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), which are the path of practice, may they easily reach the path of the Magga, Phala, and Nibbana.

## 2. The Chapter on the Rarity of the Appearance of a Buddha
## The Rarity and Difficulty of the Time when a Buddha Appears
When Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant, who was about to become the donor of the Jetavana Monastery, first arrived in Rājagaha to meet the Buddha, he heard the word "Buddha" from the merchant of Rājagaha (his brother-in-law). He said: "Ghosopi kho eso gahapati dullabho lokasmiṃ yadidaṃ Buddho Buddhoti" = O Merchant... even the mere sound of the word 'Buddha, Buddha' is very rare to hear in the world. (From Vinaya, Cuḷavagga Pali, Senāsanakkhandhaka.)
While the Buddha was staying at Āpaṇa market-town in the Anguttarāpa country, the Brahmin professor Sela—who was soon to become an Ehi Bhikkhu monk along with his three hundred followers and reach Arahantship on the seventh day—also heard the word "Buddha" from the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya. He thought: "Ghosopi kho eso dullabho lokasmiṃ yadidaṃ Buddho Buddhoti" = Even the mere sound of the word 'Buddha, Buddha' is very rare to hear in the world. (From Majjhima Nikāya, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, Sela Sutta.)
In accordance with these Pali texts, it is extremely difficult just to hear the sound "Buddha, Buddha" in the world. As for the appearance of a Buddha, it goes without saying; it is extremely and exceedingly difficult.
23:
4
In this matter, just as the word "diamond" has two types: the word referring to a real diamond and the word referring to a fake diamond, so too there are two types of words: those expressing a true meaning and those expressing a false meaning. Before the Buddha appeared, due to the "Buddha-kolāhala" (the uproar that a Buddha is about to appear), the six heretical teachers (Satthāra), who were not Buddhas but called themselves "Buddha" and "Omniscient One," had already appeared. Therefore, Anāthapiṇḍika and Sela Brahmin must have heard the word "Buddha" used to refer to those heretical teachers before.
However, just as in the presence of someone who has the wisdom to distinguish between a real and a fake gem, if both a real and a fake diamond are placed and both are called "diamond," the word referring to the fake diamond will not please his mind, but only the word "diamond" referring to the real diamond, being the true meaning and true word, will please his mind. Similarly, the word "Buddha" used to refer to the heretical teachers did not refer to a true Buddha but to a fake Buddha. Therefore, it could not please the minds of Anāthapiṇḍika and Sela Brahmin, whose wisdom and perfections (pāramī) were already mature. Only the word "Buddha" referring to the true Buddha, being the true meaning and true word, could please the minds of Anāthapiṇḍika and Sela Brahmin.
24:
5
Just as the wrong decision of those with little wisdom and merit, who mistake a fake diamond for a real one, is a decision that leads to disadvantage, so too is the disciples of other teachers (satthā) mistaking their own teachers for a true Buddha a wrong decision (micchādhimokkha) that leads to disadvantage.
In this section describing the rarity of the appearance of a Buddha (Buddhuppāda-dullabha), it is important to briefly understand these four categories in order to deeply appreciate and believe in the rarity of a Buddha's appearance:
(a) Bodhisatta (The Great Beings destined for Enlightenment)
(b) Bodhisatta-kicca (The duties and practices of the Bodhisattas)
(c) Buddha (The Great Noble Ones who have completed their tasks and attained Buddhahood)
(d) Buddha-kicca (The daily duties of the Buddha)
Among these four:
## (a) Bodhisatta (The Great Beings destined for Enlightenment)
The four Path Knowledges (magga-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) are called Bodhi. This Bodhi-knowledge is of three types: (1) Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa: the four Path Knowledges which have the special power to realize the Four Noble Truths by oneself without a teacher and to abandon all defilements along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā), and the Knowledge of Omniscience which can perceive all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) without exception. (2) Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa: the four Path Knowledges which realize the Four Noble Truths by oneself without a teacher, but
25:
6
without the ability to teach others, is called Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa. (3) Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa: the four Path Knowledges which realize the Four Noble Truths only with the help of a teacher. Thus, there are three types.
Among these: (1) The Great Noble Beings who have an intense wholesome desire for Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa are called Sammāsambodhisatta (the future Omniscient Buddhas). (2) The Great Noble Beings who have an intense wholesome desire for Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa are called Paccekabodhisatta (the future Paccekabuddhas). (3) The Great Noble Beings who have an intense wholesome desire for Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa are called Sāvakabodhisatta (the future disciples).
## Three Types of Future Buddhas
Among the three types of Bodhisattas mentioned, the Sammāsambodhisattas are further divided into three types: (1) Paññādhika Bodhisatta (those who excel in wisdom), (2) Saddhādhika Bodhisatta (those who excel in faith), and (3) Viriyādhika Bodhisatta (those who excel in energy).
Buddhahood is the attainment of the Great Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). To attain this Great Knowledge, the seekers must have a predominant element of wisdom in their mental continuum. Having a predominant element of wisdom means exercising analytical reflection and consideration in everything they do, say, and think. By doing so, their wisdom matures from life to life, and they easily reach the Great Knowledge of Omniscience, which is the pinnacle of all wisdom. Just as in the world, one easily gains money by investing money, one easily gains the Great Wisdom of Omniscience by investing wisdom. Therefore—
26:
7
The Paññādhika Bodhisattas, who excel in wisdom, always have wisdom present while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs); thus, they become Buddhas after fulfilling the perfections for four asankheyyas (incalculable periods) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappas).
Some Bodhisattas believe that "one can become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfections." In the minds of these Bodhisattas, faith (saddhā) is predominant, while wisdom is less than faith. These Great Beings are called Saddhādhika Bodhisattas (meaning Bodhisattas in whom faith alone is predominant). Because these Saddhādhika Bodhisattas fulfill the perfections led by faith rather than wisdom, they cannot become Buddhas in four asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons, but only after fulfilling the perfections for eight asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons.
Some Bodhisattas rely solely on energy (viriya). They do not primarily use the wisdom of foresight and reflection, nor do they focus on the faith that "one can become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfections." Instead, they place energy at the forefront, thinking "I will become a Buddha if I strive," and thus fulfill the perfections. Consequently, they become Buddhas only after sixteen asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons. These Great Beings are called Viriyādhika Bodhisattas (meaning Bodhisattas in whom energy alone is predominant).
It should be noted that these three names—Paññādhika, Saddhādhika, and Viriyādhika—are the names of the Bodhisattas. If one is not careful, one might think they are the names of the Buddhas. Although these three names differ during the Bodhisatta stage,
27:
8
when they become Buddhas, they are all equal in every respect. There is no longer any difference in terms of qualities or attributes between any Buddhas.
"Paññādhikānaṃ hi saddhā mandā hoti, paññā tikkhā. Saddhādhikānaṃ paññā majjhimā hoti, saddhā balavā. Viriyādhikānaṃ saddhāpaññā mandā, viriyaṃ balavaṃ." (Sutta Nipāta Commentary, Explanation of the first Khaggavisāṇa Sutta)
A special note: In Paññādhika Bodhisattas, faith is weak and wisdom is sharp. In Saddhādhika Bodhisattas, wisdom is moderate and faith is strong. In Viriyādhika Bodhisattas, both faith and wisdom are weak, and energy is strong.
## The Fundamental Reason for the Three Types of Bodhisattas
As mentioned, there are three types of Bodhisattas, and the time they spend accumulating perfections differs: four asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons, eight asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons, and sixteen asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons. Regarding the fundamental reason for this difference, the Venerable Shin Sīlavaṃsa, who was famous for his poetry in ancient Myanmar, wrote in the Pāramī-khan Pyo:
"Noble practitioners, the future Buddhas, while making their aspiration, receive the three names: Paññādhika, Viriyādhika, and Saddhādhika, and their time of liberation is determined accordingly."
The meaning is: The fulfillment of perfections by Bodhisattas follows their own aspiration, and accordingly,
28:
9
the three names—Paññādhika, Viriyādhika, and Saddhādhika—are distinct, and the three durations of time until liberation (attaining Buddhahood) are also distinct. If one aspires to become a Paññādhika Buddha while fulfilling perfections, one becomes a Paññādhika Buddha and must fulfill the perfections for four asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons. If one aspires to become a Saddhādhika Buddha, one must fulfill the perfections for eight asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons to become a Saddhādhika Buddha. If one aspires to become a Viriyādhika Buddha, one must fulfill the perfections for sixteen asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons to become a Viriyādhika Buddha. According to this verse, it seems as if these three names apply to the Buddhas. In reality, as shown before, it should be understood that these three names apply only to the Bodhisattas.
According to the view of other (apare) teachers mentioned in the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary (Pakiṇṇakakathā), the three durations for fulfilling perfections are due to the intensity of the Bodhisattas' energy (viriya) being sharp, moderate, or weak. (In this view, since a Paññādhika Bodhisatta would fulfill perfections for only four asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons because of sharp energy, it would be difficult to avoid the fault of confusion (sankara-dosa) between a Paññādhika Bodhisatta and a Viriyādhika Bodhisatta.)
The view favored by the Commentator Venerable Mahā Dhammapāla is that the difference in the duration of fulfilling perfections is due to the sharpness, moderateness, or weakness of the factors that mature liberation (vimutti-paripācanīya-dhamma).
To elaborate further... even at the time of making the aspiration and receiving the definite prophecy (niyata-byādita), the Great Bodhisattas are of three types: (1) Ugghāṭitaññū Bodhisatta,
29:
10
(2) Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta, and (3) Neyya Bodhisatta. Among them:
(1) An Ugghāṭitaññū Bodhisatta is one who, if they wished to attain Sāvaka-bodhi in that very life, has the supporting condition (upanissaya) to attain Arahantship together with the six higher powers (abhiññā) and four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) even before the third line of a four-line Dhamma verse heard from a Buddha is finished. (This refers to the 'cause' (hetu) among the eight factors for receiving a prophecy.)
(2) A Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta is one who, if they wished to attain Sāvaka-bodhi in that very life, has the supporting condition to attain Arahantship together with the six higher powers even before the fourth line of a four-line Dhamma verse heard from a Buddha is finished (before the verse ends).
(3) A Neyya Bodhisatta is one who, if they wished to attain Sāvaka-bodhi in that very life, has the supporting condition to attain Arahantship together with the six higher powers immediately after the conclusion of a four-line Dhamma verse heard from a Buddha.
As stated, because the factors for maturing liberation (vimutti-paripācanīya-dhamma) are very sharp in an Ugghāṭitaññū Bodhisatta, they fulfill the perfections for only four asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons after receiving the prophecy. In a Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta, these factors are moderate, so they fulfill the perfections for eight asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons. In a Neyya Bodhisatta, these factors are weak, so after receiving the prophecy,
30:
11
they fulfill the perfections for sixteen asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons.
An Ugghāṭitaññū Bodhisatta is the same as a Paññādhika Bodhisatta. A Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta is the same as a Saddhādhika Bodhisatta, and a Neyya Bodhisatta is the same as a Viriyādhika Bodhisatta.
## On the Impossibility of Becoming a Buddha Earlier Than the Stated Time
A variety of rice that naturally ripens in three, four, or five months cannot produce grain within fifteen days or a month, no matter how many hundreds or thousands of times it is watered and tended daily, because the grain cannot form, the stalks and leaves cannot grow as desired, and it cannot reach maturity. In the same way, even if the three types of Bodhisattas, after receiving the prophecy, were to perform great acts of giving daily like those of King Vessantara, and even if they were to fulfill the perfections such as virtue (sīla) appropriate to those acts of giving, it should be understood that they cannot reach Buddhahood—the state of being fully mature and complete in the fruit of Omniscience—before the completion of the four, eight, or sixteen asankheyyas and one hundred thousand aeons, because the substance of Omniscience cannot yet form, expand, or mature.

## (b) Bodhisatta-kicca = (The Duties of the Bodhisattas)
Just as one who desires a treasure cannot obtain it without working for it, but can only obtain the desired treasure by striving and performing the necessary work, so too the three types of Bodhisattas (beings destined for enlightenment) who respectively desire the three types of Bodhi-ñāṇa (Enlightenment Knowledge) mentioned previously, can only attain their desired Bodhi-ñāṇa by developing and striving in the practices of Pāramī (Perfections), Cāga (Sacrifice), and Cariya (Conduct), which are the means to attain the aspired Bodhi-ñāṇa.
Just as there are differences and distinctions in the profits and benefits obtained by three types of persons—one who invests great capital and strives beyond compare, one who invests moderately and strives moderately, and one who invests a small amount and strives a little—likewise, there are differences and distinctions in the attainment of the profit of Bodhi-ñāṇa based on whether the capital and foundation of striving in Pāramī, Cāga, and Cariya (known as Bodhi-paripācaka, the factors that mature enlightenment) are superior, moderate, or minimal.
The nature of these differences is as follows: (1) For the Sammāsambodhisattas, the aspirants to Omniscient Buddhahood, even before receiving the Niyata-byāditta (the definite prophecy from a Buddha stating, "This person will certainly become a Buddha with such a name in such an aeon"), they had already aspired for Buddhahood only with the mind and accumulated special merit in the preceding periods—
32:
13
"Ahampi pubbabbuddhesu, buddhattammabhipatthayiṃ.
Manasāyeva hutvāna, dhammarājā asaṅkhiyā."
Based on this Pali text from the Buddhāpadāna in the Apadāna scripture, it is stated that they aspired for Buddhahood only with the mind in the presence of countless Buddhas. Thus, it is evident that they aspired for Buddhahood mentally for a long period of time, spanning aeons that cannot be counted.
Having thus prayed for Buddhahood in the presence of countless Buddhas mentally and having accumulated special merit for a long time to become a Buddha, they receive the Niyata-byāditta (definite prophecy) in the presence of a living Buddha in a life where they are endowed with the eight factors (such as the life of the hermit Sumedha) sufficient to receive such a prophecy. (The eight factors will be explained later.)
In this regard, the aspiration for Buddhahood known as Abhinīhāra (directing the mind towards Buddhahood) should be noted with distinction. The point to note is that the Abhinīhāra of praying for Buddhahood only with the mind before the Buddhas, prior to reaching a life endowed with the eight factors, is not yet complete enough to be called a fully accomplished Bodhisatta.
Only when one reaches a life endowed with the eight factors (such as the life of the hermit Sumedha) and, based on that endowment, makes the aspiration as will be described in the section on Sumedha's prayer:
"Iminā me adhikārena, katena purisuttame.
Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, tāremi janataṃ bahuṃ."
33:
14
"By this meritorious act of supreme service (adhikāra) which I have performed towards the Omniscient Buddha, sacrificing even my life without hesitation, may I attain Omniscient Buddhahood and be able to save many beings."
Only such an Abhinīhāra of praying for Buddhahood is said to be the Abhinīhāra complete enough to receive the Niyata-byāditta.
The essence of this complete Abhinīhāra of praying for Buddhahood should be understood as a special Mahākusala (Great Wholesome) thought-process (cittuppāda) of incomparable power and capability, which serves as the root and foundation of the Pāramī, Cāga, and Cariya, arising by taking as objects the inconceivable attributes of a Buddha and the welfare of the infinite world of beings.
Simultaneously with the arising of this special Mahākusala thought-process of Abhinīhāra, the Bodhisatta is said to have entered the path of practice leading to Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Because he will certainly become a Buddha, he receives the title 'Bodhisatta' (a being destined for enlightenment). For that noble Bodhisatta, at the very moment this special Mahākusala thought-process of the complete Abhinīhāra arises, there exists the wholesome desire (chanda) to seek Omniscience fully and without remainder, as well as the ability to fulfill the Pāramī, Cāga, and Cariya—the building blocks for attaining Omniscience—beyond compare.
Precisely because they are endowed with the qualities of this special thought-process, the great Bodhisattas possess the Pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa (the knowledge that investigates and scrutinizes the perfections), which is a precursor to attaining Omniscience and enables them to realize things spontaneously without a teacher.
34:
15
Having reflected upon and undertaken the Perfections (Pāramīs) accurately and without remainder through their own intuitive wisdom, they proceed to fulfill the Perfections in order.
After having prayed for Buddhahood and received the Niyata-byāditta, the great Bodhisattas—
"Catasso hi bodhisambhāresu bhāvanā sabbasambhārabhāvanā nirantarabhāvanā cirakālabhāvanā sakkaccabhāvanā cāti"...
In accordance with the introduction (Nidānakathā) of the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, they strive and develop without rest the Pāramī, Cāga, and Cariya—the building blocks for attaining the Knowledge of the Arahatta Path and Omniscience—through four types of development (bhāvanā): (1) Sabba-sambhāra-bhāvanā, (2) Nirantara-bhāvanā, (3) Cirakāla-bhāvanā, and (4) Sakkacca-bhāvanā. Among these four:
(1) Fulfilling all the Perfections without omitting a single one is called Sabba-sambhāra-bhāvanā.
(2) Fulfilling and developing them continuously without the gap of even a single lifetime for a period of at least four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), or eight incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, or sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, is called Nirantara-bhāvanā.
(3) Fulfilling and developing the Perfections for a long duration, not decreasing by even a single aeon below the minimum of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, is called Cirakāla-bhāvanā.
(4) Fulfilling the Perfections with great respect and care is called Sakkacca-bhāvanā.

## The Noble Heart of the Great Bodhisattas
The great Bodhisattas, having prayed for Buddhahood and received the Niyata-byāditta, find themselves in the difficult and arduous journey of existence. They behold the masses of beings who are helpless and without refuge, suffering intensely and unbearably from various forms of misery: the suffering of birth (jāti), aging (jarā), sickness (byādhi), and death (maraṇa); the suffering of being killed or imprisoned in the human world; the suffering rooted in the search for food; and the suffering of the lower realms (apāya). Seeing them, their hearts are violently moved with Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) for those beings.
Prompted and urged by this Great Compassion, they endure all the suffering that arises from the wrongs committed against them by those ignorant and blind masses—such as being trespassed upon, oppressed, persecuted, or having their hands, feet, ears, nose, or head cut off—and they constantly develop only compassion and pity for a long time.
The way they develop it is thus: "What shall I do with these people who act wrongly and offensively toward me? I will surely free these very people from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha)." Thus they truly strive and fulfill the Perfections. "The power of delusion (moha) is indeed great! The strength of craving (taṇhā-lobha) is indeed great! Even toward me, who strives to free all beings from the suffering of Saṃsāra, these people, oppressed by greed and delusion, commit such great wrongs. Because of such wrongful acts, they will surely face great suffering."
(Having thus exercised a heart of Great Compassion for them...)
36:
17
They only search for and consider a good means to rescue these beings, who are oppressed by greed and delusion and who wrongly perceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful, asking: "In what way can I deliver and save them from suffering along with its causes?"
While searching and considering thus, they realize according to reality (yathābhūta) that: "Patience (Khantī) alone is the method and the good means by which I can free and rescue these beings from the bonds of existence." Even when various beings commit wrongs against them, such as cutting off their hands and feet, the great Bodhisattas do not feel the slightest anger. Instead, they blame only themselves, thinking: "I have received this present suffering due to the power of bad unwholesome kamma committed in the past. Since I myself committed unwholesome acts in the past, this suffering is very appropriate for me. I am the one who acted culpably."
Thinking thus, they place the blame only upon themselves and reflect:
"Only through patience can I rescue these people. If I were to wrong the wrongdoer in return, I would become just like him. If that were to happen, there would be no distinction between me and him. In that case, how could I free them from the suffering of the round of rebirths? I would not be able to. Therefore, I shall establish myself in the power of patience (khantī), which is the foundation of all powers, and by taking their blame upon myself and being patient,
37:
18
I shall fulfill the Perfections, preceded by Loving-kindness (Mettā) and Compassion (Karuṇā). Only by fulfilling the Perfections in this way shall I become an Omniscient Buddha. Only when I become an Omniscient Buddha shall I be able to deliver and save all beings from suffering along with its causes." Thus they see and know according to reality. (From the Bodhisambhāra-vaṇṇanā section of the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā.)
Having seen and known thus according to reality, they fulfill and develop the thirty Perfections—comprising the ten Pāramīs, the ten Upa-pāramīs, and the ten Paramattha-pāramīs, known as the Bodhi-sambhāra (requisites of enlightenment)—beyond compare through the four types of development (bhāvanā) mentioned earlier: (1) Sabba-sambhāra-bhāvanā, fulfilling all without exception; (2) Nirantara-bhāvanā, fulfilling them without the gap of even a single life from the time of receiving the prophecy until becoming a Buddha; (3) Cirakāla-bhāvanā, fulfilling them for a long duration, not decreasing by even a single aeon below the minimum of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons; and (4) Sakkacca-bhāvanā, fulfilling the Perfections with respect. (See the Anudīpanī for the classification of Pāramīs, etc.)
## Not Tending to Stay Long in Deva Realms While Fulfilling Perfections
While the great Bodhisattas are thus fulfilling the Pāramī, Cāga, and Cariya beyond compare, until they reach the final and supreme life where these practices reach their peak (such as the life of Vessantara), if they are reborn in the long-lived Deva or Brahma realms due to the power of their great wholesome merits, they do not remain there until the end of their lifespan because it is very difficult to fulfill the Perfections in those realms. Instead, they cut short their celestial lifespan through a type of death called Adhimutti-maraṇa (death by choice/will) and return to the human world.
38:
19
They are reborn only in the human world to fulfill and practice the perfections (Pāramīs). (Regarding 'Adhimutti-maraṇa'—death by resolve—see the subsequent Anudīpanī.)

## Perfections Comparable to the Ocean
The physical ocean is said to be eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, a measurable extent. It has a bottom and a surface, and its boundaries can be defined by the Cakkavāḷa mountains. However, the ocean of the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) fulfilled and developed by the Great Bodhisattas cannot be delimited by bottom, surface, or boundaries. Indeed, regarding the Dāna-pāramī of the Great Bodhisattas, the sacrifice of external wealth cannot be measured as 'this much'. The instances of sacrificing flesh, blood, eyes, and heads are likewise immeasurable. Similarly, the Perfections of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī) and others are also immeasurable. Therefore, the perfections of the Great Bodhisattas are compared to the Great Ocean (the primary metaphor being that the perfections actually exceed the ocean).

## Not Perceiving Even Great Suffering as Suffering
For example, just as a person bathing and diving into a water-filled pond during the intense heat of a summer noon does not recognize the scorching heat of the sun from above, so too the Great Bodhisattas, possessing hearts cooled by Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), seek only the welfare of beings and constantly dive and immerse themselves in the ocean of perfections. Thus, with bodies cooled by Great Compassion within the ocean of perfections...
39:
20
...because they possess such hearts, they do not regard even the extremely great suffering caused by the cruel and heartless cutting of their hands and feet by wicked beings as suffering.

## Fulfilling Perfections for a Long Duration
The Buddha taught in the Saṃyutta Nikāya that if the bones of a single person from each aeon (kappa) were piled up, they would be as large as a mountain. From the time the Great Bodhisattas made their aspiration and received the prophecy until the final life (such as the Vessantara birth) where they reached the pinnacle of perfection, if one were to count the lives spent fulfilling perfections over a period of at least four incalculables (asankheyyas) and a hundred thousand aeons, they would be more numerous than the drops of water in the Great Ocean. Among those many lives, there was not a single life that passed in vain without fulfilling perfections.

The practices of the Great Bodhisatta found in the 550 Jātaka stories and the Cariyāpiṭaka Pāḷi, which the virtuous Buddhists of today see, hear, and note, are like a single cup of water taken from the mass of the Great Ocean to demonstrate its salty taste. They are merely a few practices taught according to the occasion, selected from the perfections fulfilled over many lives, more numerous than the drops of water in the Great Ocean. If one compares the practices taught due to specific events with those not taught because no such event arose, the taught practices are like a cup of water, while the untaught...

## (C) Buddha (The Noble Ones who have reached the state of Buddhahood upon completion of their tasks)
As mentioned before, the candidates for Omniscient Buddhahood, the Sammāsambodhisattas, after receiving the definite prophecy, fulfill perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons if they are Wisdom-dominant (Paññādhika) Bodhisattas; eight incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons if they are Faith-dominant (Saddhādhika) Bodhisattas; and sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons if they are Energy-dominant (Vīriyādhika) Bodhisattas. When they reach the pinnacle of perfections, they attain Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa—comprising the Path Knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa) that realizes the Four Noble Truths by their own efforts without a teacher, and the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) that sees all knowable things without exception. They attain this along with the infinite and immeasurable attributes of a Buddha (of which it is said that even if one Buddha were to praise the virtues of another Buddha for an entire aeon without teaching anything else, the aeon would end but the virtues would not be exhausted). The noble person who has thus reached Sambodhi-ñāṇa and has no equal in the three worlds...
43:

...the peerless noble one, is called a Sammāsambuddha (The Omniscient Buddha).

Candidates for Private Buddhahood must fulfill perfections for a period of two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. When they reach the pinnacle of perfections, they attain the Path Knowledge (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) that realizes the Four Noble Truths by their own efforts without a teacher (but without Omniscience, the Ten Powers, etc.). The noble persons who have thus reached Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa are called Paccekabuddhas (Solitary Buddhas or Lesser Buddhas).

Candidates for Discipleship fulfill perfections for one incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons for Aggasāvakas, a hundred thousand aeons for Mahāsāvakas, and periods such as a hundred or a thousand aeons for Pakatisāvakas. When they reach the pinnacle of perfections, they attain the Path Knowledge (Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa) that realizes the Four Noble Truths with the Buddha as their teacher. The noble persons who have thus reached Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa are called Sāvaka Buddhas, with the respective titles of Aggasāvaka, Mahāsāvaka, and Pakatisāvaka according to their level.

## (D) Buddha-kicca (The Work of the Buddha)
Among the noble persons who have thus completed the tasks of a Bodhisatta and reached their respective states as Sammāsambuddha, Paccekabuddha, and Sāvaka Buddha (the Noble Disciple)...
44:
25
...the Sammāsambuddhas are called 'Tārayitu' persons—the most noble ones who have themselves crossed over the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) and also rescue and save the veneyya (those ready for enlightenment).

Paccekabuddhas, however, are called 'Tarita' persons—noble ones who have crossed over saṃsāra by their own power but cannot rescue others from it. Indeed, Paccekabuddhas do not appear when Omniscient Buddhas are present; they appear only in the intervals between one Buddha and another. Sammāsambuddhas realize the Four Noble Truths without a teacher and are able to make others realize them and teach them. Paccekabuddhas realize them only for themselves and cannot teach others. They personally realize the profound meaning of the Dhamma of Realization (Paṭivedha), namely the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, but they are not able to put that supramundane Dhamma into names and concepts (Nāma-paññatti) to preach to others. Therefore, the Commentaries illustrate the Paccekabuddhas' realization of the Four Noble Truths (Dhamma-abhisamaya) with the analogies of a mute person's dream or a forest dweller with little knowledge tasting various exquisite flavors in a city. Thus, those Paccekabuddhas are called 'Tarita' persons—those who can cross over saṃsāra by their own power but cannot save others.

Those Paccekabuddhas ordain others who wish to become monks and then say, 'In this way, be calm...'
45:
26
They can teach the ābhisamācārika conduct, such as "one should move forward in this manner, retreat in that manner, look in this way, speak in that way," but they cannot preach the Dhamma to others to the extent of reaching the Path and Fruition, such as "one should distinguish mind and matter and establish the vehicle of characteristics (lakkhaṇayāna)."

When observing the Uposatha, they assemble in the jeweled pavilion near the Manjūsaka celestial tree, which is one league high and one league wide, located at the entrance of the Emerald Cave—one of the three caves: the Golden Cave, the Emerald Cave, and the Silver Cave—in the Nandamūla area of Mount Gandhamādana. They perform the Uposatha in brief, either with a short exhortation such as "one should strive for the attenuation of mental defilements; one should not fall into decline," or with the mere words, "today is the Uposatha day."

The noble disciples (ariya-sāvakas) who are Sāvakabuddhas are called tārita individuals (those who are saved or carried across). Indeed, considering that the wandering ascetic Upatissa, who was to become the Venerable Sāriputta, established himself in the Path and Fruition of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-phala) upon hearing half a verse from the Venerable Assaji:

"Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā,
tesaṃ hetuṃ tathāgato"—

it might seem that noble disciples are tārayitu individuals (saviors) who, having been saved themselves, also save others. However, because the Dhamma preached by these noble disciples has the Buddha as its sole origin, and because they do not teach
46:
27
by a separate method of their own without the Buddha's guidance, those noble disciples cannot be called tārayitu individuals. In truth, they are called only tārita individuals (those who are saved) because they cannot know the Four Noble Truths without a teacher, and can only know the Four Noble Truths and attain the knowledge of the Path and Fruition with the help of a teacher.

As stated, although Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples, being tarita and tārita individuals, can live happily by entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) for their own benefit after reaching the Path and Fruition of Arahantship, the Sammāsambuddhas, the Omniscient Buddhas, cannot live for their own benefit alone in that manner. In fact, just as they had resolved while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), "Buddho bodheyyaṃ" (Having realized the Four Noble Truths myself, I shall make others realize them), they must carry out and complete the fivefold Buddha-duties (Buddha-kicca) continuously day and night.

(For the details of the five Buddha-duties, please see the explanation of the attribute 'Bhagavā' in the life of Gotama Buddha above.)

By fulfilling the "five Buddha-duties," the Buddhas have the opportunity to rest for only a brief moment after the midday meal during the day. During the night, dividing the night into three parts, they have the opportunity to rest for only one-third of the third part. During the remaining time, they spend their time by carrying out and completing the "five Buddha-duties."
47:
28
Only the Lords of Energy, who possess the supreme and incomparable glory known as "payatta," can fulfill these Buddha-duties. It is not within the range of Paccekabuddhas or disciples.

## Considering the Rarity of a Buddha's Appearance

If one deeply reflects on these four points:
(a) Bodhisatta (The Great Beings-to-be)
(b) Bodhisatta-kicca (The course of action of the Great Beings-to-be)
(c) Buddha (The Great Beings who have reached Buddhahood after completing the course of action)
(d) Buddha-kicca (The daily duties of the Buddha)

it will be evident how extremely difficult it is for a Buddha to appear.

Indeed, there are many who, after personally witnessing or hearing about the Buddha's majesty and power—such as his ability to subdue the pride of heretics and his performance of the Twin Miracle of water and fire after becoming a Buddha—desire and long for Buddhahood. For this very reason, when the Buddha descended to the city of Saṅkassa after preaching the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, due to the Buddha's "devorohana-pāṭihāriya" miracle, the space became open and clear from the highest heaven (Bhavagga) down to the lowest hell (Avīci), and similarly, the eight directions across the infinite universes became open and clear, so that humans, devas, Brahmās, and all beings
48:
29
could see one another. On that day, upon beholding the splendor of the Buddha, in the assembly which was twelve leagues in length and breadth and thirty-six leagues in circumference, there was no one who did not aspire for Buddhahood.

(That the entire vast assembly aspired for Buddhahood is mentioned in the Devorohana-vatthu of the Dhammapada Commentary and the explanation of the three kinds of miracles in the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā.)

Although there are many who desire and long for Buddhahood after witnessing or hearing about the Buddha's majesty and power, if they were to truly know the vastness of the perfections (pāramīs), the greatness of the effort required to accumulate them, the necessity of fulfilling them continuously in every life, the necessity of fulfilling them with great respect, the necessity of fulfilling them for a very long time, and the necessity of fulfilling them without regard for one's own life, those with little faith, wisdom, desire, and energy would surely be terrified. Because Buddhahood can only be attained by courageously fulfilling such fearsome perfections without fear, the attainment of Buddhahood is said to be "dullabha" (rare).

Therefore, it was preached in the second sutta of the Ekapuggala-vagga, Ekaka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya:

"Ekapuggalassa bhikkhave pātubhāvo dullabho lokasmiṃ. Katamassa ekapuggalassa? Tathāgatassa arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Imassa kho bhikkhave ekapuggalassa pātubhāvo dullabho lokasmiṃ."

"Monks, the appearance of one person in the world of beings is very rare. The appearance of which one person is very rare? The appearance of the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One who
49:
30
knows the truth by his own intuitive wisdom, is very rare."

In the commentary (Atthakathā) to that sutta, it is explained:

After raising the question, "Kasmā dullabho?" (Why is it very rare?), it is stated that one cannot become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) just once, or ten times, twenty times, fifty times, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times, ten million times, a billion times, or a hundred billion times. Likewise, one cannot become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of giving for one day, two days, ten days, twenty days, fifty days, a hundred days, a thousand days, a hundred thousand days, or a hundred billion days. Nor by fulfilling it for one month, two months, a hundred billion months; one year, two years, a hundred billion years; one great aeon (mahā-kappa), two great aeons, a hundred billion great aeons; or one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya), two incalculable periods, or three incalculable periods. (The same applies to the perfection of virtue, the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of energy, the perfection of patience, the perfection of truthfulness, the perfection of resolution, the perfection of loving-kindness, and the perfection of equanimity.) In truth, one can only become an Omniscient Buddha after fulfilling, accumulating, and developing all the requirements of the perfections without exception, continuously and without skipping a life, with great esteem, devotion, and utmost respect for a period of at least four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, which is a duration so vast it cannot be counted or limited.
50:
31
"For this reason, the one person known as the Omniscient Buddha is extremely rare in the world of beings."

In the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) to that sutta, it is also explained:

"One can become an Omniscient Buddha only by fulfilling the perfections continuously for a duration of at least four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons; it is not possible by any other means. For this reason, the appearance of the Buddhas is extremely rare."

## The Unparalleled Nature of the Perfections

The number of births as a Bodhisatta during the interval of four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons from the life of Sumedha to the life of Vessantara is even greater than the drops of water in the great ocean. The perfections fulfilled and accumulated continuously and without skipping a life are so numerous that their extent and measure cannot be described. There is no comparison or metaphor that can match them. This matter is praised and explained in the Jinālaṅkāra text:

"Mahāsamudde jalabindutopi,
tadantare jāti anappakāva.
nirantaraṃ pūritapāramīnaṃ,
kathaṃ pamāṇaṃ upamā kuhiṃ vā."

"The number of births (jāti) that occurred in the interval (tadantare) between the life of Sumedha and
51:
32
the life of Vessantara is indeed very many (anappakāva), even more than the drops of water (jalabinduto) in the great ocean (mahāsamudde). How (kathaṃ) can there be a measure (pamāṇaṃ) for the extraordinary perfections fulfilled (pūritapāramīnaṃ) continuously without interruption (nirantaraṃ)? Where (kuhiṃ vā) could there be a metaphor (upamā) to compare them?"

Not only here, but also in the Sutapātheyya Commentary and Sub-commentary, which explain the attribute of 'Satapuññalakkhaṇa' (Possessing the marks of a hundred merits), and in the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, it is explained:

From the time the aspiration for Buddhahood was made at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the donation of Queen Maddī in the life of King Vessantara, if one were to take all the merits such as giving (dāna) performed by the countless beings in the infinite universe (ananta-lokadhātu) and place them in one pile, and take the merits accumulated by a single Bodhisatta and place them in another pile, and then compare and weigh them, the collection of merits performed by the infinite beings would not reach even a hundredth or a thousandth part of the merit of the perfections performed by the single Bodhisatta.

## The Difficulty of Even Becoming a Bodhisatta

Let alone the state of a Sammāsambuddha, the Omniscient Buddha, even a life such as that of the hermit Sumedha, where the prayer for Buddhahood is fulfilled, can only be obtained when eight conditions are met. Those eight conditions are:
52:
33
(1) Being a human being,
(2) Being a male,
(3) Being a person endowed with such extraordinary merit and perfections that one could attain Arahantship in that very life,
(4) Meeting a living Buddha,
(5) Being an ascetic who believes in the law of kamma (kammavādī) or a monk within the Dispensation,
(6) Being one endowed with the noble qualities of the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti),
(7) Performing and developing the merit of the perfections to the utmost without regard for one's own life,
(8) Being one who possesses a wholesome desire (chanda) so strong that one longs for Buddhahood.

(The detailed meaning of these eight conditions will be explained upon reaching the end of the section on Perfections below.)

Since one can only receive the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa) when endowed with these eight factors, let alone Buddhahood, the state of being a person who receives a definite prophecy like the hermit Sumedha is itself an extremely rare thing.

If the state of a Bodhisatta who can receive a definite prophecy is so rare, then after receiving the definite prophecy, fulfilling the perfections for at least four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons through the four types of development (bhāvanā),
53:
34
If the state of Buddhahood, which can only be attained through the fulfillment of the Pāramīs, is so difficult to achieve, what more need be said? It is indeed extremely rare.

Because Buddhahood is so difficult to attain, the "Ninth Opportunity" (Buddhuppāda)—the rare occasion when a Buddha appears in the world—is also an extremely rare event.

In this regard, concerning the "Ninth Moment of the Arising of a Buddha" (Buddhuppāda Navama Khaṇa), one should also note the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa) mentioned in the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. These eight inopportune moments are:

1. Being born in hell (Niraya): Because one is constantly subjected to and tormented by extremely severe punishments (kammakaraṇa), a denizen of hell has no opportunity to perform meritorious deeds; thus, birth in hell is called "akkhaṇa."
2. Being born in the animal realm (Tiracchāna): Because animals have no chance to understand the Dhamma even through perception (saññā) and must live in constant fear and trembling, they have no opportunity to perform meritorious deeds; thus, birth in the animal realm is also called "akkhaṇa."
3. Being born in the realm of hungry ghosts (Peta): Because they are constantly tormented by intense hunger, thirst, and burning heat, a denizen of the Peta realm has no opportunity to perform meritorious deeds; thus, birth in the Peta realm is also called "akkhaṇa."
4. Being born in the realm of unconscious beings (Asaññasatta): Since unconscious beings lack the sensitive ear (sotapasāda) required to hear the Dhamma...
54:
35
and thus have no opportunity to perform meritorious deeds, birth in that realm of unconscious beings is also called an "akkhaṇa".)

Regarding this fourth inopportune time, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhaka Nipāta, explains only the realm of unconscious beings; however, the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭီကာ includes birth in the formless realms (arūpa-loka) as well.

Among the eight types of individuals—the worldling with three roots (ti-hetu puthujjana) and the seven noble ones (ariya) starting from the one established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phalaṭṭha)—who can be found in the formless realms, the worldling with three roots has absolutely no chance of attaining the Path and Fruit (magga-phala) because of the lack of the "voice of another" (paratoghosa), i.e., hearing the Dhamma. As for the three lower individuals established in the fruit (phalaṭṭha) who reach those formless realms, they continue to practice and develop the methods of insight (vipassanā) they had cultivated in their previous lives in the sense-sphere (kāma-loka) or the fine-material sphere (rūpa-loka) before reaching the formless realm, and thus they usually attain the higher Paths and Fruits. For this reason, the formless realm is not included in the list of inopportune times (akkhaṇa) in the Commentary.

5. Being born in the border regions (Paccanta). (Even if one possesses the sensitive ear, those born in border regions where wisdom is extremely scarce and where monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—the sons and daughters of the Buddha—do not reach, have no opportunity to hear the Dhamma and thus no opportunity to perform meritorious deeds; therefore, birth in such border regions is also called an "akkhaṇa".)

6. Holding wrong views (Micchādiṭṭhi). (Even if one is born in the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa) where the sound of the Dhamma resonates continuously during the appearance of a Buddha,
55:
36
those who hold wrong views have absolutely no opportunity to hear or practice the Dhamma; therefore, holding wrong views is also called an "akkhaṇa". (This refers to fixed wrong views, niyata-micchādiṭṭhi.)

7. Deficiency of faculties (Indriya-vekalla). (Even if one is born in the Middle Country and does not hold fixed wrong views, if one is born with no roots (ahetu-paṭisandhi) and suffers from the obstacle of kamma-result (vipākantarāya), such as being deficient in faculties like sight, etc., one has no opportunity to see the noble ones or to hear and learn the Dhamma, and thus cannot practice the holy life; therefore, deficiency of faculties is also called an "akkhaṇa".)

8. Being born when no Buddha appears. (Even if one is born in the Middle Country with complete faculties and possesses the wisdom of right view regarding kamma (kammassakatā-sammādiṭṭhi), if it is not a time when a Buddha appears, there is no opportunity to develop the three trainings (sikkhā) of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) within the Sāsana; therefore, the time when no Buddha appears is also called an "akkhaṇa".) (In this context, as long as the Sāsana has not disappeared, it is still called the period of the Buddha's appearance.)

The opportunity that escapes these eight aforementioned inopportune times (akkhaṇa), occurring during the period when the Buddha's Sāsana flourishes, with complete faculties and right view, is called the "Ninth Opportunity of the Buddha's Appearance" (Buddhuppāda Navama Khaṇa)—the ninth auspicious opportunity to develop the Dhamma after escaping the eight inopportune times.

## May the Ninth Opportunity of the Buddha's Appearance be Fruitful

All the virtuous people today who hold Buddhist views are those who are born during the flourishing of the Buddha's Sāsana, with complete faculties,
56:
37
and have attained human status along with the right view (sammādiṭṭhi). Therefore, while beautifully encountering this great "Buddhuppāda-dullabha" opportunity, if we let go of the practice of the Sāsana—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—we will be those who have bypassed this great rare opportunity.

The inopportune times (akkhaṇa), which are obstacles and barriers to the good practice of the path to Nibbāna, are many in number and occur frequently. Because Buddhas appear only once in a while after the passing of countless aeons (asankhyeyya-kappa), the "Ninth Opportunity of the Buddha's Appearance" is extremely rare to obtain.

Today, for the virtuous Buddhists, these two things—the period when the Buddha's Dhamma shines, which is extremely rare in the world, and the human status with right view—have been attained and are right before them. In this "Ninth Opportunity of the Buddha's Appearance," which is such a great and auspicious time, one should deeply and realistically reflect: "How shall I know the Dhamma? I must not let this great opportunity of the Buddha's appearance slip away. If I let it slip, I will become food for the four woeful states (apāya) and will have to suffer in weariness and distress for a long time." Having reflected thus, may you all be able to practice and develop the noble practice of the three trainings of the Sāsana—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—as taught by the Buddha, until the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), so that it can be said you have made the most of this great Ninth Opportunity of the Buddha's Appearance.

## End of the Chapter on the Rarity of the Buddha's Appearance.
