## 3. The Chapter on Sumedha the Brahmin

This Chronicle of Buddhas (Buddhavaṃsa) was taught by the Blessed One when He first visited the city of Kapilavatthu. In the assembly of His relatives, the Sakyan princes, who were very stubborn and proud and did not pay homage to Him, the Buddha created a jewelled walkway (ratana-caṅkama) in the sky, stretching from east to west across ten thousand world systems, to break their pride and make them pay homage. While He was performing the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) of water and fire on that jewelled walkway, He taught this, starting from the "Chapter on Sumedha the Brahmin," at the request of His right-hand disciple, the Venerable Sāriputta.

When the great elders such as Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Ānanda held the First Council (Paṭhama Saṅgāyana), they wished to present the Buddhavaṃsa in full, including the introduction. Thus, they established the "Vācanāmagga" (the tradition of recitation and teaching), starting with the verse "Brahmā ca lokādhipatī Sahampatī..." and including the Chapter on the Jewelled Walkway.

(The detailed introduction to this Buddhavaṃsa will be explained later in the Chapter on the Chronicle of Gotama Buddha.)

Here, I shall present and write starting from the "Chapter on Sumedha the Brahmin," as taught by the Buddha at the request of the Venerable Sāriputta. As for the story of the virtuous Sumedha the Brahmin, the Bodhisatta of this chapter:

Counting back from this aeon, four asankhyeyyas and one hundred thousand aeons (or one hundred thousand kappas) ago, the royal city named "Amaravatī" was famous and prominent. (See the Anudīpanī for details regarding the aeons and the name of the city Amaravatī.)
58:
39
The royal city of Amaravatī was a city where everything was systematically arranged and was beautiful to behold. Because it had lush, pleasant grounds, abundant shade and water, and all the food one could desire, and because it was filled with various human amenities, it could delight the hearts of all devas and humans who saw it.

It was always pleasant and bustling, never silent, with the ten sounds: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of large drums, the sound of small drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of conch shells, the sound of cymbals, and the sound of invitation (to eat and drink). (In other cities, there are many unpleasant and bustling sounds that disturb the peace, such as "Sweep the rubbish!", "Bring the hoes, pickaxes, and baskets!", "Go elsewhere, let us move!", "Bring the rice packets and food!", "Let us go to war, prepare the weapons, bows, and arrows!", etc. However, in the royal city of Amaravatī, such sounds did not exist; it means the city was always pleasant and bustling with the ten sounds like those of elephants and horses.) (See the Anudīpanī for noteworthy points regarding the ten sounds.)

Besides being endowed with all the characteristics that a great city should have, it was also full of abundant work and activities. It was also endowed with the seven jewels (diamonds, gold, silver, rubies, cat's eyes, pearls, emeralds, and corals). It was bustling and mixed with many people of different nationalities. Like a celestial realm, it was complete in every way, a place for those of great merit and power.
59:
40
## The Bodhisatta Sumedha

In that royal city of Amaravatī lived a Brahmin named Sumedha. (He was famous as "Sumedha" because he possessed praiseworthy wisdom.) This Brahmin Sumedha was of good Brahmin birth from both his mother's and father's sides, descending from a long line of Brahmins. He was conceived in the womb of a mother who was pure and free from disease. For seven generations back on both the mother's and father's sides, he was one who could not be rejected or insulted based on his birth, with anyone saying, "This person is of low birth." He was endowed with a physical appearance that was extremely beautiful, graceful, and pleasant to behold, capable of making the hearts of all who saw him clear and joyful.

In terms of wealth and education, he possessed many crores of accumulated wealth, and the wealth and grain he used daily were also very abundant. He was one who could constantly recite the Vedic scriptures by heart and was a master who had reached the far shore of the three Vedas (Iru, Yaju, and Sāma). He was also proficient in: (1) the Nighaṇḍu scripture, which is the dictionary/lexicon explaining various names; (2) the Keṭubha scripture, which explains various poetic ornaments used by the wise in composing literature; (3) the grammar scripture called Akkharappabheda, which explains various linguistic methods along with the names of letters and consonants; (4) the Itihāsa scripture (called the Purāṇas), which explains ancient legends and stories, being the fifth.
60:
41
He was one who had mastered the Vedas effortlessly, as if by merely moving his lips. 

Regarding the phrase “Itihāsa as the fifth,” according to the state of the Pāḷi Canon, it should be counted as: (1) the three Vedas, (2) Nighaṇḍu (Lexicon), (3) Keṭubha (Ritual), (4) Sadda (Grammar), and (5) Itihāsa (History). However, in the Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā, the Atharvaveda is added to the three Vedas making four, and by adding Itihāsa, it is explained as being the fifth.

He was also highly proficient in the various types of words found in grammar (Byākaraṇa), and in the nature of roots and suffixes. He was fully endowed with wisdom, without any deficiency, even in the Lokāyata texts—which do not increase merit but only prolong the cycle of birth and death—and in the Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa texts, which describe the various marks of Great Beings such as the Bodhisatta and the Paccekabuddha-to-be. He was a great professor (pāmokkha) who had reached the pinnacle of the brahminical knowledge taught by successive teachers.

While the wise Sumedha was still young, his mother and father passed away. At that time, the treasurer brought the inventory of assets and opened the treasure rooms filled with gold, silver, rubies, pearls, and so on. He presented the wealth accumulated over seven generations of ancestors, saying, “Young man, this much wealth has come down from your mother’s side; this much from your father’s side; and this much from the time of your grandfathers and great-grandfathers.”
61:
42
After presenting the wealth, he handed it over, saying, “Manage this wealth according to your will.”

The wise Sumedha accepted, saying, “Very well,” and then reflected: “My father, grandfather, and ancestors for seven generations accumulated this much wealth, yet when they passed away, they could not take even a single coin with them. As for me, I should act in such a way that I can take it with me, leaving not even a single coin behind.” Having considered this, he lived managing the household while performing meritorious deeds.

## 4. The Chapter on Sumedha’s Renunciation
One day, the wise Sumedha ascended to the upper floor of his palace, sat cross-legged in a secluded place, and reflected as follows:

“Being born in a new existence (conception) is truly painful. The destruction of the body (death) is also truly painful. Being overwhelmed and oppressed by aging, and dying in a state of confusion, is also truly painful.

Subject as I am to birth, aging, and sickness, I shall seek Nibbāna—the state where aging and death are no more, where danger is exhausted, and where there is supreme peace.

It would be well if I could abandon this foul body, filled as it is with various kinds of impurities such as urine, excrement, pus, blood, bile, phlegm, saliva, and nasal mucus, and depart without any attachment or desire for it.”
62:
43
“There must certainly be a good path leading to that peaceful Nibbāna; it is impossible for such a path not to exist. I shall seek that good path to Nibbāna to be liberated from the bonds of existence.

Just as in the world, when suffering (dukkha) is evident, happiness (sukha) is also evident; even so, when the existence of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) is evident, the non-existence of that suffering, which is Nibbāna, must also be sought (and recognized).

Just as when there is heat, there must also be cold which is distinct from it; even so, when the three fires of lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha) are evident, Nibbāna, which can extinguish these three fires, must also be sought (and recognized).

Just as when evil and unwholesome states (akusala) are evident, good and wholesome states (kusala) must also be evident; even so, when birth (jāti) is evident, Nibbāna—the state free from birth which can bring birth to an end—must also be sought (and recognized).”

After having these thoughts, he further reflected deeply:

“For example, if a man fallen into a pit of filth (or smeared with filth) sees from afar a large, clear reservoir adorned with five kinds of lotuses, but does not seek the right path to go to that reservoir, it is not the fault of the reservoir, but only the fault of the man smeared with filth. Even so, while the great reservoir of the Deathless Nibbāna exists for the washing away of the stains of defilements (kilesa), if one does not seek that reservoir of Nibbāna, it is not the fault of the reservoir of Nibbāna.”
63:
44
“For example, if a person surrounded by enemies has a path to escape but does not take it, that failure to depart is not the fault of the path, but only the fault of that person. Even so, while the great path of the factors of enlightenment (Magga) leading to the golden city of Nibbāna—the place of safety and liberation from the enemies of defilements—exists, if one who is surrounded by the enemies of defilements does not wish to go upon that path, that lack of desire and failure to go is not the fault of the excellent path of the factors of enlightenment leading to Nibbāna.

For example, if a man who is ill has a good physician who can cure him but does not have his illness treated, that failure to be treated is not the fault of the physician. Even so, if a person who is suffering and oppressed by the diseases of defilements does not seek a teacher who is clearly proficient in the path of the factors of enlightenment that leads to the cessation of those defilements, that failure to seek is not the fault of the noble teacher.”
64:
45
After having these thoughts, he further considered the abandonment of this body:

“Just as a man who desires to be beautiful, being disgusted by a foul corpse tied to his neck, would untie it and go wherever he wishes, free and happy; even so, I shall abandon this foul corpse of a body, which is a collection of various kinds of worms and impurities, and go happily without attachment or desire to the great city of Nibbāna.

For example, just as men and women who have relieved themselves at a place of excrement depart without wishing to look back even for a moment, having abandoned it; even so, I shall abandon this body, which is filled with various kinds of worms and impurities, just as one who has relieved himself abandons the latrine, and I shall go to reach the great city of Nibbāna.

For example, just as the owners of a boat that is old, decaying, and constantly leaking water abandon it without attachment or desire and depart; even so, I shall abandon this body, which has nine openings from which impure matter is constantly trickling, just as boat owners abandon an old boat, and I shall go to the great city of Nibbāna.

For example, just as a man who happens to travel with thieves while carrying treasure, seeing the danger of his treasure being plundered and destroyed, abandons the thieves and goes to a place of safety; even so,”
65:
46
“this body is very much like a great thief. (It is said that this body is like a great thief because when unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) enters and one is incited by greed and hatred, this very body becomes a great thief of life-taking (pāṇātipāta), a great thief of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), and so on, plundering and destroying all the treasures of merit.) Therefore, just as a man traveling with thieves, being greatly afraid of the danger of his treasure being plundered, abandons those thieves and departs; even so, I, being greatly afraid whenever I think of the danger of the treasures of merit being plundered and destroyed, shall abandon this body (which is like a great thief) and go to seek the path to Nibbāna, which can certainly provide the peace of the self.”

Such were his thoughts.

## The Great Almsgiving
The wise Sumedha, having reflected on renunciation through these various analogies as mentioned, thought again: “My father, grandfather, and ancestors for seven generations, having accumulated so much wealth, were unable to take even a single coin when they went to the next world. As for me, I should certainly find a good way to take this wealth with me all the way to Nibbāna.” Having thought thus, he went before the King and said:

“Great King, because I am deeply afraid in my heart, through my reflection, of the oppression of birth, aging, and so on,”
66:
47
“I shall leave the household life and become a monk. I have a collection of wealth amounting to many hundreds of millions. May the King himself take possession of that wealth.”

When he spoke thus, the King replied, “I have no need of your wealth; do with it as you wish.”

Then the Bodhisatta Sumedha, saying “Very well, Great King,” had a great drum of charity beaten throughout the city of Amaravatī, announcing, “Let those who desire wealth come and take it!” He then gave a great almsgiving to all, regardless of status, whether they had a refuge or were without one.

## The Renunciation
After giving that great almsgiving, the Bodhisatta Sumedha set out directly for the Himalayas to become a hermit.

When Sakka, the King of Devas, saw that the Bodhisatta Sumedha had entered the Himalayas with the intention of reaching Mount Dhammika this very day to renounce the world, he called the celestial architect Vissakamma and commanded, “Go, dear Vissakamma! This wise Sumedha has come to the forest to become a monk. Create a hermitage for him to reside in.”

Vissakamma, accepting Sakka’s command saying “Very well,” created a hermitage and grounds that were delightful and pleasant to the heart. Within those grounds, he created a leaf-roofed hut and a rest house that were well-secured, and a blameless walkway (caṅkama) that was pleasing to the mind.

In this regard, the walkway created by Vissakamma was as follows:
67:
48
It was a walkway free from the five faults, namely:
(1) being rough and uneven,
(2) having trees within the walkway,
(3) being overgrown with grass, creepers, and bushes,
(4) being too narrow,
(5) being too wide.

It was sixty cubits in length, with the main walkway being one and a half cubits wide, flanked on both sides by two side-paths each one cubit wide. It was a level ground spread with white sand. (For the detailed meaning of the five faults of a walkway, see the Anudīpanī.)

Furthermore, the created hermitage and grounds were such that for those residing there:
(1) there was no hoarding of wealth or grain,
(2) they sought only blameless almsfood,
(3) they partook only of food that had cooled,
(4) they were free from the kind of exhaustion experienced by citizens when kings and officials within the country forcibly collect taxes or seize gold, silver, and treasures as royal property,
(5) they were free from attachment to buildings, utensils, ornaments, and so on.
69:
In the pavilion for daytime residence, he provided drinking water pots, conch shells for drinking, and water cups. In the fire-shed, he provided fire-pots, firewood, and so on. Having thus created all the requisites pertaining to ascetics and monks, Vissakamma wrote an inscription on the wall inside the leaf-roofed hall: "Whoever wishes to ordain as a monk, let them take these requisites and ordain." Then, he returned to the celestial realm.

## Ordination

When Vissakamma had departed, Sumedha the Wise wandered along the foothills, valleys, and cliffs of the Himavanta, searching for a peaceful place suitable for his residence. He saw the delightful hermitage on the slopes of Mount Dhammika at a bend in the river, which had been created by Vissakamma and offered by Sakka, King of Devas. He walked slowly to the end of the cloister path, and seeing no footprints, he reflected: "Surely, the monks residing in this monastery must have gone to nearby villages to seek alms-food and, being exhausted, must have entered the leaf-roofed hall to rest." Thus thinking, he waited for a short while.

After some time had passed and he saw nothing unusual, he thought: "A long time has passed... I shall investigate to see if there is a monk or not." He then opened the door of the leaf-roofed hall, entered, and looked here and there. Seeing and reading the inscription on the large wall, he decided: "These requisites are suitable for me. I shall take these requisites and ordain as a monk." Having reflected upon and understood the nine faults of lay clothing and the twelve...
70:
...twelve benefits of bark garments, he discarded the pair of clothes he was wearing and donned the bark garments.

(For the nine faults of lay clothing and the twelve benefits of bark garments, see the Anudīpanī. Also, for the meaning and noteworthy points regarding bark garments, etc., see the Anudīpanī.)

## Abandoning the Leaf-Hut and Approaching the Foot of a Tree

The Bodhisatta Sumedha the Wise removed his noble pair of lay clothes and folded them neatly on the robe-rack inside the leaf-roofed hall. He then fastened around his waist a reddish bark garment, resembling a cluster of golden laburnum flowers. Over that, he draped another bark garment, bright and yellow like the color of gold. He placed a black antelope skin, complete with hooves and resembling a bed of punnaga flowers, over his left shoulder. He bound his matted hair into a topknot, securing it with an ivory pin so it would not move. He placed a coral-colored water jug in a carrying-loop that looked like a string of pearls. He took up a triple-curved carrying pole and, hanging the water jug on one end and a hook, a basket, and a wooden tripod on the other, he placed the pole with the full set of ascetic requisites on his shoulder. Holding a staff in his right hand, he stepped out of the leaf-roofed hall. Walking back and forth within the sixty-cubit-long cloister path, he looked at his own appearance and thought:

"My heart's desire has reached its pinnacle. My state as a holy recluse is truly beautiful!
72:
the three types of wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka), namely: thoughts of sensuality (kāma-vitakka), thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), and thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka), will always bite and consume him like wild gadflies. Now, it is proper for me to increase the practice of seclusion.

Indeed, I saw the faults of impediments (palibodha) in household life, which obstruct, disturb, oppress, and hinder the practice of merit, and I fled to the forest to be free. This leaf-roofed hall is also very delightful. The leveled ground is beautiful and yellow, like the color of a ripe bael fruit. The white walls are like the color of silver. The leaf-roof is beautiful and deep red, like the color of a pigeon's foot. The cane-woven couch has the appearance of an exquisite bedspread. The place is very comfortable for sitting and staying. I do not think the luxury of the house I lived in during my lay life would exceed this leaf-roofed hall."

Having reflected thus, he recognized the eight faults of a leaf-roofed hall and the ten benefits of the foot of a tree. On that very day, he abandoned the leaf-roofed hall and approached the foot of a tree endowed with the ten benefits.

(For the eight faults of a leaf-roofed hut and the ten benefits of the foot of a tree, see the Anudīpanī.)

## Practicing Dhamma by Subsisting on Fruits

The Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit, having well-discerned the aforementioned matters, entered the village for alms-food on the following day. At that time,
73:
the people living in the village where the Bodhisatta arrived offered alms-food with great effort and diligence. When the Bodhisatta had finished his meal, he returned to the hermitage and reflected:

"I did not ordain as a monk because I lacked food. Fine food tends to increase pride and the conceit of 'I am a man.' There is no end to the suffering that arises based on food. It would be better if I were to abandon food made from sown and planted grain and subsist only on fruits that have fallen naturally."

Having thought thus, from that time on, he ate only naturally fallen fruits as he had planned. Without lying down at all, he practiced the meditation work unremittingly using only the three postures of sitting, standing, and walking. Within seven days, he attained the eight attainments (eight mundane jhānas) and the five direct knowledges (abhiññā).

Regarding the series of events from the great donation given by the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Wise until his ordination and attainment of the direct knowledges and attainments, it is stated in the Buddhavamsa Pali:

*Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, nekakoṭisataṃ dhanaṃ.*
*Nāthānāthānaṃ datvāna, himavantamupāgamiṃ.*

"Dear Sāriputta,
I, the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Wise, having thought thus about renouncing the world, gave away wealth amounting to many hundreds of crores to those with and without protectors, and then I approached the Himavanta."

*Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā.*

"Dear Sāriputta,

*Aṭṭhaguṇasamupetaṃ, abhiññābalamāhariṃ.*

On the slopes of Mount Dhammika, I created a cloister path free from five faults. I created a hermitage that could provide the eight benefits of the happiness of a recluse. *Sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ tattha, navadosamupāgataṃ.*
*Vākacīraṃ nivāsesiṃ, dvādasaguṇamupāgataṃ.*

*Aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, pajahiṃ paṇṇasālakaṃ.*
*Upāgamiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ, guṇe dasahupāgataṃ.*

"Dear Sāriputta,
I abandoned the leaf-roofed hall which was beset with eight faults. I approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten benefits."

“I abandoned the food produced from sown and planted grain without remainder. I took up the food of naturally fallen fruits, which are endowed with many virtues.

Thus it was preached.

In this matter: Although the entire hermitage, the leaf-roofed pavilion, the walkway, and so forth were created by the celestial architect Vissakamma under the command of Sakka, as previously mentioned, the Buddha—referring to the time he was Sumedha—spoke as if he himself had constructed the hermitage, saying “I have well-made the hermitage,” in reference to the fact that the hermitage and other facilities appeared due to the power of his own merit. In truth, it was not built by the hermit Sumedha himself; it should be understood without doubt that it was fully created by the celestial architect Vissakamma under Sakka’s command.

## 5. The Section on the Proclamation
As previously described, while the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit was dwelling in mastery, having reached the pinnacle of success in the Dispensation consisting of the instructions of virtuous hermits and the Dhamma of Jhanas and supernormal knowledges, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Chief and Leader of the three worlds, appeared in the world.

(The lineage of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara’s life will be described later in the Section on the Twenty-Four Buddhas.)

At the four occasions—when the Bodhisatta Dīpaṅkara took conception, when he was born, when he attained Buddhahood, and when he preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka—the thirty-two great omens, such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems, clearly manifested.

(These thirty-two great omens will be described in detail in the Section on the Life of Gotama Buddha.)

The Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit did not notice those thirty-two great omens because he was dwelling in delight, absorbed only in the bliss of meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti).

After attaining Buddhahood, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka at the Sunandārāma grove, providing the medicine of the Deathless Dhamma to ten billion devas and humans. Then, like a great rain falling over the four continents, he showered the rain of Dhamma upon the multitude of people,

58

The Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit, unaware that the Buddha Dīpaṅkara had appeared, remained dwelling in the forest, delighting in the bliss of meditative attainments. Meanwhile, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, accompanied by four hundred thousand Arahant elders, gradually journeyed and arrived at the city of Rammā, staying at the great Sudassana Monastery.

The citizens of Rammāvatī heard the news that the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was staying at the great Sudassana Monastery in the city of Rammā. They took excellent medicinal requisites such as ghee and butter, and after their morning meal, holding flowers and perfumes, they went to the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. They paid respectful homage, made offerings of flowers and perfumes, and sat in a suitable place free from the six faults. After listening to the sweet Dhamma, they invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for the next day's meal. Then, they circumambulated the Buddha to the right, paid homage, and departed.

## Preparation of the Pavilion and Ceremony
When the next day arrived, the citizens of Rammāvatī prepared a great “Incomparable Almsgiving” (Asadisa Mahādāna). They erected pavilions, scattered soft and clean blue lotuses inside them, treated the ground with the four kinds of perfumes, and scattered five types of fragrant flowers including parched rice. At the four corners of the pavilion, they placed pots filled with cool, sweet water,
78:
59
covering them with emerald-green banana leaves. Above the pavilion, they hung a canopy decorated with gold, silver, and ruby stars. They hung rows of fragrant flower garlands and jewel garlands in abundance. After preparing the alms-pavilion in this manner, they swept and cleaned the entire city of Rammāvatī. They placed water pots decorated with banana trees bearing fruit and flowers, and erected banners, streamers, and jasmine garlands. They fenced both sides of the main royal road with curtains and prepared everything necessary within the city. Then, they decorated the entire path along which the Buddha Dīpaṅkara would travel, filling up the gullies eroded by water, leveling the uneven and muddy ground, spreading white sand like pearls, scattering parched rice and flowers, and planting fruit-bearing banana trees. Thus, they managed the preparatory services for the almsgiving.

At that time, the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit flew into the sky from his hermitage. While traveling through the air above the citizens of Rammāvatī, he saw them joyfully and delightedly clearing and decorating the road. He reflected, “What is the reason for this?” and while the people were watching, he descended from the sky and stood in a blameless spot, saying:

“This great crowd is joyful, elated, and thrilled; they are clearing the road, the path, and the way. For whom is this road being cleared?”

“This great crowd is joyful and elated in heart; they are clearing the road. For whom are they clearing the road?”

inquire. Since the lifespan during the time of Buddha Dīpaṅkara’s appearance was one hundred thousand years, it can be inferred that Sumedha the Hermit was already very old, his age being countable by thousands of years.)

## Taking a Portion of the Road and Preparing It
At the moment the citizens of Rammāvatī spoke, the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit, upon hearing the word “Buddha,” experienced a great surge of rapture (pīti). Expressing the overflowing rapture within him by repeating “Buddha... Buddha...”, he rejoiced greatly and experienced mental bliss.

Standing right where he had descended from the sky, Sumedha the Hermit rejoiced and felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) through wisdom, thinking: “I shall sow the seeds of noble merit in the presence of this Buddha Dīpaṅkara, who is like a fertile field for sowing the seeds of merit. The ninth auspicious occasion of a Buddha’s appearance (Buddhuppāda), which is free from the eight inopportune places, is very rare to obtain and rare to encounter. I have now obtained such a rare and difficult-to-encounter auspicious occasion of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara’s appearance. Let this auspicious occasion not pass me by.” Thus he thought deeply.

Having thought so, he requested a place, saying: “O people, if you are clearing the road for the Buddha Dīpaṅkara’s arrival,

Then the wise Sumedha, generating rapture with the Buddha’s virtues as the object, thought: “I am capable of repairing and clearing this place through psychic power to make it the best and most excellent. However, if I clear it through psychic power (as it would be finished easily in a moment), it would not bring me complete satisfaction. Today, I should perform physical service (veyyāvacca) myself.” Having so decided, he carried earth from afar and filled that large muddy swamp.

Before the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit could finish repairing his assigned portion, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, endowed with the six supernormal knowledges, the virtue of being unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, and the virtue of being free from the stains of defilements, came along the road accompanied by four hundred thousand Arahants.

The Buddhavamsa Commentary further explains that these four hundred thousand Arahants were endowed with many other virtues, such as having few desires, being easily contented, being capable of giving instructions, respectfully receiving advice, being secluded from the five cords of sensual pleasure and defilements, avoiding improper social mingling, and being perfected in the five types of Vinaya.

## The Strong Aspiration to Become an Omniscient Buddha

The way the hermit Sumedha's mind was set on becoming a Buddha while lying face down in the mud was as follows: "If I so desired, I could today burn away the defilements and become a pure Arahant, having exhausted the four asavas (taints). But what benefit is there for an excellent person like me to realize Nibbāna through the Fruit of Arahantship in the guise of an obscure disciple monk under the teaching of Dīpaṅkara Buddha? I shall strive to reach the state of an Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

Being a man of great character who recognizes the power of wisdom, the power of faith, and the power of effort, what benefit is there for me to cross over the ocean of Saṃsāra alone, thinking only of my own benefit? I shall strive to reach the state of an Omniscient Buddha...

66
...and after striving, I shall rescue the multitude of beings, including devas, from the ocean of suffering in the cycle of rebirth (Saṃsāra).

By this extraordinary act of devotion (adhikāra), in which I have disregarded my own life and lay in the mud to offer my back as a bridge for the Great Man Dīpaṅkara Buddha, I shall myself reach the state of an Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and then rescue and save the multitude of beings from the ocean of suffering in Saṃsāra.

Having cut the current of Saṃsāra and destroyed the three realms of existence, and having first boarded the raft of the Noble Eightfold Path myself, I shall rescue and save the multitude of beings, including devas." Thus, the thought of becoming a Buddha arose in him.

(The points to be noted here will be explained in the Anu-dīpanī.)

Although she strongly wished to offer something, she had nothing other than the eight lotuses. She said:

"O Hermit, for as long as you are fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) to become a Buddha, may I be your equal companion."

The Bodhisatta hermit Sumedha accepted the five lotus flowers given by the young Brahmin lady Sumittā and, in the midst of the assembly, offered them to Dīpaṅkara Buddha who was approaching, while making the aspiration for Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa).

Seeing this, Dīpaṅkara Buddha, also in the midst of the assembly, spoke these words of prophecy:

"O noble hermit known as Sumedha, this lady Sumittā will be your companion with the same intention and the same destiny for the sake of your Buddhahood. She will be one who is beloved through the three actions of body, speech, and mind. She will be exceedingly beautiful, charming, pleasing to the heart, and a speaker of pleasant words. Later, in your final birth, she will receive the inheritance of the supramundane Dhamma in your liberating dispensation (niyyānika-sāsana), reaching the Fruit of Arahantship and becoming a female disciple endowed with psychic powers (iddhi-pāda)."

Thus He delivered the prophecy.

(This collection of events was recounted by the Great Elder Nun Yasodharā herself to the Buddha, as recorded in the Therī Apadāna Pāḷi.)

## The Proclamation of the Prophecy

In this context, the hermit Sumedha did not aspire to become a Buddha without possessing the necessary qualifications to receive a prophecy (unlike the vast assembly of thirty-six yojanas when the Buddha descended from Tāvatiṃsa). In fact, he was already endowed with the eight factors for receiving a prophecy, as previously mentioned in the ninth chapter on the 'Appearance of a Buddha': (1) Being a human being; (2) Being a male; (3) Being a person endowed with the specific merit to attain Arahantship in that very life if desired; (4) Meeting a living Buddha in person; (5) Being a hermit who believes in the law of kamma (kammavādī); (6) Being endowed with the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) and five supernormal powers (abhiññā); (7) Having sacrificed his life for Dīpaṅkara Buddha—for if Dīpaṅkara Buddha and the four hundred thousand Arahants had actually trodden upon Sumedha's back as he intended, he would not have survived, yet knowing this, he sacrificed his life boldly and without hesitation. This kind of merit is called 'adhikāra' merit in the scriptures. Being endowed with such extraordinary merit; (8) Having such a strong desire for merit that even if the entire universe were filled with glowing coals and spear-points, and he were told he could only attain Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) by crossing them without retreating, he would still be willing to cross them to attain Buddhahood. Because he was perfected in these eight factors for receiving a prophecy, his aspiration to become a Buddha was firm.

Therefore, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara also approached the place where the Bodhisatta, the hermit Sumedha, was lying. Standing at the head of the Bodhisatta Sumedha, He sent forth and contemplated with His Anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa (the knowledge that can see and know the future without obstruction), thinking: "This hermit Sumedha has made a firm resolve to become a Buddha and lies here in the soft mud. Will this hermit's aspiration be fulfilled, or will it not?"

Having contemplated, He saw clearly and definitively: "After four asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons from this world, he will become the Buddha named Gotama." While still standing in the midst of the assembly, He proclaimed the prophecy with nine verses beginning with "Passatha imaṃ tāpasaṃ, jaṭilaṃ uggatāpanaṃ":

"Monks, behold this hermit with matted hair, who is endowed with fierce austerity. This hermit Sumedha, in an era more than many incalculable aeons (four asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons) from now, will surely become a Buddha in the three worlds."

"In the life when he is to become a Buddha, this hermit Sumedha will renounce the world from the wonderful and delightful royal city of Kapilavatthu. After practicing the work of meditation and performing the difficult practice (dukkharacariyā), the Bodhisatta will reside at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree. Having accepted 'milk-rice' at that banyan tree, he will proceed to the banks of the Nerañjarā river."

(Regarding the Nerañjarā river, one may refer to the later section in the Anu-dīpanī.)

Upon reaching the foot of the Bodhi tree, keeping the Mahābodhi-maṇḍa (the Great Seat of Enlightenment)—the place where the Omniscient Knowledge clearly arises—to his right, he will circumambulate from south to west, west to north, and north to east. Then, that Blessed One, who possesses great fame and glory with no one superior to him, will penetrate and realize the Four Noble Truths at the foot of the Assattha tree. (Meaning, he will truly become a Buddha.)

His biological mother will be named Māyādevī; his biological father will be named Suddhodana; and this Buddha will be named Gotama.

Kolita and Upatissa, who are free from the taints (āsavas), devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and firm concentration, will be the pair of Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka).

The monk named Ānanda will be the attendant and will serve this Buddha. Khemā Therī and Uppalavaṇṇā Therī, who are free from the taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and firm concentration, will be the pair of Chief Female Disciples (Aggasāvikā).

## The Rejoicing of Devas and Humans
Upon hearing this prophecy of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, who has no equal in the three worlds and who always seeks only noble virtues, the devas and humans, greatly rejoicing that "this hermit Sumedha is indeed the seed of a future Buddha," shouted and raised cheers of applause, joyfully clapping their hands. The devas and Brahmās from the ten thousand world systems, along with the multitude of humans, raised their joined palms in reverence and paid homage.

"Even if we fail to fulfill and thus miss the teachings of this Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the refuge of the whole world, may we, in the future, behold this noble hermit with our own eyes when he becomes a Buddha and be among those who attain the extraordinary Dhamma."

"Just as a person crossing a river, if unable to reach the intended landing place due to the force of the current and being swept away, would cross the river by grasping a landing place further downstream; in the same way, even if all of us miss (attaining the Dhamma under) this Blessed One Dīpaṅkara,

may we, in the future, behold this noble hermit with our own eyes when he becomes a Buddha and be among those who attain the Dhamma."

Thus, they made their aspirations and prayers.

## The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara’s Departure to the City of Ramma
The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Master of the attribute 'Lokavidū' who clearly knows the three worlds and is worthy of receiving offerings brought from afar, having delivered the prophecy to the hermit Sumedha (and having honored him with eight handfuls of flowers), stepped over the hermit Sumedha with His right foot and departed.

At that place of prophecy, the four hundred thousand Arahant elders, the sons of the Blessed One, (having honored the Bodhisatta Sumedha with flowers and scents), kept the hermit Sumedha to their right and departed. Humans, Nagas, and Gandhabba devas also respectfully paid homage to the hermit Sumedha, honored him with flowers and scents, and then left.

The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahants and being worshipped and honored by the citizens of Ramma and many devas, proceeded along the decorated path. He sat upon the Buddha-seat prepared within the city of Ramma, like the young sun appearing over the peak of Mount Yugandhara, in order to make the lotus-like people who were ready for liberation blossom by maturing them with the four levels of Truth. The four hundred thousand Arahants also sat down in their respective places in order.

## The Rapturous Joy of the Bodhisatta Sumedha
As soon as the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the leader of the three worlds, along with the four hundred thousand Arahants, had passed beyond the sight of the hermit Sumedha, the Bodhisatta Sumedha rose joyfully from his prone position. With a heart moistened by exceedingly noble happiness, joy, and rapture, he sat cross-legged upon the great heap of flowers offered and scattered by devas and humans. To contemplate and reflect upon the Pāramīs (Perfections), he thought thus:

"I have attained mastery (vasībhāva) in the sphere of Jhana; I have reached the pinnacle of the five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). Within the ten thousand world systems, there are no hermits equal to me. In terms of psychic power and the Dhamma, I am indeed peerless."

Having reflected thus, he attained an exceptionally superior state of mental happiness.

## 6. Section on Reflecting on the Perfections
When all the devas and brahmas had departed, the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit, having heard the words of both the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and the devas, was greatly pleased and joyful, and he reflected thus:

"The Buddhas do not have the custom of speaking words that are doubtful (thinking it might be so, or it might not be so);
100:
81
they do not have the custom of speaking words that are in vain. There is no such thing as the words of the Buddhas being false. (Therefore) I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.

Just as a stone thrown into the sky surely and certainly falls back to the ground, even so, the words of the glorious Buddhas are surely and certainly firm; thus, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.

Just as the nature of death is surely and certainly firm for all beings, even so, the words of the glorious Buddhas are surely and certainly firm; thus, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.

Just as the rising of the sun is surely and certainly firm when the night ends, even so, the words of the glorious Buddhas are surely and certainly firm; thus, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.

Just as the nature of the lion's roar when emerging from its cave is firm, even so, the words of the glorious Buddhas are surely and certainly firm; thus, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.

Just as the delivery (birth) of the fetus by pregnant women is firm, even so, the words of the glorious Buddhas are surely and certainly firm; thus, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha.
101:
82
Having reflected with various such similes and having decided that he would definitely become a Buddha according to the words of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, he thought:

"Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make one a Buddha (Buddhakarā dhammā), investigating thoroughly all those fundamental principles that exist in the upper realm (deva world), the lower realm (human world), and the ten directions (realms divided into kāma, rūpa, and arūpa)."

Thus, he investigated and reflected upon the Buddhakarā dhammā—the causes that can make one a Buddha.

(In this context, the knowledge that reflects on and investigates the perfections is called Pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa. That Pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa within the Bodhisatta Sumedha the Hermit was of great power. In reflecting on the perfections (pāramī), the great sacrifices (cāga), and the conducts (cariya) which are the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) to attain Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), he could see and understand them without any obstruction. It was self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) without the help of a teacher. It is explained in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Anuṭīka that this is the precursor and omen for attaining the Golden Omniscient Knowledge.

To make it clearer: the Buddha Dīpaṅkara only spoke the words of prophecy to Sumedha the Hermit, saying "You will become a Buddha." He did not preach that such and such qualities must be practiced and developed to become a Buddha. The Bodhisatta Sumedha had to reflect, investigate, and search for those qualities that make one a Buddha only through his own Pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa. When he reflected and investigated those qualities with that knowledge, they appeared fully in the Bodhisatta's knowledge without any obstruction. Regarding that:)
102:

With the eightfold path and the Māyā-gaṅga, having fulfilled the duties and possessing distinct knowledge, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya Dhamma) serve as a protective hand. In this realm of humans, where enemies are crushed, he remained close to the fifteen hundred defilements, yet destroyed the twelve great leaders of the thieves (defilements) through four stages of path-knowledge. Having attained the prize of victory and peace, and being praised as one who has achieved total eradication (samuccheda), he stands amidst the Saṅgha. Such is the one whose wisdom is vast and whose virtues are extraordinary and radiant—the famous Great Elder, the noble Sāriputtra...

That noble being, who seeks the welfare of others, your father in faith, has brought forth numerous traditions and methods. Correctly establishing the truth, he spoke from here with a singular desire, aspiring for the great prize of enlightenment. Those who are so named strive for a long time, sacrificing much, using the Buddha's wisdom as a scaffold to build and support. Like a hook that does not miss anything great or small, he taught the conduct to be practiced with a clear and melodious voice, explaining the causes and effects in full, even if the Great Noble Lord did not explicitly preach it... Upon receiving the consecration and prophecy, immediately and without delay, he possessed the power of penetrating and comprehensive knowledge. With self-enlightened knowledge (Swayambhū-ñāṇa) that does not rely on others, and coupled with wisdom, he saw the entire surface of the earth, above and below, without exception.

Thus, he desired to establish the practice—so it is composed in the 'Poem on the Chapter of Perfections' (Pāramī-taw-khan Pyo).

In the aforementioned passage, according to the original Pali term 'Dhamma-dhātu' (intrinsic nature/fundamental principle), that which bears its own nature and arises is called 'Dhātu' in Pali and 'Dhāt' in Burmese. Bearing its own nature means that it arises automatically according to its causes, without being created or fashioned by others. If it were created or fashioned by others, it would no longer be an intrinsic nature (Dhātu). Therefore,
103:
84
A phenomenon that arises purely according to its causes, without being connected to the efforts of others, is called 'intrinsic nature' in Burmese and 'Dhamma-dhātu' in Pali.

If one wishes to search for the causal factors that make one a Buddha (the factors that enable one to become a Buddha), one should search only within the intrinsic nature (Dhamma-dhātu). Thus, it is preached: 'Vicinnāmi dhammadhātuyā' (I search within the Dhamma-dhātu). If the intention is to speak of a person rather than the nature of Dhamma, the term 'Loka-dhātu' (world-element) should be used. (This means that Dhamma is to be searched for in the Dhamma-dhātu, while a person is to be searched for in the Loka-dhātu.) The usage is seen in expressions such as: 'Two Buddhas cannot arise simultaneously in a single world-element (Loka-dhātu).' In this context, since the subject is the person of the Buddha, the term 'Loka-dhātu' is used, not 'Dhamma-dhātu'.)

## (a) Dāna Pāramī (The Perfection of Generosity)

When he investigated and reflected in this manner, the Bodhisatta Sumedha first saw the Dāna Pāramī, which is like a great and noble path leading to Buddhahood, a path constantly followed and practiced by previous Bodhisattas.

(Having seen it thus, he admonished himself:) 'Friend Sumedha... if you desire to reach the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscient Knowledge (to become a Buddha), first firmly establish and undertake this Dāna Pāramī, and become one who is perfected in Dāna Pāramī (fulfill the Dāna Pāramī to the highest degree).'

(Continuing further:) 'In the world, if a pot filled with anything (such as water or milk) is overturned, it pours out all the water it contains without leaving any behind. Similarly, when you see recipients of alms—whether they be low, middle, or high—

...give like the overturned water pot, without leaving any remainder of what you have to give.' Thus, he admonished himself again.

(Noteworthy points regarding this Dāna Pāramī are presented extensively in the Anudīpanī.)

## (b) Sīla Pāramī (The Perfection of Virtue)

After the hermit Sumedha had found, seen, and reflected upon the Dāna Pāramī—

'The factors that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to this Dāna Pāramī alone. There must be other factors that can mature the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscient Knowledge. I shall investigate and search for those factors as well...'

When he investigated and reflected thus, he saw the second perfection, Sīla Pāramī, which was constantly followed and practiced by previous Bodhisattas.

(Having seen it thus, he admonished himself:) 'Friend Sumedha... if you truly desire to reach and attain the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscient Knowledge, firmly establish and constantly undertake this second perfection, Sīla Pāramī, and strive to become one who is perfected in Sīla Pāramī (fulfill the Sīla Pāramī to the highest degree).'

(Continuing further:) 'In the world, the animal known as the Camari (the yak) protects its tail-hair. If its tail becomes snagged in any place, it would rather face death in that very spot than let its tail-hair be damaged. Similarly,'

'In the same way, friend Sumedha, you should fulfill the virtues to perfection in the four bases of wholesome Dhamma, namely: (1) Pātimokkha-saṃvara (restraint by the monastic code), (2) Indriya-saṃvara (restraint of the sense faculties), (3) Ājīva-pārisuddhi (purity of livelihood), and (4) Paccaya-sannissita (reflection on the use of requisites). Just as the Camari deer protects its tail-hair even at the cost of its life, you should protect your virtue at all times.' Thus, he admonished himself again.

(Continuing further:) 'Just as the King of Lions, the Kesarasīha, possesses unwavering energy in all postures—sitting, standing, and walking—and always has an uplifted heart, similarly, friend Sumedha, you should firmly uplift your energy in all existences where you may be born. When you have reached the pinnacle of Viriya Pāramī, friend Sumedha, you will attain the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscient Knowledge.' Thus, he admonished himself again.

**********

## (f) Khantī Pāramī (The Perfection of Patience)

After the hermit Sumedha had found, seen, and reflected upon the Viriya Pāramī—

'The factors that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these five alone. There must be other factors that can mature the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscient Knowledge. I shall investigate and search for those factors as well...'
109:
When he investigated and reflected in this manner, he saw the sixth perfection, the Perfection of Patience (Khantī Pāramī), which the previous Bodhisattas had constantly resorted to, practiced, and developed.

(Having seen it, he admonished himself:) "Friend Sumedha, if you wish to reach and attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge, you must firmly undertake and constantly practice this sixth Perfection of Patience. If you can fulfill this Perfection of Patience without a divided mind, such as 'sometimes being patient and sometimes not,' or 'being patient with some people and not with others,' then you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

(Continuing further:) "Just as this Great Earth (Mahāpathavī) does not feel any hatred or love toward anything thrown upon it, whether it be pure and excellent or impure and base, but remains patient, even so, Friend Sumedha, you must endure the adoration and offerings of all people as well as their contempt. When you reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Patience, you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

**********
## (g) The Perfection of Truthfulness (Saccā Pāramī)

After the hermit Sumedha had found, seen, and reflected upon the Perfection of Patience:

"The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be only these six. There must be other qualities that can mature the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship
110:
and Omniscient Knowledge. I shall search for those qualities as well."

When he investigated and reflected in this manner, he saw the seventh perfection, the Perfection of Truthfulness (Saccā Pāramī), which the previous Bodhisattas had constantly resorted to, practiced, and developed.

(Having seen it, he admonished himself:) "Friend Sumedha, you must firmly undertake and constantly practice this seventh Perfection of Truthfulness. If you can fulfill the Perfection of Truthfulness by speaking only the single truth without double-talk, such as 'sometimes being truthful and sometimes not,' or 'telling the truth to some and not to others,' then you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

(Continuing further:) "Just as the Venus star (Osadhi-tārakā), which is like a great standard of truth for the whole world including the devas, travels straight along its fixed course without deviating, whether in the rainy season, winter, or summer, even so, Friend Sumedha, you must not deviate from the eightfold path of truth: what is seen, what is heard, what is sensed (reached), what is known, and what is not seen, what is not heard, what is not sensed, and what is not known. (Speak only that you have seen what was seen; speak only that you have heard what was heard; speak only that you have sensed what was sensed; speak only that you have known what was known; speak only that you have not seen what was not seen; speak only that you have not heard what was not heard;
111:
speak only that you have not sensed what was not sensed; speak only that you have not known what was not known.) When you reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Truthfulness in this way, you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

(In this context, only when one says they have seen what was seen by the eye is it called speaking while established in the path of truth. Only when one says they have heard what was heard by the ear is it called speaking while established in the path of truth. What is smelled by the nose, tasted by the tongue, and touched by the body is called 'sensed' (reached). Only when one says they have sensed what was sensed is it called speaking while established in the path of truth. Only when one says they have known what was known by the mind is it called speaking while established in the path of truth. The same applies to what is not seen, not heard, not sensed, and not known. This kind of speaking while established in the path of truth is called Noble Usage (Ariya-vohāra) by the Blessed One.)

*********
## (h) The Perfection of Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī)

After the hermit Sumedha had found, seen, and reflected upon the Perfection of Truthfulness:

"The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be only these seven. There must be other qualities that can mature the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge. I shall search for those qualities as well..."

When he investigated and reflected in this manner, he saw the eighth perfection, the Perfection of Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī), which the previous Bodhisattas had constantly resorted to, practiced, and developed.
112:
(Having seen it, he admonished himself:) "Friend Sumedha, you must firmly undertake and constantly practice this eighth Perfection of Resolution. If you can fulfill it by being unshakable in that Perfection of Resolution, then you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

(Continuing further:) "Just as a great stone mountain (selo pabbato), which is without trembling and naturally well-established in the world, does not tremble at all because of the wind blowing fiercely but stands firmly in its place, even so, Friend Sumedha, you must fulfill your practice to completion without ever failing or wavering in the meritorious deeds of the perfections you have undertaken. When you reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Resolution in this way, you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

(In this context, Adhiṭṭhāna means the mental state or decision to perform a certain task or to be in a certain way, such as 'I will do this task; I will make it happen in this manner.' (For example) The mental state or decision of the Bodhisatta Prince Temiya to act as if he were crippled, mute, and deaf—though he was not—until he could go forth into the forest, is called Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna).)

## (i) The Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā Pāramī)

After the hermit Sumedha had found, seen, and reflected upon the Perfection of Resolution:

"The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be only these eight. There must be other qualities that can mature the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge. I shall search for those qualities as well..."

When he investigated and reflected in this manner, he saw the ninth perfection, the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā Pāramī), which the previous Bodhisattas had constantly resorted to, practiced, and developed.

(Having seen it, he admonished himself:) "Friend Sumedha, if you desire to reach and attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge, you must firmly undertake and practice this ninth Perfection of Loving-kindness. Strive and exert yourself to practice through the meditation of loving-kindness in a way that is unlike others."

(Continuing further:) "Just as water (udaka) in the world, without discrimination between the virtuous and the wicked, pervades all who use it with its coolness and cleanses them by washing away dust and impurities, even so, Friend Sumedha, you must develop loving-kindness equally toward both those who do not wish for your welfare (enemies) and those who do wish for your welfare (friends). When you reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Loving-kindness, you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge (you will become a Buddha)."

114:
## (j) The Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā Pāramī)

After the hermit Sumedha had found, seen, and reflected upon the Perfection of Loving-kindness:

"The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be only these nine. There must be other qualities that can mature the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge. I shall search for those qualities as well..."

When he investigated and reflected in this manner, he saw the tenth perfection, the Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā Pāramī), which the previous Bodhisattas had constantly resorted to, practiced, and developed.

(Having seen it, he admonished himself:) "Friend Sumedha, you must firmly undertake and practice this tenth Perfection of Equanimity. Just as the tongue of a balance scale, which is equally weighted on both sides, does not rise up nor fall down but remains level and straight, even so, Friend Sumedha, if you remain firmly in a neutral state without leaning toward either side in pleasure or pain (if greed arises due to pleasure, it is called leaning toward the side of pleasure; if anger arises due to pain, it is called leaning toward the side of pain. It means one must remain in the middle without greed for pleasure or anger for pain), then you will reach the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge (Buddhahood)."

(Continuing further:) "Friend Sumedha, as a worldly analogy, just as this Great Earth (Mahāpathavī) remains indifferent without any hatred or love toward both the impure things and the pure things that someone might throw upon it,
115:
even so, Friend Sumedha, you must always practice, undertake, and develop neutrality like a balance scale, without love or hatred in both pleasure and pain. When you reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Equanimity, you, Friend Sumedha, will attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge (you will become a Buddha)."

**********
## The Great Earthquake upon Reflecting on All Ten Perfections

After reflecting on the Perfection of Equanimity, the hermit Sumedha thought: "In this world, these ten are the only qualities that mature the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge, and that make one a Buddha, which Bodhisattas must accumulate and fulfill. There are no others beyond these ten. These ten perfections, the excellent qualities for becoming a Buddha, do not exist in the sky above, nor do they exist in the Great Earth below, nor do they exist in the cardinal directions such as the East. Indeed, they exist only within my heart." Having seen and reflected that these ten perfections are well-established only in his own heart, he firmly resolved: "Friend Sumedha, you must fulfill and remain in these ten perfections, the excellent qualities for becoming a Buddha, without deviation."

Then, he reflected on them in forward order (anuloma): the Perfection of Generosity (Dāna Pāramī), the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī), the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma Pāramī), the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā Pāramī), the Perfection of Energy (Vīriya Pāramī), the Perfection of Patience (Khantī Pāramī), the Perfection of Truthfulness (Saccā Pāramī), the Perfection of Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī), the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā Pāramī), and the Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā Pāramī). Then, in backward order: the Perfection of Equanimity, the Perfection of Loving-kindness, the Perfection of Resolution, the Perfection of Truthfulness,
116:
...in reverse order: Khantī-pāramī, Vīriya-pāramī, Paññā-pāramī, Nekkhamma-pāramī, Sīla-pāramī, and Dāna-pāramī. By the method of starting from the middle and ending at both ends: Vīriya-pāramī, Khantī-pāramī, Paññā-pāramī, Sacca-pāramī, Nekkhamma-pāramī, Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī, Sīla-pāramī, Mettā-pāramī, Dāna-pāramī, and Upekkhā-pāramī. By the method of starting from both ends and ending in the middle: Dāna-pāramī and Upekkhā-pāramī, Sīla-pāramī and Mettā-pāramī, Nekkhamma-pāramī and Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī, Paññā-pāramī and Sacca-pāramī, Vīriya-pāramī and Khantī-pāramī. Thus, he reviewed and contemplated the ten perfections like oil being squeezed out from both sides of a mechanical press.

He reviewed and contemplated without omission all the facts that should be known regarding the ten perfections which are the causes of Buddhahood: that the sacrifice and practice of various external goods and wealth is called Pāramī; the sacrifice and practice of limbs and organs is called Upapāramī; and the sacrifice and practice of even one's life is called Paramatthapāramī.

Due to the power of the Pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa (Knowledge of Investigating the Perfections) of the Bodhisatta Hermit Sumedha, who was contemplating these ten perfections along with their respective essential characteristics and functions, this great earth, comprising ten thousand world-systems, shook violently in six ways: tilting to the left, tilting to the right, moving forward, moving backward, sinking down, and rising up. It also made a great echoing roar. Like a sugar-cane press being squeezed by the hands of the pressers,
117:
and like the rotating wheel in an oil mill, this great earth turned and shook all around.

(As previously described in the latter part of the Sumedha-kathā), after the Buddha Dīpaṅkara had given the prophecy to the Hermit Sumedha, He proceeded to the homes of the lay devotees who had invited Him into the city of Rammavatī and was partaking of the alms-food and other offerings. During that time, the Hermit Sumedha was reflecting on and analyzing the ten perfections one by one. At the conclusion of his reflection on all ten, when the great earthquake occurred, the entire assembly of people who were serving alms to the Buddha Dīpaṅkara at the alms-giving ceremony in Rammavatī were unable to remain standing due to the force of the violent earthquake. They fell to the ground in a daze, like great Sāla trees blown down by a fierce gale descending from Mount Yugandhara.

At that place, thousands of pots containing alms-food and hundreds of water jars collided with one another and were smashed to pieces.

Then, many people, being terrified and trembling with distressed minds, gathered together in unison, approached the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, and said:

"O Lord, endowed with the five types of eyes (the Buddha-eye, Dhamma-eye, Samanta-eye, Divine-eye, and Wisdom-eye)... will this be for the benefit of the people, or will it be for their harm?"
118:
"All the people are now oppressed by a great and terrifying danger. O Lord, please dispel and remove that danger!"

When they pleaded thus, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara said, "Be free from agitation, be comforted, and do not be afraid because of this earthquake. This very day, I have prophesied to the wise Sumedha that 'This person will become an Omniscient Buddha in the world in the future.' That wise Sumedha has now reviewed and contemplated the ten noble perfections which were practiced by previous Bodhisattas. Because of that wise Sumedha's reflection on the ten perfections—the excellent qualities for becoming a Buddha—without omission, this great earth, comprising ten thousand world-systems in the world including the devas, has shaken violently." Thus He preached to the citizens of Rammavatī, explaining the cause of the earthquake and assuring them that there was no danger for the people.

**********
## The Worship and Prayers of Humans and Devas
Upon hearing the words of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the anxiety in the hearts of the citizens of Rammavatī was immediately dispelled and calmed. Having found peace of mind, they became extremely joyful and delighted. Taking offerings such as flowers and perfumes, they departed from the city of Rammavatī, approached the Bodhisatta Sumedha, and once again worshipped and honored him with those flowers and perfumes.

At that time, the Bodhisatta Hermit Sumedha, having undertaken the ten perfections which are the traditional practice of Bodhisattas,
119:
kept his mind firm and steady. He paid homage to the Buddha Dīpaṅkara in his mind and rose from his cross-legged sitting position.

To the Bodhisatta Hermit Sumedha, who had risen from his seat after contemplating the perfections, the devas brought celestial flowers and the humans brought human flowers. Both devas and humans honored him by scattering and offering these celestial and human flowers.

Both devas and humans proclaimed auspicious words of praise, saying: "The Hermit has aspired for the noble prize of Buddhahood. May you obtain that aspired prize of Buddhahood according to your wish!"

"May all dangers that the Noble Hermit might encounter be completely avoided and never occur. May all sorrows, anxieties, and illnesses disappear and be cleared away without being met. May no harm whatsoever befall the Noble Hermit's body. May you swiftly and thoroughly reach the noble Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge."

"O Sumedha of great effort and energy... just as in this world, when the flowering season arrives, the trees that usually bloom do so; in the same way, may you bloom with the qualities of knowledge such as the Fourfold Intrepidity (Catuvesārajja-ñāṇa), the Sixfold Unique Knowledge (Cha-asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and the Ten Powers (Dasabala), which are the fruit and property of all Buddhas."
120:
"O Sumedha of great effort and energy... just as all the Buddhas fulfilled the ten perfections, in the same way, may you also fulfill the ten perfections; may you be able to fulfill them."

"O Sumedha of great effort and energy... just as all the Buddhas realized the Four Noble Truths at the foot of the Bodhi tree and became Buddhas, in the same way, may you also realize the Four Noble Truths at the Great Bodhi, the victory ground, and become a Buddha."

"O Sumedha of great effort and energy... just as all the Buddhas preached the first sermon, the Dhammacakka (or, as they turned the Jewel of the Wheel of Dhamma), in the same way, may you also be able to preach the first sermon, the Dhammacakka (or, may you be able to turn the Jewel of the Wheel of Dhamma). (In this context, the Buddha's knowledge of preaching is called the Dhammacakka Jewel.)"

"Just as on the full moon day, the great moon is exceedingly beautiful when it is entirely free from the five impurities: frost, mist, clouds, Rāhu (Asurinda), and smoke; in the same way, may you, with your heart's desires fulfilled, be exceedingly beautiful in the ten thousand world-systems."

"Just as the sun, released from the mouth of Asurinda (called the planet Rāhu), is radiant and beautiful with its own light; in the same way, may you be released from all worlds of existence and be radiant and beautiful with the glory of a Buddha."
121:
"Just as all river waters flow into and gather in the great ocean, in the same way, may all humans together with devas gather only in your presence."

In this manner, the devas and humans spoke words of auspicious prayers and declarations of success.

Thus, the Bodhisatta Sumedha, who received such great praise and the sound of prayers from the assembly of devas and humans, firmly resolved to undertake the ten perfections and entered the great Himavantā forest to fulfill those perfections.

## Introduction
The word 'Anudīpanī' is purely a Pali term. (Anu = further/subsequent, Dīpanī = explanation/exposition). A discourse that further explains a collection of matters that might not be clear or obvious in the original text is called an 'Anudīpanī'. The Most Venerable Ledi Sayadaw wrote a commentary on the Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha titled 'Paramattha-dīpanī'; in that Paramattha-dīpanī, he wrote another volume titled 'Anudīpanī' to further explain the collection of facts that might not be clear or obvious.

Similarly, in this Mahā Buddhavaṃsa text, if the original text and the noteworthy Anudīpanī facts were written and printed together in a mixed fashion, it would be difficult for the virtuous readers to distinguish between the text and the meaning, leading to confusion. Therefore, the facts and matters that are particularly advanced, extensive, and worth noting for the Buddhavaṃsa text are included, described, and printed as a supplement under the name 'Anudīpanī'.

By looking at this 'Anudīpanī = Supplementary Explanation', those matters that are not clear or obvious in the original words of the Mahā Buddhavaṃsa will become well-clarified and obvious, and the meanings that are deep in wisdom and hidden will be easily understood.
123:
...it will become clear. Therefore, may the virtuous audience who read the Mahābuddhavaṃsa, after reading the text of the Chronicle of Buddhas, not neglect or ignore this Anudīpanī (Explanatory Supplement), but examine it thoroughly and easily understand the profound and hidden meanings worthy of note.

## The Meaning of Pāramī
The ten groups of Dhamma such as Dāna (generosity), Sīla (morality), etc., are called Pāramīs. (The Great Bodhisattas who are endowed with the ten qualities such as Dāna and Sīla are called Parama = Noble Persons. The state of these Great Bodhisattas is called Pāramī, derived from the word 'Paramānaṃ bhāvo', as it is the cause for the arising of the knowledge and the verbal expression of others who see or hear them, saying 'This person is indeed a Great Bodhisatta'.)
(Alternatively, it is derived from 'Paramānaṃ kammaṃ', meaning the work or the practice of the Great Bodhisattas, which is the collection of the ten Dhammas such as Dāna, Sīla, etc., and is thus called Pāramī.)

That sequence of ten Pāramīs should be known according to this verse:
Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ.
Khanti sacca madhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettūpekkhāti te dasa.
(Generosity, morality, renunciation, wisdom, and energy as the fifth;
Patience, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.)

Among these ten Pāramīs, each is divided into three: Pāramī, Upapāramī, and Paramatthapāramī. (For example, in Dāna: 1. Dāna-pāramī, 2. Dāna-upapāramī, 3. Dāna-paramattha-pāramī. It is the same for Sīla and the others.) Because they are thus divided into three each, there are thirty Pāramīs in detail.

## Distinction between Pāramī, Upapāramī, and Paramatthapāramī
For these three, one should first note: (1) external possessions such as children, wife, gold, silver, and other utensils; (2) one's own major and minor limbs such as hands and feet; and (3) one's life. Regarding Dāna—
124:
(1) Sacrificing external possessions is Dāna-pāramī; (2) sacrificing major and minor limbs is Dāna-upapāramī; (3) sacrificing one's life is Dāna-paramattha-pāramī. This is how it should be noted.

Similarly, the three types of observing Sīla without transgression for the sake of external possessions, for the sake of limbs, and for the sake of life should be understood as Sīla-pāramī, Sīla-upapāramī, and Sīla-paramattha-pāramī respectively. For the remaining eight, the same method should be applied.

(a) If one can sacrifice external things, animate or inanimate, it is the basic Pāramī.
(b) If one can sacrifice various major and minor limbs with a detached mind, it is Upapāramī.
(c) If one can sacrifice one's life (jīva), it is called Paramattha.
(d) Thus the ten Pāramīs expand into thirty distinct types.

Regarding these three—Pāramī, Upapāramī, and Paramatthapāramī—please refer to the detailed explanations of various teachers in the Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā, Pakiṇṇakakathā, under the heading 'Ko vibhāgo...'.

## Adhimuttimaraṇa
Death by resolving the mind is called Adhimuttimaraṇa. It is a type of death that occurs immediately after resolving, "Let my death occur right now." This kind of death can only happen to Bodhisattas; it cannot happen to others.

When the Great Bodhisattas are occasionally reborn in the long-lived realms of Devas or Brahmas, they reflect: "For me, residing in this Deva or Brahma realm, there is no opportunity to fulfill the Pāramīs, Cāga (liberality), and Cariya (conduct)." Thus, they become weary of staying long in those Deva or Brahma realms. At that time, they enter their celestial mansion, close their eyes, and resolve: "From this moment on, let the continuity of my life-faculty (jīvitindriya) not proceed further." Immediately after this resolution—
125:
The death-consciousness (cuti-citta) arises, and their celestial or Brahma life ends. This is true... because their Pāramīs are exceptionally developed, they have purified the continuity of their aggregates (khandha) through higher knowledge (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti) in various lives. Therefore, because their attachment (sineha) to the physical body is extremely thin, and because their compassion (karuṇā) for beings is supreme, their resolutions (adhiṭṭhāna) are sharp and pure, and all the wishes of the Great Bodhisattas are fulfilled.

Since they have mastery over Kamma just as they do over the mind, after ending their celestial or Brahma life through the aforementioned Adhimuttimaraṇa, they take rebirth in the human world as kings, brahmins, etc., where they can fulfill their desired Pāramīs. For this reason, our Bodhisatta, even in this present Bhadda-kappa, was reborn in the Brahma realm after passing away from many lives without losing his jhāna. However, he stayed in that Brahma realm for only a short time, passed away through Adhimuttimaraṇa to end his Brahma life, and was reborn in the human world to practice and accumulate the foundations of the Pāramīs.

The Eye of the Three Worlds, the Incomparable One (Cinteyya), in his lives as a Bodhisatta during that time, though he reached the Brahma realms repeatedly, he desired to save the multitude of beings. Thus, he did not remain until the end of those long aeons of Brahma bliss, but with mindfulness established, he resolved to pass away, ended his life, and took rebirth in the human realm. He fulfilled the Pāramīs, Cāga, and Cariya life after life. Oh, how wondrous is the power of the Great Lord's compassion!
