## Kappa = About the Aeon
What is called 'Kambhā' (Kappā) in the Burmese language is expressed by the Pali word 'Kappa'. Therefore, in the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, it is taught as: "Kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye"... and so on.

A period of time called a Kappa cannot be counted in numbers of years; it is something that can only be understood through contemplation. The way to understand it through contemplation is—
126:
If there were a great granary one yojana in length, breadth, and height, filled with tiny mustard seeds, and one seed were removed every hundred years, that great heap of mustard seeds would be exhausted before the period of time called one Kappa is over. This is how it should be understood through contemplation. (Considering this statement, one should note that Kappa in Pali = Kambhā in Burmese = an extremely long period of time.) Nowadays, however, without noticing that "an extremely long period of time is called a Kappa," people use the term 'Kambhā' only for the physical mass of the earth, such as the earth's surface or the globe.

## Divisions of Kappa
One should note that Kappa and Kambhā are the same. There are six types of Kappa: (1) Mahākappa, (2) Asaṅkhyeyyakappa, (3) Antarakappa, (4) Āyukappa, (5) Hāyanakappa, and (6) Vaḍḍhanakappa.

Among them, each Mahākappa (No. 1) is defined by the four types of Asaṅkhyeyyakappa (No. 2): (a) Saṃvaṭṭakappa = the aeon of dissolution; (b) Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyīkappa = the aeon when it remains dissolved; (c) Vivaṭṭakappa = the aeon of evolution; (d) Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīkappa = the aeon when it remains evolved. (That is to say, these four Asaṅkhyeyyakappas together are called one Mahākappa.)

Among these four Asaṅkhyeyyakappas, the period from the falling of the world-destroying rain until the flames cease (if the world is destroyed by fire), or until the water ceases (if by water), or until the wind ceases (if by wind), is called Saṃvaṭṭakappa (the dissolving aeon).

The period from the time it has been destroyed by fire, water, or wind until the falling of the world-creating rain is called Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyīkappa (the aeon that remains destroyed).

The period from the falling of the world-creating rain until the appearance of the sun, moon, and stars in the world is called Vivaṭṭakappa (the evolving aeon).

The period from the appearance of the sun, moon, and stars until the falling of the next world-destroying rain is called Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīkappa (the aeon that remains evolved).
127:
In this explanation, two types of world-destroying rains are included. One type is the rain that inevitably falls when any world—whether it is to be destroyed by fire, water, or wind—is about to perish. The manner of its falling is that a great rain falls heavily, covering the entire world-system that is to be destroyed. People, seeing the heavy rain, plant crops, and after the plants have grown enough for cattle to eat, the rain stops completely and never falls again. This is the foundational rain for the destruction of the world.

The other type is the rain that falls specifically to destroy the world in a world destroyed by water. That rain is not ordinary rainwater; it is a special kind of water that can destroy even stone mountains and rocks upon contact.

(For a detailed account of how the world is destroyed by fire, water, and wind, please read the chapter on the higher knowledge of recollecting past lives (Pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā) in the translation of the Visuddhimagga.) The four types mentioned, such as Saṃvaṭṭakappa, are equal in duration. The length of each of these four parts cannot be counted in number of years. Therefore, these four Kappas are called Asaṅkhyeyyakappa (Incalculable Aeons).

Only when these four Asaṅkhyeyyakappas are combined does it become one Mahākappa (or one Kambhā). The Burmese use the word 'Kambhā' to denote the meaning of the Pali 'Mahākappa'. As for the term 'Asaṅkhyeyyakappa', they do not use a separate vocabulary but use the Pali-derived term 'Asaṅkhyeyyakap' (Asaṅkhyeyya-kappa).

## (3) Antarakappa etc.
Among those four Asaṅkhyeyyakappas, at the beginning of the Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-asaṅkhyeyyakappa (alternatively, the beginning of the world), humans have an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) lifespan. As time passes, unwholesome states such as greed (lobha) and hatred (dosa) enter and destroy them, and the lifespan gradually decreases until it reaches ten years. This period of decline is called Hāyanakappa in Pali, and 'Soke-kap' (Descending Aeon) in Burmese.

Then, from the ten-year lifespan, because wholesome states such as loving-kindness (mettā) and the sublime abidings (brahmavihāra) enter and support them, the lifespan increases generation after generation until it reaches an incalculable age again. From the ten-year lifespan—
128:
The period of time during which the lifespan increases until it reaches the incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) age is called Vaḍḍhanakappa in Pali, and 'Tet-kap' (Ascending Aeon) in Burmese. (If one wishes to know the details of these two—the descending and ascending aeons—one should look and note in the Cakkavatti Sutta of the Pāthika-vagga, Dīgha Nikāya 3, in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.)

In this way, the lifespan of humans fluctuates, rising when wholesome states increase and falling when unwholesome states overwhelm, between the ten-year age and the incalculable age. One such pair of an ascending aeon and a descending aeon is called one Antarakappa.

## Three Types of Antarakappa
At the beginning of the world, from the Asaṅkhyeyyakappa, when the lifespan reaches ten years, a change of aeon (kappa) occurs. In the process of decline, if it occurs because greed (lobha) is particularly dominant, a "great danger of famine" occurs during the final seven days, and all wicked people perish. That aeon is called Dubbhikkhantaraka-kappa.

In the process of decline, if it occurs because delusion (moha) is particularly dominant, a "great danger of dire disease" occurs during the final seven days, and all wicked people perish. That aeon is called Rogantaraka-kappa.

In the process of decline, if it occurs because hatred (dosa) is particularly dominant, during the final seven days, "they kill each other with weapons," and all wicked people perish. That aeon is called Satthantaraka-kappa.

(According to the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā: if greed is dominant, the Rogantaraka-kappa occurs; if hatred is dominant, the Satthantaraka-kappa occurs; if delusion is dominant, the Dubbhikkhantaraka-kappa occurs, and wicked people perish.)

The reason why one pair of an ascending and a descending aeon is called one Antarakappa is that it occurs every time the lifespan reaches ten years before the total destruction by fire, water, or wind at the end of the Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-asaṅkhyeyyakappa.
129:
(Indeed)
It refers to the period of change and destruction that occurs intermittently before the final great destruction, based on the fact that all wicked people perish due to the perils of famine, disease, and weapons.

Based on the perils that occur during the final seven days of these interim aeons (antarakappa)... the names Rogantarakappa (aeon of plague), Satthantarakappa (aeon of weapons), and Dubbhikkhantarakappa (aeon of famine) are used. If a contagious disease breaks out in certain towns or regions (not worldwide) during the period before the ten-year lifespan era, it is said that the Rogantarakappa is striking that town or region. If warfare occurs, it is said that the Satthantarakappa is striking. If famine strikes, it is said that the Dubbhikkhantarakappa is striking. Such expressions are merely metaphorical, based on their similarity to the actual conditions of a true interim aeon. The phrase "four planes of misery and three perils (kappas)" used in Buddhist prayers and aspirations also refers only to these metaphorical aeons.

When sixty-four of these interim aeons, consisting of pairs of increasing and decreasing periods, have passed, one Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī Asaṅkhyeyyakappa (incalculable aeon of world-duration) ends. In the Saṃvaṭṭa Asaṅkhyeyyakappa, Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī Asaṅkhyeyyakappa, and Vivaṭṭa Asaṅkhyeyyakappa, although they are not measured by the pairs of increasing and decreasing interim aeons because beings do not exist (in the human and deva realms), each of these great incalculable aeons lasts approximately the same duration as sixty-four interim aeons. Therefore, they should be understood as being equal in time to the Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī Asaṅkhyeyyakappa.

## Āyukappa (Lifespan Aeon)
An Āyukappa is an aeon defined according to the prevailing lifespan of beings. (Āyu = life/lifespan). This means that if the lifespan is one hundred years, then one hundred years is one Āyukappa; if the lifespan is one thousand years, then one thousand years is one Āyukappa.

When the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Ānanda, the Tathāgata has developed the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda); if the Tathāgata so desired, he could remain for a kappa or slightly more than a kappa"... the term 'kappa' here refers to the Āyukappa. An Āyukappa refers to the lifespan of humans during that particular period.
130:
This refers to the measure of the human lifespan. Therefore, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, explains that the Buddha meant he could remain for a hundred years or slightly more.

However, Mahāsīva Thera argued that it refers to the Mahākappa (Great Aeon) known as Bhadda. (He stated this considering that the kamma which produces the final rebirth of a Bodhisatta has the potential to sustain life for an incalculable number of years. He also based this on the Pali texts which mention that the Āyupālaka Phalasamāpatti—the Fruition Attainment for sustaining life—can maintain the life-continuum known as āyusaṅkhāra and ward off dangers to life.) The commentators (Aṭṭhakathā teachers) do not accept the view of this Elder.

In the Saṅghabhedaka Khandhaka of the Vinaya Cūḷavagga Pali, it is taught: "One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is reborn in hell and must be boiled there for a kappa." The commentary on that text explains that this 'kappa' is the Āyukappa of the beings in Avīci Hell. In the great Vinaya sub-commentary (ṭīkā) called the Terasakanḍa, it is explained that the Āyukappa of these Avīci beings is equal to one-eightieth (1/80) of a Mahākappa. That same sub-commentary specifically notes that this one-eightieth duration is designated as an Antarakappa. By defining one-eightieth of a Mahākappa as an Antarakappa (the Antarakappa of Avīci beings), it implies that one Mahākappa contains eighty Antarakappas according to the count of Avīci beings.

Regarding this statement, it should be clarified that, as previously mentioned, one Mahākappa consists of four Asaṅkhyeyyakappas, and each Asaṅkhyeyyakappa consists of sixty-four Antarakappas. Therefore, one Mahākappa contains two hundred and fifty-six (256) Antarakappas according to the human count.

If those 256 kappas are divided by 80, the result is three and one-fifth (3 1/5) kappas each. Thus, three and one-fifth human Antarakappas equal one Antarakappa of the Avīci beings. (In Avīci Hell, there are no increasing and decreasing aeons as in the human world; it is a state of constant suffering and destruction.
131:
Therefore, there is no need to distinguish periods by the three great perils that occur at the end of a decreasing aeon as in the human world. One-eightieth of a Mahākappa, which is the lifespan (āyukappa) of those Avīci beings, is simply called an Antarakappa. Thus, it means one Avīci Antarakappa equals three and one-fifth human Antarakappas.)

According to this method, it can be said that in one Asaṅkhyeyyakappa, there are sixty-four Antarakappas by human count, and twenty Antarakappas by the count of Avīci beings. Therefore, when some Pali texts (such as the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā, Ṭīkā-kyaw, etc.) explain that one Asaṅkhyeyyakappa has sixty-four Antarakappas or twenty Antarakappas, it is not a difference in doctrine. It is merely a difference in the method of counting between the human scale and the Avīci scale (64 vs. 20). The actual duration of time should be understood as being exactly the same.

A special point to note is found in the Sammohavinodanī, the commentary on the Ñāṇavibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga: "Only the kamma of Saṅghabhedaka (causing a schism in the Saṅgha) can cause one to remain for a kappa. If one commits Saṅghabhedaka kamma at the beginning or middle of a kappa and falls into Avīci Hell, one is released only when the kappa is destroyed. If the kappa were to be destroyed tomorrow, and one caused a schism today and fell into hell, one would suffer for only one day and be released tomorrow; however, such an occurrence is impossible."

Based on this passage, some people believe and record that "Saṅghabhedaka kamma causes one to stay in hell for an entire Mahākappa and one is released only when the world is destroyed." In truth, that Vibhaṅga commentary uses the general term 'Kappatthitiyo' (staying for a kappa); it does not specifically say 'Mahākappatthitiyo' (staying for a Mahākappa). Furthermore, the explanation of 'Kappatthitiyo' is based on the Vinaya Cūḷavagga Pali: "Āpāyiko nerayiko, kappaṭṭho saṅghabhedako... Having split the unified Saṅgha, he boils in hell for a kappa." Since the commentator Venerable Mahābuddhaghosa himself explained in the Cūḷavagga commentary that "Kappa means Āyukappa" (Kappanti āyukappaṃ),
132:
the duration of suffering in Avīci Hell due to Saṅghabhedaka kamma should be taken as an Āyukappa, not the Mahākappa (the entire world-cycle). In the commentary on the Kappatthiti chapter of the 13th division of the Abhidhamma Kathāvatthu, it is explained that the Pali passage "Āpāyiko nerayiko" refers to the Āyukappa (of Avīci beings), which is one-eightieth of a Mahākappa.

## Varieties of Mahākappa
The Mahākappa, also called a world-cycle, is of two types: (1) Suññakappa (Empty Aeon) and (2) Asuññakappa (Non-empty Aeon).

Among them, an aeon in which no Buddhas appear is called a Suññakappa. It means an aeon void of Buddhas.

An aeon in which Buddhas appear is called an Asuññakappa. It means an aeon not void of Buddhas.

In a Suññakappa, only Fully Enlightened Buddhas do not appear. However, Paccekabuddhas and Cakkavattis (Universal Monarchs) can arise, as can be inferred from the Upāli Thera Sutta of the first chapter of the Apadāna Pali and other texts.

Indeed, in the Upāli Thera Sutta and its commentary, it is stated: "Counting back from this aeon, in the second aeon, Prince Khattiya, the son of King Añjasa, insulted the Paccekabuddha Devala upon leaving the garden." There is no mention in the scriptures that a Fully Enlightened Buddha appeared in that aeon. Also, in the commentary on the Bhaddaji Thera Sutta of the Apadāna, it is mentioned: "In a great Suññakappa void of Buddhas, he had formerly served five hundred Paccekabuddhas," showing that Paccekabuddhas appear in Suññakappas. In the Kusumāsanīya Thera Sutta of the Apadāna Pali, it says: "In the aeon immediately preceding, the Bodhisatta of Kusumāsanīya Thera was once a Universal Monarch named Varadassī." Similarly, in the Tiṇasanthara Thera Sutta of that Pali, it says: "Counting back from this aeon, in the second aeon, the Bodhisatta of Tiṇasanthara Thera was once a Universal Monarch named Migasammata." These texts show that Universal Monarchs can arise in a Suññakappa.
133:
The Asuññakappa (Non-empty Aeon) in which Buddhas appear is further divided into five types: (a) Sārakappa, (b) Maṇḍakappa, (c) Varakappa, (d) Sāramaṇḍakappa, and (e) Bhaddakappa. Among them:

(a) If one Buddha appears, it is called a Sārakappa.
(b) If two Buddhas appear, it is called a Maṇḍakappa.
(c) If three Buddhas appear, it is called a Varakappa.
(d) If four Buddhas appear, it is called a Sāramaṇḍakappa.
(e) If five Buddhas appear, it is called a Bhaddakappa.

(Mnemonic verse:)
One is Sāra, two Maṇḍa, Vara is for three,
Sāramaṇḍa shows four, five is Bhaddaka,
If even one does not appear, it is a Suññakappa.

The aeon four incalculables (asaṅkhyeyya) and one hundred thousand cycles ago, mentioned in the section on Sumedha the Brahmin, was a Sāramaṇḍakappa in which four Buddhas appeared. It should be noted that the city of Amaravatī flourished during the period after the appearance of the first three Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and Saraṇaṅkara—among those four.

## The Reason for the Name Amaravatī
Amara = Deva (a race that does not die/immortals); Vatī = possessing. It means a royal city where devas reside. The reason for this name is as follows:

In the Bhesajjakkhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga and other texts, it is taught that as soon as the Brahmins Sunidha and Vassakāra planned to establish the city of Pāṭaliputta, devas first came and took up positions to mark the sites. The areas marked and taken by powerful devas became the residential quarters for kings, ministers, and wealthy merchants of great merit. The areas marked by devas of medium power became the residential quarters for people of medium merit. The areas marked by devas of lesser power became the residential quarters for people of lesser merit.
134:
(b)
Based on this statement, it is understood that many deities (devas) would come to mark and occupy the site where the greatest royal capital is to be established. To signify the presence of these many deities who have marked, protected, and resided there, the name "Amaravatī" was given.

The Pali suffix "-vatī" and the Burmese word "shi-the" (to have/possess) indicate abundance. In the world, one who possesses only a small amount of wealth is not usually called a wealthy person (dhanasī); only one who possesses wealth far exceeding others is called wealthy. Therefore, as this great city is a magnificent royal capital, the name Amaravatī makes it known that it is a great city where many powerful deities come to protect and reside.

## The Ten Sounds
Regarding the ten sounds, the Buddhavaṃsa Pali does not show all ten sounds completely, but only six. However, the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya Mahāvagga and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary present all ten in order. In that presentation, because 'samma' and 'tāḷa' are distinguished as separate sounds, the count of ten is reached at the sound of 'tāḷa', making the sound of invitation (nimantana), such as "Please eat, please drink," the eleventh.

In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta Pali, the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, the Jātaka Commentary, and the Mūlaṭīkā, it is taught and explained that the sound of invitation is the tenth sound. Accordingly, if 'samma' and 'tāḷa' are not taken separately as the sound of cymbals and the sound of bronze gongs, but are taken together as the single sound of rhythm (musical timing), then the sound of invitation (nimantana) becomes the tenth sound, which would then agree with the aforementioned Pali, Commentaries, and Sub-commentaries.

In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta Commentary, it is also explained: "Samma-saddo ti kaṃsatāḷa-saddo," showing that 'samma' and 'tāḷa' have the same meaning. In the Abhidhāna-ṭīkā, it is similarly explained: "Sammañca taṃ tāḷañcāti sammatāḷaṃ." Considering that the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries explain 'sammatāḷa' as a single entity, and in order for the sound of invitation to be the tenth sound as stated in the Pali, one may translate them separately as "samma = wooden clappers, tāḷa = bronze gongs" if desired, but to include both meanings without separating them, they are translated as "the sound of rhythm (musical timing)."
135:
(bha)
(Note: In translating 'samma' as 'khwet-khwin' (clappers), some might assume it refers to cymbals. In truth, it should be understood that 'khwet-khwin' refers to wooden or bamboo slats. One should consult the Abhidhāna-nissaya of the Abhayārāma Sayadaw and the Panyat-net-kyan of the Myataung Sayadaw.)

In the Nidāna-kathā of the Jātaka Commentary, the ten sounds are explicitly listed as: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of the great drum, the sound of the mutinga drum, the sound of the lute, the sound of wooden clappers, the sound of bronze gongs, the sound of the conch, and the sound of invitation with food and drink. In the Sri Lankan version of the Jātaka Nidāna, however, the sound of the conch is omitted, and the sound of singing is included to make ten. Given this discrepancy between the Burmese and Sri Lankan versions, since the original Buddhavaṃsa Pali itself directly mentions the conch, it is not appropriate to omit it from the ten sounds; thus, the Burmese version should be upheld. The sound of singing from the Sri Lankan version can be included within the sound of the lute if one wishes; it does not need to be mentioned separately.

## 4. The Section on Sumedha's Renunciation
Regarding the five defects of a walking path (caṅkama) on page 48:

If the ground is uneven, or rough and hard, or if trees are within.
If bushes, grass, and vines grow in a messy tangle within the path.
If it is too narrow, or too wide—these are the five defects to be noted.

One should know according to this verse. Among those five defects of a walking path...

(1) On a path that is rough and uneven, the feet of the one walking become painful and develop blisters or calluses; concentration (samādhi) cannot be attained, and the work of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) cannot be fulfilled. On a soft and even path, however, the work of meditation can be fulfilled due to the comfort of dwelling. Therefore, "rough and uneven ground" should be known as the first defect. Regarding this, in the Sutaung-khan Pyo (Poem on the Prayer Section), it is composed:

Where earthworms' mounds and sharp stones rise on high ridges, where one must turn and double back, walking daily with effort, the soles of the feet become sore and split, causing hesitation and a lack of clarity; even if one tries to restrain the mind, when walking for a long time, it is not stable...

Thus it is composed.
136:
(bhi)
(2) If there is a tree within, in the middle, or at the edge of the walking path, it is likely to strike the forehead or the head of one who walks without mindfulness or attention. Therefore, "the presence of a tree within the walking path" should be known as the second defect. Regarding this, in the Sutaung-khan Pyo, it is composed:

On the right or left, or within the path, if there are twin trees very close by, and if one walks without reflection and strikes them, the feet may stumble, the hands may be pierced, and the forehead or head may be severely bruised and swollen...

Thus it is composed.

(3) On a walking path where the ground is covered with grass, vines, and such, a person walking in the dark might tread on snakes and the like, and might even die (even if one does not intend to kill, it is called killing); or one might be bitten by those snakes and suffer great misery. Therefore, "the presence of grass, vines, etc., on the surface of the walking path" should be known as the third defect. Regarding this, in the Sutaung-khan Pyo, it is composed:

Where vines and rotten vegetation are tangled on the track, even if one covers the feet and walks, if one treads mistakenly without foresight, one might be harmed by insects and creatures...

Thus it is composed.

(4) In constructing a walking path (with a quartz base, of even width, two spans across, with a wall-like border, a small side-path on both left and right—and the main path sixty cubits long, perfectly straight, not crooked, not shifting front or back, three spans wide, with cross-planking, so that even if one treads heedlessly, there is no slipping, as if fixed firmly), according to this, there should be small side-paths of one cubit width each, slightly raised like a wall to provide support in case of an accidental slip to either side. In the middle of these two, the main walking path, exactly sixty cubits long and one and a half cubits (three spans) wide, must be laid straight and even. This is the standard system from the texts for constructing a walking path. If the main path is less than the described width, being only one cubit or one span wide, it is extremely narrow. For one walking on such a narrow path, if they strike against the boundary between the main path and the side-paths and slip,
137:
(bhī)
their toenails or fingernails may be torn off, or their toes or fingers may be broken. Therefore, "being too narrow" should be known as the fourth defect. Regarding this, in the Sutaung-khan Pyo, it is composed:

If the side-path is narrow and the main path is only a cubit or a span wide, if one slips and treads mistakenly, the fingertips or toes may be broken, leading to terrifying pain in that narrow place...

Thus it is composed.

(5) On a walking path that is too wide, the mind of the one walking tends to wander here and there; stability of mind cannot be attained. Therefore, "being too wide" should be known as the fifth defect. Regarding this, in the Sutaung-khan Pyo, it is composed:

If the path is excessively wide like a broad stone slab, as one walks back and forth, lifting the feet and treading with uneven strides, the mind wavers and the steps are not balanced; with burning agitation and arrogant thoughts arising, the voice of meditation does not proceed correctly...

Thus it is composed.

This collection of statements consists of words from the Atthasālinī Commentary. The verses of the Pyo are also presented here as they were composed by the Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa in the Sutaung-khan Pyo, following the Atthasālinī Commentary, as they are worthy of devotion.

In the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, however, regarding the term 'pañca-dosa' (five defects) mentioned in the Pali "pañca-dosa-vivajjitaṃ," the first method explains the five defects of the walking path exactly as in the Atthasālinī Commentary. Then, a second method is explained. According to the second method, 'pañca-dosa' refers to the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). According to this second method, being free from the five defects would no longer concern the walking path itself. It would only concern the term 'abhiññā-bala' (power of direct knowledge) to be mentioned later; it is explained to connect the words as "the power of direct knowledge free from the five defects of the hindrances."

This second interpretation is not very advantageous. The reason is that the five hindrances are already abandoned at the moment of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) just before attaining the first jhāna. Therefore, for the direct knowledge (abhiññā) which is the fifth jhāna, it is not necessary to specifically say "the power of direct knowledge free from the five defects of the hindrances."
138:
(khu)
(It is not that the hindrances are abandoned only upon reaching the direct knowledge of the fifth jhāna; since they were already abandoned before the first jhāna, there is no need to qualify the direct knowledge with the attribute of being free from hindrances.)

Alternatively, there are two types of 'dosa': 'dosa' in the ultimate sense (paramattha-dosa, referring to the mental factor of hatred/anger) and 'dosa' in the conventional sense (vohāra-dosa, referring to faults or defects as used by people). In the context of Sumedha's walking path, cell, robes, and leaf-roofed monastery, the 'dosa' mentioned are only conventional defects (vohāra-dosa). Only by taking them as conventional defects such as the unevenness of the ground, etc., will the context remain consistent.

In connection with the eight joys of a recluse (samaṇa-sukha) mentioned on pages 48 and 49, one should also note the eight blessings of a recluse (samaṇa-bhadra) from the Soṇaka Jātaka in the Saṭṭhi-nipāta. A brief summary of the Soṇaka Jātaka is as follows:

In the distant past, the Bodhisatta was the son of the King of Magadha in the city of Rājagaha, and was named Prince Arindama. Born on the same day as the Bodhisatta was the son of the court chaplain (purohita), the youth Soṇaka.

Both of them grew up together from childhood. When they reached the proper age, they went together to the city of Takkasilā to study. After completing their education and becoming proficient in all beliefs, arts, and regional customs, they left Takkasilā together and traveled from place to place in order. They eventually reached the park of the King of Bārāṇasī and entered the city of Bārāṇasī the following day.

That day, some people were preparing milk-rice and arranging seats to hold a recitation of the Vedas and a feast for brahmins, known as Brāhmaṇa-vācaka. Seeing Prince Arindama and the youth Soṇaka entering the city, they invited them into the house and gave them seats. When he saw that a white cloth was placed for Prince Arindama and a red rug for himself, the youth Soṇaka knew by the omen: "Today, my friend Prince Arindama will become the King of Bārāṇasī, and he will appoint me to the position of Commander-in-Chief (Senāpati)."
139:
(Khu)
After the two friends had finished their meal, they returned to the park of the King of Vārāṇasī. That day happened to be the seventh day since the King of Vārāṇasī had passed away, and it was the day the ministers sent out the ceremonial state carriage (mangalā ratha) to find a successor to the throne. The state carriage left the city, headed for the park, and stopped at the park gate. At that time, the Bodhisatta Prince Arindama was sleeping on the ceremonial stone slab with his head covered, while the youth Soṇaka sat near the Bodhisatta. When Soṇaka heard the sound of musical instruments, he thought, "The state carriage has come for Prince Arindama. He will become king today and will offer me the position of commander-in-chief (senāpati). However, I truly have no desire for any official rank or position. Once King Arindama leaves this park, I shall depart for the forest and become a monk." Having made this plan, he went to hide in a secluded thicket.

The chaplain (purohita) and the ministers of Vārāṇasī consecrated Prince Arindama on that very stone slab, crowning him king, and led him into the city with great royal ceremony. Thus, Prince Arindama became the King of Vārāṇasī. Surrounded by immense royal luxury and attendants, Prince Arindama completely forgot his friend Soṇaka.

As for Soṇaka, after King Arindama entered the city, he went and sat on that ceremonial stone slab. At that moment, seeing a withered sal leaf fall directly in front of him, Soṇaka was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "Just like this sal leaf, my body too will surely reach old age and decay, and will undoubtedly fall to the earth in death." He then practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and, in that very sitting, attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). Immediately, his lay appearance vanished and he took on the form of a monk. He joyfully uttered an inspired exclamation (udāna), "Natthi dāni punabbhavo = There is now no more rebirth for me in a new existence," and departed for the Nandamūla cave.

King Arindama, intoxicated by royal luxury, only remembered his childhood friend Soṇaka after forty years had passed. He longed for him repeatedly, wondering, "Where might my friend Soṇaka be living now?" but could find no trace of news about him.
140:
(Khe)
"To whom shall I give a hundred pieces of silver for bringing good news of Soṇaka? To whom shall I give a thousand pieces of silver for reporting a direct sighting that leads to finding Soṇaka? Who, whether great or small, will report to me about my friend Soṇaka, my childhood playmate?"

King Arindama repeatedly recited this verse (gāthā) expressing this meaning:

Kassa sutvā sataṃ dammi, sahassaṃ daṭṭhu soṇakaṃ.
Ko me soṇakamakkhāti, sahāyaṃ paṃsukīḷitaṃ.

As the King recited it frequently, the citizens also began to recite this verse, regarding it as the King's favorite song.

After fifty years had passed, King Arindama had many sons and daughters, the eldest son being named Prince Dīghāvu. At that time, Soṇaka Paccekabuddha thought, "King Arindama wishes to see me. I shall go and shower him with the rain of Dhamma, explaining the faults of sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation, and thus provide the cause for King Arindama to become a monk." He traveled through the air to the royal park. Near the park, he heard a boy gathering firewood and repeatedly singing the aforementioned song. The Venerable Soṇaka Paccekabuddha then taught the boy a response verse.

The boy went to King Arindama and recited the response verse. Consequently, King Arindama came to the park with his fourfold army. After paying homage to Soṇaka Paccekabuddha, the King, being himself a person of defilements, looked down upon the Venerable Soṇaka Paccekabuddha as a lonely, wretched pauper. He spoke disparagingly with the verse beginning with "Kapaṇo vatāyaṃ bhikkhu."

In response, the Venerable Soṇaka Paccekabuddha countered by explaining that one who experiences the Noble Path (Ariya-magga) within their mental body (nāma-kāya) is not a lonely pauper. Rather, only one who lives lawlessly and practices unrighteousness is a lonely pauper; furthermore, such a person is himself a base individual and a great refuge for other base people.
##
141:
(Khai)
Then King Arindama, with the verse beginning "Arindamo ti me nāmaṃ," declared that his name was Arindama and that he was known to all as the King of Kāsi. He then asked, "O Venerable One, having arrived in this royal park, do you sleep in comfort?"

In response, the Venerable Soṇaka Paccekabuddha recited eight verses, preaching the eight Samaṇabhadra—the auspicious blessings or comforts of a recluse. These eight Samaṇabhadra are:

1. Sadāpi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno.
Tesaṃ koṭṭhe openti, na kumbhiṃ na kaḷopiyaṃ.
Paraniṭṭhitamesānā, tena yāpenti subbatā.

"Great King... for the monk who has renounced the home life and is free from anxiety, there is auspicious blessing and comfort at all times and in all places (not just at this time in your park). Great King... such monks do not store wealth or grain in granaries, pots, or baskets (unlike laypeople who increase their greed for long-term storage). They sustain themselves only with alms-food already prepared in the houses of donors, obtained through the noble search, and consumed with proper reflection (paccavekkhaṇā)." (This verse shows the Samaṇabhadra or recluse's happiness of not possessing stored wealth and grain.)

2. Dutiyampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno.
Anavajjapiṇḍo bhottabbo, na ca kocūparodhati.

(In the Vinaya texts, alms-food obtained through the twenty-one improper ways of searching (anesana), such as practicing medicine, or through the five types of wrong livelihood, or even rightfully obtained requisites consumed without proper reflection, are called "savajja-piṇḍa"—blameworthy food.)

"Great King... a good and noble monk consumes rightfully obtained alms-food with proper reflection, in a blameless manner.
142:
(Kho)
When a noble monk consumes blameless food in a blameless manner, not even the slightest defilement can oppress him. This state of not being oppressed by defilements through the blameless consumption of blameless food is the second auspicious blessing and comfort of a monk who is free from longing and anxiety. (This verse shows the Samaṇabhadra or recluse's happiness of seeking and consuming blameless alms-food.)

3. Tatiyampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno.
Nibbuto piṇḍo bhottabbo, na ca kocūparodhati.

(Alms-food obtained rightfully and consumed with reflection by a worldling is called "nibbuta"—cooled food. However, in the ultimate sense, only the alms-food of an Arahant is truly "nibbuta"—cooled food.)

"Great King... a good and noble monk consumes only cooled alms-food; because of such consumption, not even the slightest defilement can oppress him. Consuming such cooled food and not being oppressed by defilements is the third auspicious blessing and comfort of a monk who is free from longing and anxiety. (This verse shows the Samaṇabhadra or recluse's happiness of consuming only cooled alms-food.)

4. Catutthampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno.
Muttassa raṭṭhe carato, saṅgo yassa na vijjati.

"Great King... for the good monk who wanders through the towns and villages, free from attachment and greed toward the donors of the four requisites, there can be no attachment of lust (rāga-saṅga) or attachment of hatred (dosa-saṅga). (Attachment that strikes or offends an object, like the pricking of a thorn, is called the attachment of hatred.) Such freedom from attachment is the fourth auspicious blessing and comfort of a monk who is free from longing and anxiety.
143:
(Khaw)
(This verse shows the Samaṇabhadra or recluse's happiness of being free from attachment to donors and not living in entanglement with them.)

5. Pañcamampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno.
Nagaramhi ḍayhamānamhi, nāssa kiñci aḍayhatha.

"Great King... (A monk who has many requisites and, thinking 'let not thieves steal my belongings,' entrusts his surplus requisites to the houses of familiar donors, will feel worried and exhausted upon hearing news that a certain donor's house in the town is on fire. Such a monk cannot have auspicious blessing or comfort.) A monk who (like a bird whose only possessions are its wings, which go wherever it goes) possesses only the requisites he is currently using and attached to his person, suffers no loss even if the town or village is burned. This immunity from loss by fire is the fifth auspicious blessing and comfort of a monk. (This verse shows the Samaṇabhadra or recluse's happiness of not being affected by fire.)

6. Chaṭṭhampi bhadramadhanassa, anāgārassa bhikkhuno.
Raṭṭhe vilumpamānamhi, nāssa kiñci ahīratha.

"Great King... when rebels plunder and destroy a town or village (monks with many extra requisites stored in the town suffer loss as their belongings are stolen or destroyed, and thus lack the blessing of peace), for a monk like myself, whose only possessions are the eight requisites attached to his person, nothing is plundered by thieves. This is the sixth auspicious blessing and comfort of a monk who does not store property. (This verse shows the Samaṇabhadra or recluse's happiness of being at peace from the danger of thieves.)
144:
(b)
7. "O Great King, the monk who possesses only the eight requisites as his own property can travel happily along roads guarded by thieves or paths patrolled by guards without being questioned, interrogated, or arrested, taking only his bowl and robes. This is the seventh blessing and happiness of a monk." (This verse illustrates the Recluse's Blessing and Happiness (samaṇabhadra, samaṇasukha) of being able to travel safely even on roads guarded by thieves and officials.)

8. "O Great King, the monk who possesses only the eight requisites attached to his person can go to whatever direction he desires without any lingering attachment (to his former place), without even looking back. Such ability to travel is the eighth blessing and happiness of the monk who does not store up wealth and property." (This verse illustrates the Recluse's Blessing and Happiness of being able to go to another place without attachment to the old location.)

Thus—
While the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka was preaching these Recluse's Blessings, King Arindama interrupted him, saying, "Venerable Sir, although you praise and preach these Recluse's Blessings, I, as one who lusts after sensual pleasures, will not be able to follow them. I greatly delight in human sensual pleasures and divine sensual pleasures. By what means or good path can I attain human and divine lives?" When he asked this, the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka preached the faults of sensual pleasures, explaining that those who lust after them go to woeful states (duggati), and only by abandoning them can one avoid such states. He used the simile of a crow that, greatly rejoicing, perches on a dead elephant carcass floating in the middle of a river...
145:
(bā)
...and reaching the middle of the ocean, finds no foothold and perishes. After preaching the faults of sensual pleasures using this simile, the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka departed through the air.

King Arindama also gained great spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He handed over the throne to his eldest son, Dīghāvu, entered the Himavantā, became an ascetic, lived on fruits, practiced the Sublime Abodes (brahmavihāra) and meditative absorptions (jhāna), and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

## The Eight Kinds of Recluse's Happiness (Samaṇasukha)
1. Not storing wealth or grain; this is the foremost noble happiness of a monk.
2. Seeking alms food blamelessly; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
3. Consuming alms food with prior reflection and composure; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
4. Being free from the oppression of taxes and punishments by the ruler of the land; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
5. Not being attached to buildings or thinking of them as 'mine' like laypeople; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
6. Being free from the dangers and harassment of thieves and robbers; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
7. Being free from association with ministers and officials, thus attaining peace; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
8. Being unhindered and free to go in all four directions; this is the noble happiness of a monk.
(These eight kinds of Recluse's Happiness and the eight Recluse's Blessings are mostly identical. Compare them accordingly.)

The nine faults of lay clothing mentioned on page 51 are:
1. The high value and cost of the cloth worn is one fault.
2. The fact that it can only be produced through dependence on others who weave it is one fault.
3. It becomes soiled easily when used; (being soiled, it must be frequently washed and dyed) is one fault.
4. It wears out quickly due to frequent washing and dyeing; (worn-out clothes must be frequently sewn and patched) is one fault.
5. It is difficult to find and acquire again is one fault.
146:
(ga)
6. It is unsuitable and inappropriate for the state of a hermit is one fault.
7. It is associated with enemies; (since enemies desire lay clothing, one must guard it securely so they cannot take it) is one fault.
8. For the wearer, it becomes an object of vanity, elegance, and ornamentation is one fault.
9. If one carries it without wearing it, it becomes an extra burden on the shoulder, leading to great greed—this is one fault.

These nine faults are composed in the Sutaung-khan Pyo as follows:
"This garment, woven from thousands of threads and worth hundreds of thousands, is bright and vivid, yet for me, it is hard to obtain and its price is bitter... If one wears it without knowing its distinction, one is no different from an ignorant person... When worn on a sweaty body, it does not last long and soon appears soiled... Even with a small amount of cloth, if it is perceived as dirty, it must be washed and dyed; through much dyeing and washing, it becomes thin and torn, yet even then, one must sew and patch it as if it were new... Even with effort, acquiring a piece of cloth is difficult and causes distress to the heart... For one called a hermit, cotton cloth and robes are highly unsuitable... Without avoiding the appearance of a monk, even while wearing it, there is the worry that strangers might strip it off; though one fears wearing it, one must constantly guard it... Even if one wears and uses good things, it appears as vanity, elegance, and a pretense of ornamentation... If not worn but kept as a precious item, it remains a lingering attachment, a sign of great greed and a burden for a monk; thus, virtuous people may find cause for blame."
This is composed in verse 82.

High cost, dependence on others, easily soiled, easily worn out, difficult to obtain, unsuitable for a monk, many dangers, vanity in use, and the burden of carrying—remember these nine as the faults of lay clothing.

The twelve benefits of bark-fiber robes (vākacīra) are:
1. They are inexpensive, good, and suitable for hermits; this is one benefit.
2. They can be made by one's own hands; this is one benefit.
3. They become soiled slowly during use, and there is no great trouble when washing them; this is one benefit.
4. Even when worn out through use, there is no need to sew or patch them; they are simply discarded; this is one benefit.
5. When seeking to obtain new ones, they can be easily made; this is one benefit.
6. they are appropriate and suitable for the state of a hermit; this is one benefit.
7. They are not the belongings of enemies or wicked people; this is one benefit.
8. For the user, they do not serve as ornamentation; this is one benefit.
9. They are light to carry and wear; this is one benefit.
10. They lead to fewness of wishes regarding the requisite of robes; this is one benefit.
11. Since bark-fiber robes can be produced simply by pounding and processing the fibers, their production is righteous and blameless; this is one benefit.
12. If a bark-fiber robe is lost or destroyed, there is no lingering attachment or regret; this is one benefit.
These are the twelve. The detailed meaning is found in verse 84 of the Sutaung-khan Pyo.

## Bark-fiber Robes
Bark-fiber robes (vākacīra) are... robes made by stripping the fibers of phrū-chan grass and joining or knotting them together to be worn. (This is stated according to the Atthasālinī Commentary.)
148:
(gi)
However, the master of poetry, Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa, composed in verse 83 of the Sutaung-khan Pyo:
"Joining and sewing smoothly the fibers of phrū-chan grass, twisted and entwined, processed to be soft and wondrous, the edges of the bark-fiber are held and recognized as the inner and outer robes—"
According to this poem, merely stripping and joining the phrū-chan grass fibers is not enough; they must be pounded and processed (te) until they are smooth and soft. Therefore, it is explained that they are called "lyaw-tay" (bark-processed).

In Pali, these bark-fiber robes are called vākacīra, vakkala, or tirīṭaka. Among these:
The robe denoted by the word vākacīra, as explained in the Atthasālinī Commentary, is a robe made from phrū-chan grass. If translated directly into Burmese, it should be "phrū-chan grass robe." However, past famous teachers did not translate it so; they only translated it as "bark-fiber robe" (lyaw-tay thin-gan).

The two names vakkala and tirīṭaka refer to robes made from fibers obtained from tree bark. In the word vakkala, the term vakka means tree bark. Although it says tree bark, one should not take the thick outer bark, but only the thin inner bark (fiber) that covers the wood. It should be understood that they are called bark-fiber robes because these fibers are stripped, sewn together, and then pounded (te) to be soft. Although the term vākacīra means "phrū-chan grass robe," because robes made from tree bark fibers were more common than those made from phrū-chan grass, the term "phrū-chan grass robe" did not become prominent, and only "bark-fiber robe" became well-known. For this reason, in verse 91 of the Sutaung-khan Pyo, it is composed:
"Removing the stench of lay life, wearing tree bark, discarding lay clothes and human scents, washing away human impurities, I have abandoned lay clothing—"
Thus, even the bark-fiber robe is described as being made of tree bark.

## The Wooden Triple-Staff
The wooden triple-staff called tidaṇḍa (or tayo-thuli) is a type of hermit's requisite. It refers to three sticks used for supporting a water pot. (Tedaṇḍiko'ti kuṇḍikaṭṭhapanatthaya tidaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā caranto. — Tika, Tirīṭivacchajātakaṭṭhakathā). Some also say it is a single-legged stand with three branches.
**********
## Water Pot and Shoulder Pole
The water pot called kuṇḍikā is also a type of hermit's requisite. Regarding the Pali term khārikāja, some ancient teachers decided that khāri and kāja have the same meaning, referring to a shoulder pole that carries loads at three points. Other teachers say that khāri refers to a collection of hermit's requisites such as a fire-drill (mī-son), needles, and fans. According to these teachers, khārikāja should be translated as "a shoulder pole on which various hermit's requisites are hung."

According to Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa, the author of Sutaung-khan Pyo, the Pali word khāri should be translated into Burmese as pyā-sit. Since he wanted to show that pyā-sit is a water gourd, he composed it as "pyā-sit water gourd" in verse 66. A water gourd is a vessel for holding and drinking water, similar to modern-day thermoses.
**********
## Ajinacamma = Black Leopard Skin
"The hide of a beast along with its hooves, called ajinacamma," is also a hermit's requisite. Let us examine this further.

Ancient teachers unanimously translated this Pali term ajinacamma as "black leopard skin" (thit-net-yay). Because of this translation, many assume that a leopard whose entire body is black is called "thit-net." In the Magadha Dictionary, verse 611, two words for leopard appear: saddūla and dīpi. The word ajina does not appear as a word for leopard. In the Amarakoṣa Dictionary (Vagga 17, Verse 47), the word ajina appears as a synonym for camma, meaning leather or hide. This statement from the Amarakoṣa should be noted.
150:
(gu)
In the commentaries such as the Aṭṭhasālinī, it is stated: "punnāgapupphasantharasadisaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ," which is translated into Burmese as "the hide of a black antelope with hooves, resembling a bed of Punnāga flowers in color and appearance." In this phrase, the word 'sakhuraṃ' (with hooves) indicates that it is the hide of an animal. Regarding the comparison to a bed of Punnāga flowers, one might wonder whether it refers to the color or the softness. Since it is well-known that Punnāga flowers are not exceptionally soft compared to other flowers, this metaphor should be understood as referring to the color rather than the texture. If the metaphor refers to the color, it is clear that it is not a "black leopard" (thit-net).

However, the Monywe Zetawon Sayadaw stated: "The phrase 'resembling a bed of Punnāga flowers' is not a metaphor for the color of the black antelope hide. It is a metaphor used to compare it with the spotted leopard (thit-pyauk), which is commonly known today, to show that hermits and monks are permitted to use spotted leopard skins."

Because ancient teachers translated the Pali word 'ajina' as 'thit-net' (black leopard), it seems as if there were a species of leopard with a purely black color. In the Magadha Dictionary (Abhidhānappadīpikā), all leopard-like creatures are called 'dīpi' or 'saddūla' without distinguishing their colors. 'Ajina' is a synonym for 'camma' (hide/skin); it is a Pali term for skin. Therefore, in the Janaka Jātaka and Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, it is preached: "ajinamhi hanyate dīpi" (the leopard is killed for its skin). In the Janaka Jātaka Commentary, 'ajina' is also explained using the synonym 'camma' as: "ajinamhīti cammatthāya cammakāraṇā."

In the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, it is also preached: "kese muñcitvāhaṃ tattha, vākacīrañca cammakaṃ," describing how the hermit Sumedha, before making his aspiration and offering himself as a bridge before the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, loosened his hair and spread his bark-garment and hide over the mud. The word 'cammaka' (hide) in this Pali verse refers to the 'ajinacamma' created by the celestial architect Vissakamma.
151:
(gū)
Considering the aforementioned reasons, 'ajinacamma' is not from the feline family (tigers, leopards, or cats which have claws). Based on the attribute 'sakhuraṃ' (with hooves), it is the hide of a hoofed animal like a buffalo, ox, or horse. This hide, in terms of appearance, resembles a bed of Punnāga flowers as shown in the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary. Its texture is extremely soft and delicate. This species of animal is a special creature found only in the Himālaya region or areas near the Himālaya, similar to the Eṇī deer. Because the hide of this creature is beautiful in color, soft, and very difficult to obtain, people treasure it and designate it as an auspicious hide.

When the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha was born, the four Great Kings received him from the hands of the Arahant Brahmas of the Suddhāvāsa realm using this special animal hide (black antelope hide), which is regarded as auspicious in the world and pleasant to the touch. This is stated in the Jātaka Commentary Nidāna and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary as: "brahmānaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno maṅgalasammatāya sukhasamphassāya ajinappaveṇiyā gaṇhiṃsu."

What has been stated above is the critical analysis by the late Aggamahāpaṇḍita U Lin (the original compiler of this Great Buddhavaṃsa), regarding the ancient masters' translation of the Pali 'ajinacamma' as 'thit-net' (black leopard hide).

Among the noble teachers who translated it as 'thit-net', the Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa, in verse 85 of the 'Su-taung-khan Pyo', wrote: "Like large cool blossoms, like Punnāga flowers, adorned with floral spots, most beautiful, with divided claws, without missing a mark, the black leopard hide, a sign of glory, smoothly and perfectly folded, placed upon the left shoulder..." (Here, he did not translate 'sakhuraṃ' as 'with hooves' but as 'with divided claws', directly composing it as a black leopard).

The Great Manle Sayadaw also wrote in the second stanza of the Renunciation Section, Part Five of the Maghadeva Laṅkā:
152:
(ge)
"Lurking in the forest depths, watching the flocks of birds and beasts, when striking for food, if it falls to the right, they eat according to their custom; following the steadfast law of the black leopard's habit, taking it as a witness and a sign, constantly keeping it in heart, to practice and follow that way, precisely with its hooves, beautiful and smooth, that hide, without losing its form, carried upon the shoulder, without failing the Dhamma, firmly undertaking the practice—"

Thus, he composed that just as black leopards eat only the prey that falls to their right and not to their left when they strike, so too hermits and monks resolve to carry the black leopard hide as a vow to use only possessions obtained righteously (like the right side) and not those obtained unrighteously (like the left side).

## Jaṭā, Jaṭāmaṇḍala = Matted Hair and Hair-Coil
Regarding hermits, one should distinguish between 'jaṭā' (matted hair) and 'jaṭāmaṇḍala' (hair-coil). The distinction is as follows: 'Jaṭā' is what naturally exists on the hermit's body. A person who becomes a hermit should tie their hair firmly and compactly so that they do not have to spend time cleaning and combing it. This compact tying of the hair should be understood as 'jaṭā'.

In the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary, among the requisites created by the celestial architect Vissakamma inside the leaf-roofed hut, there is an item called 'jaṭāmaṇḍala' (hair-coil). Therefore, the hair-coil is a separate object created by Vissakamma, not a natural part of the hermit's body. It should be understood that it was not an original part of Sumedha's body. Based on the description that when Sumedha entered the leaf-roofed hut, he placed the hair-coil on his head and inserted an ivory pin (hatthidantasuci) to keep it and his topknot from moving, it is clear that the 'jaṭāmaṇḍala' is distinct from Sumedha's own topknot. This hair-coil that is worn over the topknot is what is called 'htauk-char' in modern times. ('Htauk-char' refers to an accessory used to support and cover the topknot to prevent dust and debris from falling on it.)
153:
(gai)
The Monywe Zetawon Sayadaw, in the first volume of the Samantacakkhudīpanī, first explained that compactly tied hair is called 'jaṭā', and later, citing various reasons, stated that the 'htauk-char' is also called 'jaṭā'. (See Samantacakkhudīpanī, Vol. 1, Question No. 48).

In the 'Su-taung-khan Pyo', it is also composed: "The noble monk is not bald, but with a protruding topknot, tying the jaṭā." This can be interpreted as: the hermit is not bald, but has his hair tied compactly into a topknot. In this sense, it means "compactly tied hair is called jaṭā." (Alternatively) It can be interpreted as: tying the protruding topknot by covering it with a 'jaṭā' from above. In this sense, it means "the object covering the hair (htauk-char) is called jaṭā." In another part of the same poem, it says: "Arranging the head-wrap, wearing the jaṭā, and fixing the topknot-pin." This implies that the object worn over the hair is called 'jaṭā'.

In the poem Catu-dhammasāra (also known as Ko-khan Pyo), it is written: "Smoothly and perfectly, the jaṭā topknot, beautifully all around." According to the author of this poem, Shin Mahā Raṭṭhasāra, the meaning is clearly that "the topknot itself, tied well and beautifully, is called jaṭā."

In the Magadha Dictionary (Abhidhānappadīpikā), verse 257: "tāpasānaṃ tahiṃ jaṭā" shows that the word 'jaṭā' refers to the mass of hair (hair-bundle) of hermits. Furthermore, in verse 948: "veṇvādi śākhājālasmiṃ, laggakese jaṭālaye," it is shown that the word 'jaṭā' has three meanings: a tangled web of branches like a bamboo grove, the tangled hair of hermits, and craving (taṇhā). Thus, according to the Magadha Dictionary, it is evident that "tangled and tied hair is called jaṭā." The Pali word 'jaṭā' is translated into Burmese as 'san-kyit' (matted hair).

In the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary, when listing the requisites created by Vissakamma, there is no mention of creating 'jaṭā'. It only mentions the creation of 'jaṭāmaṇḍala' (hair-coil). Therefore,
154:
(go)
it is clear that 'jaṭā' refers to the hair (or topknot) which is a part of the hermit's own body.

In the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, the Buddha preached regarding the hermit Sumedha loosening his hair before the Buddha Dīpaṅkara: "kese muñcitvāhaṃ tattha." The phrase "loosened the hair" implies that he untied the 'jaṭā' which had been compactly tied.

Furthermore, in the Mātaṅga Jātaka of the Vīsatinipāta Pali, there is the phrase: "jaṭā ca kesā ajinā nivatthā." The commentary explains this as: "jaṭā ca kesāti tāta maṇḍavya tava dakkhiṇeyyasu ekaccānaṃ kesā jaṭā katvāna baddhā. ajinā nivatthāti sakhurāni cammāni nivatthā." (The grammatical connection in the commentary is: 'jaṭā ca kesāti' means matted hair and hair. 'tāta maṇḍavya', O dear Maṇḍavya... 'tava dakkhiṇeyyesu', among those worthy of your offerings... 'ekaccānaṃ kesā', the hair of some persons... 'jaṭā katvā', having made into matted locks... 'baddhā', are tied (knotted)). By saying that the hair itself is compactly bound and knotted, it means that the compactly bound hair is called 'jaṭā'.

Therefore, based on the Pali, Commentaries, and the Magadha Dictionary which state that "compactly tied hair is called jaṭā," one should accept this without doubt.

Moreover, in the Catu-dhammasāra (Ko-khan) Pyo, verse 18:
"To the bird of the Eightfold Path, when it rests in the diverse mind, to trap it, showing the great jaṭā snare, with the requisites of the forest-dwelling hermit closely following..." and so on.

In the Maghadeva Laṅkā Thit, Part Five, Renunciation Section, stanza 2:
"'kesamassuṃ ohāretvā', as the Pali text says, all the noble ones who become hermits, first shave off the hair and beard of their human appearance, and thereafter, whatever grows back, without cutting it at all, they tie it into a jaṭā until the end of their lives."
155:
...they set it... indeed, that matted hair, like a snare set to catch a bird flying in the sky, is kept on the head to catch the bird of the Eightfold Path."

Considering these poems, it is clear that "jaṭā" refers to a hair-knot. These poems show that "jaṭā" is not an ordinary hair-knot, but one tied in a loop like a snare. The meaning in these poems is: just as in the world a snare is set to catch a flying bird (like the Htī-hlaing bird), hermits tie their hair in the form of a snare to catch the bird of the Noble Eightfold Path when it appears in the forest of the mind. Such a hair-knot tied with a loop is called "jaṭā".

## Eight Types of Hermits
The name "Rasay" (hermit) is derived from the Magadha (Pali) word "Isi" and the Sanskrit word "Rishi". It refers to a noble person who seeks and accumulates virtues such as morality (sīla-kkhandha). From the Sanskrit "Rishi", the "Ri" becomes "Ra", and in "shi", the "i" becomes "e" with a low tone, resulting in "thay". Combined, they form the Burmese term "Rasay". Thus, in the New Maghadeva Alaṅkāra, verse 421, it is composed:

"Isi and Rishi are the Pali and Sanskrit terms. According to both languages, among the existing terms, the Pali term is derived from the root 'Is', meaning one who constantly seeks and accumulates special virtues such as the refined and calm morality (sīla-kkhandha). In the Sanskrit name Rishi, 'Ri' is written as 'Ra', and 'i' becomes 'e' with a low tone, forming the new term 'Rasay' used by the people of the Burmese era to refer to virtuous and moral persons."
156:
The name "Rasay" (hermit) does not belong to those within the Buddha's Dispensation; it is a name for those outside the Dispensation. Nevertheless, they should be regarded as noble persons according to their era.

The different types of hermits are described in the Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā, in the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, as being of eight kinds:
1. Saputtabhariya hermit,
2. Uñchācariya hermit,
3. Anaggipakkika hermit,
4. Asāmapāka hermit,
5. Ayamuṭṭhika hermit (also known as Asmamuṭṭhika),
6. Dantavakkalika hermit,
7. Pavattaphalabhojana hermit,
8. Paṇḍupalāsika hermit.

Among these eight:
1. The type of hermit who accumulates wealth and lives with a wife and children is called a Saputtabhariya hermit. (This is like the hermit Keṇiya during the Buddha's time. That hermit Keṇiya, in the market town of Āpaṇa in the Aṅguttarāpa country, gave bribes to the king and built a leaf-hut monastery in a fertile area. Being a businessman, a thousand households lived depending on him. This hermit Keṇiya was from a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla) family and became a hermit only to protect his wealth. During the day, he wore saffron-dyed robes and tied his hair in matted locks, appearing as a true virtuous hermit, but at night, he enjoyed the five cords of sensual pleasure with his wife and children.)

2. The hermit who does not accumulate wealth or take a wife, but approaches donors in the fields during harvest time to receive grain, collects what he gets, and cooks it himself is called an Uñchācariya hermit. (Uñchā = searching for grain in the threshing floors; Cariya = one whose practice is such a livelihood.)
157:
3. Thinking, "It is not proper to wander from one threshing floor to another to receive and collect grain, then pound and cook it to eat," the hermit who receives raw rice in villages and market towns and then cooks and eats it is called an Anaggipakkika hermit. (Anaggipakkika = a hermit who lives on raw rice that has not been cooked with fire.)
(Note: The Uñchācariya hermit goes to the threshing floor to receive unhusked grain and beans. The Anaggipakkika hermit goes from house to house in towns and villages to receive rice that has already been husked.)

4. Thinking, "Being a hermit, it is not at all suitable to cook for oneself," the hermit who enters the village and receives only cooked food to eat is called an Asāmapāka hermit. (Asāmapāka = one who lives by receiving only cooked food without cooking it himself.)

5. Thinking, "It is painful for a hermit to have to go for alms daily," the hermit who peels and eats the bark of edible trees (such as the marking nut tree) using a hammer or stone is called an Ayamuṭṭhika hermit. (The term Asmamuṭṭhika also exists.) (Aya = hard like iron; Muṭṭhika = one who crushes and eats tree bark with a stone the size of a fist.)

6. Thinking, "It is painful to wander about crushing tree bark with a stone," the hermit who no longer carries stones or hammers but bites and peels the bark with his own teeth to eat is called a Dantavakkalika hermit. (Danta = with teeth only; Vakkalika = one who splits and eats tree bark for sustenance.)

7. Thinking, "It is very painful for a hermit to bite and peel with the teeth," the hermit who eats only fruits that fall after being struck with stones or sticks is called a Pavattaphalabhojana hermit. (Pavatta = fallen by being struck with stones or sticks; Phala = fruit only; Bhojana = one who habitually eats.)

8. The hermit who lives by eating only flowers, fruits, and leaves that fall naturally without being struck by stones or sticks is called a Paṇḍupalāsika hermit. (Paṇḍupalāsa = with withered leaves, flowers, and fruits; Ika = one who lives and sustains himself.)
158:
This Paṇḍupalāsika hermit is further divided into three types: (1) If he eats only the leaves, flowers, and fruits that fall within his reach without getting up from his seat, he is an Ukkaṭṭha-paṇḍupalāsika. (2) If he does not move to another tree but eats only the leaves, flowers, and fruits that fall naturally from a single tree, he is a Majjhima-paṇḍupalāsika. (3) If he goes under various trees to search for and eat naturally fallen leaves, flowers, and fruits, he is a Mudū-paṇḍupalāsika.

These are the eight types of hermits mentioned in the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga.

The eight types of hermits mentioned in the commentary on the Hiri Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta are:
1. Saputtabhariya hermit,
2. Uñchācārika hermit,
3. Sampattakālika hermit,
4. Anaggipakkika hermit,
5. Ayamuṭṭhika hermit,
6. Dantalūyyaka hermit,
7. Pavattaphalika hermit,
8. Vaṇumuttika hermit.

Among these:
1. Those like the hermit Keṇiya, who become hermits along with their wives and children and live by plowing fields, trading, etc., are called Saputtabhariya hermits.

2. The hermit who builds a dwelling at the city gate and teaches arts and sciences to the sons of kings and Brahmins, and who does not accept gold or silver but only accepts and uses items suitable for virtuous persons, such as sesame and rice, is called an Uñchācārika hermit.

3. The hermit who accepts and sustains himself with food that arrives exactly at mealtime is called a Sampattakālika hermit.
159:
4. The hermit who sustains himself by eating leaves and fruits that are not cooked with fire is called an Anaggipakkika hermit.

5. The hermit who wanders carrying a hammer, stone, or a billhook, knife, etc., and when hungry, peels and eats the bark of the tree he reaches, then observes the Uposatha and develops the four Brahma-vihāras, is called an Ayamuṭṭhika hermit.

6. The hermit who wanders without carrying a hammer, stone, etc., and when hungry, bites and peels the bark with his teeth from the tree he reaches to eat, then observes the Uposatha and develops the four Brahma-vihāras, is called a Dantalūyyaka hermit.

7. The hermit who lives near a natural pond or a forest, and (if living at a pond) eats lotus stalks and roots from that pond, or (if living in a forest) eats flowers when they are in season or fruits when they are in season (and if there are no flowers or fruits, does not go elsewhere for food but eats even the outer bark of the tree), then observes the Uposatha and develops the four Brahma-vihāras, is called a Pavattaphalika hermit.

8. The hermit who performs good deeds by observing the Uposatha and developing the Brahma-vihāras after eating only the leaves that have fallen to the ground from their stems is called a Vaṇumuttika hermit.

Among these eight types of hermits, the later ones are more noble in practice than the earlier ones.

As stated, among the eight types of hermits mentioned in the Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā and the Sutta Nipāta-aṭṭhakathā, excluding the Saputtabhariya hermits (such as Keṇiya), the remaining seven types are all virtuous persons as they observe the Uposatha and develop the Brahma-vihāras to the best of their ability. Therefore, they are called "Isi" or "Tāpasa". "Isi" means one who seeks virtues, and "Tāpasa" means one who strives in practice.
160:
(ghi)
Among the eight types of hermits mentioned in the Sīlakkhandha Commentary, Sumedha the Hermit was an "Asāmapāka" hermit (one who does not cook) for only one day, and in the following days, he became a "Paṇḍupalāsika" hermit (one who lives on fallen leaves), the eighth type. According to the eight types of hermits in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, he should be classified as the eighth type, a "Vaṇumuttika" hermit.

A hermit is also called (in Pali) "Jaṭila" (one with matted hair) or "Jaṭādhara" (one who wears matted hair). Having or wearing matted hair can be done by anyone, whether virtuous or wicked. Because both virtuous and wicked people can be called Jaṭila or Jaṭādhara, in verse 440 of the Magadha Abhidhāna (Dictionary), these two terms are listed alongside synonyms for "Acelaka" (naked ascetics). The terms "Isi" and "Tāpasa," however, are listed in verse 433 of the Magadha Abhidhāna alongside synonyms for "monks" (bhikkhus).

## Three Types of Renunciants (Shin)

The Pali word "Pabbajjā" was translated by ancient teachers as "Shin-pyu" (making a 'Shin' or renunciant). It means avoiding the life of a layperson wearing white clothes. This renunciation is of three types:

(1) Isi-pabbajjā = Becoming a hermit,
(2) Samaṇa-pabbajjā = Becoming a monk,
(3) Sāmaṇera-pabbajjā = Becoming a novice.
According to these three types of renunciation, the meaning of the word "Pabbajita" (Shin) is divided into three: hermit, monk, and novice.

## Eight Disadvantages of a Leaf-Roofed Hermitage

1. The great effort required to collect and seek out wooden materials for construction.
2. The need for constant maintenance and repair when the grass roof, leaf roof, or mud walls rot, decay, or fall away.
161:
(dhi)
3. Since a monastery belongs to those of high seniority, if another senior person arrives, one must vacate it at any time; thus, concentration (samādhi) cannot be attained.
4. By warding off cold and heat, it leads the dweller to make themselves soft and delicate.
5. One who enters a roofed monastery can commit misdeeds; it is as if the building conceals blameworthy actions.
6. It becomes a cause for attachment through craving (taṇhā), thinking "my monastery."
7. Living in a monastery is like living with a companion (a wife).
8. It involves contact with lice, bedbugs, house lizards, and so on.
These are the eight defects of a leaf-roofed monastery as reflected upon and realized by the Bodhisatta Sumedha. Therefore, in the Su-taung-khan Pyo, verse (95):
Once again, this monastery, sought and acquired with great effort and planning, causing anxiety and exhaustion, was built by combining all the materials... (1).
With old, rotting, and swaying roofs, floorboards and thatch, bamboo strips decaying, the floor unstable, and walls leaning, carrying mud and red earth, burdened time and again, it was extremely exhausting to build... (2).
When noble elders of great seniority and grace, traveling from other lands across borders, happen to arrive at my place at an inconvenient time or late at night, though I must show respect, I find no stability and must arise and move elsewhere... (3).
Though sheltering the body in a good shade, one becomes overly fond of comfort and idleness; not avoiding specific times, one cannot endure the touch of heat, cold, softness, or hardness... (4).
Thinking "no one knows or hears, it is hidden," and failing to contemplate the Dhamma, if one commits impure deeds, it conceals them from the sight of the public, leading to shameless conduct... (5).
162:
(dhu)
Deeply attached to the monastery and its surroundings, thinking "my cell," such intense craving becomes a cause for becoming a hungry ghost (peta), a heavy burden indeed... (6).
When considering all matters, if one builds a hut and lives there for months, it is said that one has a companion (like a wife)... (7).
Furthermore, there are lice, bedbugs, various kinds of rats, spiders, geckos, and house lizards—thousands and tens of thousands of insects living together with the dweller... (8).
Thus it was composed.

## The Ten Virtues of the Foot of a Tree
(1) Having minimal construction is one virtue. (Unlike a leaf-roofed monastery, there is no need for effort in building; it is already available by nature, and one simply enters and takes shelter.)
(2) The absence of the need for cleaning and guarding is one virtue. (Whether the foot of a tree is swept or not, it is easy and comfortable to use.)
(3) The absence of the need to vacate and stand up when senior elders arrive is one virtue.
(4) If one commits a misdeed at the foot of a tree, others will see it; thus, out of fear and shame, it does not act as a concealment for blameworthy actions (unlike a monastery).
(5) The absence of physical stiffness is one virtue. (A person living in the open air without shelter may experience physical stiffness. However, a person living at the foot of a tree does not experience such stiffness.)
(6) The absence of taking possession is one virtue.
(7) Being able to abandon the attachment of "my place" is one virtue.
(8) Unlike in a monastery shared with many, there is no need to evict others by saying, "I will clean this monastery, you all must leave," is one virtue.
163:
(dhū)
(9) Obtaining the delight of the dweller is one virtue.
(10) Since a tree-root dwelling is easily found wherever one goes, the absence of concern or longing for "my place" is one virtue.
These are the ten virtues of the foot of a tree as reflected upon and realized by the Bodhisatta Sumedha. Therefore, in the Su-taung-khan Pyo, verse (98):
The foot of a tree, a pure dwelling for all noble ones (Ariyas), requires little effort in tying or binding with bamboo, thatch, or fiber... (1). When approaching it, it is pleasant; one can choose a desirable spot as one likes. Whether the ground is swept or not, it is rarely unpleasant or dull... (2).
At an inconvenient time, in the dark of night or past midnight, even if a senior arrives, one does not have to vacate the place as one would in a monastery; thus, one is free from the anxiety of checking seniority... (3).
Though it is wide open and lacks privacy, because there is little concealment, one avoids and loathes improper, base, and impure conduct; such behavior is far away... (4).
Between the cold and heat of the open field and the shelter of a monastery building, living here permanently is more capable than others; it is peaceful and the temperature is just right... (5).
Unlike using a very beautiful cell or hut, one is free from the disturbance of taking possession... (6).
Without guarding or attachment, thinking "this is my tree," and without being stingy toward those who might drive one away, the heart remains pure... (7).
Unlike a house shared with companions where one must clean insects and dust, creating a burden within, and repeatedly shouting to move things back and forth, there is no such burden here... (8).
Furthermore, even a celestial mansion provided by Sakka or a fine emerald coverlet cannot surpass the excellence of this. Shimmering with a dark-greenish hue, cool and spacious,
164:
(dhe)
Reaching almost to the sky, when one lives under a young tree, it is peerless. Filled with rapture (pīti) as if drenched in oil, with a joyful heart and a settled mind, one is fully satisfied and greatly delighted... (9).
Trees are abundant upon the earth; thus, one does not greedily or obsessively cling to a specific spot or store possessions there; attachment is minimal... (10).
Thus it was composed.

## 5. The Section on the Declaration
As stated on page (66), when the hermit Sumedha was reflecting, he thought: "What is the use of me crossing [the ocean of Saṃsāra] alone?" This is recorded in the Buddhavamsa Pali as: *Kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena*.
Based on this Pali text, people often say and criticize: "One should not seek only one's own benefit in the world; one who seeks only one's own benefit is an *attahita* person (one who practices only for self-interest). One who seeks only his own benefit is useless in the world."
However, if one looks further in that same Pali text, one will find the specific phrase: *Purisena thāmadassinā*, meaning "by a man who sees his own strength [in wisdom, faith, and effort]." Considering this subsequent specific phrase, criticism should only be directed at those who have the strength and ability to serve the interests of many but choose not to, seeking only their own benefit. If a person has absolutely no strength or ability to serve the interests of many, yet says "I will serve the interests of many" and fails to do so, being untruthful, such a person—not knowing their own limitations—is the one who deserves criticism and reproach.
In truth, if one does not have the strength to serve the interests of many, one must serve one's own interest. Therefore, in the twelfth chapter, the Attavagga of the Dhammapada Pali:
165:
(dhai)
*Attadatthaṃ paratthena, bahunāpi na hāpaye.*
*Attadatthamabhiññāya, sadatthapasuto siyā.*
"One should not neglect one's own welfare for the sake of another's, however great. Having clearly understood one's own welfare, one should be intent on one's own goal."
The meaning of this Dhammapada teaching is that if one cannot serve the interests of others but plans and speaks as if they will, they will fail to serve both others' interests and their own, resulting in a loss on both sides. Therefore, it is taught that one who lacks the ability to serve others should clearly understand and realize their own welfare and strive for it. According to this method, a person who knows their own limitations and strives only for their own welfare should not be criticized as a mere *attahita* person; rather, it should be said that they are doing what they can and are a good person. Criticism as a mere *attahita* person is only deserved by someone like the hermit Sumedha, who has the power and ability to serve the interests of many but chooses to serve only their own.
In summary, it means: serve the interests of many only if you are truly capable of doing so; if you are not, serve your own interests without neglect. One who merely pretends to serve the interests of many while actually seeking only their own benefit is a wicked and deceitful person.

The letter 'l' is changed to 'r', and a nasal sound (niggahīta) appears in the first syllable; that niggahīta is changed to 'ñ' and joined with 'j', resulting in the Pali word *Nerañjarā*. (Just as the names Sāvatthī

and Vesālī are used according to their original Pali forms, the original Pali form Nerañjarā should also be called "Nerañjarā River" in Burmese usage.)
Alternatively, it comes from the root *Nīla-jala*. *Nīla* = blue-green; *jala* = water. Blue-green water refers to clear water. Even nowadays, people say of very clear water, "The water is so clear it looks blue-green." It means a river with blue-green, pure, and clear water.
In the Abhidhāna-ṭīkā written by the minister Caturangabala during the prosperity of Pinya city, in addition to the aforementioned meanings, it states: "Nerañjarā is the name of a type of musical instrument.
