## Notes Regarding the Declaration (Vyākaraṇa)
The word *Vyāditta* (Declaration/Prophecy) is widely considered to be derived from Pali. During the reign of King Alaungmintaya, the wise poet U Aw, who held the title Cintakyawthu, wrote in the conclusion of his *Kavi-lakkhaṇa* orthography: "Regarding the word *Vyāditta*, the old orthography spelled it with a final 'p' as *Vyādhip*. However, most scholars spell it only with a final 't' as *Vyāditta*. Furthermore, in grammar, there are forms like *Vyāditta* and *Vyākata*. Therefore, only the final 't' spelling should be accepted."
167:
(Ghaw)
According to this writing, just as the Burmese word 'kaw-zaw' (carpet) originated from the Pali word 'kojava', the Burmese word 'byadeik' (prophecy) originated from the Pali word 'byādita'.

In the scriptures, the special words spoken by the Buddha are customarily referred to as 'byākaraṇa' or 'byākata'; (the term 'byādita' is not customarily used). When referring to a person who has received a prophecy, the scriptures use the term 'laddhabyākaraṇa'. Former teachers have translated this Pali term into Burmese as 'one who has obtained a prophecy' or 'one who has received a prophecy'. Therefore, the Burmese word 'byadeik' currently in common use is not Pali; it is a word used by ancient scholars in their Burmese translations, following the Pali terms 'byākaraṇa' and 'byākata' as closely as possible in sound.

To give an example... among the world-trees (trees at the head of the islands), the tree that grows at the head of the Eastern Island is indeed a world-tree, yet it is not called 'kapparukkha' in Pali. Because it is a well-known and widely recognized tree called 'siriṣa' in Pali, and it is the 'kokko' tree in Burmese, it is only referred to as 'siriṣarukkha' in Pali. In Burmese translations, it is also translated simply as 'kokko tree'.

Similarly, the tree that grows at the head of the Southern Island is also a world-tree, but it is not called 'kapparukkha' in Pali. Because it is a well-known and widely recognized tree called 'jambu' in Pali, which is the 'thabye' (rose-apple) tree in Burmese, it is referred to as 'jamburukkha' in Pali and 'thabye tree' in Burmese. In this regard, the tree at the head of the Southern Island is not called merely 'thabye tree', but is referred to as 'jambu-thabye', and people regard it not as an ordinary thabye tree, but as a wondrous one. In truth, it is not a different species of thabye; it is called 'jambu-thabye' by combining the Pali name 'jambu' and the Burmese name 'thabye'. (This is similar to the usage 'Buddha-Phayar'.)

Even though the tree that grows at the head of the Western Island is also a world-tree, it is not called 'kapparukkha' in Pali. Because it is a well-known and widely recognized tree called 'kadamba' in Pali, which is the 'htein' tree in Burmese, it is referred to as 'kadamba' in Pali and 'htein tree' in Burmese.
168:
(Ghaṃ)
As for the tree that grows at the head of the Northern Island... this species of tree does not exist in any other land. While all other trees bear only one type of flower or fruit according to their respective 'bījaniyāma' (biological laws), this tree at the head of the Northern Island is a tree that yields whatever those who desire it wish for. Therefore, because it is impossible to give it a specific name based on a single etymological reason, it was named simply 'kapparukkha' (the world-tree/wish-fulfilling tree).

Ancient scholars created a distinct Burmese vocabulary for this Pali term 'kapparukkha' and translated it as 'padesā-bin'. It might be thought that this word 'padesā' is Pali. In reality, it is not Pali. The Pali word 'padesa' denotes two meanings: (1) a measure of length equal to a span of the forefinger, and (2) a partial region or place. The nature of the tree at the head of the Northern Island is not connected to a span of the forefinger, nor is it a partial region. The special quality of this tree is simply the ability to obtain desired material objects. Therefore, the word 'padesā' is not Pali; it should be considered merely a Burmese word designated as a vocabulary term by ancient scholars.

In one sense, this word 'padesā' and the word 'byadeik' are similar in that they appear to be Pali despite not being so. Thus, the word 'byadeik' is not a word directly descended from the Pali 'byādita', but is related only to the Pali 'byākaraṇa'. Therefore, it is necessary to examine and understand the meaning of the original Pali word 'byākaraṇa'.

Upon examination, the term 'byākaraṇa' is a Pali word formed by combining 'vi', 'ā', and 'karaṇa'. ('vi' = special, 'ā' = distinctly/separately, and 'karaṇa' = declaring/speaking). In this context, the special and distinct declaration made by the Blessed One is called 'byākaraṇa'. It means the special and distinct declaration such as, 'This hermit Sumedha will become a Buddha at such a time'. Ancient Burmese scholars translated this very declaration as 'giving a prophecy' (byadeik-kyar-khring).
169:
(Ghā)
This term 'byākaraṇa' is a noun, and in its verbal form, it is used in the Pali Canon and other texts as 'byākāsi', which Burmese scholars have translated as 'He gave a prophecy'. The meaning is that He made a special and distinct declaration.

This term 'byākaraṇa' does not only denote the special and distinct prophetic words of the Blessed One; it also refers to secular grammatical treatises such as Pāṇini. In the context of questions and answers, the word 'byākaraṇa' denotes 'answering', as in 'ekaṃsabyākaraṇa' (answering categorically). Furthermore, 'veyyākaraṇa', which is one of the nine components (aṅgas) into which the Buddha's teachings are divided, is also this same word 'byākaraṇa'. The 'veyyākaraṇa' component within the ninefold teaching consists of the collection of Dhamma taught distinctly in pure prose (cuṇṇiya) without being mixed with verses (gāthā). The point is that the word 'byākaraṇa' denotes the meaning of giving a prophecy, the meaning of secular grammatical treatises, the meaning of answering, and the meaning of a component of the Dhamma taught in pure Pali prose (such as the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) without verses.

In the times of ancient kings, the people exalted the king almost to the level of the Buddha, and when acknowledging what the king said, they would say, 'According to the noble prophecy (byadeik), my Lord', thus using the term 'byadeik' to refer to the king's commands.

After considering and examining all these aforementioned points, one should understand without doubt that the word 'byadeik' used in relation to the Buddha originated from the Pali 'byākaraṇa'. It refers to the special and distinct declaration, which is as unerring as a strike upon the earth, made by a certain Buddha concerning a certain Bodhisatta, an aspirant for Paccekabuddhahood, or an aspirant for discipleship, stating that 'In such an aeon, you will become a Buddha (or Paccekabuddha, etc.) by such a name'.

Regarding the statement on page 73:

In the Pali text 'dakkhiṇaṃ pādamuddhari', which describes the Buddha stepping forth with His right foot from the side of the hermit Sumedha... some have the opinion that, in the world, if women who are standing still are asked to step forward, they customarily start with the left foot. This interpretation seems too simple and superficial for the wise to favor. In truth, the custom is that if one wishes to avoid and show respect to an object of importance and reverence, one must go by keeping that object on one's right side. Since the hermit Sumedha was a person of importance, it should be understood that the Dipankara Buddha, out of regard for him, kept the hermit Sumedha on His right and stepped forth by lifting His right foot.

To make it clear... if the hermit Sumedha were lying prostrate from east to west with his head to the east, and if the Buddha, coming from the head (the east), had avoided him by passing on the hermit Sumedha's northern side, He would have been passing with the hermit Sumedha on His left. To prevent this, He avoided him by passing on the hermit Sumedha's southern side (from the south). This is the meaning.

As stated in the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, it is only mentioned that the Dipankara Buddha, after giving the prophecy to the hermit Sumedha, departed keeping him on His right. In the Jātaka Commentary and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, it is specifically explained that He departed after honoring him with eight handfuls of flowers (aṭṭhahi pupphamuṭṭhīhi pūjetvā).

In this matter, some ask, 'Is it appropriate for the noble personage Dipankara, who was already a true Buddha, to honor the hermit Sumedha, who was merely an aspirant (Bodhisatta), with eight handfuls of flowers?' To that question, some answer, 'The Dipankara Buddha did not honor the hermit Sumedha with him as the target;
171:
(Ngā)
He did not honor him personally, but honored only the Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) that he would obtain when he became the Gotama Buddha in the future. Therefore, it is appropriate'.

Some are satisfied with this answer, while others are not. The reason for dissatisfaction is the view that it is not a sound reason for a noble personage who currently possesses Omniscient Wisdom to honor an Omniscient Wisdom that will only arise in the future.

Both sides of this question and answer take the meaning of the word 'pūjā' (honor/worship) to be the same as the 'pūjā' in the phrase where humans and devas 'worship' (pūjā) the Buddha. In the context of humans and devas worshipping the Buddha, the meaning of the word 'pūjā' is 'I worship with great reverence and salutation'. The word 'pūjā' in the context of the Dipankara Buddha honoring the hermit Sumedha with eight handfuls of flowers and the word 'pūjā' in the context of humans and devas worshipping the Buddha cannot have the same meaning. If one considers carefully... the Burmese word 'pū-zaw' (honor/worship) originated from the Pali word 'pūjā'. In the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, 'pūjā' is explained as 'pūjāti sakkāra mānana vandanā', meaning that 'pūjā' refers to performing well (sakkāra), honoring (mānana), and saluting (vandanā). Therefore, the meaning of the Burmese word 'pū-zaw' must also be performing well, honoring, and saluting.

Thus, regarding the statement 'The Dipankara Buddha honored (pū-zaw) the hermit Sumedha with eight handfuls of flowers', the 'pūjā' therein can be translated as 'He treated him well with eight handfuls of flowers' or 'He honored him with eight handfuls of flowers'; it cannot be translated as 'saluting' (vandanā).

In summary... the worship of the Triple Gem by humans and devas and the honoring of the hermit Sumedha by the Dipankara Buddha do not have the same meaning; they are distinct. In the worship by humans and devas, it means revering and saluting as the highest state. In the case of the Dipankara Buddha honoring the hermit Sumedha, it means performing well (treating well).
172:
It means showing great respect. Therefore, it should be answered that there is no contradiction. At the beginning of the commentary known as the Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī, it is stated: 'I pay homage to the Dhamma which was worshipped by the Buddha.' In the sub-commentary named Maṇisāramañjūsā, it is explained that the Buddha's worship of the Dhamma consists of proper reflection, practice, cultivation in the mind, repeated attention, careful consideration, respectfully preaching the Dhamma to those to be tamed, and praising the Dhamma, etc.; it is not the offering of material things.

On page 77:
One should note the words of praise from the devas and brahmas, taking the conjunction of the moon with the Visākhā constellation as a sign. The time when the moon is in conjunction with Visākhā is the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha). Just as the Bodhisattas of the past received their prophecies on the full moon day of Kason, the day the Hermit Sumedha received his prophecy was also the full moon day of Kason; thus, they declared that he would certainly become a Buddha.

The reason devas and brahmas spoke of Kason as a special occasion is that Kason is the first and most distinct month of the year. (One might ask: Is not Tagu the first month of the year? Tagu can never be the first month of the year for its entire duration in any year; the first part belongs to the old year, and only the latter part enters the new year. Sometimes the entire month falls within the old year. Therefore, it cannot be the first month of the year. Kason, however, is the first month that should be the beginning for the entire month in any year; only occasionally do four or five days fall into the old year, and mostly the entire month belongs to the new year, making it the special first month of the year.)

In the world, being the first in anything is a special point. The first building of a house (house-warming), the first establishment of a factory (opening ceremony), the first establishment of a department store (opening ceremony)—thus, giving importance and value to the first beginning is a type of worldly auspicious custom (maṅgala).
173:
The act of receiving a prophecy is also a very extraordinary matter, and according to worldly auspicious customs, it pertains only to a special day. Therefore, because the prophecy was received on the full moon day of Kason, the devas and brahmas declared that he would certainly become a Buddha.

The full moon day of Kason is not only the day of receiving the prophecy; it is also the day when the Great Bodhisattas in their final existence (pacchimabhavika) are born, the day they attain Buddhahood, and the day they enter Parinibbāna. The reason these noble events occur only on the full moon day of Kason is, as previously shown, due to the special nature of Kason as the first month of the new year.

Not only in Buddhahood but also in worldly affairs, ancient kings usually had the custom of being consecrated (abhiseka) in the month of Kason. Therefore, in the Consecration Chapter of the New Maghadeva Laṅkā, it is composed: 'Great poets and wise men, in accordance with royal records and balanced wisdom, without exceeding, as the new year turns and Tagu ends, in the month of Kason, the consecration festivals were traditionally held, marking the time by custom.'

According to this method, the festival of pouring water on the Bodhi tree is also held only in Kason, the first month. The reason is... as previously shown, at the beginning of things, followers of any religion pray and seek blessings by cherishing what they rely on. Thus, at the beginning of the year, to ensure peace and freedom from danger throughout the coming year, in ancient times (before the Buddha appeared), people used to pour water on Banyan trees and pray for blessings.

In the world, when the Buddha had not yet appeared, people worshipped various things as they saw fit, mostly worshipping tree deities (rukkha-deva) who were close to humans. Among the various trees that were the dwellings of tree deities, they gave special importance to the Banyan tree, and when praying for blessings, they usually did so at the Banyan tree. To make this reason clear, as an example (sādhaka)...
174:
Shortly before the Buddha appeared, Sujātā, the daughter of a wealthy man from Senānigama in the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, went to a large Banyan tree in her youth and prayed: 'When I reach the proper age, may I be united with a man of equal status and give birth to a firstborn son; if you assist me, I will hold a grand worship ceremony costing one hundred thousand every year.'

As she prayed, when her firstborn son (Yasa) was born, she held a grand worship ceremony every year on the full moon day of Kason. On the full moon day of Kason in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj), while the Bodhisatta was staying at the foot of that Banyan tree, Sujātā came and offered the most excellent milk-rice (ghana-pāyāsa), as clearly explained in the Nidāna of the Jātaka Commentary.

In this Jātaka Commentary, although it is not stated which day she first prayed or the days she held the annual worship, since it is clearly explained that the final day of worship when she met the Bodhisatta was the full moon day of Kason, it can be inferred that the day of the prayer and the annual worship days were also the full moon day of Kason.

In the scriptures, it only mentions Sujātā offering milk-rice. It does not mention pouring water. Therefore, it might be said that the story of Sujātā should not be evidence for water pouring. While Sujātā certainly would have cleaned the ground and poured water at that large Banyan tree, it should be understood that the commentator only explained the important and prominent act of offering milk-rice, and did not explain the water pouring as it was not the primary act.

In the Dummedha Jātaka, the 50th Jātaka of the Ekanipāta, water pouring is directly mentioned. The summary of this Dummedha Jātaka is...

In the past, when King Brahmadatta ruled in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the son of that king, also named Brahmadatta. While he was living as the Crown Prince...
175:
The citizens, placing great trust in deities, performed worship by killing goats, chickens, pigs, etc., and offering their blood and flesh, as well as flowers and perfumes.

The Bodhisatta Crown Prince thought, 'When I become king, I will bring an end to these evil deeds (without harming or oppressing anyone).' Seeing many people holding a worship festival at a large Banyan tree, he entered the Banyan tree, offered flowers and perfumes (like the others), poured water, circumambulated the Banyan tree to the right, and returned.

In this way, he went to that Banyan tree from time to time and performed worship like one who truly trusted the deity. Later, when his father passed away and he became king, he gathered all the ministers and said, 'O ministers... did you not see me go to the large Banyan tree and perform worship by pouring water when I was Crown Prince? At that time, I promised: "If I successfully inherit my father's position, I will worship the deity with the blood and flesh of a thousand fools." Now, I wish to worship the Banyan tree deity with the blood and flesh of fools. From today, you must investigate, list, and bring the fools within the kingdom.'

This is the Jātaka story which teaches how the country became peaceful and good, such that there was no one who dared to commit acts like killing.

In this Jātaka, it is directly mentioned that the Bodhisatta himself (using a stratagem like the others) poured water. According to what has been shown... the story of Sujātā shows that the day and month of worshipping the Banyan tree was the full moon day of Kason, and the Dummedha Jātaka shows the act of pouring water.

When these two accounts are combined, it becomes clear that before the Buddha appeared, people in the world approached the Banyan tree deities whom they relied on and worshipped...
176:
...and held worship festivals by pouring water on the Banyan tree on the full moon day of Kason, the beginning of the year.

Later, when the Buddha appeared, they no longer worshipped the Banyan tree deity but worshipped only the Buddha. However, because water was poured at the Banyan tree before the Buddha appeared, the term 'Nyaung-ye' (Banyan water) did not change, and the water offered to the Buddha is also called 'Nyaung-ye'.

To give a clear example... in the front room of every Buddhist household, they build a shelf as they are able, and on that shelf, they place three pots filled with water and suitable flowers. Everyone consistently calls that shelf 'Nyaung-ye-o-zin' (Banyan water pot stand), those pots 'Nyaung-ye-o' (Banyan water pots), the flowers 'Nyaung-ye-o-pan' (Banyan water pot flowers), and the water in the pots 'Nyaung-ye' (Banyan water).

Would there be an intention to go and pour water on a Banyan tree with the water from the Nyaung-ye pots kept in the front of one's house? In truth, there is no intention to go and pour it on a Banyan tree; the intention is only to worship and offer to the Triple Gem (Ratanattaya). These types of pots and flowers do not get the names Nyaung-ye-o and Nyaung-ye-pan only when flowers are placed in them in the front of the house; even while they are piled up and sold in the market, they are called Nyaung-ye-o and Nyaung-ye-o-pan. As shown at the end, they are simply pots and flowers for worshipping and offering to the Triple Gem.

Thus, although it is said that from the time the Buddha appeared, all Buddhist devotees clearly and widely practiced the act of offering water to the Triple Gem and calling it Nyaung-ye while praying for blessings, the custom of pouring water and praying for blessings with the intention of worshipping the great Banyan tree deities according to the tradition before the Buddha appeared was so strongly ingrained that even now, when people see large Banyan trees, they give them more attention than other trees, and the custom of offering flowers and lighting lamps at large Banyan trees remains prominent. Those who do so...
177:
(Nge)
They do not intend the Bodhi tree where the Buddha attained enlightenment, but only recognize it as the banyan tree where the great tree-deity (Rukkha-deva) resides. They are merely followers of the ancient tradition from before the Buddha's enlightenment (without much scrutiny).

## Various Views on the Month of Kason and the Water-Pouring Ceremony

(a) The water-pouring ceremony (Nyaung-yay) refers to the pouring of water on the Bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa). The reason for pouring water specifically in the month of Kason is... the word Kason is derived from the Pali word (Kasinna). (Ka = water, sinna = severed/depleted); Kasinna means the month when water is depleted in the earth element. The author of the *Vohāralīnattha Dīpanī* explains that in the month of Kason (derived from the Pali Kasinna), it is far from the previous year's rain and the coming year's rain has not yet fallen, making it the month when water is most depleted in the earth; thus, water must be poured to prevent the Bodhi tree from dying.

(The Pali word Kasinna meaning the month of Kason is not found in the Piṭaka scriptures; furthermore, scholars might criticize this by asking whether the Bodhi tree is only given strength when it is extremely weak, rather than pouring water in the months of Tabaung and Tagu when water is also somewhat scarce.)

(b) Some scholars also say that the water-pouring ceremony originated based on the Ānanda Bodhi tree (planted by the Venerable Ānanda within the Jetavana Monastery), as mentioned in the introduction to the *Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka*, the sixth Jātaka of the Terasa Nipāta.

(In that *Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka* Commentary, regarding the Bodhi tree managed by the Venerable Ānanda, it is specifically mentioned that scented water was placed in eighteen gold and silver pots (according to Burmese versions) or one hundred and eight pots (according to Sri Lankan versions), and various flowers like blue lotuses were planted and arranged around the banyan tree for worship; there is no specific mention of 'pouring water'. However, water would certainly have been poured on that Bodhi tree. Nevertheless, the arrangement and worship with scented flower pots, the surrounding with railings made of the seven kinds of gems, and the spreading of white sand mixed with gold,
178:
(Ngo)
the construction of walls, and the building of gateways adorned with the seven kinds of gems were the more extraordinary matters, and thus the commentator specifically explained those matters. If the specific practice of pouring water had become prominent from that time, the commentator would have explained it specifically; however, it was not explained. Therefore, it is difficult to say that the water-pouring festival began based on the Ānanda Bodhi, which does not directly show the pouring of water.)

(c) Other scholars say that the Full Moon Day of Kason is a great and noble day because, as previously mentioned, it is the day the Bodhisattas received the prophecy, the day of birth in the final life to become a Buddha, the day of attaining Enlightenment, and the day of entering Parinibbāna; therefore, the merit of pouring water on the Bodhi tree is performed on the Full Moon Day of Kason.

(The practice of pouring water on the banyan tree existed even before the Buddha appeared, as mentioned earlier. It should be noted that after the Buddha appeared, the practice changed from worshipping deities to Buddhist followers pouring water on the Bodhi tree in worship of the Buddha, focusing on the aforementioned great and noble days.)

## Notable Points Regarding Omens (Nimitta)

The term 'Nimeit' is a Burmese word derived from the Pali 'Nimitta'. The word 'Nimitta' denotes the cause for knowing (the cause for the arising of knowledge) that either a good result or a bad result will occur. The word 'Nimitta' by itself can denote both a good cause (good omen) and a bad cause (bad omen); when referring to a bad cause or omen, it is usually used in combination with the prefix 'du' as 'dunnimitta'. In this chapter on the Prophecy, however, only good causes are taught as 'Nimitta'.

Regarding the factors related to causes recognized by worldly people, they say there are five types: Teit, Nimeit, Tabaung, Sanni, and Ba-waw. The distinctions between these five are also noted as follows:

Visible signs are 'Nimeit', a gift is 'Teit', and a sound is 'Tabaung'. It is said that if one sees something good upon waking up and opening one's eyes in the morning, that day is a day of good 'Nimeit'; if one sees something bad, that day is a day of bad 'Nimeit'. Thus, what is seen with the eyes is called 'Nimeit'.
182:
(Ca)
The word 'Teit' is also called 'Atate'. (Although it is called Atate, it is not the 'Atate' that refers to the past time.) It is merely a word for a gift. A gift sent by friends to oneself is called 'Teit' (or 'Atate'). If that gift is an item one likes, it is said that the 'Teit' is good (the 'Atate' is good); if it is an item one does not like, it is commonly said that the 'Teit' is not good (the 'Atate' is not good).

'Tabaung' is the sound that is heard. It is said that the sounds sung or shouted from the mouths of performers, madmen, or children, which are heard without intentionally listening, are called 'Tabaung'.

A sound that is known only by intentionally lurking and listening is called 'Sanni'. Therefore, if one wishes to know whether something is good or bad, one should 'listen for Sanni' by lurking and listening secretly.

(In the *Maghadeva Laṅkā Thit*, it is composed: "Take Sanni from the south and Tabaung from the north; such is the traditional saying." The meaning is... although Sanni and Tabaung are both sounds, a sound heard from the south of one's residence is Sanni, and a sound heard from the north is Tabaung.)

Matters spoken by deities through possession are called 'Ba-waw'. Therefore, in the *Maghadeva Laṅkā Thit*, it is composed: "The omens of the country, Atate, and Ba-waw, which the deities speak and bring."

These various names have existed since around the time of Shin Mahā Sīlavaṃsa in the 800s of the Burmese Era. Shin Mahā Sīlavaṃsa, however, wished to show that since only 'Nimitta' is taught in the Pali scriptures, there is no need to distinguish between Teit, Nimeit, Tabaung, Sanni, and Ba-waw. For the Nimitta mentioned in the Pali, he composed: "This earth also, with great respect, resounds with a deep sound and remains upright; such a Sanni, a wonder of the city, we have seen," and also: "With greed and passion diminished, and with anger, ignorance, and pride not healthy, the water recedes. These strange and extraordinary Tabaung, we now note in the city, some..."
183:
...I cannot bear to forget)," thus the signs are composed and written under the names of 'Sane' (prophetic signs) and 'Tabaung' (omens) in verses (30) and (32) of the Pāramī-khaṇḍa-pyo.

## Points to Note Regarding the Appearance of Omens

In saying that "the 32 great omens appeared," it should be noted that some omens appeared simultaneously and in competition with one another, while other great omens, being contradictory in nature, did not appear simultaneously but appeared in turns.

For example, it is said that land flowers and water flowers bloomed at the same time, and fruit trees bore fruit at the same time. In this case, flowers and fruits are not contradictory in nature and are distinct physical entities; therefore, they can appear simultaneously and in competition.

In the case where it is said that the ten thousand world systems became silent and musical instruments played by themselves, silence and the sounding of music are contradictory in nature and do not have separate physical forms (unlike flowers and fruits). Thus, they cannot exist together at the exact same moment. It should be understood that during the moment the sound was silent, it was so quiet that gods and humans could clearly perceive it, and when the instruments played, they played so that gods and humans could clearly hear them.

Similarly, regarding the stopping of normally flowing river waters and the whirlpools turning in the ocean, these cannot occur simultaneously. While the river water is stopped, whirlpools would not be able to turn in the ocean (where they do not normally turn). In truth, coinciding with the occasion of the Prophecy, the river water showed a sign by ceasing to flow, which was an unprecedented and extraordinary wonder. While this sign was being shown, even the surface of the ocean would remain as calm as the river water, without even a wave, let alone a whirlpool. When it was the ocean's turn to show a sign, it would show it by turning in whirlpools, and at that time, the river water would flow as usual without stopping.

I shall now extract and present the verses (29, 30, 31, 32, 33) from the Pāramī-khaṇḍa-pyo concerning these 32 great omens for easy understanding...

27. And celestial fragrances wafted from the windward side, as if the air were filled with fine powder.

28. All beings, from the Brahma realm down to the lowest, could see each other clearly as they were, leaving only the four formless realms empty.

29. The various hells in the lower regions were not hidden or submerged but were clearly visible, both large and small, as if being pointed out.

30. Doors and mountain ranges did not stand in the way; fences and walls seemed to show compassion and did not block the view, leaving everything open and without boundaries.

31. No one passed away with the death-consciousness (cuti-citta),

32. Nor did any new being undergo rebirth or enter a womb.

All these events occurred exactly as described during the time of the Lord, and we encounter them now; the traditional accounts remain intact.

## The Anu-dīpanī on the Section of the Prophecy is finished.
187:
## 6. Pāramī-khaṇḍa
## (A) Dāna Pāramī

Regarding this Perfection of Generosity (Dāna Pāramī):

In the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi, it is clearly stated that the great Bodhisattas of the past fulfilled the Perfection of Generosity first. The hermit Sumedha, the Bodhisatta, admonished himself, saying, "O Sumedha, you too should fulfill the Perfection of Generosity first..." Thus, it is well-known and evident that among the ten Perfections, the Perfection of Generosity is the one to be fulfilled first and is of special importance.

However—

In the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi, the Buddha preached: "Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sappañño..." meaning, "A wise man, established in rebirth with the three noble roots, being mature and possessed of keen effort, if he establishes himself in virtue (sīla) and develops concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), he can untangle the tangle of craving." In this teaching, there is not even a hint of Dāna (generosity); only the three factors of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom are included.

Not only that, in the great Visuddhimagga treatise (which consists of over 600 pages) that elaborates on the meaning of this single verse from the Saṃyutta Pāḷi, there is no mention of Dāna. Furthermore, among the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path that lead to Nibbāna, only those related to Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom are included. There is no path factor related to Dāna. Consequently, some have come to believe and say that "Dāna is not a teaching desired by the Buddha, nor is it a teaching that leads to Nibbāna; it is only a teaching that expands the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra)," and thus "Dāna should not be practiced."

The famous Yaw Mingyi U Hlaing, in his treatise Vimuttirasa, wrote: "Dāna was preached by the Buddha only for ordinary people (the unlearned), such as the son of the wealthy man Sigāla."

There are many devout Buddhists who cannot accept and are deeply disturbed by such statements that "Dāna should not be practiced" and Yaw Mingyi's writing that "Dāna was preached by the Buddha only for ordinary people."
188:
There is no benefit in being displeased or disturbed by these statements and writings. In fact, it is very important to understand the correct meaning according to the Buddha's intention, as it truly is (yathābhūta), which will be beneficial. The correct meaning to be understood is as follows:

The aforementioned great Saṃyutta Pāḷi was preached by the Buddha for those noble individuals (ājānī) who had the capacity to strive and become Arahats, exhausting all defilements within this very life without being reborn again. If a person truly has the potential to become an Arahat in this life, and if they indeed become an Arahat according to that potential, there is no longer a need to establish a new future life. Dāna is a Dhamma that can bring about new lives and new wealth. For a person who is to end the affairs of saṃsāra in this very life, there is no future new life; therefore, even if they perform Dāna, there is no new life for that Dāna to yield its results, making Dāna redundant. For this reason, in the aforementioned great Saṃyutta Pāḷi, the Buddha emphasized only the three trainings of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom, which can exhaust defilements in this very life, as they are more important than Dāna for those noble individuals. It is by no means because Dāna should not be practiced that the Buddha did not mention it.

Dāna is a Dhamma that softens the heart. A person who performs any act of charity has their heart softened for the undertaking of virtue, the development of concentration, and the development of wisdom, due to the support and sufficing condition (upanissaya) provided by that Dāna. It is a personal experience of every devout Buddhist with faith that when going to a monastery or pagoda without any offering, one's heart is not softened and feels awkward, hesitant, and conflicted about undertaking the precepts, listening to the Dhamma, or practicing meditation. That is why, during the time of the Buddha, noble disciples like Visākhā and others, when going to the monastery, always took offerings such as food in the morning and drinks or medicinal items like catumadhu (the four sweets) in the evening.

If one is not a person who will exhaust defilements and become an Arahat in this very life, one must inevitably travel through saṃsāra to a greater or lesser extent. Without Dāna, the journey of saṃsāra...
189:
If one must travel [in saṃsāra], it is difficult to attain a good destination (sugati) because of the lack of generosity (dāna). Even if one attains it, it is difficult to be endowed with necessary requisites. At that time, even if one wishes to seek wholesome states (kusala dhamma), one will not be able to do so. (One might argue that they will seek only the merits of the three trainings—virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—without dāna. However, such a point can only be spoken of; in reality, it is not possible to practice. Indeed, only when supported by the benefit of dāna can the successful practice of virtue, concentration, and wisdom arise.) Therefore, for those who have not yet ceased their journey in saṃsāra, it is extremely important to make a special effort in dāna. Only when one possesses the provisions of dāna (dāna-rikkhā) will one reach a good destination in saṃsāra, be endowed with necessary requisites in that life, and be able to strive for the wholesome deeds one wishes to practice.

Among the travelers of saṃsāra, the Great Bodhisattas are the greatest travelers. After receiving the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa), the Bodhisattas must wander and strive in saṃsāra for a minimum of four asaṅkheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas)—a duration incalculable by billions of years—to fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) to attain Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Aspiring Paccekabuddhas must fulfill perfections for two asaṅkheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons; Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka) for one asaṅkheyya and a hundred thousand aeons; and Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) for a hundred thousand aeons. Since these Great Bodhisattas are the greatest travelers of saṃsāra, the perfection of generosity (dāna pāramī) is of utmost importance. Accordingly, in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi, it is taught that dāna pāramī must be firmly undertaken and fulfilled first.

Therefore, based on the teachings in the Saṃyutta Pāḷi intended for those great individuals who will become Arahants in this very life, it is not appropriate for those whose perfections are not yet complete to say, "Generosity is redundant."

Some also have the habit of asking:
"Can one reach Nibbāna with dāna alone?" If it is said "alone," then one cannot reach Nibbāna with dāna, nor with sīla, nor with bhāvanā (mental development).
190:
This must be the answer. For the reason that... when one says "dāna alone," it implies that sīla and bhāvanā are excluded; similarly, if one says "bhāvanā alone," it implies that dāna and sīla are excluded. Without sīla, one is merely a mass of vice, an embodiment of evil practicing misconduct. No matter how much such a mass of vice develops bhāvanā, just as a very good seed placed on a red-hot iron ball cannot sprout and turns to ash in an instant, the bhāvanā developed by a mass of vice does not become true bhāvanā; its nature will be destroyed immediately. Therefore, it should be understood that applying the word "alone" to dāna and asking such a question is inappropriate.

In this section on dāna pāramī in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi, it is clearly taught that one should give to recipients regardless of whether they are of low, middle, or high status. Considering this teaching, it should be understood that one should not select recipients when giving; there is no need to choose.

However, in the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi, the Buddha taught the classification of recipients into seven types of communal offerings (saṅghika dāna) and fourteen types of individual offerings (puggalika dāna). Among the fourteen individual offerings, He taught that the benefits increase as one ascends from the lowest, which is an animal, and finally, He taught the great fruitfulness of communal offerings (saṅghika dāna).

Also, in the Aṅkurapeta-vatthu Pāḷi, when the Buddha was residing on the Paṇḍukambalā stone throne to teach the Abhidhamma in Tāvatiṃsa, the devas Indaka and Aṅkura came to pay their respects. Whenever devas of great power arrived, the deva Aṅkura had to vacate his place and move back further and further, eventually having to attend from a distance of ten yojanas from the Buddha.

As for the deva Indaka, he did not have to move from his original place where he first arrived; he could remain where he was. The reason for this was that although the deva Aṅkura was a great donor who had cooked and offered alms for a long time during a ten-thousand-year lifespan using a row of hearths twelve yojanas long, his recipients were only ordinary worldlings (puthujjanas).
191:
The deva Indaka, on the other hand, had once offered a single spoonful of alms-food to the Arahant Venerable Anuruddha.

Thus, although Indaka's gift was as small as a single spoonful, because the recipient was an Arahant and it was a noble deed, he could remain in his place without moving. As for the deva Aṅkura, although his offerings were vast, because the recipients were only ordinary worldlings and the power of the merit was not great, he had to move back whenever devas of great power arrived. Therefore, it is stated in the scriptures: "Viceyya dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ," meaning, "If one wishes to give, one should select and give to the recipient where the gift will yield great fruit."

Regarding the apparent inconsistency and contradiction between the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi and the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta Pāḷi, etc., the way to understand them harmoniously is as follows: The method taught in the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta Pāḷi and others is intended for ordinary devas and humans. For the Great Bodhisattas, as stated in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi, their primary aim and intention is to attain the Buddha's Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). In the Buddha's Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), there is no low, middle, or high; it is of one kind only. Thus, they must give their available offerings to all recipients who come, without discriminating between low, middle, or high. There is no reason to think, "This recipient is low; if I give to him, I will attain a low and inferior Buddha's Wisdom. This recipient is only of middle status; if I give to him, I will attain only a middle-status Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa." Therefore, giving without selecting recipients is the custom of Bodhisattas who desire Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa. The intention of ordinary devas and humans, however, is to desire various worldly pleasures, and thus they should select the best recipient.

In this way, since the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi was taught with the Bodhisattas in mind, and the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta Pāḷi and others were taught with ordinary devas and humans in mind, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency or contradiction.
192:
## Meaning of Pāramī

The Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) provides various definitions for the meanings that can be derived from the word "Pāramī." To present them clearly:

In the word "Pāramī," the terms "parama" and "ī" are combined. The preceding term "parama" signifies nobility or supremacy. In this context, it refers to the noble Bodhisattas as "parama."

Alternatively, in the Pāḷi word "parama," there is the root "par" and the suffix "ma." The root "par" signifies fulfillment and protection. Because they fulfill and protect virtues such as generosity (dāna), the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama."

Alternatively, the root "mav" (associated with "parama") signifies binding. Because they attract and bind other beings to themselves through special qualities, the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama."

Alternatively, the root "maj" (associated with "paraṃ") signifies purity, and the word "paraṃ" signifies excellence. Because they are purified from the defilements (kilesas) that cause impurity in an incomparable, excellent, and noble manner, the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama."

Alternatively, the root "may" (associated with "paraṃ") signifies going, and the word "paraṃ" signifies the supreme. Because they specifically go towards the supreme Nibbāna, the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama."

Alternatively, the root "mu" (associated with "paraṃ") signifies defining or discerning. Because they discern the world beyond just as they do the present world, the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama." (The meaning is: just as they discern with wisdom to make the present world and present life good, happy, and faultless, they can also discern with wisdom to make the future world beyond good, happy, and faultless; they are able to act for its betterment.)
193:
Alternatively, the root "mi" (associated with "paraṃ") signifies inserting or incorporating, and the word "paraṃ" signifies excellence. Because they exceedingly incorporate virtues such as morality (sīla) into their own continuity, the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama."

Alternatively, the word "paraṃ" signifies "other" or "opposite." The root "mi" signifies oppressing. Because they oppress the host of enemies known as defilements (kilesas), which are the opposite of themselves—that is, the host of the Dhamma of the virtuous—the Great Bodhisattas are called "parama."

Alternatively, the root "maj" (associated with "pāra") signifies purity. The word "pāra" signifies the "far shore." Here, saṃsāra should be taken as "this shore" and Nibbāna as the "far shore." Because they are themselves pure and also purify other beings at the far shore of Nibbāna, the Great Bodhisattas are called "Pāramī."

Alternatively, the root "mav" (associated with "pāra") signifies binding or connecting. Because they connect beings to Nibbāna, the Great Bodhisattas are called "Pāramī."

Alternatively, the root "may" signifies going. Because they go to the far shore of Nibbāna, the Great Bodhisattas are called "Pāramī."

Alternatively, the root "mu" signifies knowing. Because they know Nibbāna, the far shore of saṃsāra, as it truly is, the Great Bodhisattas are called "Pāramī."

Alternatively, the root "mi" signifies inserting or placing. Because they place and deliver beings into Nibbāna, the far shore of saṃsāra, the Great Bodhisattas are called "Pāramī."

Alternatively, the root "mi" signifies oppressing. Because they oppress and eliminate the defilements (kilesas), which are the enemies of beings, at Nibbāna, the Great Bodhisattas are called "Pāramī."
194:
(g)
(This method of considering various meanings is to demonstrate the collection of meanings that can be derived according to natural linguistics. It is not a presentation of arbitrary meanings.)

'Paramānaṃ ayaṃ pāramī': This is the property or practice of the supreme ones (Bodhisattas). Thus, it is Pāramī, the practice that is the property of the Bodhisattas. (Alternatively) 'Paramānaṃ kammaṃ pāramī': This is the work or task performed by the supreme ones. Thus, it is Pāramī, the task performed by the Bodhisattas. 'Pāramissa bhāvo pāramitā. Pāramissa kammaṃ pāramitā.' These are explained as the state of a Bodhisatta or the tasks that are the cause of enlightenment.

According to this explanation, "The collection of dhammas such as generosity (dāna), etc., which the Bodhisattas practice and perform, is called Pāramī (or Pāramitā)."

In the Zinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, it is stated: 'Pāraṃ nibbānaṃ ayanti gacchanti etāhīti paramiyo, nibbānasādhakā hi dānacetanādayo dhammā pāramīti vuccanti'—meaning, those dhammas such as the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā), etc., which are the means to reach Nibbāna, the other shore of saṃsāra, are to be called Pāramī.

In the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is explained: 'Taṇhā-māna-diṭṭhīhi anupahatā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā dānādayo guṇā pāramiyo...'—meaning, "The virtues such as giving (dāna), etc., which are not destroyed (or grasped) by craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi), and are embraced by compassion (karuṇā) for beings and skill in means (upāya-kosalla) [i.e., performed with compassion and wisdom as the precursors], are called Pāramīs." (This explanation focuses primarily on the Pāramīs of the Bodhisattas.)

Those Pāramīs are:

'Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ.
Khantisaccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettūpekkhāti te dasa.'—
According to this verse—
195:
(ghā)
Generosity (Dāna), Morality (Sīla), Renunciation (Nekkhamma), Wisdom (Paññā), and Energy (Viriya);
Patience (Khanti), Truthfulness (Sacca), Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna), Loving-kindness (Mettā), and Equanimity (Upekkhā).

According to this mnemonic verse, there are ten types: (1) Dāna-pāramī, (2) Sīla-pāramī, (3) Nekkhamma-pāramī, (4) Paññā-pāramī, (5) Viriya-pāramī, (6) Khanti-pāramī, (7) Sacca-pāramī, (8) Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī, (9) Mettā-pāramī, and (10) Upekkhā-pāramī. (The nature of these ten will be explained clearly later.)

In this regard, one should reflect with devotion on the noble foundational practice of the Great Bodhisattas, noting the point mentioned in the section on 'The Rarity of the Appearance of a Buddha' regarding continuous practice (nirantara-bhāvanā): "From the life in which the Great Bodhisattas aspire for Buddhahood and receive the definite prophecy (niyata-byāditta) until the final life of becoming a Buddha, there is not a single life in which they did not fulfill the Pāramīs at all; at the very least, they fulfilled the Pāramī of generosity (dāna)."

## Characteristics, Function, Manifestation, and Proximate Cause of the Pāramīs

Just as a yogi who wishes to practice Vipassanā meditation reaches the Purification of View (diṭṭhi-visuddhi) only after thoroughly knowing materiality (rūpa) and mentality (nāma) through these four aspects—Characteristic (lakkhaṇa), Function (rasa), Manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and Proximate Cause (padaṭṭhāna)—so too will one's knowledge regarding the Pāramīs be purified only after thoroughly knowing them through these four aspects. Thus, the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary explains the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes of these Pāramīs in a separate chapter. Among them, the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes applicable to all ten Pāramīs are:

All ten Pāramīs have the characteristic of supporting others (parānuggaha-lakkhaṇā). They have the function (kicca-rasa) of benefiting others; (alternatively) they have the function (sampatti-rasa) of stability (akampana). They have the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of seeking the welfare and benefit of beings; (alternatively) they have the manifestation of appearing in the wisdom of those who reflect on them as the noble dhammas for attaining Buddhahood. They have Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) as their—
196:
(ghi)
proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna); (alternatively) they have Great Compassion and wisdom skillful in means (upāya-kosalla) as their proximate cause.

To explain a bit further... The general nature (sāmañña-sabhāva) of various phenomena (which is shared with other dhammas) and the specific nature (visesa-sabhāva) (which is unique to that dhamma and not shared with others) are called 'Characteristic' (lakkhaṇa). (For example, within materiality, the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), which is a primary element, has two types of characteristics: the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of hardness. Since the characteristic of impermanence is shared with other dhammas, it is called a general characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa). The characteristic of hardness, however, is not shared with other dhammas and belongs only to the earth element; therefore, it is called a natural characteristic (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa).)

'Sāmaññaṃ vā sabhāvo vā, dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ mataṃ.'
Whether general or specific, it is known as the characteristic of dhammas. If it is not shared, it is the true natural characteristic; if it is common, it is the general type; these two are to be understood as 'Characteristic'.

The distinct work or function (kicca) and the accomplishment (sampatti) of various phenomena are called 'Rasa'. (For example, when a wholesome state (kusala) arises, it arises by destroying unwholesome states (akusala). The destruction of unwholesome states is the function of the wholesome state; thus, it is said that the wholesome state has the function-rasa (kicca-rasa) of destroying unwholesome states. The final accomplishment of that wholesome state is the yielding of desired and noble results. Thus, it is said that the wholesome state has the accomplishment-rasa (sampatti-rasa) of producing desired and noble results.)

'Kiccaṃ vā tassa sampatti, rasoti paridīpaye.'
Either the function or its accomplishment should be explained as 'Rasa'. Function is the activity; accomplishment is the fulfillment; understand 'Rasa' as these two.

When one considers various phenomena deeply, they may appear in the wisdom of the contemplator in relation to their nature, or in relation to their function, or in relation to their—
197:
(ghī)
cause, or in relation to their effect. Such a mode of appearance is called 'Manifestation' (paccupaṭṭhāna). (Example: If one considers deeply what kind of dhamma 'wholesome' (kusala) is, it may appear in the wisdom of the contemplator as "Kusala is a pure nature" in relation to its nature. It may appear as "Kusala is a dhamma that destroys unwholesome dhammas" in relation to its function. It may appear as "Kusala is a dhamma that can only arise through association with good friends (kalyāṇa-mitta)" in relation to its cause. It may also appear as "Kusala is a dhamma that produces desired results" in relation to its effect.)

'Phalaṃ vā paccupaṭṭhāna-mupaṭṭhānanayopi vā.'
Nature, function, or cause—these three modes of appearance—and the effect—this one mode of appearance—are to be taken as 'Manifestation'.

The nearest and most powerful cause of various dhammas is called 'Proximate Cause' (padaṭṭhāna). (Example: Among the many causes for the arising of wholesome states, wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra) is the nearest and most powerful cause; therefore, wise attention is explained in the scriptures as the proximate cause of wholesome states.)

'Āsannakāraṇaṃ yaṃ tu, padaṭṭhānanti taṃ mataṃ.'
That which is the powerful and nearest cause of an effect is to be understood as 'Proximate Cause'.

## Notable Points Regarding Generosity (Dāna)

In connection with the term 'Dāna-pāramī', the fundamental nature to be understood is that whatever is given (or the act of giving itself) is 'Dāna'. This act of giving, Dāna, should be noted as having two types:

(1) Giving that is a sphere of merit (puṇya-visaya-dāna),
(2) Various types of giving that are not a sphere of merit but are practiced as worldly duties (loka-visaya-dāna).
198:
(ghu)
All giving performed with clear and pure faith (saddhā) is called 'puṇya-visaya-dāna', and only this meritorious giving is relevant to Dāna-pāramī. All giving that is not performed with clear and pure faith—such as giving out of affection, giving out of anger, giving out of fear, giving out of ignorance, up to the lowest forms like giving a penalty or a death sentence—is called 'loka-visaya-dāna'. This worldly giving is not relevant to Dāna-pāramī.

## Dāna and Pariccāga

In the context of meritorious giving (puṇya-visaya-dāna) related to Dāna-pāramī, one should understand and note whether 'Dāna' (translated into Burmese as 'လှူဒါန်းခြင်း' - offering/giving) and 'Cāga' or 'Pariccāga' (translated into Burmese as 'စွန့်ကြဲခြင်း' - relinquishing/giving away) are the same or different in nature.

In the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka of the Asīti-nipāta:
'Dānaṃ sīlaṃ pariccāgaṃ, ajjavaṃ maddavaṃ tapaṃ.
Akkodhaṃ avihiṃsañca, khantiñca avirodhanaṃ.'—
When the ten royal virtues (rāja-dhamma) were taught, Dāna and Pariccāga were taught as separate items.

In the Jātaka Commentary, it is explained: 'Dasavatthukā cetanā dānaṃ, deyyadhammacāgo pariccāgo...' (In the Burmese version, the letter 'da' is missing in 'savatthukā'). According to this Jātaka Commentary:

(a) The volition (cetanā) of offering the ten types of gift-objects (dāna-vatthu) known as: (1) Anna = food, (2) Pāna = drink, (3) Vattha = clothing, (4) Yāna = conveyances such as umbrellas and shoes that provide comfort in travel, (5) Mālā = flowers, (6) Gandha = scented powder, (7) Vilepana = perfumed paste or ointment, (8) Seyya = bedding, (9) Āvasatha = rest houses, pavilions, or monasteries, (10) Padīpeyya = lamps or electric lights—the volition of offering these ten gift-objects is 'Dāna'.

(b) The volition of relinquishing and giving other types of gift-objects is 'Pariccāga'. Thus, Dāna and Pariccāga should be distinguished according to the material objects involved.
199:
(ghū)
In the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) of that Jātaka, it is explained: "Teachers have stated the distinction between Dāna and Pariccāga as follows: relinquishing a gift-object with a view toward benefits to be enjoyed in the future saṃsāra is 'Dāna'; giving rewards and properties to heroes, employees, etc., with a view only toward benefits in the present life, according to the principle of 'Purisamedha' (skillfulness in supporting employees according to their abilities), is 'Pariccāga'."

Alternatively, one should note in brief the story of the Bodhisatta Akitti the Wise, which appears in the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary and the Terasa-nipāta Jātaka Commentary. It is as follows: When his parents passed away, the Bodhisatta Akitti the Wise looked at the vast wealth and was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "The parents and grandparents who accumulated this wealth have gone, leaving it behind. I, however, shall take this wealth with me." After asking permission from the King, he had it announced throughout the country and gave away all his possessions for seven days. When the wealth was still not exhausted, he thought, "There is no benefit in me staying to give these things away as if it were a game. Let anyone who wants them come and take them." He then left his house, buildings, and granaries open and departed for the forest.

Regarding the practice of this Great Bodhisatta, it can be said in worldly terms that during the first seven days, he performed the act of 'Dāna' (offering). After that, he performed the act of 'Pariccāga' (relinquishing).

The reason is that Dāna is complete if it has four factors: (1) the giver, (2) the gift-object, (3) the clearly present recipient, and (4) the volition to give. In the first part of Akitti the Wise's giving, all four factors were present. After the seven days, however, he relinquished the property and left before the recipients had arrived or were clearly present; therefore, it is not called 'Dāna' but is called 'Pariccāga'.

Even in matters not related to merit, if one gives something to another, it is called 'giving' (Burmese: ပေးသည်; Pali: deti). If one leaves one's property saying, "Let him who wants it take it; if not, let it be as it may"—
200:
The act of discarding something with the thought, "Let it be," is not called giving (dāna); it is only called letting go or discarding. In Pali, it is not called dāna, but cāga.

The essential point to note is: transferring one's own property to another is called giving or dāna, whereas removing the mental attitude of wanting to possess one's own property is called discarding or relinquishing. (In the world, even discarding something because it is useless is called relinquishing.)

Alternatively, giving to noble recipients is called performing dāna or donating, while giving to lowly recipients is called distributing or pariccāga. Accordingly, it is taught that kings should practice two types of royal conduct: the dāna of donating when meeting noble monks and brahmins, and the pariccāga of distributing when meeting lowly beggars and paupers.

This is the explanation to note the distinction between dāna and pariccāga when they are taught separately.

## Similarity between Dāna and Pariccāga

Although dāna and pariccāga are distinct in worldly usage, such as in the definition of the Ten Royal Virtues, in terms of the Dhamma, they cannot be entirely separate. If dāna occurs, pariccāga also occurs; if pariccāga occurs, dāna also occurs. The reason is that giving one's manifest property to a recipient, whether far or near, is dāna, and destroying or removing the mind that clings to the property as "mine" is pariccāga. Anyone, when giving their property to others, first develops the nature of relinquishment (pariccāga) with the thought, "I will no longer use this property," and only then gives it to others. Therefore, in the context of meritorious deeds, if there is the dāna of giving, there is also the pariccāga of relinquishing.

In the Buddhavamsa Pali, among the ten perfections, only Dāna Pāramī is taught, and Cāga Pāramī is not mentioned. This is because cāga is included within dāna. According to the nature of the Dhamma (without regard for worldly usage),
201:
in the Buddhavamsa Pali as taught, giving to anyone regardless of whether they are lowly, middling, or noble is called Dāna Pāramī. There is no longer any grounds to say that it is Dāna Pāramī only if the recipient is noble, and only Pariccāga Pāramī if the recipient is lowly.

Similarly, in the Anguttara Nikaya and other texts, when the seven treasures of the noble ones (saddhamma) are taught—namely, faith (saddhā), virtue (sīla), learning (suta), relinquishment (cāga), wisdom (paññā), moral shame (hiri), and moral dread (ottappa)—only cāga appears, and dāna is not included. This absence is because when cāga is mentioned, dāna is already included within it.

This is the point to note when dāna and cāga are taught as one without distinction.

## Calling Dāna as Pariccāga

Although all acts of giving can be called Dāna Pāramī, very great acts of giving are described in the scriptures as Mahāpariccāga (Great Sacrifices). In classifying these great sacrifices into five types:

In the Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā, Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā, and Anguttara-aṭṭhakathā (in the commentary on the word 'Tathāgata'):
(1) Aṅgapariccāga = Sacrifice of limbs (major and minor),
(2) Nayanapariccāga = Sacrifice of the eyes,
(3) Dhanapariccāga = Sacrifice of wealth,
(4) Rajjapariccāga = Sacrifice of the kingdom,
(5) Puttadārapariccāga = Sacrifice of children and wife.
Thus, the five great sacrifices are explained.

In the commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā:
(1) Aṅgapariccāga = Sacrifice of limbs,
(2) Puttadārapariccāga = Sacrifice of children and wife,
(3) Rajjapariccāga = Sacrifice of the kingdom,
202:
(4) Attapariccāga = Sacrifice of one's self (including life),
(5) Nayanapariccāga = Sacrifice of the eyes.
Thus, five types are presented.

In the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā:
(1) Attapariccāga = Sacrifice of one's self (including life),
(2) Nayanapariccāga = Sacrifice of the eyes,
(3) Dhanapariccāga = Sacrifice of wealth,
(4) Rajjapariccāga = Sacrifice of the kingdom,
(5) Puttapariccāga = Sacrifice of children.
Thus, five types are presented.

In the Suttamahāvā-ṭīkā (commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta):
(1) Aṅgapariccāga = Sacrifice of limbs,
(2) Nayanapariccāga = Sacrifice of the eyes,
(3) Attapariccāga = Sacrifice of one's self (including life),
(4) Rajjapariccāga = Sacrifice of the kingdom,
(5) Puttadārapariccāga = Sacrifice of children and wife.
Thus, five types are presented.

In the commentary on the first sutta of the second vagga of the Dukanipāta in the Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā:
(1) Aṅgapariccāga = Sacrifice of limbs,
(2) Attapariccāga = Sacrifice of one's self,
(3) Dhanapariccāga = Sacrifice of property and wealth,
(4) Puttadārapariccāga = Sacrifice of children and wife,
(5) Rajjapariccāga = Sacrifice of the kingdom.
Thus, five types are presented.

In the Buddhavamsa-aṭṭhakathā:
(1) Aṅgapariccāga = Sacrifice of limbs,
(2) Jīvitapariccāga = Sacrifice of life,
203:
(3) Dhanapariccāga = Sacrifice of property and wealth,
(4) Rajjapariccāga = Sacrifice of the kingdom,
(5) Puttadārapariccāga = Sacrifice of children and wife.
Thus, five types are presented.

In the Vessantara Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā:
(1) Dhanapariccāga = Sacrifice of property and wealth,
(2) Aṅgapariccāga = Sacrifice of limbs,
(3) Puttapariccāga = Sacrifice of children,
(4) Bhariyapariccāga = Sacrifice of the wife,
(5) Jīvitapariccāga = Sacrifice of life.
Thus, five types are presented. (The Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā also presents these same five with a slightly different order.)

Although the names differ slightly in each source, the underlying meaning is the same. Indeed, among external objects (bāhiraka), the sacrifice of the most external property is Dhanapariccāga; the sacrifice of children and wife, who are as dear as life, is Puttadārapariccāga; and the sacrifice of the kingdom (royal luxury), which is vital for personal status, is Rajjapariccāga. These three sacrifices are defined for external objects. Regarding one's own body, the sacrifice of limbs that does not result in death is Aṅgapariccāga. The sacrifice that involves giving up one's life is presented in some texts as Nayanapariccāga, in some as Jīvitapariccāga, and in others as Attapariccāga. Since sacrificing the eyes or the body can lead to death, they are essentially the same as Jīvitapariccāga (sacrifice of life). Thus, two types of sacrifice are explained regarding one's own body. In summary, there are three types of great sacrifice for external objects and two types for one's own body (those that can cause death and those that do not). Therefore, one should not consider the scriptures to be in conflict.

In the commentary, King Vessantara's great gift, which included seven hundred of each item, is explained as the Sattasataka Mahādāna (meaning the Great Gift of Seven Hundreds).
204:
Although it is not explicitly described as Mahāpariccāga (Great Sacrifice), among the five types of great sacrifices mentioned, King Vessantara's great gift can certainly be called Dhanamahāpariccāga if one wishes to do so.

## Various Noteworthy Points regarding Dāna

In this section on the Perfections (Pāramī), for the three types of future Buddhas (Bodhisattas)—those striving to attain Sammāsambodhi, Paccekabodhi, and Sāvakabodhi—I shall present the section called Pakiṇṇakakathā (Miscellaneous Discussion) to provide diverse knowledge and expertise regarding Dāna, which is part of the Bodhisambhāra (the requisites for attaining their desired Bodhi-enlightenment). In this section, I will provide detailed answers based on the following six investigative questions:

1. What things are called dāna?
2. Why is it called dāna?
3. What are the characteristics (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of dāna?
4. How many varieties of dāna are there?
5. What causes the greatness of the power of dāna?
6. What causes the decline of the power of dāna?

(In subsequent perfections, I will follow this same method.) Regarding these six investigative questions:

1. According to the question "What things are called dāna?", the summary answer is: "Both the volition (cetanā) that desires to give and the material object (vatthu) that is given are called dāna." This will become clearer in the detailed explanation later.

2. According to the question "Why is it called dāna?", it is called dāna because the volition to give is the cause that enables the act of giving. To explain more clearly: without volition, one cannot give; only when there is volition can one give. Regarding volition:
(a) One should note the muñca-cetanā, which arises at the very moment of giving. Muñca means relinquishing. The volition that occurs at the moment of relinquishing and giving is called muñca-cetanā. This muñca-cetanā alone is the actual essence of dāna.
205:
(b) The group of volitions that occur beforehand, prior to the act of relinquishing, is called pubba-cetanā. This pubba-cetanā is counted within dāna (it may even be called dāna). Although it is called "beforehand," it refers to the time when the gift-object is already manifest and one intends, "I will give this object." The volition involved in merely thinking or imagining giving without having the material object may be called pubba-cetanā if one wishes, but it cannot be included within dāna; it can only be a type of ordinary merit.

Regarding the word dāna when it takes volition as its meaning, according to grammatical treatises (forming the definition as 'dīyati anenāti dānaṃ'), it must be translated as "the cause of giving."

As for the material object, it is called dāna because of its nature of being given. Regarding the word dāna when it takes the material object as its meaning, according to grammatical treatises (forming the definition as 'dīyatīti dānaṃ'), it must be translated as "the thing that is given."

Based on these two meanings of dāna as volition and object, it is stated in the scriptures that there are two types of dāna: (1) cetanā-dāna and (2) vatthu-dāna.

Some may ask: "In the ripening of results, only volition can produce a result, while the object cannot. Why then is the material object called dāna if it cannot produce a result?" The answer is that although only volition acts as kamma and can produce a result, that volition can only be included within the kamma of dāna as previously shown if it arises because a material object is manifest. Therefore, the material object is also an important cause for the fulfillment of the kamma of dāna. Although the material object cannot produce a result directly, it must be said that it can do so through its connection as a cause.

For example, it is like the saying, "The rice is cooked because of the firewood." In direct terms, only the fire cooks the rice. However, that fire burns only when there is firewood. Because of the firewood, the fire burns; because of the fire,
206:
(h)
Just as it is correct to say "the rice is cooked because the firewood is good" when connecting causes, it is also correct to say "one obtains good results because of the object of charity (dāna-vatthu)."

Because the material object is also important for the fulfillment of the act of dāna (dāna-kamma), various types of dāna are classified and explained in the scriptures based on the material object.

The explanation is as follows... According to the Vinaya teachings, it is explained that there are four types of dāna: the dāna of alms-food (piṇḍapāta), the dāna of robes (cīvara), the dāna of dwellings (senāsana), and the dāna of medicine (bhesajja). Although the Vinaya does not primarily intend to show four types of dāna, since the Buddha permitted four requisites for the use of monks, the offerings also naturally become fourfold; thus, it is explained that there are four types of dāna according to the Vinaya. Fundamentally, the reason for these four divisions is based on the material object.

According to the Abhidhamma teachings, where all existing phenomena in the world are classified and taught through the six sense objects, it is explained that there are six types of dāna: giving of forms (rūpa-dāna), giving of sounds (sadda-dāna), giving of smells (gandha-dāna), giving of tastes (rasa-dāna), giving of tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-dāna), and giving of mental objects or Dhamma (dhamma-dāna).

In this case, too, although the Abhidhamma teachings do not directly teach six types of dāna, because the six sense objects are taught, it implies that if those objects are respectively given, there are six types of dāna according to the variety of objects. Therefore, the scriptures explain that there are six types of dāna according to the Abhidhamma.

According to the Suttanta teachings, there are: giving of various kinds of food (anna-dāna), giving of various kinds of drink (pāna-dāna), giving of clothing (vattha-dāna), giving of vehicles or means of transport (yāna-dāna), giving of various kinds of flowers (mālā-dāna), giving of various kinds of scents (gandha-dāna), and giving of various kinds of unguents (vilepana-dāna).
207:
(za)
(Since the word 'vilepana' means something to be smeared, any substance, whether liquid or powder, that is used for smearing or anointing should be considered 'vilepana'. In ancient times, substances like orpiment and realgar, which were commonly used for anointing, should also be called 'vilepana'.)

Giving of couches, benches, and bedding (seyya-dāna); giving of dwellings such as houses and monasteries (āvasatha-dāna); and giving of oil and other materials for lighting lamps (padīpeyya-dāna)—thus, it is explained that there are ten types of dāna.

These ten types were originally taught only as the ten objects of dāna (dāna-vatthu). Since there are these ten objects of dāna, if those objects are respectively given, there should also be ten types; therefore, the scriptures explain that there are ten types of dāna according to the Suttanta.

In this regard, one should not assume that only these ten types are worthy of being given, citing that the Buddha only taught these ten objects of dāna. These ten types were taught as objects of dāna because they are generally the most common offerings in the world. Alternatively, since all material objects can be included within these ten categories based on their nature, by showing these ten, it should be understood that any material objects commonly used by virtuous people can be offered.

From these aforementioned statements, it should be well understood that material objects are important causes for the dāna of intention (cetanā-dāna). In the various classifications of dāna to be explained later, one should note that many types of dāna related to material objects are included.

In this section, 'cetanā' (intention) is called dāna because it is the cause of giving. The 'vatthu' (object) to be offered is called dāna because it is that which is given.

3. Regarding the question "What are the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of dāna?"—dāna is as follows:
208:
(zi)
(a) It has the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of relinquishing (giving up).
(b) It has the function (rasa) of destroying attachment to the objects of charity. (Alternatively) It has the function of achievement (sampatti-rasa) in being blameless.
(c) It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of non-attachment. (Meaning, it appears to the yogi's knowledge as a state free from attachment.) (Alternatively) It has the manifestation of the fulfillment of existence (bhava) and the fulfillment of wealth (bhoga). (Meaning, it appears to the knowledge of one who reflects as a state that brings about the result of fulfillment in human or celestial existence and fulfillment of wealth and possessions.)
(d) It has the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the material object to be relinquished. (Meaning, if there is no object to be relinquished, dāna cannot occur by mere thought alone; only when there is an object to be relinquished can true dāna occur. Therefore, the material object to be relinquished is the closest cause, the padaṭṭhāna, of dāna.)

4. Regarding the question "How many divisions does that dāna have?", the answer is very extensive. (May you all note this with great mindfulness and wisdom.)

## Collection of Dāna in Pairs
Dāna is divided into two types: āmisa-dāna and dhamma-dāna. Material objects such as alms-food are called 'āmisa'. Giving those material objects is called āmisa-dāna. Since 'āmisa' and 'paccaya' (requisite) are the same, it can also be called paccaya-dāna. Giving the Dhamma by preaching to others is called dhamma-dāna. The Buddha taught that among all types of dāna, dhamma-dāna is the supreme. (This division into two is also based on the material object.)

In connection with these two types of dāna, it is necessary to examine what kind of dāna it is when people in the world build and worship great pagodas (cetiyas) and Buddha statues.

Regarding this matter—
Some individuals say, "Although those who build great pagodas and Buddha statues relinquish much wealth, it cannot be dāna. Dāna occurs only when the three factors—the recipient (paṭiggāhaka), the object of charity (dāna-vatthu), and the donor (dāyaka)—are complete.
209:
(zī)
In building great pagodas and Buddha statues, although the donor is clearly present, there is no recipient. To whom should these great pagodas and Buddha statues be offered? Since there is no recipient in this way, it cannot even be dāna. It should only be a state of Samatha meditation related to Buddha-anussati (recollection of the Buddha). Repeatedly reflecting on the attributes of the Buddha is Buddha-anussati, and the builder of pagodas and statues does not intend to relinquish them to any specific recipient. It is merely building a physical form to enable clear reflection when repeatedly contemplating the attributes of the Buddha. Because worshipping these pagodas and statues can make the Buddha's attributes especially vivid, it should be noted that it only pertains to Buddha-anussati kammaṭṭhāna."

Other teachers say, "The builder of great pagodas and Buddha statues builds them to pay respect and offer worship to the Buddha, who is most worthy of respect. Therefore, among the ten bases of meritorious action (puṇya-kiriya-vatthu), it is the merit of humility (apacāyana-kusala). That apacāyana-kusala must be included within virtue (sīla). The reason is... paying respect to that which is worthy of respect is a type of conduct-virtue (cāritta-sīla). Therefore, the merit of building pagodas and statues should not be included in Buddha-anussati, but only in sīla."

The Buddha-anussati samatha-kusala and apacāyana-kusala mentioned by these teachers do not involve the relinquishing of material objects. Now, in building great pagodas and Buddha statues, since many material objects must be relinquished, it pertains only to the act of dāna.

One might ask, "If it pertains to the act of dāna, can dāna occur without a recipient?"

In the scriptures, there is a statement that "the truest nature of any phenomenon can be obtained by analyzing it through the four factors: lakkhaṇa, rasa, paccupaṭṭhāna, and padaṭṭhāna." Therefore, according to the method previously mentioned regarding the characteristics of dāna, the scriptures state that "dāna has the characteristic of relinquishing the objects of charity."
210:
(zu)
For the donor who builds pagodas and statues, the characteristic of dāna (relinquishing material objects), the function of dāna (destroying attachment to those objects), the manifestation of dāna (the result of fulfillment in existence and wealth), and the proximate cause of dāna (the material objects)—since these four factors are complete, it should be understood as dāna.

Alternatively, it would not be wrong to say that all devas and humans who wish to have faith in, behold, and worship the pagodas and statues are indeed the recipients. Since the great pagodas and statues are objects to be used by humans and devas for beholding and worshipping, they can be called objects of charity (dāna-vatthu).

In the world, various material objects are used according to their purpose. Food items are used by eating; clothing items are used by wearing; and objects worthy of faith, devotion, and worship are used by having faith, devotion, and worshipping them.

If one digs large wells or ponds on a road where many people travel, even if those wells and ponds are not dedicated to anyone by pouring water (libation), if people who arrive there drink and bathe as intended for the public, would it be proper to say that the donor of those wells and ponds does not achieve dāna? It would not be proper. That owner of the well or pond does not intend to give to any specific person, but digs them with the intention for whoever happens to come by to drink and use them; just as that constitutes dāna, so it is here.

Therefore, it is appropriate to analyze that those who build pagodas and statues are the donors (dāyaka), the great pagodas and statues are the objects of charity (dāna-vatthu), and all devas and humans who worship and behold them are the recipients (paṭiggāhaka).

One might want to ask, "Is it appropriate to call great pagodas and Buddha statues 'objects of charity'? Would there not be some fault?"

The answer should be that just as the cabinets and shelves where the Piṭaka scriptures (Dhamma-cetiya) reside, pagodas are the dwelling places of the bodily relics (sārīrika-dhātu) known as Dhātu-cetiya, and thus they are worthy of being called objects of charity.
211: ## Whether Dāna is Accomplished Only After Libation  The question of whether a gift (dāna) is valid or not when the act of libation (pouring water) is not clearly performed during the consecration of a pagoda or statue is often considered.
