2. *Asakkacca-dāna*: Giving carelessly without properly preparing the object of donation to be pure and excellent. (Due to this dāna, although one may have wealth, followers and attendants may not obey one's words.)
3. *Akāla-dāna*: Giving at an inappropriate time. (Due to this dāna, although one may have wealth, one may not obtain many desired results at the time they are needed.)
4. *Ananuggaha-dāna*: Giving as a mere formality without the desire to support the recipient. (Due to this dāna, although one may have wealth, one may not have the desire to use or may not get to use excellent requisites.)
5. *Upaghāta-dāna*: Giving while harming or affecting one's own reputation or the reputation of others. (Due to this dāna, although one may obtain wealth, it may be destroyed by the five enemies.)

It can be understood that there are five such types of *asappurisa-dāna*. Considering the *kāla-dāna* and *akāla-dāna* mentioned in these *sappurisa* and *asappurisa* dānas, even if done with good intention, one should be careful not to light lamps for the Buddha during the day or offer food and snacks after noon.

Donations that are regarded as meritorious deeds by people but are in fact only unwholesome demerit are...
253:
(ဋား)
(1) Majjadāna = The gift of intoxicants.
(2) Samajjadāna = The gift of theatrical shows or festivals.
(3) Itthidāna = The gift of providing prostitutes for those who desire them.
(4) Usabhadāna = The gift of releasing a bull into a herd of cows for mating as desired.
(5) Cittakammadāna = The gift of painting and donating inappropriate images.
These five are taught in the Parivāra of the Vinaya Piṭaka.

It is taught that only demerit (akusala) arises from giving these five because it is impossible to maintain a wholesome intention (cetanā) when donating these things. People often have a misconception; for instance, if they see an opium addict who is on the verge of death due to withdrawal and think, "If this person does not have opium, he will surely die; I will give him opium to save his life," they might believe this is the merit of giving life (jīvitadāna). In reality, it cannot be merit. This is because the desire for someone to consume opium, which should not be consumed, is not a wholesome mind but an unwholesome one. The same principle should be understood regarding alcohol and similar substances.

In the Vessantara Jātaka, the Commentaries state that when the Bodhisatta, King Vessantara, arranged the materials for his great offering (mahādāna), he included even intoxicants.

Regarding this point, the reason given for King Vessantara including alcohol—which is not a proper gift—in his arrangement is that he had absolutely no desire for drunkards to consume it. Only the intention to have others drink is unwholesome. King Vessantara, however, had no such intention; he included it merely to avoid being accused by others that his great offering was incomplete and lacked intoxicants.
254:
(ဌ)
Upon careful scrutiny, a great noble person like King Vessantara would not fear or worry about being blamed by others when he is blameless. In truth, the fault lies only in drinking the intoxicant. If it is used as medicine, such as for external application or other appropriate ways without drinking it, no demerit (akusala) can occur. It should be understood that he included it because he wished to give to those who might need it for such blameless purposes as external application.

As for the other four, such as the gift of theatrical shows (samajjadāna), they are types of giving where it is impossible to have a wholesome intention under any circumstances.

## The Five Great Gifts (Mahādāna)
In the Anguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, the fourth (4) Dānavagga, ninth Sutta, beginning with the words "Pañcimāni bhikkhave dānāni mahādānāni...", the Buddha taught the Five Precepts themselves as the Five Great Gifts in detail.

In this great Sutta, because the Five Precepts are taught in detail as the Five Great Gifts, one should not conclude that "virtue (sīla) is called giving (dāna)." The Buddha did not intend to teach that virtue and giving are identical in essence (sabhāva). Virtue is the proper restraint of body and speech, whereas giving is the act of relinquishing something. Therefore, it should not be understood that virtue itself is called giving. In reality, if one observes the precept of abstaining from taking life (pāṇātipāta-virati) and is endowed with virtue, that virtuous person no longer kills beings and is said to give the gift of safety (abhaya-dāna), which is the gift of being free from danger to all beings. In this manner, by observing all five precepts, one gives the gift of safety to beings, and since the act of giving based on virtue is accomplished, the Buddha taught the five precepts as the Five Great Gifts. This should be noted with special attention.

## The collection of gifts in groups of five is finished.

255:
(ဌာ)
There is no direct teaching in the Pāḷi Canon that Dana is of four types by its inherent nature. However, according to the Vinaya method, based on the four requisites, it can be presented as four: the gift of robes, the gift of alms-food, the gift of monasteries, and the gift of medicine. Similarly, based on the four types of purity of the gift (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi), it can be presented as four: a gift where only the donor is virtuous and the recipient is not, a gift where only the recipient is virtuous and the donor is not, a gift where both are not virtuous, and a gift where both are virtuous.

Although there is no direct teaching in the Pāḷi Canon that Dana is of six types by its inherent nature, according to the Abhidhamma method, based on the six sense objects, these six objects can be made the objects of giving. This is explained in detail in the Atthasālinī Commentary (Sixth Edition, page 119, etc.) as six types: rūpadāna (the gift of forms), saddadāna (the gift of sounds), and so on.

Likewise, although there is no direct teaching in the Pāḷi Canon that Dana is of seven types, if one wishes to present the seven types of Saṅghika-dāna (offerings to the Order) mentioned previously as a group of seven gifts, it may be so presented. (Since it has been shown before, it is not shown here.)

## The Group of Eight Gifts
In the Anguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, the fourth (4) Dānavagga, first Sutta, the Buddha taught that there are eight types of gifts. These eight are:
1. Giving with attention and without delay when a recipient arrives.
2. Giving out of fear of being blamed or fear of falling into the four woeful states (apāya).
3. Giving with the thought, "This person has given to me in the past."
4. Giving with the intention, "If I give to this person now, he will give back to me in the future."
5. Giving with the reflection, "Giving is a good deed."
256:
(ဌိ)
6. Giving with the reflection, "I am one who cooks and eats; it is not proper for me to eat without giving to those who do not cook."
7. Giving with the reflection, "If I give this gift, my good reputation and fame will spread far and wide."
8. Giving with the intention that the gift may serve as an equipment or ornament for the mind to become well-concentrated when it is not yet concentrated during the practice of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation.
These are the eight.

Among these eight, only the last gift is the most noble. This is because this last gift encourages and supports the mind to become calm and joyful during the practice of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation, and it is a special gift that is highly beneficial to Samatha and Vipassanā, which lead to the attainment of Jhāna, Path (Magga), and Fruition (Phala). The first seven gifts cannot support the mind of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation in this way. Among those that cannot, the 1st and 5th gifts are also noble gifts (meaning paṇīta-dāna). The 7th gift is an inferior gift (hīna-dāna), while the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 6th gifts are merely a group of middling gifts (majjhima-dāna).

Regarding giving, there are the two types mentioned before: puññavisaya-dāna (merit-oriented giving) and lokavisaya-dāna (worldly-oriented giving). In the eight types of gifts just described, they should be distinguished as lokavisaya or puññavisaya as appropriate. The way to understand them is: the 1st, 5th, and 8th gifts are types of puññavisaya-dāna, while the remaining five should be considered only as lokavisaya-dāna.

Alternatively:
1. Giving out of affection and desire.
2. Giving reluctantly with anger because it is unavoidable.
3. Giving out of foolishness and confusion, not knowing cause and effect.
257:
(ဌီ)
4. Giving out of fear of being blamed by many, fear of falling into the woeful states, or fear that the recipient might cause some harm.
5. Giving with the thought, "My parents and grandparents for generations have performed the act of giving; it is not proper for me to diminish this lineage and tradition of my ancestors."
6. Giving with the aim of reaching the celestial realm (deva-loka) after death as a result of this gift.
7. Giving with the expectation of mental joy, thinking, "If I give this gift, my mind will be clear, delighted, and joyful."
8. Giving with the intention that the gift may serve as an equipment or accessory for the mind to become well-concentrated when it is not yet concentrated during the practice of Samatha and Vipassanā.
This was taught in the Anguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, (4) Dānavagga, third Sutta.

Among these eight as well, only the eighth gift is the most noble. The 6th and 7th gifts are appropriate and noble gifts, belonging to the group of puññavisaya-dāna. The other five types of gifts are inferior and belong only to the group of lokavisaya-dāna.

Alternatively:
In the same (4) Dānavagga, fifth Sutta, the eight types of Dānūpapatti are taught in detail. The Pāḷi term 'Dānūpapatti' means "the rebirth in a future existence obtained because of giving." The gift is divided into eight types based on the eight kinds of future rebirths. The brief classification is:
1. Seeing wealthy people in the human world, one gives a gift and makes a wish to become like them. Being also endowed with virtue (sīla), one is reborn as a wealthy human after death according to the wish. This is one type.
258:
(ဌု)
2. Having heard that the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) possess great power, luxury, and happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that realm. Being also endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Cātumahārājika realm after death according to the wish. This is another type.
3. Having heard that the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa realm possess great power, luxury, and happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that realm. Being also endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm after death according to the wish. This is another type.
4. Having heard that the devas of the Yāma realm possess great power, luxury, and happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that realm. Being also endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Yāma realm after death according to the wish. This is another type.
5. Having heard that the devas of the Tusita realm possess great power, luxury, and happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that realm. Being also endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Tusita realm after death according to the wish. This is another type.
6. Having heard that the devas of the Nimmānarati realm possess great power, luxury, and happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that realm. Being also endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Nimmānarati realm after death according to the wish. This is another type.
7. Having heard that the devas of the Paranimmitavasavatti realm possess great power, luxury, and happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that realm. Being also endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Paranimmitavasavatti realm after death according to the wish. This is another type.
8. Having heard that the Brahmas are long-lived, beautiful, and possess much happiness, one gives a gift and makes a wish to be born in that Brahma realm.
259:
(Ṭhū)
Because of giving gifts with a prayerful aspiration and being endowed with virtue, one is reborn in the Brahma realm after death according to that aspiration. This is one point.
(Regarding this 8th type of dāna, although it is taught as if the state of a Brahma can be attained through dāna alone, in reality, the state of a Brahma cannot be attained by dāna alone. It is taught based on the fact that by the eighth type of dāna included in the two sets of eightfold dāna mentioned before, one possesses a gentle mind, and after developing the Brahma-vihāras (Sublime Abodes), one can be reborn in the Brahma realm.)
Furthermore...
In the seventh sutta of that Dānavagga, the eight kinds of Sappurisa-dāna (Giving of a Good Person) are taught. The eight are:
1. Giving after making the gift clean, pure, and beautiful.
2. Giving what is choice and excellent.
3. Giving at the proper and appropriate time.
4. Giving only items that are allowable for the recipients.
5. Giving after careful discrimination of the recipient and the object to be given (Viceyya-dāna).
(In this Viceyya-dāna, there are two types of discrimination: choosing the recipient and choosing the object. Among these, setting aside recipients outside the Dispensation (bāhiraka) who are completely devoid of virtue, and giving to recipients within the Dispensation who are endowed with virtues such as morality, is called discrimination of the recipient. When one has two types of objects, good and bad, setting aside the inferior object and giving the better one is called discrimination of the object.)
6. Giving regularly as much as one is able.
7. Giving with a clear and bright mind at the time of giving.
8. Being able to maintain a joyful mind after having given.
These are the eight.
260:
(Ṭhe)
In this context, although Asappurisa-dāna (Giving of an Unworthy Person) is not taught separately in succession, if one reverses the eight kinds of Sappurisa-dāna that were taught, the eight kinds of Asappurisa-dāna can be obtained. The eight that can be obtained are:
1. Giving in an unclean and improper manner.
2. Giving only inferior things.
3. Giving at an inappropriate time.
4. Giving items that are not allowable for the recipients.
5. Giving without discriminating between the recipient and the object.
6. Giving intermittently instead of giving as much as one is able.
7. Giving without a clear mind at the time of giving.
8. Feeling regret or being reluctant after having given.
These are the eight.
## The group of eightfold dāna ends.
**********
## The group of ninefold dāna
In the Vinaya Parivāra Pāḷi, it is taught that there are nine kinds of Adhammika-dāna (Unrighteous Giving). In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), regarding the phrase 'Nava adhammikāni dānāni', it is explained as: 'diverting a gain intended for the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a Cetiya, or to an individual...'
1. Diverting a gain already intended for the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha.
2. (Or) diverting it to a Cetiya.
3. (Or) diverting it to a particular individual.
4. Diverting a gain already intended for a Cetiya to another Cetiya.
261:
(Ṭhai)
5. (Or) diverting it to the Saṅgha.
6. (Or) diverting it to a particular individual.
7. Diverting a gain already intended for an individual to another individual other than the one intended.
8. (Or) diverting it to the Saṅgha.
9. (Or) diverting it to a Cetiya.
Thus, the nine types are explained.
In this context, according to the Pāḷi term 'pariṇata', 'intended gain' means the four requisites and utilities that have been verbally promised or dedicated, saying, 'We shall offer or build this for the Saṅgha, the Cetiya, or the individual.'
The origin story for teaching these nine Adhammika-dānas should be noted. That story appears in the Pārājika-kaṇḍa and Pācittiya Pāḷi of the Vinaya. The account is as follows:
While the Blessed One was staying at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, a certain association in Sāvatthī consulted and agreed, saying, 'After offering a meal to the Saṅgha, we shall also offer robes.' They prepared both robes and food to be offered to the Saṅgha (according to their annual custom).
At that time, the Chabbaggī monks went to that association and spoke so insistently that the people could not refuse, asking for those robes to be given to them. Consequently, they gave the robes to the Chabbaggī monks and offered only the meal to the Saṅgha.
When the monks learned of this and spoke words of blame and reproach, they reported it to the Blessed One. In that context, He laid down the training rule: 'Whatever monk should knowingly divert to himself a gain that was already intended for the Saṅgha, there is an offense of Pācittiya involving forfeiture (Nissaggiya).'
262:
(Ṭho)
In the Padabhājanī, which analyzes this training rule in detail, it is taught: If one knowingly diverts to oneself a gain intended for the Saṅgha (verbally promised) and receives it, there is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. If one diverts it to another Saṅgha or to a Cetiya, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. If one knowingly diverts a gain intended for a Cetiya to another Cetiya, or to the Saṅgha, or to an individual, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. If one knowingly diverts a gain intended for another individual to a different individual, or to the Saṅgha, or to a Cetiya, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. Thus it is analyzed and taught.
The reason for presenting this origin story is to clarify how a donor's gift acquires the bad name of 'Adhammika-dāna' due to the interference and agitation of donation brokers or middlemen. Indeed, if a donor has verbally stated, 'I shall offer this object to the Saṅgha, the Cetiya, or the individual,' that object partially becomes the property of the Saṅgha, Cetiya, or individual who was mentioned. Knowing that it is thus intended for the Saṅgha, Cetiya, or individual, if donation brokers or middlemen (like the Chabbaggī monks) unrighteously interfere and agitate, causing the gift to be diverted to another Saṅgha, Cetiya, or individual, and the donor follows their words, that dāna becomes Adhammika-dāna because of that unrighteous interference.
The nine ways of receiving such Adhammika-dāna, diverted from the original intended Saṅgha, Cetiya, or individual due to the unrighteous interference of brokers, are also taught as the nine Adhammika-paṭiggaha (Unrighteous Acceptances). The nine ways of using them are taught as the nine Adhammika-paribhoga (Unrighteous Uses).
Although the act of donation brokers unrighteously interfering and causing a diversion, and the subsequent giving to another Saṅgha, Cetiya, or individual, is called Adhammika-dāna, it is not called Adhammika if the diversion from the original intent is done righteously...
263:
(Ṭhor)
...or if the donor themselves gains right understanding and changes the original intended gift to another. Therefore:
The Blessed One instructed His foster mother, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, to offer to the Saṅgha the pair of new robes she had woven and brought with the verbal intention of offering them to the Blessed One Himself. If it were unrighteous (adhammika) or blameworthy, the Blessed One would not have given such an instruction. King Pasenadi of Kosala also, in the beginning, accepted a bribe of one hundred thousand coins from the heretics (titthiyas) and gave permission for the heretic teachers to build a monastery near Jetavana. When the heretics' disciples brought timber and bamboo to build the monastery, at the Buddha's command, first Venerable Ānanda and the monks, and secondly Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna, went to the palace (to prevent it). However, because he had taken the bribe, King Pasenadi did not dare to meet them. On the following day, the Buddha Himself went and taught the Bharu Jātaka from the Dukanipāta. Consequently, the King gained right vision, confiscated the original land and the timber as royal property, and built a monastery there, offering it to the Blessed One. Because that monastery was the meritorious work of King Pasenadi of Kosala, it became known as the Rājakārāma (the King's Monastery). If offering this Rājakārāma Monastery to the Blessed One were an Adhammika-dāna, the Blessed One would not have accepted it.
Furthermore, the quality of Pāhuneyya, which is among the nine qualities of the Saṅgha, should be taken as evidence. An object prepared for guests (āgantuka) who are expected to arrive is called pāhuna. When encountering the Noble Saṅgha, it is proper to set aside the guests for whom the items were intended and offer those items only to the Noble Saṅgha. The Noble Saṅgha is also worthy of receiving such gifts. They are also worthy of using them after receiving. This worthiness to receive is called the quality of Pāhuneyya.
If, according to the donor's own wish (without the unrighteous interference of middlemen), they divert their own property from the original intention...
264:
(Ṭhaṃ)
If it were unrighteous, the Buddha would not have taught that a gift intended for guests should be given to the Noble Saṅgha, nor that it is worthy of being accepted.

## Three Types of Righteous Giving (Dhammika-dāna)
1. Giving to the Saṅgha a gift that was already intended for the Saṅgha.
2. Giving to a Cetiya a gain that was already intended for that Cetiya.
3. Giving to a specific individual a gain that was already intended (and verbally declared) for that specific individual.
These three are taught as the three types of righteous giving.

In explaining these nine types of unrighteous giving and three types of righteous giving, the commentator (in the Vinaya Parivāra Commentary) explains unrighteous giving as: 'saṅghassa pariṇataṃ aññasaṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā puggalassa vā pariṇāmeti'—diverting a gain intended for the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a Cetiya, or to an individual, etc. This 'diverting' is not the act of the donor, but the act of intermediaries or 'alms-brokers' who unrighteously interfere and arrange for the gift to be transferred. Therefore, it should be firmly understood that unrighteous giving occurs only because intermediaries (like the Chabbaggiya monks) unrighteously interfere and manage the transfer of the gift.

## The Group of Nine Gifts is Finished.
**********
Regarding the group of ten gifts, there is no direct teaching in the Pāḷi Canon stating that there are ten types based on the inherent nature of dāna, as there are for the groups of four, six, or seven. Rather, the commentator explains the ten types of dāna according to the Suttanta method, based on the ten common objects of alms (dāna-vatthu). Similarly, if one wishes to distinguish fourteen types of dāna based on the fourteen types of individual offerings (puggalika-dāna) mentioned in the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta, it would be appropriate to do so.

## The Classification of Dāna is Finished.
**********
265: (Thā) 5. 'What is the cause for the greatness of the power of that gift?' 6. 'What is the cause for the decline of the power of that gift?' Based on these investigative questions: The causes for the greatness and decline of the power of Dāna should first be understood by referring to the Dāna Sutta, the seventh sutta of the Devatā Vagga in the Chakkanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. In that sutta... While the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, he saw with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) the laywoman Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇḍaka offering a great gift endowed with six factors to the Saṅgha led by the two chief disciples. [He said:] 'Monks, the laywoman Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇḍaka is offering a gift endowed with six factors to the Saṅgha led by Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The three factors on the part of the donor are: 1. Being joyful before giving. 2. Having a clear and pure mind while giving. 3. Being delighted and joyful after having given. The three factors on the part of the recipients are: 1. Being free from lust (rāga), or practicing for the removal of lust. 2. Being free from hatred (dosa), or practicing for the removal of hatred. 3. Being free from delusion (moha), or practicing for the removal of delusion. She is offering a gift endowed with these six factors. Monks, just as it is impossible to measure the water in the great ocean, so too it is impossible to measure the merit of a gift endowed with these six factors. Indeed, just as the mass of water in the great ocean...'
266: (Ḍa) ...can only be called an incalculable mass of water, so too a gift endowed with these six factors must be called a gift that yields immeasurable results. According to this Pāli text: The intensity of the three-fold intention (cetanā) on the part of the donor, and the recipients being free from greed, hatred, and delusion (or practicing for their cessation)—these six factors are the causes for the greatness of the power of Dāna. If these factors are complete, the power of Dāna is great. If these factors are deficient, the power of Dāna declines. Furthermore, in the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka of the Dasakanipāta, the Great Teacher (Disāpāmokkha) asked the Brahmin Mahādhammapāla (the father of King Suddhodana in a previous life), 'Why is it that in your Mahādhammapāla clan, young people do not die before reaching their full lifespan?' In response, he said: 'Pubbeva dānā sumanā bhavāma, Dadaṃpi ve attamanā bhavāma. Datvāpi ve nānutappāma pacchā, Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā n mīyare.' 'We are well-pleased before giving; we are truly delighted while giving; and after giving, we truly have no regret or anxiety. Because of these three reasons, the young ones in our Mahādhammapāla clan do not die (before their time).' Based on this, it should be understood that this 'consistency of the three-fold intention' has the power to produce the immediate benefit of long life.
267: (Ḍā) Furthermore... (1) The gift must be righteously obtained (dhammiyaladdha). (2) The gift must be offered with intense faith and consistency in the three-fold intention (cetanā-mahatta). (3) The recipient must be an Arahant or an Anāgāmī (vatthu-sampatti). (4) The recipient must have just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) (guṇātireka). Because the Atthasālinī Commentary and the Dhammapada Commentary explain that a gift endowed with these four factors can yield results in this very life—as in the cases of the wealthy man Puṇṇa, the wealthy man Kākavaliya, and the florist Sumana—it should be understood without doubt that these four factors are also causes for the greatness of the power of Dāna. (In the Atthasālinī, these four factors are explained as the four purities of offerings (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi), and in the Dhammapada Commentary, they are explained as the four accomplishments (sampadā) of Dāna.) Furthermore... In the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāli, the four purities of offerings (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi) are taught. The intended meaning of these four is: (1) A type of gift that is purified by the donor, though not by the recipient. (This means that even if the recipient is immoral, if the donor is virtuous, offers righteously obtained goods, possesses the three-fold intention, and has faith in Kamma and its results, then that gift is purified by the donor and can be of great fruit.)
268: (Ḍi) (2) A type of gift that is purified by the recipient, though not by the donor. (This means that even if an immoral donor offers unrighteously obtained goods without intense three-fold intention or faith in Kamma and its results, if the recipient is virtuous, then that gift is purified by the recipient and can be of great fruit.) (3) A type of gift that is purified neither by the donor nor by the recipient. (This means that if an immoral donor offers unrighteously obtained goods to an immoral recipient without intense three-fold intention or faith in Kamma and its results, then that gift is like planting poor seeds in poor soil; it is a gift that does not yield great fruit.) (4) A type of gift that is purified by both the donor and the recipient. (This means that if a virtuous donor offers righteously obtained goods to a virtuous recipient with intense three-fold intention and faith in Kamma and its results, then that gift is like planting good seeds in good soil; it is a gift that yields great fruit.) Among these four points, although the third point involves only impurity (lack of abundant fruit) rather than purity, it is included in the count of purities because it occurs as a counterpart to the others; thus, they are taught as the four purities (visuddhi). Considering this teaching on the four purities of offerings, in the matter of Dāna: 1. The donor being virtuous and endowed with good conduct. 2. The recipient being likewise. 3. The gift being righteously obtained.
269:
4. The strength of the three types of volition (cetanā).
5. Having faith (saddhā) and belief in kamma and its results.

These five factors are the causes for the great power of generosity (dāna).
If one is endowed with these five factors, the power of dāna is great; if these factors are deficient, it should be understood that the power of dāna diminishes.

## Matters to Note Regarding Faith (Saddhā)
Among the five factors for the great power of dāna mentioned above, it is important to understand the faith (saddhā) shown in item (5), which is belief in kamma and its results. The word 'saddhā' is translated into Burmese as 'belief' (yone-kyi-chin). If translated according to its root meaning, it should be rendered as 'the state that bears or holds well.' Just as very clear water that has settled its sediment can reflect the image of the moon or the sun, this faith, being free from the impurities of defilements (kilesa), is like bearing the qualities (guṇa) of the Buddha and other objects of meditation well within itself.

As a worldly analogy, just as people without hands cannot pick up jewels even if they see them, or as one without wealth cannot be fully equipped with various utensils, or as one without seeds cannot be endowed with crops and so on, similarly, without faith, one cannot gather the jewels of merit such as dāna, sīla, and bhāvanā. Because one cannot attain or be endowed with the bliss of humans, devas, and Nibbāna without it, the Blessed One taught that this faith is like a hand, like wealth, and like a seed.

In texts such as the Milindapañhā and the Atthasālinī, it is mentioned that this faith is like the water-clearing gem of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). Just as the water-clearing gem of a Universal Monarch can instantly make even the most turbid water clear when placed into it, faith can instantly remove all impurities of defilements in the mind and make it clear. This means that when faith is present, no disturbances such as sorrow (soka) can enter.
270:
Therefore, if Buddhist devotees repeatedly reflect on how long their minds have remained clear while focusing on the Buddha, they will realize how difficult it is to achieve a state where the mind is purely clear without any defilement while focusing on the Buddha.

Setting aside ordinary times, if while worshipping the Buddha, one's mind remains purely clear for about five minutes, focusing only on the Buddha without other objects entering, one should consider that faith (saddhā) has arisen for those five minutes. One should also practice to make this state continuous for a long time.

Regarding the belief in Kamma in the act of giving (dāna), it is called "believing in Kamma" when one can maintain a clear mind, thinking: "By giving now, a certain amount of my wealth will be spent. However, it is not spent in vain. I have gained the volition of dāna-kamma, which is many times more valuable than the wealth spent. Although the five kinds of enemies can destroy wealth, no enemy can destroy the volition of dāna-kamma. Only this volition of dāna-kamma will follow me throughout saṃsāra until I reach Nibbāna."

If one further reflects on the results of Kamma, thinking, "Because of this Kamma, I can obtain beneficial results throughout saṃsāra; there is no doubt about it," a very clear state of mind will arise in practice. This state of great clarity, arising from reflecting on the results of Kamma, is called "believing in the results of Kamma."

As explained, one should be mindful to be endowed with the Dhamma that makes the power of the fifth dāna great, by focusing on either Kamma or its results so that the clarity of mind clearly arises.

## The Chapter on the Perfection of Giving (Dāna Pāramī) ends.
271:
## (b) The Perfection of Virtue (Sīla Pāramī)

## The Camarī Animal

In this chapter on the Perfection of Virtue, the creature named Camarī used as an example should be understood only as a four-legged animal (it should not be mistakenly recorded as a species of winged bird). Both the terms 'Camara' and 'Camarī' can refer to this animal.

In the Magadha Abhidhāna (dictionary), only the term 'Camara' is included. Ancient teachers translated this term 'Camara' into Burmese as 'Aung'. The Kyaw Aung San Htar Sayadaw and the Pyay Sayadaw also translated it both as 'Aung' and as 'the animal named Camarī'. Because this animal with a magnificent tail is called 'Aung', it is composed in the Kavi-lakkhaṇa orthography text as: "The Galon (Garuda) connects, the flying spear, the Aung-tail hangs profusely." This describes hanging the Camarī tail-hair at the base of a spear to make the flying spear look beautiful.

To accurately identify this four-legged animal (translated as 'Aung' by ancient teachers) denoted by the terms 'Camara' and 'Camarī':

The Abhayārāma Sayadaw and the Taung Pauk Sayadaw of Mawlamyine, who reached the pinnacle of proficiency in various Sanskrit and Magadha (Pali) scriptures, wrote in their Abhidhāna-nissaya and Amarakoṣa-nissaya as follows:

Camaro: The animal named Camarī. The Camarī is a species of long-haired Tibetan ox (yak). Since the tail-hair of that animal is long, it is used to make fly-whisks in India and Tibet. This is called the "Cāmarī-tail fly-whisk." In Tibet, this animal is used for carrying loads, for milk, and for meat. This meaning is given based on Sanskrit medical texts and books that show animal illustrations with Pali names and describe their nature.
272:
(This is provided based on...) (From Abhayārāma Sayadaw's New Abhidhāna-nissaya, Verse 618.)

Camara: Tibetan ox. (From the same, Amarakoṣa-nissaya, Chapter 15, Verse 10.)

Camara: The noble animal named Camarī. (Vāladhippiya and Girippiya are also its names. This animal named Camarī resembles an ox and has long hair; it is used in Tibet for carrying loads, etc. The Cāmarī-tail fly-whisk is a type of fan made from its tail-hair. In Sanskrit texts, it is said to resemble a buffalo. In the Sinhalese Amarakoṣa-nissaya, it is also said to be a special animal named Camarī that resembles a buffalo and originates in the Uttarāpatha region.)

Known as Camarī, understand it as the Tibetan ox.
Its body is larger than this ox, noted for its bushy tail-hair.
In form and appearance, it is similar to a buffalo, not different.
Just as oxen are used here, they are used there.
Called the Cāmarī fly-whisk, it is made from its tail-hair.
It approaches and delights in mountainous and forested areas.
Therefore, it is widely known by the name Girippiya.
By the name Vāladhippiya, it is one that dearly loves its tail-hair.
(From Taung Pauk Sayadaw's New Abhidhāna-nissaya)

Regarding the Camarī animal in this context of Sīla Pāramī, in the Pāramī-taw-khan-pyo, Verse 71:

Until reaching the end of the four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), practicing austerity and virtue with strong effort, not considering the goal as small, the great ascetic Sumedha, who was wise and prosperous... like the Camarī, which has a beautiful and bushy tail, the pride of the forest, with a shimmering golden hue; this species of animal, by its natural habit, avoids danger, yet if its tail-hair happens to get caught in a tangled thicket or vine...
273:
...even if it gets caught and entangled, it cherishes and protects even a single strand of hair as if it were its own life. Though the animal exhausts its strength and becomes dizzy from struggling, fearing that the tip of the tail might break, it does not move even a step but stays still, ready to sacrifice its life. Without thinking foolishly that it is not worth dying for a single strand of hair, it thinks, "Even if I die, let my tail, which is a rare treasure used for royal regalia, remain undamaged and beautiful." Thus, that noble forest animal lies down and dies. May you, Sumedha, keep the extraordinary conduct of this animal in your heart.

Thus, it is composed in a way that inspires devotion.

It means that just as the Camarī animal, if even a single strand of its tail-hair gets caught in a thicket due to an unfortunate move, cherishes that hair so much that it fears it will break if it struggles with all its might (and without thinking, "I should not die for a single strand of hair"), it sacrifices its life and lies there (not allowing the tail-hair to be damaged) so that its tail, which is a rare treasure for royal regalia, may remain intact after its death; so too, you, Sumedha, should take that Camarī animal as an example and protect the tail-hair of virtue (sīla) even at the cost of your life. This is how he admonished himself.

## Detailed Points to Note Regarding Virtue (Sīla)

In this section on the Perfection of Virtue, as in the previous section on Giving, the details to be noted according to the Visuddhimagga Commentary are as follows:

(1) What state is called virtue (sīla)?
(2) For what reason is it called virtue?
(3) What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?
(4) What are the benefits of that virtue?
(5) How many kinds of virtue are there?
274:
(6) What are the causes of the defilement of virtue?
(7) What are the causes of the purification of virtue?

I shall explain by answering these seven questions as the basis. Among those seven questions:

## The Definition of Virtue (Sīla)

(1) To the question "What state is called virtue?": In the mental continuum of those who abstain from killing and so on, and those who fulfill major and minor duties, virtue consists of the Abhidhamma factors of volition (cetanā), the mental factors of abstinence (virati) known as Right Speech (sammā-vācā), Right Action (sammā-kammanta), and Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) which is non-greed (alobha), non-ill will (avyāpāda) which is non-hatred (adosa), Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) which is non-delusion (amoha), the fivefold restraint (saṃvara) to be explained in detail later, and non-transgression (avītikkama).

There are five groups of states called virtue. They are: (a) Volition (cetanā) in the continuum of one who abstains from bodily and verbal misconduct, and volition in the continuum of one who fulfills major and minor duties; (b) The three mental factors of abstinence (virati) that abstain from bodily and verbal misconduct; (c) The three states of mental good conduct, namely non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view; (d) The fivefold restraint; (e) The wholesome consciousness and mental factors that arise when one does not transgress the training rules (sikkhāpada) that should be observed, called non-transgression (avītikkama). These are the five groups of states.

## (a) Volition-Virtue (Cetanā-sīla) and (b) Abstinence-Virtue (Virati-sīla)

Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct—these three are bodily actions (kāyakamma).
Lying, slandering, harsh speech, and frivolous talk—these four verbal actions (vacīkamma) lead to the lower realms.

According to this, killing (pāṇātipāta), stealing (adinnādāna), and sexual misconduct (kāmesu micchācāra) are called the three bodily misconducts. False speech (musāvāda), slandering (pisuṇavācā), harsh and abusive speech (pharusavācā), and useless, frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) are called the four verbal misconducts.
275:
Committing these three bodily misconducts and four verbal misconducts can be done for the sake of livelihood (such as the killing done by hunters, fishermen, etc.). There are also instances of killing, etc., that are not for the sake of livelihood (such as the killing done by princes hunting for sport).

Just as there are two ways of committing these bodily and verbal misconducts—for the sake of livelihood and not for the sake of livelihood—abstaining from these misconducts is also of two kinds: abstaining from misconducts that involve livelihood and abstaining from misconducts that do not involve livelihood.

Abstaining from the three bodily misconducts not involving livelihood is called Right Action Abstinence (sammā-kammanta-virati). Abstaining from the four verbal misconducts not involving livelihood is called Right Speech Abstinence (sammā-vācā-virati). Abstaining from those three bodily and four verbal misconducts that have livelihood as their root cause, as well as from various types of wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) specifically taught for monks, is called Right Livelihood Abstinence (sammā-ājīva-virati).

The three aforementioned mental factors of abstinence are called Abstinence-Virtue (virati-sīla), and the mental factor of volition (cetanā) that arises together with those mental factors of abstinence is called Volition-Virtue (cetanā-sīla). The volition present in great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala citta) when performing major and minor duties toward teachers, preceptors, and others is also called Volition-Virtue (cetanā-sīla).

## (c) Non-covetousness and Other Virtues

Greed that looks toward the wealth of others, thinking, "If only this wealth were mine," is called the mental misconduct of covetousness (abhijjhā). In the continuum of one who abandons that mental misconduct of covetousness, the volition that causes the abandonment and the mental factor of non-greed (alobha) called non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) are called virtue. The mental factor of anger that intends the destruction of others (thinking, "May that person be ruined or die," etc.) is called the mental misconduct of ill will (vyāpāda). In the continuum of one who abandons that mental misconduct of ill will, the volition that causes the abandonment and the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa) called non-ill will (avyāpāda) are called virtue. Thinking, "There is no such thing as giving (dāna)..."
276:
The wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi cetasika) which holds that "there is no result [of actions]" and so forth, is called mental misconduct of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi manoduccarita). The volition (cetanā) that arises in the continuum of one who abandons that mental misconduct, along with the mental factor of non-delusion (amoha cetasika) known as right view (sammādiṭṭhi), is called virtue (sīla).

If the three mental misconducts—covetousness (abhijjhā), ill-will (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi)—exist, then failures in virtue (dussīlya) such as killing and so forth can occur. When the three mental wholesome conducts (manosucarita) and the volitions that abandon those mental misconducts arise, failures in virtue called dussīlya, such as killing and so forth, cannot occur. Therefore, the three mental wholesome conducts—non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill-will (abyāpāda), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi)—are called virtue (sīla).

Whenever consciousness arises, volition (cetanā) is always present. It is this volition that urges and connects the mind with its object. Just as soldering is called joining together, the act of connecting and joining the mind with its object is called urging (cetanā). If volition does not urge, the mind will not be connected with the object as the perceiver and the perceived; the mind will not stay on the object; the mind will not take the object as its focus. Because volition solders and urges, the mind can be connected with the object as the perceiver and the perceived. The mind is able to stay on the object. The mind is able to take the object as its focus. Therefore, since volition is present every time consciousness arises, all volitions associated with consciousness related to virtue should be understood as virtue (sīla).

## (d) Restraint Virtue (Saṃvara-sīla) and (e) Non-transgression Virtue (Avītikkama-sīla)

The previously mentioned virtue of volition (cetanā-sīla), virtue of abstinence (virati-sīla), and the virtues of non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view are virtues common to both laypeople and monks. Furthermore, the virtues specifically related to monks are restraint virtue (saṃvara-sīla) and non-transgression virtue (avītikkama-sīla). Among these two, restraint virtue (saṃvara-sīla) is:

(1) Pātimokkha-saṃvara = (This refers to the virtue of the training rules which causes the person who guards it to be liberated from dangers such as the four woeful states.)
277:
(2) Sati-saṃvara = (This refers to guarding the six sense faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—with unremitting mindfulness so that the thieves of unwholesome states cannot enter.)

(3) Ñāṇa-saṃvara = (This refers to the wisdom that restrains the unwholesome states of craving, wrong view, ignorance, and misconduct which tend to flow continuously like a stream. Virtue dependent on requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla) is also included in this ñāṇa-saṃvara.)

(4) Khanti-saṃvara = (This refers to restraint through patience, enduring cold, heat, and so forth, so that unwholesome states do not arise.)

(5) Vīriya-saṃvara = (This refers to the effort and restraint exercised so that sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty (micchāvitakka) cannot arise or persist in the mind. Virtue of livelihood purification (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) is also included in this vīriya-saṃvara.)

Pātimokkha, Sati, Ñāṇa, Khanti, and then Vīriya.
Guarding against and abandoning unwholesome states, these are the five restraints (saṃvara).

Non-transgression virtue (avītikkama-sīla) refers to the non-transgression of the undertaken training rules through body and speech.

The actual ultimate realities (dhammas) of the aforementioned five restraints and non-transgression are:

For pātimokkha-saṃvara, the ultimate realities are the mental factors of volition (cetanā), abstinence (virati), non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha) as shown at the beginning of the section on virtue.

For sati-saṃvara, the ultimate reality is the mental factor of mindfulness (sati). (Volition must also be present whenever mindfulness arises.)

For ñāṇa-saṃvara, the ultimate reality is the mental factor of wisdom (paññā). (Volition must also be present whenever wisdom arises.)

For khanti-saṃvara, the ultimate reality is the group of wholesome mental states led by the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa), which has the characteristic of not being angry; or simply the mental factor of non-hatred.

For vīriya-saṃvara, the ultimate reality is the mental factor of energy (vīriya). (Volition must also be present whenever energy arises.)
278:
As for avītikkama, the ultimate reality is the group of wholesome mental states that occur in the manner of not transgressing the undertaken training rules.

In the matter of giving (dāna), volition (cetanā) is the foundation. In the matter of virtue (sīla), volition is also the foundation; furthermore, the three mental factors of abstinence (virati), the three mental factors of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as the mental factors of mindfulness, wisdom, and energy, each leading in their respective roles, can be included in the group of wholesome mental states.

This concludes the explanation of the states called virtue (sīla).
**********
## Reasons for the Name Sīla

(2) Regarding the question "In what sense is it called sīla?": The word "sīla" is a Myanmar term used according to the Pali. While the Myanmar phrase "performing dāna," used according to the Pali, can be explained as "performing acts of giving and generosity," the Myanmar phrase "undertaking sīla" is often not clearly understood by many.

The word "sīla" conveys two meanings: natural character (pakati) and good conduct. Among these two:

The meaning of "natural character" is used interchangeably with the word "habit" (alaye). The usage is as follows: (pāpakaraṇasīlo) one who has the habit of doing evil, (dubbhasanasīlo) one who has the habit of speaking bad words, (abhivādanasīlo) one who has the habit of paying respect to those worthy of respect, (dhammakathanasīlo) one who has the habit of preaching the Dhamma, and so forth. The good or bad natural character of a person is expressed as "sīla" in Pali and "habit" (alaye) in Myanmar. This usage of "habit" is also applied to things where "good" or "bad" is not specifically mentioned, such as: (vassānasamaye rukkhā ruhanasīlā) trees tend to grow in the rainy season, (gimhasamaye pattā patanasīlā) leaves tend to fall in the summer, and so forth.

The meaning of "good conduct" refers only to noble things. This meaning of noble things or good conduct is what the word "sīla" in this section on virtue conveys. Regarding noble things, the word "sīla" has two meanings: (1) composing well (sīlana), and (2) upholding well (dhāraṇa).
279:
(1) "Composing well" (sīlana) means preventing bodily and vocal actions from being scattered or disordered. In the continuum of those who do not observe virtue, bodily actions and vocal speech tend to occur in a scattered manner, like an uncontrolled ball of thread. When virtue is observed, those bodily and vocal actions no longer become scattered. (Even if a person is sharp-minded or harsh, if someone else treats them in an unbearable way while they are undertaking virtue, that person might have reacted with violent bodily and vocal actions if they were not undertaking virtue. However, because they have undertaken virtue, they can control their mind and compose themselves well so that there is no violence in bodily or vocal actions. The virtue they observe restrains them so that bodily and vocal actions do not become scattered or uncontrollable.) This is the detailed meaning of the first sense, "composing well."

(2) The meaning of the second sense, "upholding well" (dhāraṇa), is that no wholesome state (kusala) can arise well without virtue. Wholesome states can arise well only in the continuum of those who possess virtue. Therefore, since virtue is the fundamental basis and root of all wholesome states, it is the state that upholds and carries out the arising of the four levels of wholesome states (catubhūmaka-kusala).

In this section on the Perfections (Pāramī), the Hermit Sumedha first contemplated the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) with his wisdom and thus admonished himself that "the Perfection of Giving must be practiced first." This does not mean that one should practice only giving (dāna) first without observing virtue (sīla). When contemplating the factors that can lead to Buddhahood, the Perfection of Giving appeared first in the Hermit Sumedha's wisdom of investigating the perfections (pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa). Therefore, it was stated: (imaṃ tvaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya) "First of all, undertake this Perfection of Giving firmly and fulfill it to the highest degree." It does not mean that one must practice giving first before practicing virtue at all.
280:
The perfections are arranged and taught as first, second, and so forth, not to show the order of practice, but to show the order in which they appeared in the wisdom of investigating the perfections (pāramī-pavicaya-ñāṇa). All ten perfections cannot appear in wisdom simultaneously at the same moment. Because it appeared first in wisdom, the teaching began with the Perfection of Giving. However, in practice, only when one practices giving while established in virtue can there be purity of the gift (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi) on one's own part. Only when giving is preceded by the undertaking and practice of virtue can it yield greater benefits.

For this reason, when lay devotees invite the Saṅgha to offer robes and other offerings, the monks (even if the original invitation did not include a request to give precepts) first administer the precepts (sīla) before allowing the offerings to be made.

Based on these points, if asked "Why is it called sīla?", one should answer clearly: (1) because it composes bodily and vocal actions well, making them refined and gentle instead of allowing them to be coarse and violent; and (2) because it serves as the fundamental basis to uphold and bring about the four types of wholesome states—namely, sense-sphere wholesome, fine-material-sphere wholesome, immaterial-sphere wholesome, and supramundane wholesome states.

In this regard:

Virtue composes well, and concentration (samādhi) also composes well. How does the composing of virtue differ from that of concentration? Also, the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) supports well, and virtue also supports well. How does their supporting differ? These are possible questions.

The answer is: Virtue prevents bodily and vocal actions from being scattered; it composes them well so they are calm and peaceful. Concentration...
281:
(ဎီ)
It well-establishes the mind and mental factors associated with it so that they do not scatter toward various objects but remain concentrated on a single object. This manner of well-establishing is distinctive.

Virtue (sīla) is the fundamental cause for the arising of wholesome states of the four planes (catu-bhūmaka kusala). This being the fundamental cause for the arising of these wholesome states is what is meant by saying it "well-carries" (rūpaharana) them so that they arise. Just as a nurse carries a prince to prevent him from wandering aimlessly and falling into disorder, or as the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) provides support for co-nascent (sahajāta) material phenomena so they are well-established and do not scatter—this providing of support is called "well-carrying." Thus, the earth element well-carries co-nascent material phenomena so they do not scatter. Virtue carries wholesome states of the four planes by being their fundamental cause for arising. This manner of well-carrying is distinctive. (From the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, Sīlaniddesa).

In the Visuddhimagga Commentary, it is stated: "Only the two meanings previously shown are the meanings permitted by grammarians for the word 'sīla.' Other teachers, however, say that the word 'sīla' is derived from 'sira' or 'sīsa.' The words 'sira' and 'sīsa' mean 'the head.' Just as when the head of a living being is severed, the entire body perishes, so too when virtue perishes, all wholesome states perish. Therefore, because virtue is like the head of all wholesome states, it is intended to be 'sira' or 'sīsa,' but through the transformation of letters, it is called 'sīla.'

Alternatively, in the world, the cooling of heat is called 'sītala' in Pali. Since virtue cools all the heat of defilements within the continuity of beings, it is intended to be 'sītala,' but by dropping the middle letter 'ta,' it is called 'sīla.' In such ways, they explain the meaning of the word 'sīla.'"
282:
(ဎု)
The explanations of those other teachers do not provide the meaning derived from the actual root of the word 'sīla'; they are merely conceptual derivations based on the linguistic nature of the words 'sira,' 'sīsa,' and 'sītala,' which are phonetically similar to 'sīla.' Only the two meanings previously shown—'well-establishing' and 'well-carrying'—are the original meanings of the word 'sīla.'

The collection of meanings for the term 'sīla' mentioned above is based on the second of the two meanings—'natural disposition' (sabhāva) and 'good conduct' (suvatta)—found in verse 1092 of the Magadha Abhidhāna: "Sīlaṃ sabhāve suvatte..."

The reason for calling it 'sīla' can also be understood through the first meaning, 'natural disposition.' How can this be understood? Although the meaning 'natural disposition' can include various types of nature, both good and bad, as previously shown, it is the habit of the noble ones and Bodhisattas of the past to practice and cultivate virtuous conduct. In the world, although the word 'Dhamma' includes both wholesome and unwholesome states, when taking refuge with the words "I go to the Dhamma for refuge," one must take only the noble supramundane Dhamma which is worthy of refuge. Similarly, although 'Saṅgha' means a group or assembly, and there are various types of assemblies such as human assemblies (manussa-saṅgha) or bird assemblies (sakuṇa-saṅgha), when taking refuge with the words "I go to the Saṅgha for refuge," one must take only the assembly of the highest Noble Ones (ariya). Likewise, in this context, although there are various habits, in the matter of the practice related to the Perfections (pāramī) that must be fulfilled, one must take only the habitual practice of the noble ones and Bodhisattas of the past. If the meaning is taken in this way, the first meaning from the Abhidhāna, 'natural disposition,' should also be used in this context of virtue. According to this view, the reason for being called 'sīla' should be answered as: it is called 'sīla' because it is the habitual practice of the noble ones and Bodhisattas of the past.

This is the reason for being called 'sīla.'

283:
(ဎူ)
## Characteristics, etc., of Virtue
(3) To the question: "What are the characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause of virtue?"
The answer is: Virtue has the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of well-composing, so that bodily actions and so on do not fall into disorder. (Alternatively) It has the characteristic of being the fundamental basis of all wholesome states. It has the function (rasa) of destroying the state of being one who lacks virtue, such as bodily and verbal misconduct. (Alternatively) It has the function of achievement (sampatti), being endowed with the quality of faultlessness. (Being in a state of Dhamma that is not blamed by wise and noble ones is called being endowed with the quality of faultlessness). It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of the state of purity of bodily actions and so on. (This means that when wise and noble ones reflect on what kind of thing virtue is, it appears in their knowledge that virtue is indeed the purity of bodily action, the purity of verbal action, and the purity of mental action). It has the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the two states: shame (hirī) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa). (Hearing the True Dhamma and so on are distant causes for the arising of virtue; since one can only undertake and guard virtue when shame and fear of wrongdoing are present, these two are the proximate causes of virtue.)

This is the explanation of the characteristics and so on of virtue.
**********
## The Benefits and Advantages of Virtue
(4) To the question: "What are the benefits of that virtue?"
The answer is: Virtue has the benefit and advantage of being able to make the heart of the practitioner joyful and pleasant, and of obtaining many other qualities. By the words "and so on," it is meant that for one whose heart is joyful and pleasant, there arises gladness (pāmojja), which is tender rapture. For one who has gladness, there arises rapture (pīti), which is mature joy. For one who has rapture, there arises tranquility (passaddhi) of body and mind. For one who has tranquility, there arises happiness (sukha) of body and mind. For one who has happiness, there arises concentration (samādhi). For one who has concentration, there arises the knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa).
284:
(ဎေ)
For one who has the knowledge of things as they really are, there arises strong insight knowledge (balava-vipassanā-ñāṇa) known as disenchantment (nibbidā) with the suffering of the round of rebirth and conditioned things. For one who has strong insight knowledge, there arises the Path (magga), which is free from craving. For one who has the Path, there arises the Fruition of Arahantship, which is called liberation (vimutti). For one who has the Fruition of Arahantship, there arises reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), which reflects on the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. For one who has reviewing knowledge, one can attain Parinibbāna without any remaining aggregates. In this way, virtue has the benefit of enabling one to obtain many qualities up to the attainment of Parinibbāna. (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 3, p. 515).

Alternatively:
1. A virtuous person, being endowed with virtue, can acquire great wealth based on heedfulness (appamāda) in guarding their virtue.
2. A virtuous person can have a good reputation and fame that spreads and prevails.
3. A virtuous person, when approaching any of the four assemblies—the assembly of rulers, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, or the assembly of monastics—can enter confidently without fear or hesitation, and with a bright countenance (because of their own virtue).
4. A virtuous person, when dying at the end of their lifespan, dies unconfused. (A non-virtuous person always feels remorse near the time of death, thinking, "I have not done good deeds," etc. A virtuous person has no such remorse; because their wholesome kamma and so on appear at that moment, they die with a clear mind, without confusion or fear, like one who discards an earthenware pot to receive a golden one).
5. A virtuous person, after death, is reborn in a happy destination (sugati), such as the human or celestial realms.

These benefits and advantages can be obtained. (Dīgha Nikāya, Vol. 2, p. 73; Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 2, p. 221; Vinaya, Vol. 3, p. 322.)
285:
(ဎဲ)
Furthermore, in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya, it is taught that one can obtain benefits starting from being loved and respected by fellow practitioners up to the Fruition of Arahantship. Please take the details from the Burmese translation of the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta.

This is the explanation of the benefits and advantages of virtue.

## Classifications of Virtue
## Dyads of Virtue
(5) To the question: "How many classifications of virtue are there?"
The classifications of virtue that should be obtained are: Virtue is of two kinds, namely, virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla) and virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla). Among these two:

Regarding the types of training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed Buddha, there are two kinds: one kind of training rule that is prescribed as "this action must be performed" (referring to duties toward a preceptor, duties toward a teacher, etc.), and another kind of training rule that is prescribed as "this action must not be performed" (referring to Pārājika training rules, etc.). Among these two, following, performing, and fulfilling the training rules such as duties toward a preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta) and duties toward a teacher (ācariya-vatta) according to the Buddha's intention is called *cāritta-sīla*. Guarding by abstaining and not performing the Pārājika training rules and so on, which are prescribed as "this action must not be performed," according to the Buddha's intention is called *vāritta-sīla*. This is the summary of the meaning.

The distinction between these two, *cāritta-sīla* and *vāritta-sīla*, is commonly explained as follows:

"The kind of virtue where there is no fault if not practiced, but if practiced, it leads to progress and purity of virtue, is called *cāritta-sīla*. The virtue of guarding and not transgressing, even at the cost of one's life, those things forbidden by the Blessed Buddha as 'not to be done,' is called *vāritta-sīla*."

This is often answered without distinguishing between monastics and laypeople. In fact, for monastics, there are duties such as the *upajjhāya-vatta* prescribed by the Blessed Buddha as "these actions must be performed." For pupils (saddhivihārika) and others who do not fulfill or perform these duties, it concerns *cāritta-sīla*.
286:
Because failing to fulfill duties results in the Vinaya offense of the dukkhaṭa of breaking a duty (vattabheda), for monks, one should not say "there is no fault even if not practiced." Rather, it should be answered that following and fulfilling the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Buddha as "this must be done" according to His will is called Cāritta Sīla (morality of performance).

For laypeople, in distinguishing between Cāritta and Vāritta, even if the unwholesome acts to be avoided are the same: (1) Any unwholesome act that has the nature of definitely yielding rebirth in the lower realms (apāya-paṭisandhi); abstaining from such unwholesome acts that definitely yield rebirth in the lower realms is called Vāritta Sīla (morality of avoidance). (2) Any unwholesome act that may or may not yield rebirth in the lower realms; abstaining from such unwholesome acts, as well as showing respect to elders and so on, should be answered as Cāritta Sīla.

For example, among the Five Precepts practiced by laypeople, the unwholesome acts to be avoided—killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, speaking falsehood, and drinking intoxicants—can definitely yield rebirth in the lower realms if committed. Therefore, abstaining from such unwholesome acts that can definitely yield rebirth in the lower realms (the Five Precepts) is called Vāritta Sīla.

Among the Eight Precepts practiced by laypeople, the four—pāṇātipāta, adinnādāna, musāvāda, and surāmeraya—are only Vāritta Sīla as previously stated. Regarding the remaining four, such as abrahmacariya (unholy conduct) or engaging with one's own spouse, eating at the wrong time (after noon), watching or listening to dancing, singing, and music, and sleeping on high and noble seats—when Noble Ones like Sotāpannas and Sakadāgāmīs engage in these, they do so only with a mind dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhi-vippayutta), which does not lead to the lower realms. Ordinary worldlings (puthujjanas), however, may engage in them with either a mind associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi-sampayutta) or dissociated from wrong view, which may or may not lead to the lower realms. Therefore, in abstaining from these remaining four, such as abrahmacariya, it should be called Cāritta Sīla out of consideration for the Sotāpanna and Sakadāgāmī Noble Ones.
287:
A lay devotee (upāsaka) established in the Three Refuges can become a virtuous upāsaka simply by strictly observing the Five Precepts. Observing the Eight Precepts is an advancement to practice a higher noble life. There is no teaching stating that "only by observing the Eight Precepts can one avoid the lower realms; one cannot escape the danger of the lower realms by merely observing the Five Precepts." Therefore, the latter four precepts included in the Eight Precepts, such as abrahmacariya-virati and vikālabhojana-virati, should be included under Cāritta Sīla.

For monks, however, since the Buddha has taught and forbidden engaging in unholy conduct, eating at the wrong time, watching or listening to dancing, singing, and music, and sleeping on high and noble seats, the morality of abstaining from (not doing) these four types of actions must definitely be called Vāritta Sīla.

## Points to Note

In the aforementioned Eight Precepts, one might read the explanations distinguishing Cāritta Sīla and Vāritta Sīla superficially or without care. Or, by superficially and lightly considering the domestic life, eating after noon, watching shows, and using noble seats by Noble Ones like Visākhā, one might wrongly believe that "engaging in sensual pleasures with one's own property, eating after noon, watching shows, and using noble seats are entirely without fault." Having thus erred, one might further indulge in these things in association with wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), becoming more and more mistaken. Special care should be taken to avoid such errors.

One should consider with great mindfulness: acts such as killing living beings, stealing others' property, misconduct in forbidden objects (others' spouses), and drinking intoxicants can in no way be performed such that they do not become unwholesome courses of action (akusala kamma-patha) or causes for rebirth in the lower realms. If these acts are committed, they definitely constitute unwholesome kamma-patha that leads to the lower realms. If these acts are committed, they can cause one to reach the lower realms. Therefore, Noble Ones—
288:
—even if forced to do those acts with a sword over their heads, would rather sacrifice their lives than commit them. They have already completely uprooted, by means of the Path (Magga), the unwholesome roots and underlying tendencies (anusaya) that cause such acts.

As for eating after noon and so on, worldlings (puthujjanas) do them, and Noble Ones like Sotāpannas and Sakadāgāmīs also do them. In doing so, it is not proper to say that because the manner of eating or acting is the same, the internal mental state is also the same. Indeed, the perception of any conditioned thing (saṅkhāra) as happiness (sukha) by Noble Ones is not the same as the perception by worldlings. (The manner in which Noble Ones use sensual objects (vatthukāma) is not the same as the manner in which ordinary worldlings use them.) Regarding the perception and use of any conditioned thing or sensual object as happiness by Noble Ones, it is explained (in the Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 353):

"Diṭṭhi-vippayutta-cittena pana ariyasāvako pariḷāhābhibhūto pariḷāhavūpasamatthaṃ mattahatthi-parittāsito viya cokkhabrāhmaṇo gūthaṃ kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati" = Just as a very pure Brahmin, being chased by a rutting elephant, might resort to a place with excrement and filth despite his loathing and lack of desire to go there, simply to escape the danger of that elephant; so too, when a Noble Disciple is oppressed by the heat of sensual lust (kāmarāga) which has not yet been abandoned by the Path (and which does not lead to the lower realms), the Sotāpanna or Sakadāgāmī perceives a certain conditioned thing as happiness only with a mind dissociated from wrong view, in order to cool the danger of that heat of defilement.

This commentary explanation should be deeply reflected upon and noted. Using Visākhā and others as a basis or shield for their words, some ordinary worldlings might wrongly think that their own enjoyment of sensual pleasures is no different and is identical to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by Visākhā and others. Considering the cited commentary, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by Sotāpanna and Sakadāgāmī Noble Ones is—(like the pure Brahmin who, only because he is chased by an elephant, runs into a place with excrement to escape the elephant's danger despite his loathing)—
289:
—enjoyed only with a mind dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhi-vippayutta) to cool the heat of the danger of sensual lust (kāmarāga) which has not yet been abandoned. The enjoyment of sensual pleasures by ordinary worldlings is mostly done with a mind associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi-sampayutta).

The point is: engaging in one's own sensual objects, eating after noon, watching shows, and using noble seats—these four acts can be done with a mind associated with wrong view, or they can be done with a mind dissociated from wrong view which does not lead to the lower realms. Therefore, (since they do not definitely lead to the lower realms but are uncertain), the meaning is that abstaining from these four (morality) should be included in Cāritta Sīla rather than Vāritta Sīla.

Such a distinction of the Eight Precepts into four Cāritta and four Vāritta is for the morality where each training rule (sikkhāpada) is undertaken individually, as is done nowadays. If, however, they are not undertaken individually but are undertaken collectively as "Aṭṭhaṅga-samannāgataṃ uposatha-sīlaṃ samādiyāmi" (I undertake the Uposatha Sīla endowed with eight factors), then that collectively undertaken Uposatha Sīla should only be Cāritta Sīla. The reason is that one may observe the Uposatha Sīla (Eight Precepts) if one wishes, or remain without observing it if one does not wish. (For a person who holds Buddhist views, only if the minimum Five Precepts are intact can they be a virtuous upāsaka. Beyond that, if capable, one should observe the Eight Precepts. Even if one cannot and does not observe them, if the Five Precepts are intact, one can still be a virtuous upāsaka. Only when the Five Precepts are complete and intact for anyone holding Buddhist views does one become a Buddhist according to the Buddha's will.) In the Eight Precepts undertaken collectively in this way, there is no longer a need to distinguish one part as Cāritta and another as Vāritta; only in the case of undertaking each training rule individually should they be divided into Cāritta and Vāritta as appropriate.
290:
In the case of the Five Precepts, whether they are undertaken individually or collectively, they are only Vāritta Sīla. For laypeople, following the group of practices that the Buddha taught as being good to practice like monks is indeed Cāritta Sīla. (The details of how to practice and abstain from these Cāritta Sīla and Vāritta Sīla were described above in the Miscellaneous Section.)

Between these two, Cāritta Sīla and Vāritta Sīla, only a person who has both faith (saddhā) and effort (vīriya) can strive to fulfill Cāritta Sīla. Believing that "if I practice these, it will be a good practice and will yield good results in the future" is faith. Striving to carry them out without laziness is effort. It means that Cāritta Sīla can be fulfilled only by one who, after believing that there will be benefit in practicing this, strives to complete the practice according to that belief. In Vāritta Sīla, there is no special effort or exertion to be made; it can be fulfilled simply by abstaining from and not doing the unwholesome acts that the Buddha taught should not be done. There is no need to exert special effort; it can be fulfilled simply by having faith in the Buddha's teaching.

Alternatively, there are two types: Ābhisamācārika Sīla and Ādibrahmacariyaka Sīla. Among these two, the group of morality excluding Ājīvaṭṭhamaka Sīla, which will be explained later, is called Ābhisamācārika Sīla. (Abhi = excellent/noble; samācāra = good conduct; abhisamācāra = noble and good conduct. Abhisamācāra refers to the morality of the Path and Fruition by the method of excellence. The morality taught and prescribed to fulfill that Path and Fruition morality is called Ābhisamācārika Sīla.)

Ājīvaṭṭhamaka Sīla is called Ādibrahmacariyaka Sīla. (Ādi = beginning; brahmacariya = the noble practice of the Ariyan Path; ādibrahmacariya = the very beginning of the noble practice of the Ariyan Path. The morality taught as the group of dhammas that must be practiced and fulfilled at the very beginning to attain that noble practice of the Ariyan Path is called Ādibrahmacariyaka Sīla.)
291:
(ṇā)
This Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla (Morality with Livelihood as the Eighth), known as Ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla (Morality of the Beginning of the Holy Life), consists of these eight factors: the three wholesome bodily actions of abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct; the four wholesome verbal actions of abstaining from false speech, abstaining from slandering speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous or mythical talk that lacks essence like empty husks but is spoken to make others believe; and abstaining from wrong livelihood. It is called Ājīvaṭṭhamaka because livelihood (ājīva) is the eighth (aṭṭhamaka) factor of this morality. In the Visuddhimagga Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, this Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is explained as Ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla according to the first method. This commentary is often misinterpreted, misunderstood, and misspoken.

The way it is misinterpreted and misspoken is as follows: Based on the statement that the beginning of the Noble Ariya Path is Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla, some mistakenly say that only Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is the morality to be practiced at the start to attain the Noble Path. They wrongly claim that the five precepts, eight precepts, and ten precepts commonly used today are not the kind of morality to be practiced at the start to attain the Noble Path. A certain sect even emerged holding such views.

Others say, "We have never heard of Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla; this Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla being spoken of so strangely now is not the Buddha's teaching, but a later, useless form of morality." In truth, Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is indeed a morality taught by the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught this Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla as recorded in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi, page 337 (Vagga 5, Sutta 7), which the commentator himself points out in the Visuddhimagga Aṭṭhakathā, Volume 1, page 12, quoting: "Tenāha pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotīti." Therefore, it should not be said that it is not the Buddha's teaching.

The Blessed One appeared in a world overwhelmed by the darkness of misconduct (duccarita). To those who were initially steeped in misconduct,
292:
(ṇi)
When the Buddha wished to discipline beings with the practice of morality, because they were beings with gross misconduct, he initially disciplined them with Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla, which was suitable for those with such coarse misconduct. After disciplining them with this Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla and when their (gross) misconduct had diminished and decreased, he ceased using Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla and consistently taught and used only the five precepts and eight precepts.

Thus, although Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla was prevalent when the Blessed One first began teaching and disciplining those with gross misconduct, as beings became more refined, Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla was set aside. Consequently, up to the present time, teachers and the Saṅgha do not specifically preach its use, and laypeople no longer specifically undertake and practice it. (This is because Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is intended for those with very thick, coarse misconduct.)

A question may arise: "Since this Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is the beginning practice of the Noble Path and was the morality used when the Buddha first appeared, would it not be even more appropriate to undertake and practice it now?" The answer is: The "beginning" of the Noble Path refers to the start of practice only for those who previously had no foundation in the Noble Path's practice at all. While those transitioning from false views to Buddhist views should practice Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla at the start, for those whose Buddhist views are already mature, they have already matured in the practice of Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla from before; thus, even if they undertake it now, it should no longer be called the practice that is the "beginning" of the Noble Path. For those with mature Buddhist views, let alone the parents, even the children of such good parents, according to their parents' instructions, believe and know from a young age that committing gross misconduct such as killing results in great hell, and thus they abstain. When these children grow up and undertake morality, (since they have already
293:
(ṇī)
abstained from the gross misconduct that should be avoided through Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla since childhood), they should proceed to fulfill the five precepts, eight precepts, and ten precepts in order. To put it another way, Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is the morality taught to discipline those who are steeped in misconduct and have never had even a scent of morality, to make them abstain from those coarse misdeeds. It is very clear that for the aforementioned children who received parental guidance from a young age, they are no longer steeped in gross misconduct, and thus there is no special need to fulfill Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla. This statement is made based on the present era where the Sāsana is flourishing.
