However, if one realizes of oneself, "Although it is said that most people abstain from gross misconduct from the age they can understand their parents' words, I have never abstained and have only committed every gross misconduct I encountered," then that person must indeed undertake Ādibrahmacariyaka (Ājīvaṭṭhamaka) morality. This is because, for such a person, the practice to attain the Noble Ariya Path must begin only now.

Regarding this Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla, if someone were to preach, "Since this morality does not include the Surāmeraya (alcohol) precept, one can keep this morality while drinking; since it does not include the Naccagīta (dancing and singing) precept, one can keep this morality while watching shows. Therefore, this morality can be easily practiced without any strictness or difficulty. It is also the true cause for attaining the Path and Fruition," those who prefer the easy way would be very pleased.

In the world, beings generally prefer the easy way in everything. Although people strive day and night to obtain treasures like gold and silver, they cannot always get them as planned. Despite knowing how difficult they are to obtain, if some scammers claim they can easily turn one tical of gold into two ticals, people become very excited and entrust all their bits of gold and silver to the teacher. In the end,
294:
(ṇu)
when the teacher cannot make it increase and instead runs away with all the gold and silver given, they suffer great mental distress because they were cheated of their gold and silver. This happens because they preferred the easy way.

Just as with worldly wealth and treasures, there can be teachers who entice and deceive regarding the Path and Fruition, which are extremely difficult to attain. If they preach, "If you practice my method, you can become a Sotāpanna in seven days; if your wisdom is sharp, you can progress to become a Sakadāgāmi, etc.," those who like the easy way believe they will easily become Sotāpanna, Sakadāgāmi, and so on, and they do whatever that teacher commands. When seven days have passed and the teacher says, "You have become a Sotāpanna, you have become a Sakadāgāmi, you have succeeded in so many stages," they truly believe it just as the teacher says.

In this matter, a point worth noting is that in the world, if a block of brass is melted and struck with alchemical mercury and truly becomes gold, the state of the original brass and the state after becoming gold will be vastly different. Similarly, the state of an ordinary worldling (puthujjana) and the state of an Ariya (Noble One) who has attained a Path and Fruition must be immensely different in terms of the coarseness or refinement of their bodily, verbal, and mental actions. One should not remain satisfied and truly believe just because a teacher says one has become an Ariya. Instead, one should reflect on oneself: "How have my bodily, verbal, and mental actions changed in terms of coarseness or refinement compared to my previous state?" Only when one finds a truly extraordinary condition should one consider and believe the teacher's words that one has become an Ariya. Believing too easily will only lead to error.

In the same way, regarding morality, even the lowest level, the five precepts, is difficult and impossible for a drinker to maintain. As for the eight precepts and others, it goes without saying; they are even more difficult.
295:
(ṇူ)
Thus, whether in the matter of morality or anything else, those who prefer the easy way should be very careful and mindful that they may not obtain the genuine thing and may live believing a counterfeit to be real.

All morality other than the aforementioned Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is called Ābhisamācārika-sīla. Even the five precepts are a practice superior to Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla. Here, a question arises again:

"In the five precepts, only one of the four verbal misconducts, Musāvāda (false speech), is included for abstention. In Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla, however, all four verbal misconducts are included for abstention. Considering this point, should it not be said that the five precepts are inferior to Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla?"

The answer is: Among the four verbal actions (verbal misconduct), the misconduct of Musāvāda is the root cause for committing all other misconducts. The Buddha taught that for one who commits Musāvāda, there is no misconduct they would not dare to do. One who can abstain from Musāvāda can easily abstain from the remaining three verbal misconducts. How could one who does not even speak a lie speak slandering speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech? Therefore, among the four verbal misconducts, only abstaining from Musāvāda is primarily included in the teaching of the five precepts. Thus, there is no reason to say that Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is superior to the five precepts. Again, a question arises:

"The act of abstaining from wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) is not in the five precepts, but only in Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla. Because of this abstention from wrong livelihood, can it not be said that Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla is nobler than the five precepts?"

The brief answer is: For one who maintains the five precepts, there is no longer much specific wrong livelihood to be avoided. Indeed...
296:
(ṇa)
Wrong livelihood (micchājīva) refers to making a living by consuming resources obtained through misconduct. The misconducts that generally lead to the acquisition of wealth and property are: killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), taking what is not given (adinnādāna), and false speech (musāvāda). In the world, wealth is mostly acquired by engaging in these three misconducts. For a person who strictly observes the Five Precepts, they have already directly abstained from these three misconducts. Furthermore, by abstaining from false speech, they no longer engage in making a living through other misconducts. Therefore, it should not be said that for laypeople, the Morality with Livelihood as the Eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) is superior to the Five Precepts for the sake of abstaining from wrong livelihood. (This explanation is provided for laypeople.)

For monks... the collection of training rules and morality regarding abstaining from minor offenses and even smaller offenses is called ābhisamācārika-sīla (morality regarding minor conduct). The collection of training rules and morality regarding abstaining from major offenses (gross offenses) is called ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla (morality fundamental to the holy life). (This means that the collection of training rules observed to avoid the Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa offenses, which are designated as heavy offenses (garuka-āpatti), is called ādibrahmacariya-sīla. The collection of training rules observed to avoid the remaining five groups of offenses, which are designated as light offenses (lahuka-āpatti), is called ābhisamācārika-sīla.)

Alternatively... among the five books of the Vinaya, the collection of training rules contained in the first two books (Pārājika-pāḷi and Pācittiya-pāḷi, known as the Ubhatovibhaṅga) is called ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla. The collection of training rules included in the Mahāvagga-pāḷi and Cullavagga-pāḷi, known as the Khandhakavagga, is called ābhisamācārika-sīla. (The final book, Parivāra-pāḷi, is mostly a summary of the teachings found in the preceding four books of the Vinaya.)

(For monks, only when ābhisamācārika-sīla is fulfilled can ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla be fulfilled. Indeed, if a monk abstains even from light offenses (lahuka-āpatti)—offenses of minor consequence—it goes without saying that he will certainly abstain from the very heavy offenses (garuka-āpatti).)
297:
(ṇe)
Alternatively, there are two types: morality of abstinence (virati-sīla) and morality of non-abstinence (avirati-sīla). Between these two, as previously explained in the section "What is called Sīla?" on page (ḍo) where the essence of morality is identified, the three mental factors of abstinence—Right Speech (sammā-vācā), Right Action (sammā-kammanta), and Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva)—are called virati-sīla. The remaining group of states, such as volition (cetanā), is called avirati-sīla.

In another way, morality is of two types: dependent morality (nissita-sīla) and independent morality (anissita-sīla). Of these two, morality observed depending on either craving (taṇhā) or wrong view (diṭṭhi) is called nissita-sīla. (Morality practiced with the desire for success in future lives or success in wealth, thinking, "By this morality, may I attain a noble life and noble wealth in the next existence," is called morality dependent on craving. The kind of morality practiced by those with wrong views, such as the cow-practice or dog-practice, mistakenly believing that they will be purified from the cycle of rebirth through such habits, is called morality dependent on wrong view (diṭṭhi-nissita-sīla). Noble Buddhist followers would not observe this diṭṭhi-nissita-sīla; they might only mistakenly observe taṇhā-nissita-sīla. One should be mindful not to observe it in this way.) Morality observed without depending on the aforementioned craving and wrong view, but with the sole intention of "I shall practice the holy life," (or) morality associated with the Paths and Fruits (magga-phala), and the mundane morality that serves as the foundation for that supramundane morality, are called independent morality (anissita-sīla).

In another way, there are two types: time-limited morality (kālapariyanta-sīla) and life-long morality (āpāṇakoṭika-sīla). Of these two, morality observed by defining a desired period of time is called kālapariyanta-sīla. Morality observed for the rest of one's life without defining a time limit is called āpāṇakoṭika-sīla.

Regarding time-limited morality, the Visuddhimagga Commentary explains it as "morality undertaken after making a time limit" (kālaparicchedaṃ katvā samādinnaṃ sīlaṃ). The Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā further explains "making a time limit" as "making a limit by way of time, such as 'for this night and for this day'" (kālaparicchedaṃ katvāti imañca rattiṃ imañca divanti ādinā viya kālavasena paricchedaṃ katvā). The meaning is that according to the Commentary...
298:
(ṇo)
...the method of defining the time should be done by the power of time, such as defining it as "for this whole night and for this whole day," and so on.

When people nowadays receive precepts, there is no explicit definition of time. They undertake them by saying, "Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi" (I undertake the training rule of abstaining from killing living beings). Although it seems as if they are undertaking it for their whole life, since the intention in the mind of the practitioner is only for a single day, that undertaken morality is merely time-limited morality (kālapariyanta-sīla) defined by the period of one day. Considering the explanations in the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries, one should undertake the precepts by including words that indicate the desired time for kālapariyanta-sīla. Even if those words defining the time limit are not included, there is no fault; it remains kālapariyanta-sīla.

In the current practice of undertaking precepts, although the words of limitation are absent, the purpose of one day is fulfilled by intention. Thus, some might think, "Morality is only good to observe if it is kept for the whole day, the whole night, or a full day and night." However, in the commentary to the Sīlamayañāṇa-niddesa of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is stated:
(Katamoti kālapariyanto, upāsakopāsikā dānaṃ dadamānā parivesanapariyantaṃ sīlaṃ samādiyanti, vihāragatā vihārapariyantaṃ sīlaṃ samādiyanti, ekaṃ vā dve vā tayo vā bhiyyo vā rattidivāni paricchedaṃ katvā sīlaṃ samādiyanti, ayaṃ kālapariyanto.)

The meaning is: What is morality with a time limit (kālapariyanta-sīla)? Laymen and laywomen who frequently visit the Three Jewels undertake precepts while giving alms, until the completion of the act of giving. (This means they observe the precepts while inviting the Saṅgha to their home and offering food; after the offering, they do not continue to observe them.) This is what is called "one-sitting morality" (tathaing-thila) nowadays. When they go to a monastery, they undertake morality for the duration of their stay at the monastery.
299:
(ṇau)
They observe morality by defining nights and days, such as for one day, or two days, or even more than that. Such observed moralities are called time-limited morality (kālapariyanta-sīla).

Based on this Commentary, it is evident that one can observe morality not just for a whole day, but even for the duration of offering alms to the Saṅgha at home, or for the duration of one's stay at a monastery. Such observed morality is called kālapariyanta-sīla. Therefore, if one wishes to undertake it by defining a period during the night, one can do so; if one wishes to undertake it by defining a period during the day, one can do so. For this reason, teachers have said, "Children who cannot yet abstain from the evening meal on Uposatha days should be encouraged to undertake the Uposatha precepts by defining the time for the morning period." As they have said, it is also logically appropriate. The reason is that it cannot be said that merit is gained only if the holy life is practiced for a whole day, and not if it is practiced for a part; merit is gained for as much as one is able to practice.

Evidence for this can be found in the Petavatthu Pāḷi, (3) Cūḷavagga, (7) Migaluddaka-petavatthu and (8) Dutiya-migaluddaka-petavatthu. A summary of these two stories is as follows:

During the time of the Buddha, there was a hunter in the city of Rājagaha who made a living by killing and harming deer both day and night. One of the hunter's friends was a lay follower (upāsaka) who took refuge in the Three Jewels. That lay friend spoke to and tried to stop the hunter from the misconduct of killing animals entirely, but when he could not succeed, he finally persuaded him, saying, "Friend, come. If you cannot abstain for the whole day, then abstain from the misconduct of killing living beings during the night." Thus, during the night...
300:
(ṇaṃ)
...he established him in the practice of merit. Following the instructions of his lay friend, that hunter abstained from his usual misconducts (such as preparing arrows and traps) during the night, and performed the act of killing animals only during the day.

Later, when that hunter died, he became a Vemānika-peta (a ghost with a mansion, experiencing mixed results) near the city of Rājagaha. He suffered great misery during the day, but at night, he enjoyed sensual pleasures, being fully endowed with the five types of sensual objects.

When the Venerable Nārada saw that ghost and inquired about his past meritorious deeds, the ghost replied that he had been a hunter in his past life. Although his friend, a lay follower with great faith, had forbidden him from doing evil, he had been accustomed to and enjoyed evil for a long time, and thus could not fully follow his friend's advice (following only half of it without total opposition). Due to the meritorious deed of undertaking and practicing morality only at night while continuing to commit the misconduct of killing living beings during the day as usual, he had now become a Vemānika-peta. Because of the unwholesome kamma of the misconduct committed during the day, he suffered great misery during the day. Because of the wholesome merit of the morality undertaken and practiced at night, he enjoyed celestial pleasures during the night. (This is the summary of the 7th Migaluddaka-peta story.) In the 8th story of the hunter-ghost, it is the story of a hunter who did not listen to his lay friend's warnings but only observed morality at night after being exhorted by an Arahant who came to that lay follower's house for alms.

Based on these stories of the hunter-ghosts, it is clear that even if one cannot observe morality during the day and only observes it during the night, that morality can yield good results during the night. Therefore, it is very appropriate to observe morality within whatever period of time one is capable of.
301:
Alternatively, there are two kinds of virtue: (1) Saparitanta-sīla and (2) Aparitanta-sīla. In essence, this means virtue that is limited and virtue that is unlimited.

(1) If a person who has undertaken the Uposatha virtue for the whole day is told by someone, "Friend, break your virtue now and I will give you a thousand [pieces of money]," and they break it, that virtue is called limited (saparitanta) virtue. (This means the virtue ends at the moment it is broken, not lasting the intended full day because of wealth.) Similarly, virtue that is broken because one is told that followers will be given if it is broken, or that relatives will be killed if it is not broken, or that limbs will be severed, or that one's life will be taken—such virtue is called limited (saparitanta) virtue. In short, virtue that is broken because of any of these five—wealth, followers, relatives, limbs, or life—is called limited (saparitanta) virtue.

(2) Virtue that is well-observed as intended and cannot be broken by these five means is called unlimited (aparitanta) virtue. (This means virtue that does not perish or end due to disturbances before the intended time is reached.)

(In the case of the former saparitanta-sīla, although it is destroyed due to bribery etc., the virtue observed prior to its destruction is still a meritorious deed of virtue that can produce good results. It should not be said that it is not virtue. Considering that even if virtue undertaken for a whole day is broken later, it remains a virtue that can bring benefits for the earlier portion, one should believe without doubt that virtue undertaken for a specific period to the best of one's ability is noble virtue.)

Alternatively, there are two kinds: Lokiya-sīla (mundane virtue) and Lokuttara-sīla (supramundane virtue). Virtue that is an object of the taints (āsavas) (i.e., virtue that can be taken as an object by the taints) is called Lokiya-sīla.
302:
Virtue that is not an object of the taints (āsavas) (i.e., virtue that is not taken as an object by the taints) is called Lokuttara-sīla. Between these two, Lokiya-sīla can lead to specific states of existence (human or deva life) and can also be a foundation and cause for liberation from existence (Vin. v, 288). Lokuttara-sīla, however, leads to liberation from existence. It is also the domain that is the object of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Thus, virtue is divided into these pairs.

The section on the pairs of virtue is finished.
**********
## The Threefold Group of Virtue
Alternatively, virtue is divided into three: (1) Hīna-sīla, (2) Majjhima-sīla, and (3) Paṇīta-sīla. Among these three, as explained in the previous section on Generosity (Dāna), virtue undertaken and practiced with inferior desire (chanda), energy (viriya), consciousness (citta), or investigation (vīmaṃsā) is called Hīna-sīla (inferior virtue). Virtue undertaken and practiced with medium desire, energy, consciousness, or investigation is called Majjhima-sīla (medium virtue). Virtue undertaken and practiced with superior desire, energy, consciousness, or investigation is called Paṇīta-sīla (superior virtue).

Alternatively: (1) Virtue undertaken and practiced out of a desire for fame and reputation is called Hīna-sīla. (2) Virtue undertaken and practiced out of a longing for the bliss of existence as a result of merit is called Majjhima-sīla.

(The longing for future benefits, such as thinking that by practicing this virtue one will attain noble bliss in a future life, is indeed a state of greed (lobha). Because it is virtue practiced without being free from this greed, it is only medium (majjhima). However, the longing for future bliss (longing for the deserved fruits of one's own merit) is not as low or base as the longing for prestige, influence, fame, and followers in the present life. In the world, prestige can be obtained merely by pretending,
303:
without sincere intention (cetanā) or faith (saddhā). The fruits of merit, however, cannot be obtained merely by pretending without sincere intention and faith; only with good intention can good results be obtained. The more one desires good results, the better one's intention must be. Therefore, the desire for the fruits of merit is more noble than the desire for prestige. Although the intention aimed at obtaining many such fruits of merit is purely wholesome (kusala), because it is associated with the impulse of greed (lobha-javana) that craves the benefits to be enjoyed, it cannot be superior and is only medium.)

(3) Virtue undertaken and practiced by reflecting only on the nobility of the Dhamma, without desiring prestige or future benefits, thinking, "This virtue is a noble practice. It is proper for me to practice this noble way," is called superior (paṇīta) virtue. This is because it is virtue practiced with a purely wholesome mind, unassociated with greed. Only this kind of virtue should be regarded as the true Perfection of Virtue (sīla-pāramī).

(As shown in the section on the Perfection of Generosity below, the Naga kings Campeyya and Bhūridatta could not observe this superior virtue and observed it while longing for the fruit of merit, namely human life; thus, they are said to have observed only medium virtue. However, it should also be noted that the virtue observed by those Naga kings is indeed the Perfection of Virtue, because they observed it even at the cost of their lives, without allowing the virtue to be broken.)

Alternatively: (1) Virtue that is defiled by unwholesome states such as self-exaltation and the disparagement of others, thinking, "I am one possessed of virtue; others have no virtue and are of base nature," is called Hīna-sīla. (2) Mundane virtue observed without such defilement is called Majjhima-sīla. (3) Virtue associated with the supramundane Path and Fruit is called Paṇīta-sīla.
304:
Alternatively: (1) Virtue undertaken and practiced to obtain and enjoy good wealth and bliss in a good future life is called Hīna-sīla. (2) The virtue of aspiring Disciples (Sāvaka-bodhisattas) and aspiring Private Buddhas (Pacceka-bodhisattas) practiced with the aim of liberating oneself from the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) is called Majjhima-sīla. (3) The virtue of aspiring Buddhas (Bodhisattas) practiced with the aim of being able to rescue and liberate all beings from the round of rebirths is called Paṇīta-sīla (which constitutes a Perfection). (In this context, the Commentaries explain only Paṇīta-sīla as the virtue that constitutes a Perfection, referring only to the highest form of virtue. Such an explanation is called the 'method of the sublime' (ukkaṭṭha-naya) in the scriptures. Therefore, it should be understood that the virtues of aspiring Private Buddhas and aspiring Disciples, who practice for their own liberation from the round of rebirths, are also Perfections of Virtue, even if they are not the most supreme.)

Alternatively, there are three kinds: Attādhipateyya-sīla, Lokādhipateyya-sīla, and Dhammādhipateyya-sīla. (1) Virtue undertaken and practiced by giving weight to oneself, desiring to abandon conduct and thoughts unsuitable for oneself, is called Attādhipateyya-sīla (virtue with self-dominance). (2) Virtue undertaken and practiced by giving weight to the world, desiring to avoid the blame and reproach of the public, is called Lokādhipateyya-sīla (virtue with world-dominance). (3) Virtue undertaken and practiced by giving weight to the Dhamma, desiring to honor the noble qualities of the Dhamma, thinking, "The Dhamma of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna taught by the Blessed One is of great power and is truly the Dhamma that leads out of the round of rebirths; that Dhamma should be honored only through the practice of the way; therefore, I shall honor that Dhamma of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna through the practice of virtue," is called Dhammādhipateyya-sīla (virtue with Dhamma-dominance).

Alternatively, there are three kinds: Parāmaṭṭha-sīla, Aparāmaṭṭha-sīla, and Paṭippassaddha-sīla. Among these three:

(1) The virtue described as Nissita-sīla in the section on pairs of virtue is called Parāmaṭṭha-sīla because it is misapprehended wrongly through craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). While observing virtue, if one wrongly attends to it with the attachment of craving, thinking, "My virtue is
305:
an extremely noble virtue that can certainly give the bliss of existence I desire; others cannot practice my kind of virtue," or with the obsession of personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) that mistakenly perceives virtue itself as the "self-soul" or "essence," then that virtue is called Parāmaṭṭha-sīla.

(That Parāmaṭṭha-sīla is indeed virtue ignited by the fire of craving and views. This great fire of craving and views can consume not only mundane sensual pleasures but even the practices of generosity and virtue. Only when one reaches true meditation (bhāvanā) can the fire of views be prevented from burning. One who wishes to develop true meditation should, before developing it, clearly reflect, "There is no such thing as 'I'; there is only a collection of mentality and materiality," and only after removing personality view (atta-diṭṭhi) can true meditation be developed. One should reflect, consider, and strive to develop true meditation that is not consumed by the fire of personality view.)

(2) Virtue that is the true foundation and cause for the Path, as practiced by noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjanas), as well as virtue occurring at the moment of the Path for noble persons in training (sekha-ariya), is called Aparāmaṭṭha-sīla. (3) Virtue present in the four Fruition consciousnesses is called Paṭippassaddha-sīla.

Alternatively, there are three kinds: Visuddha-sīla, Avisuddha-sīla, and Vemātika-sīla. Among these three: (1) The virtue of a pure person is called Visuddha-sīla. (Virtue practiced without committing an offense, or the virtue of a person who has rehabilitated an offense after committing it, is called Visuddha-sīla.) (2) The virtue of an impure person is called Avisuddha-sīla. (The virtue of a person who has committed an offense and left it without rehabilitation is called Avisuddha-sīla.) (3) The virtue of a person who has doubt—whether regarding an object, such as "Is this bamboo-shoot or pork?"; or regarding an offense, such as "Is this a Pācittiya offense or a Dukkaṭa offense?"; or regarding the transgression itself, such as "Did I transgress against that object or did I not?"—is called Vemātika-sīla.

(Among these three, a noble yogi who strives in the work of meditation should make impure virtue pure;)
306:
(If one has committed a light offense (lahuka-āpatti), one must purify one's virtue by confessing (desanā). If one has committed a grave Saṅghādisesa offense, one must purify one's virtue by undergoing the Parivāsa and Mānatta penance. If there is doubt, one should clear that doubt by investigating the matter oneself or by questioning those learned in the Vinaya; once the doubt is cleared, if the action is allowable, one may perform it, and if it is not allowable, one should abandon it.)

Alternatively, there are three types of virtue: Sekha-sīla, Asekha-sīla, and Nevasekha-nāsekha-sīla. (1) Virtue associated with the four Paths and the three lower Fruits is called Sekha-sīla (virtue of the trainee). (2) Virtue associated with the Fruit of Arahantship is called Asekha-sīla (virtue of the one beyond training). (3) The remaining collection of mundane virtue is called Nevasekha-nāsekha-sīla (virtue of neither). This is the virtue of worldlings (puthujjana).

The section on the Threefold Virtue is finished.
**********
## The Fourfold Virtue
Alternatively, there are four types:
Hānabhāgiya-sīla,
Ṭhitibhāgiya-sīla,
Visesabhāgiya-sīla,
Nibbedhabhāgiya-sīla.

Among these: (1) Virtue that partakes of decline (or that which will only decline) is called Hānabhāgiya-sīla. (A monk who associates only with immoral persons and does not associate with or attend to virtuous persons, who does not see the fault in transgressing the causes of offenses, who does not know them, who frequently dwells on unwholesome thoughts, and who does not guard the sense faculties such as the eye—the virtue of such a monk does not progress but declines day by day.)

(2) Virtue that partakes of stability (or that which will remain stable without increasing or decreasing) is called Ṭhitibhāgiya-sīla. (A monk who...
307:
...lives with a mind that only finds joy and satisfaction in being endowed with virtue, but has no intention to further develop meditation (kammaṭṭhāna); being content with mere virtue and not striving for anything higher than virtue—the virtue of that monk neither progresses forward nor slides backward, but remains merely stable.)

(3) Virtue that partakes of distinction (or that which will become distinguished) is called Visesabhāgiya-sīla. (A monk who, after being endowed with virtue, is not content with mere virtue but strives for the attainment of concentration (samādhi); the virtue of that monk is called virtue partaking of distinction, namely the distinction of concentration. It means virtue that yields the special benefit of concentration.)

(4) Virtue that partakes of the penetration of the mass of defilements (yielding benefit) is called Nibbedhabhāgiya-sīla. (A monk who is not content with mere virtue but strives diligently to attain strong insight knowledge (balava-vipassanā-ñāṇa) that is weary of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha); the virtue of that monk is called virtue partaking of penetration, which yields the benefit of penetrating the mass of defilements by attaining the Path and Fruit.)

Alternatively, there are four types:
Bhikkhu-sīla,
Bhikkhunī-sīla,
Anupasampanna-sīla,
Gahaṭṭha-sīla.

(1) The collection of training rules prescribed by the Buddha for male monks, and those rules prescribed for female monks (bhikkhunīs) which male monks should also observe and maintain, is called Bhikkhu-sīla.

(2) The collection of training rules prescribed for female monks, and those rules prescribed for male monks which female monks should also observe and maintain, is called Bhikkhunī-sīla.
308:
(3) The ten precepts observed and practiced by male and female novices (sāmaṇeras and sāmaṇerīs) are called Anupasampanna-sīla. (Those who are not monks are called 'anupasampanna'. Although laypeople are also technically 'anupasampanna', because they will be mentioned separately as 'gahaṭṭha', the Commentator takes 'anupasampanna' here to refer only to male and female novices. There is also the category of Sikkhamānā; however, since these are senior female novices practicing special rules to become bhikkhunīs, they should be understood as included within the category of female novices without being mentioned separately.)

(4) The virtue practiced by lay devotees, both male (upāsaka) and female (upāsikā), is called Gahaṭṭha-sīla.

Regarding this Gahaṭṭha-sīla, the Visuddhimagga Commentary explains: "Upāsakaupāsikānaṃ niccasīlavasena pañcasikkhāpadāni sati vā ussāhe dasa uposathangavasena aṭṭhāti idaṃ gahaṭṭhasīlaṃ = The five training rules to be constantly observed by laymen and laywomen, or ten training rules if there is capability, or eight training rules by way of the factors of the Uposatha—this collection of virtue is called Gahaṭṭha-sīla, practiced by laypeople." (One should first note that the five precepts to be constantly observed, and if capable, the ten precepts or the eight precepts, are called Gahaṭṭha-sīla.)

In this passage from the Visuddhimagga Commentary, there is a disagreement and debate regarding the meaning of the phrase "sati vā ussāhe" (if there is capability). The disagreement is as follows: Some teachers translate it (connecting the word 'niccasīlavasena', which was stated for the five precepts, with the subsequent word 'dasa') as: "For laypeople, not only the five precepts but also the ten precepts are 'nicca-sīla', virtue that must be observed permanently."

"For the five precepts, whether one has the capability or not, there is no need to choose; they are virtue to be observed constantly. As for the ten precepts, although they are said to be virtue to be observed constantly...
309:
...they must be observed by one who has the capability. 'Capability' means the ability to completely abandon and renounce gold and silver without keeping, handling, or trading them in any way. If one is such a person who can renounce them, one must observe the ten precepts constantly for life. They should not be observed for just a few days or months. If one intends to avoid gold and silver only while observing the precepts but intends to use them again after finishing, or if there is still attachment and longing for gold and silver, those teachers say one should not observe them."

Because it is very difficult for laypeople to renounce their own gold and silver without attachment, there are some who think and say that it is not even suitable for laypeople to practice the ten precepts. (Also in the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā): "Dasāti sāmaṇerehi rakkhitabbasīlamāha ghaṭīkārādīnaṃ viya"—In the commentary's words 'sati vā ussāhe dasa', the word 'dasa' (ten) refers to the ten precepts observed by novices, meaning virtue like that observed by Ghaṭīkāra the potter and others. Because of this explanation, those who were mistaken became even more mistaken. The misunderstanding is this: In the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta (Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, 4. Rājavagga, 1), just as Ghaṭīkāra the potter abstained from handling and using treasures like gold and silver for his whole life, others also cannot fulfill the ten precepts merely by refraining from receiving new gold and silver; they must be able to abandon all existing gold and silver treasures they possess and be like Ghaṭīkāra the potter. This is the extreme view taken by some regarding the Mahāṭīkā teacher's statement.

To clarify these views:
As mentioned, the doctrine that "one must be able to renounce gold and silver without attachment before observing the ten precepts" arose based on the Jātarūpa training rule included in the ten precepts. Those teachers' view is that the nature of the Jātarūpa rule is such that it can only be kept secure if one can abandon all one's treasures without attachment to avoid receiving, handling, or using them. Ghaṭīkāra the potter was a Great Anāgāmī who had abandoned gold and silver without attachment. For people today, although they do not newly receive, handle, or use them on the day they observe the precepts...
310:
...since their old treasures still exist in their homes and so on, it contradicts the Jātarūpa training rule. Therefore, they believe that without being able to renounce gold and silver without attachment, one should not undertake the ten precepts, and even if one does, one will not obtain the virtue.

This should not be viewed in such a way. The reason is: for monks, there is the great Rūpiya training rule concerning the acceptance of gold and silver, which is more subtle and noble than the Jātarūpa training rule of laypeople. According to that rule, if gold and silver are offered, one must not accept them oneself, nor should one have another accept them. If there is no one to accept them and they are left nearby, one must not remain satisfied; one must refuse, saying, "This is not allowable for us monks, we do not wish to accept this offering." If one does not refuse, an offense is committed, and furthermore, that gold and silver must be forfeited. This is how it was taught and prescribed. However...

If a donor comes to a monk and offers money, and although the monk refuses and rejects it according to the Vinaya to remain free from offense, the donor insists on leaving it and departs. When another donor arrives and the monk explains the situation, if that donor asks, "In that case, please show me a secure place to keep the money," the monk may even go up to a seven-storied mansion, take the donor there, and say, "This is a secure place." He must not say, "Put it here." When the donor places it properly in the spot shown by the monk and leaves, the monk may lock the door securely and guard it. There is a clear explanation in the Commentary to the Rūpiya training rule (Vinaya Vol. 2, p. 270) that by acting in this way, no offense is committed.

If it were the case that one must not possess any gold or silver because of undertaking the Jātarūpa training rule, then the aforementioned monk (who must be more subtle than a layperson) would not be able to guard gold and silver by any means. Just as that monk is free from offense even though he guards the gold and silver left securely by a donor, it should be understood that for laypeople, even while observing the ten precepts, there is no hindrance to their virtue regarding the gold and silver treasures they have kept in appropriate places.
311:
In the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā, the citation of Ghaṭīkāra the potter’s Ten Precepts as an example is not intended to mean that “a layperson who wishes to observe the Ten Precepts must be able to abandon gold and silver without attachment, just like Ghaṭīkāra the potter.” Rather, it is merely to present Ghaṭīkāra the potter, the most excellent observer of the Ten Precepts, as a model so that “a layperson observing the Ten Precepts should not be satisfied with merely fulfilling them, but should strive to become one who possesses the Ten Precepts of the highest standard.” It should be understood that this example was given to encourage one to strive to emulate him as much as possible, even if one cannot fully reach the level of Ghaṭīkāra the potter.

The evidence for this interpretation is as follows: In the commentary to the first sutta of the second vagga of the Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā, the author of the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā himself, the Venerable Dhammapāla Thera, explained: “Sīlamayanti niccasīlauposathaniyamādivasena pañca aṭṭha dasa vā sīlāni samādiyantassa.” In this writing, he makes it known that there are three types of undertaking virtue: (1) the Five Precepts as Nicca-sīla (permanent virtue), (2) the Eight Precepts as Uposatha-sīla (observance virtue), and (3) the Ten Precepts as Niyama-sīla (determined/periodic virtue). According to this commentary, it is clear that the Ten Precepts are not Nicca-sīla but are Niyama-sīla.

Similarly, in the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi, Sakka-saṃyutta, Vagga 2, Sutta 8: When Sakka, the King of Devas, was about to descend from the Vejayanta Palace to go to the park, he paid homage to the eight directions just before mounting his chariot. When the charioteer Mātali asked whom he was worshipping, Sakka replied:

Ye gahaṭṭhā puṇṇakarā, sīlavanto upāsakā.
Dhammena dāraṃ posenti, te namassāmi mātali.

“Friend Mātali, those laypeople who are doers of merit, who are endowed with virtue (sīlavanto), who are lay devotees (upāsakā), and who righteously support their wives and children—them I worship, Mātali.”
312:
Regarding the word “Sīlavanto” (virtuous) in this reply by Sakka, the commentary explains: “Sīlavanto ti upāsakatte patiṭṭhāya pañcahipi dasahipi sīlehi samannāgatā = The virtuous ones are those who, established in the status of a lay devotee (upāsaka), are endowed with either the Five Precepts or the Ten Precepts.” (According to this commentary, it is clear that the people Sakka worships are laypeople who observe the Five or Ten Precepts while still living with their wives and children.)

In the Saṃyutta-ṭīkā, the sub-commentary to that sutta, it is also explained: “Niccasīlavasena pañcahi niyamavasena dasahi = By way of permanent virtue (nicca-sīla), the five should be taken; by way of determined virtue (niyama-sīla), the ten should be taken.” In this sub-commentary as well, the Ten Precepts are not called Nicca-sīla but are referred to only as Niyama-sīla.

## Niyama-sīla
The meaning of the term Niyama-sīla is summarized in verse 444 of the Magadha Abhidhāna (Pali Dictionary): Virtue that is to be observed constantly is called Yama-sīla. Virtue that is not constant but observed from time to time is called Niyama-sīla. The use of the terms Yama-sīla and Niyama-sīla is a usage derived from Brahmanical doctrines. This can be known by referring to verse 49 of the Brāhmaṇavagga (Chapter 17) of the Amarakoṣa Dictionary, which states: (Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-acceptance of gifts—these five are called Yama-sīla, to be guarded constantly. Purification, contentment, austerity, recitation of the Vedas, and mindfulness of Brahma—these five are called Niyama-sīla, to be guarded occasionally.)

According to the Saṃyutta Pāḷi and its commentary already cited, it is clearly known that even laypeople who righteously support their wives and children can observe the Ten Precepts. Therefore, the view that “laypeople should only observe the Ten Precepts if they can completely abandon gold and silver without attachment like Ghaṭīkāra the potter” is not a correct view, but an extreme one.

Furthermore, in the commentary to the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka of the Asītinipāta, regarding the Tenfold Virtue of Kings (Rājadhamma), the commentary explains the meaning of “Sīla” as both the Five Precepts and the Ten Precepts.
313:
Since both are explained, it is clear that kings also observe the Ten Precepts as part of the royal virtues. If it were true that the Ten Precepts must be observed permanently to be valid, then kings—who have queens and concubines related to the Abrahma-cariya precept, and whose treasuries are filled with gold and silver related to the Jātarūpa precept—would not be able to observe the Ten Precepts (Dasa Sīla). If it were impossible for kings to observe them, the commentator would not have included the Ten Precepts under the category of “Sīla” within the Tenfold Virtue of Kings. Because the commentator specifically included the Ten Precepts as part of the royal virtues, it should be understood without doubt that the Ten Precepts are not Nicca-sīla (permanent virtue), but are virtue to be observed only when one is able to do so from time to time.

Furthermore, in the Khuddakapāṭha Pāḷi, the Ten Training Rules are taught starting with “Dasa sikkhāpadāni.” In the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: “Among these ten training rules, the first two—abstaining from taking life and taking what is not given—and the fourth and fifth—abstaining from false speech and intoxicants—apply to both lay devotees (upāsakas) and novices (sāmaṇeras) by way of permanent virtue (nicca-sīla). (The third precept, abstaining from unchastity, is omitted here because it cannot be a permanent virtue for laypeople. It is a training rule to be observed only when one is able.) By way of observance virtue (uposatha-sīla), for laypeople, among the ten training rules, the seventh (dancing and music) and eighth (garlands and scents) are made into a single factor, and excluding the final precept on gold and silver, all training rules apply to novices. (This means all the eight training rules to be practiced by laypeople apply to novices.) The final training rule regarding gold and silver is a specific training rule for novices.”

If one considers this explanation from the commentary, it means that for laypeople, the training rules from the Ten Precepts that must be permanently avoided are the four: taking life, taking what is not given, false speech, and intoxicants. For laypeople,
314:
they will not be able to permanently abstain from unchastity, nor will they be able to permanently abstain from the later training rules such as untimely eating, dancing, and music. Thus, it is clear that all ten of these are the type of Niyama-sīla (determined virtue) to be guarded only when one is able.

Although the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā states that “the training rule on gold and silver is a specific training rule only for novices,” even if novices transgress the gold and silver training rule, they do not lose their status as novices. The reason is that in the Mahākhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, when the ten factors (dasa liṅga) that cause the loss of novice status were taught, only the first five of the Ten Precepts were included. The latter five were not. Therefore, even if one of the latter five is transgressed, the novice status is not lost; the novice merely becomes one liable to punishment (daṇḍa). If he undergoes the punishment assigned by his teachers, such as the sand-carrying penance or water-carrying penance, he becomes a good novice again.

In this way, considering that even for novices—for whom the Ten Precepts are indispensable—the transgression of the gold and silver training rule does not destroy their novice status, it is clear that the latter five of the Ten Precepts are not as critical as the first five even for novices. Since it is not that critical even for novices, it is inappropriate to make the gold and silver training rule a matter of great urgency and strictness specifically for laypeople in speech and writing.

It is recognized that the Venerable Mahā Buddhaghosa wrote both the Visuddhimagga-aṭṭhakathā and the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā. Since these two texts were written by the same teacher, their meanings cannot be divergent. The meaning of the Visuddhimagga-aṭṭhakathā, “Upāsakānaṃ niccasīlavasena pañca sikkhāpadāni sati vā ussāhe dasa,” should be understood without doubt in accordance with the Khuddakapāṭha and Itivuttaka commentaries: “The Ten Precepts are not Nicca-sīla for laypeople, but are Niyama-sīla to be observed only when able.” The assertion that “the Ten Precepts must be observed permanently if one is able,” adding the word “permanently” to the side of the Ten Precepts, contradicts the aforementioned Khuddakapāṭha and Itivuttaka commentaries.
315:
Furthermore, in explaining the manner in which virtue is broken, the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā states: “For novices, if one training rule is broken, all are destroyed. Indeed, for novices, the Ten Precepts stand in the place of the Pārājika (offenses of defeat) for monks. However, one is bound by unwholesome kamma only for the specific training rule that is transgressed. For laypeople, if they transgress one training rule after undertaking the Five Precepts, only that transgressed training rule is broken. If that broken training rule is undertaken again, the Five Precepts are complete once more. Other teachers (Apare), however, explain: (If the Five Precepts were undertaken individually, one by one, then if one is broken, only that one is broken and the remaining training rules are not. If at the time of undertaking, one said ‘Pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ sīlaṃ samādiyāmi = I undertake the virtue endowed with five factors’ and undertook them collectively, then if one is broken, all are destroyed, because they were undertaken collectively. Regarding the weight of kamma, kamma is incurred only for the transgressed training rule, not for the remaining ones.)”

Although the view of some great teachers is that “in a collective undertaking, if one is broken, all are broken,” meaning without exception, the remaining training rules cannot truly be destroyed without a transgression. Therefore, when it is said they are “broken,” if one took the precepts saying “virtue endowed with five factors,” then if one is broken, the five factors no longer exist; only virtue endowed with four factors remains. If we take the view of the “Other teachers” (Apare) as referring only to the fact that the original five-fold undertaking is broken, then there will be no difference in doctrine. For novices, it is not like this; if one is broken, all are destroyed, because for novices, the Ten Precepts are virtue that must be guarded permanently.

Considering these statements on how virtue is broken, it is clear that for laypeople, since only one is broken if one is transgressed, there is no absolute Nicca-sīla in the same way as for novices. The reason is that just as a novice is a novice only if he has the Ten Precepts, and if he lacks them he is not a novice, one cannot say that a person is a human only if they have a certain virtue, or that if they lack such virtue they are not human. Therefore, in the commentary to the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga of the Sammohavinodanī...
316:
(Thi)
"Whatever training rule laypeople transgress, only that specific one is broken or destroyed; the remaining ones are not destroyed. Why? Because laypeople possess 'unfixed' virtue (anibaddhasīla); they do not have a virtue that must be guarded constantly [in its entirety] to be considered 'guarded.' Whatever training rule they are able to observe, they guard only that specific one." This is how it is explained.

The point intended in this Sammohavinodanī Commentary is that novices (sāmaṇeras) must always observe the ten precepts; if they transgress even one or two, the entire set of training rules is destroyed, and they are no longer novices. Just as novices must always possess the ten precepts, there is no such requirement for laypeople that they must possess a specific virtue to be considered human, or that they are not human if they do not possess it. Based on this statement, it should be understood that laypeople should observe as many of the five precepts as they can, let alone the ten. If they cannot observe all five but can only observe one or two, one cannot say, "It is not good to observe them because the five are not complete," or "Even if observed, no merit is gained and it does not constitute virtue."

One should understand that "Even if the five are not complete, merit is gained and it constitutes genuine virtue by observing as many as one can." Supporting evidence is found in the Commentary to the Paṭisambhidāmagga, Volume I, page 188, in the explanation of Pariyantapārisuddhisīla (the meaning of this virtue will be clarified later): "There are two kinds of limits for the purified virtue observed with a limit: the limit of training rules and the limit of time. Regarding the limit of training rules, lay disciples (upāsakas and upāsikās) have sets of training rules consisting of one, two, three, four, five, eight, or ten rules according to their regular undertaking. Probationary nuns (sikkhamānās) and male and female novices (sāmaṇeras and sāmaṇerīs) have ten training rules. This is what is called the limit of training rules."

The point intended in this commentary is that laypeople may undertake one, two, three, four, five, eight, or ten training rules and...
317:
(Thī)
...if they guard them securely, it is Sikkhāpadapariyantapārisuddhisīla, meaning 'purified virtue with a limit on the training rules.' Therefore, although in the world there are no [standard] sets of one, two, three, or four precepts, and only the five precepts are well-known, it is not the case that one should only undertake them if all five can be kept. It is clear that if one can manage only one, one can observe one; if two, then two; if three, then three; if four, then four.

A question may arise: "While there is the opportunity to observe from one to four precepts, why does the Visuddhimagga Commentary mention only the five precepts by saying 'pañca sikkhāpadāni niccasīlavasena' (the five training rules by way of permanent virtue) for lay disciples?"

The answer is: In the Visuddhimagga Commentary, the focus is not primarily on the people who will observe them, but on the fundamental nature of the virtue to be observed. The fundamental nature of virtue is such that all five should be observed constantly. It cannot be said that one may choose not to observe any of these five training rules; if they are not observed, it will simply result in a fault. Focusing on this fundamental nature of the training rules that ought to be observed constantly, the statement "pañca sikkhāpadāni niccasīlavasena" was made. Not only in the Visuddhimagga Commentary but also in other scriptures, the five precepts are presented as permanent virtue (niccasīla) according to this fundamental nature.

One should not misinterpret this by shifting the meaning toward the person who must observe them, thinking, "I must observe these five precepts only if I can do so constantly; if I cannot, I should not observe them, and it is not good to observe them partially," based on the scriptural focus on the fundamental nature of virtue. (The fundamental nature of the five precepts is that all five should be observed constantly; however, the nature of people is to observe as many as they can, whether it be one or two, as stated in the Sammohavinodanī and Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentaries. The point is that one should not judge or understand the nature of people based solely on the fundamental nature of the virtue.)
318:
(Thu)
## The Five Precepts with Celibacy as the Fifth (Brahmacariyapañcamasīla)
In addition to the five, eight, and ten precepts practiced by laypeople, there is also the Brahmacariyapañcamasīla. This Brahmacariyapañcamasīla is essentially the five precepts. In the ordinary five precepts, the third training rule is undertaken as "Kāmesu micchācārā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi." If one replaces that Kāmesu micchācāra rule with "Abrahmacariyā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi," it becomes the Brahmacariyapañcamasīla. (The name Brahmacariyapañcamasīla means the virtue where complete abstinence from sexual intercourse is the fifth. Based on this literal meaning, it might seem that the Abrahmacariyā rule should be undertaken last, but it is not necessary to do so. One simply undertakes "Abrahmacariyā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi" in the place of the Kāmesu micchācāra rule, just as when receiving the ordinary five precepts.)

The undertaking of this Brahmacariyapañcamasīla by Ugga the Householder of Vesālī and Ugga the Householder of Hatthigāma in the Vajjī country is mentioned in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, 3-Gahapati Vagga, Suttas 1 and 2. In the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Pañcakanipāta, 3-Upāsaka Vagga, 10-Gavesī Sutta (page 189), it is mentioned that Gavesī Upāsaka observed it during the time of Kassapa Buddha.

Both Ugga householders mentioned in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, were Non-Returner (Anāgāmī) lay disciples who, after undertaking the Brahmacariyapañcamasīla from the Buddha, married off their eldest wives to the men of their choice and renounced their other wives, living without taking any more wives for the rest of their lives. Those who wish to practice this Brahmacariyapañcamasīla today should not wrongly assume that they must completely renounce their wives and children like those Ugga householders before they can undertake and practice it. Nor should it be assumed that those who cannot completely renounce their wives and children cannot observe it. The reason is that, as stated in the previously mentioned Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, only the four rules—abstinence from killing, stealing, lying, and intoxicants—are presented as permanent virtue (niccasīla). Thus, the Abrahmacariyā rule, along with...
319:
(Thū)
...the subsequent set of training rules such as Vikālabhojanā, are not permanent virtue (niccasīla), but are clearly 'regulated virtue' (niyamasīla) to be undertaken occasionally. Although one may not be able to practice exactly like Ghaṭīkāra the Potter, it has been shown through various scriptures as mentioned below that one can observe the ten precepts as regulated virtue (niyamasīla) to the best of one's ability. Regarding this Brahmacariyapañcamasīla, although the two Ugga householders, being Anāgāmī Ariyas, completely renounced their current wives and observed it for life—and it would indeed be excellent if others could follow and practice exactly like them—it should be well understood that if one cannot follow them exactly, one can still observe it to the extent of one's own ability.

## The Five Precepts with Celibacy and One Meal (Brahmacariyapañcama-ekabhattikasīla)
Furthermore, there is also the Brahmacariyapañcama-ekabhattikasīla (also known as Ekabhattikasīla). Ekabhattika means eating only one meal in the morning. Therefore, if one wishes to observe this Brahmacariyapañcama-ekabhattikasīla, one can simply add one more training rule, "Vikālabhojanā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi," at the end of the method for undertaking the Brahmacariyapañcamasīla. Alternatively, if one wishes to undertake it all at once, one can say, "Brahmacariyapañcama-ekabhattikasīlaṃ samādiyāmi." The observation of this Brahmacariyapañcama-ekabhattikasīla by Dhammika the lay follower, Nandamātā the laywoman, and others is mentioned in the Suttanipāta Commentary, Volume I, in the explanation of the Dhammika Sutta. The Buddha also taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Pañcakanipāta, 3-Upāsaka Vagga, 10-Gavesī Sutta, that Gavesī Upāsaka and five hundred lay followers observed it during the time of Kassapa Buddha.

## The Eight Uposatha Precepts (Aṭṭhaṅgauposathasīla)
A question may arise: "Just as the five precepts are referred to simply as 'pañca' (five) and the ten precepts as 'dasa' (ten), why is the eight precepts specifically referred to by adding 'uposathaṅgavasena' (by way of the Uposatha factors)?"
321:
Considering the explanations that the Jātarūpa precept is a distinctive precept for novices (sāmaṇeras), it is very clear that the Ten Precepts are specifically the virtue (sīla) of novices.

Therefore, among the two types of virtue particularly relevant to them, the ancient wise and virtuous ones referred only to the Eight Precepts—which are superior and observed on specifically designated days—as 'Uposatha'. In the Visuddhimagga Commentary, this is specifically stated as 'uposathaṅgavasena' (by virtue of the factors of the Uposatha).

Virtuous people, not being satisfied with the act of virtue alone, also wish to perform acts of generosity (dāna). To perform these acts of generosity well, they are unable to observe the Jātarūpa precept (abstaining from gold and silver). If one observes the Jātarūpa precept, one cannot fully manage the seeking and purchasing of items to be offered. Therefore, it should be well noted that the ancients observed only the Eight Precepts on specifically designated days.

## The Nine-factored Uposatha

Regarding this Nine-factored Uposatha (navaṅga-uposatha), it is introduced in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Navaka Nipāta, 2-Sīhanāda Vagga, 8th Sutta: "The Nine-factored Uposatha, when practiced to fulfillment, is of great fruit, great benefit, and great majesty." In detailing these nine factors, the text lists the same Eight Precepts from the precept of abstaining from taking life (pāṇātipāta) up to the precept of abstaining from high and large beds (uccāsayana-mahāsayana), and at the end, it is taught: "mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati" (he dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness).

The essential meaning intended by this teaching is that after undertaking the regular Eight Precepts, one must cultivate loving-kindness (mettā). If a person keeps the Eight Precepts securely and cultivates loving-kindness, that person is practicing the Nine-factored Uposatha. Loving-kindness is a form of meditation (bhāvanā), whereas only virtue (sīla) is to be formally undertaken. Meditation is a type of Dhamma that must be cultivated continuously. Therefore, a person who wishes to practice the Nine-factored Uposatha does not need to formally undertake a separate precept for loving-kindness; after receiving the regular Eight Precepts, if they continue to cultivate and practice loving-kindness as much as they can...
322:
...it should be well noted that they are said to be practicing the Nine-factored Uposatha which has nine components.

In the teaching of this Nine-factored Uposatha, the phrase 'ekaṃ disaṃ' (one direction) was included regarding loving-kindness. This indicates that in cultivating loving-kindness, focusing on specific directions is more effective than pervasiveness without such focus. Therefore, when one wishes to pervade the ten directions with loving-kindness, it should be noted that one ought to cultivate it by specifically taking each direction as an object, one by one, starting from the direction of one's choice until all ten directions are completed.

Although there are four Sublime States (brahmavihāra), the reason why loving-kindness (mettā) alone was specifically extracted and combined with the Eight Precepts to be taught as the Nine-factored Uposatha should be understood as being due to the great power of loving-kindness. For this very reason, the Buddha taught the Mettā Sutta, which is prominently found in the Khuddakapāṭha Pāḷi and the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi.

Furthermore, in the Aṅguttara Pāḷi, Ekādasaka Nipāta, 2-Anussati Vagga, 5th Sutta, it is taught that if one repeatedly cultivates loving-kindness, one can obtain eleven benefits:

1. Sleeping in comfort,
2. Waking in comfort,
3. Not seeing evil dreams,
4. Being dear to human beings,
5. Being dear to non-human beings (deities, ogres, hungry ghosts),
6. Deities protecting one,
7. Not being harmed by fire, poison, or weapons,
8. The mind concentrating easily,
9. Having a clear facial complexion,
10. Dying unconfused,
11. If one cannot yet penetrate the higher Paths and Fruits in this life, one will go to the Brahma realm.

Because of these reasons, it is evident that loving-kindness possesses greater power and majesty.
323:
## Three Kinds of Uposatha

There are three kinds of Uposatha virtue:
(1) Gopāla-uposatha = The Herdsman's Uposatha,
(2) Nigaṇṭha-uposatha = The Nigaṇṭhas' (Jain ascetics') Uposatha,
(3) Ariya-uposatha = The Noble Uposatha.
This was taught by the Buddha in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Tika Nipāta, 2-Mahā Vagga, 10th Sutta, the Visākhūposatha Sutta. The intended meanings are:

(1) The Uposatha observed with a mental attitude similar to that of herdsmen is called Gopāla-uposatha. When herdsmen return home in the evening after tending cattle and handing them over to the owners, they usually think only: "Today I grazed the cattle in such a place and gave them water in such a place; tomorrow I will graze them in such a place and give them water in such a place." Similarly, if a person observing the Uposatha spends the day with greed, longing only for food, thinking: "Today I ate such and such food; tomorrow I will eat such and such food," their mental attitude is like that of a herdsman. Therefore, the Buddha called that Uposatha 'Gopāla-uposatha'.

(2) The kind of Uposatha practiced by the Nigaṇṭhas is called Nigaṇṭha-uposatha. (Those who do not wear clothes and hold false views are called Nigaṇṭhas.) These Nigaṇṭhas, for example, regarding the act of taking life, would say not to kill beings that exist beyond a hundred yojanas in the four directions: East, West, South, and North. (Consider carefully: is it even possible to kill a being existing beyond a hundred yojanas?) By setting geographical limits regarding the taking of life, they devise ways to allow for the commission of misconduct, distinguishing between areas where misconduct may be committed and where it may not. The Uposatha practiced by those who follow this method is called 'Nigaṇṭha-uposatha' by the Buddha.
324:
(3) The Uposatha observed by purifying the defilements that cling to the mind through repeated reflection on the qualities of the Buddha and so forth is called Ariya-uposatha. This Ariya-uposatha is again divided into six types:

(a) Brahmūposatha = The Brahma Uposatha,
(b) Dhammūposatha = The Dhamma Uposatha,
(c) Saṅghūposatha = The Sangha Uposatha,
(d) Sīlūposatha = The Virtue Uposatha,
(e) Devatūposatha = The Deities Uposatha,
(f) Aṭṭhaṅgūposatha = The Eight-factored Uposatha.

Among these six:

(a) The Uposatha observed by undertaking the Eight Precepts and repeatedly reflecting on the qualities of the Buddha, such as 'Arahaṃ', is called Brahmūposatha.
(b) The Uposatha observed by undertaking the Eight Precepts and repeatedly reflecting on the qualities of the Dhamma is called Dhammūposatha.
(c) The Uposatha observed by undertaking the Eight Precepts and repeatedly reflecting on the qualities of the Sangha is called Saṅghūposatha.
(d) The Uposatha observed by undertaking the Eight Precepts, practicing so that the virtue is unbroken, untorn, unspotted, and unsplattered, and repeatedly reflecting on the merits of that virtue is called Sīlūposatha.
(e) In the world, there are deities and Brahmas. These deities and Brahmas were born in those celestial and Brahma realms because they were endowed with the qualities of pure and noble faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in their previous lives. One observes the Uposatha by taking deities and Brahmas as a standard, reflecting: "In me also, these pure and noble qualities are evident." This is called Devatūposatha. (In this context, both deities and Brahmas are called 'devatā'.)
325:
(f) The Buddha taught that the virtue observed by undertaking the Eight Precepts and reflecting on all eight factors in this way: "Just as the Arahants always have compassion and kindness without ever killing or harming living beings, so too I have now practiced kindness and compassion without killing or harming; by this practice, I am following the example of the Arahants," is called Aṭṭhaṅgūposatha (the Uposatha characterized by reflection on the eight factors).

These divisions of the Uposatha into three or six types should be understood as Uposathas taught according to the manner of practice. In terms of the virtue to be practiced, as previously shown, there are only two: the Eight-factored Uposatha and the Nine-factored Uposatha.

## Three Kinds of Uposatha Days

According to the days on which they are observed, there are three kinds of Uposatha:
(1) Pakati-uposatha,
(2) Paṭijāgara-uposatha,
(3) Pāṭihāriya-uposatha.

That there should be these three types of Uposatha can be known by relying on the Pāḷi texts such as the Rāja Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Tika Nipāta, 4-Devadūta Vagga, 7th Sutta) which states: "uposathaṃ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti" (they observe the Uposatha and keep the watch),

And the Pāḷi verse:
"Cātuddasiṃ pañcaddasiṃ, yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī.
Pāṭihāriyapakkhañca, aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ."
(On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight, and during the extraordinary fortnight, one should observe the eight-factored Uposatha.)

Among these three kinds of Uposatha:

## (1) Pakati-uposatha = Regular Uposatha Day

In the aforementioned Pāḷi text, the phrase "Cātuddasiṃ pañcaddasiṃ, yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī" indicates the Pakati-uposatha days (Regular Uposatha days). According to this Pāḷi, Pakati-uposatha consists of three observances per fortnight: the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the fifteenth day.
326:
Since there are three observances per fortnight, it should be understood that there are six observances (six Uposathas) in a month that are Pakati-uposatha. According to the Commentary: the 5th, 8th, 14th, and 15th days of the waxing fortnight make four observances; and the 5th, 8th, 14th, and 15th days of the waning fortnight also make four observances. Thus, a total of eight observances (eight Uposathas) in a month are Pakati-uposatha—the regular, customary Uposathas.

(In the present time, however, people generally speak of, recognize, and practice four observances in a month as Pakati-uposatha. These four Uposathas are the 8th day of the waxing moon, the full moon day, the 8th day of the waning moon, and the new moon day.)

## (2) Paṭijāgara-uposatha = The Watchful Uposatha

Paṭijāgara-uposatha refers to the practice of adding one day before and one day after each of the eight Pakati-uposatha days mentioned in the Commentary. (Paṭi = repeatedly; jāgara = waking/watchful; meaning the virtue that repeatedly wakes one from the sleep of defilements.) Counting by days: for the 5th day Pakati-uposatha, the 4th day is the preparatory day and the 6th day is the extra day. For the 8th day Pakati-uposatha, the 7th day is the preparatory day and the 9th day is the extra day. For the 14th day Pakati-uposatha, the 13th day is the preparatory day (there is no extra day as it leads into the next). For the Full Moon Pakati-uposatha, there is no preparatory day (as it follows the 14th), but the 1st day of the waning moon is the extra day. Counting the days in order like this: the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 13th, 14th, 15th (Full Moon), and the 1st day of the waning moon make ten days for the waxing side. Similarly, there are ten days for the waning side. Thus, it should be well noted that in a month, there are eight Pakati-uposatha days and twelve Paṭijāgara-uposatha days.

## (3) Pāṭihāriya-uposatha

The Uposatha that is even more intensive and powerful than the Paṭijāgara-uposatha is called Pāṭihāriya-uposatha. In Paṭijāgara-uposatha, there are still intervening days free from the precepts in both the waxing and waning fortnights. In Pāṭihāriya-uposatha, however...
327:
(Dā)
Precepts must be practiced daily without any gaps or interruptions. 

If one wishes to observe this Pāṭihāriya-uposatha, it should be observed without any missing days throughout the three months of the Rains Retreat (Vassa). If one cannot observe it for the full three months, it should be observed for the entire month from the full moon of Thadingyut to the full moon of Tazaungmon. If one cannot observe it for the entire month, it should be observed for fifteen days from the full moon of Thadingyut to the new moon of Thadingyut. This is the explanation found in the Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary (from Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 2, pp. 122-123).

In the commentary to the Dhammika Sutta of the Cūḷavagga in the Sutta Nipāta (Sutta Nipāta Commentary 2-108), it is stated that the observance of the Uposatha without any gaps for five months—namely Āsāḷha, Sāvaṇa, Poṭṭhapāda, Assayuja, and Kattika—is called Pāṭihāriya-uposatha. Other teachers, however, say that the observance of the Uposatha without gaps for three months—Āsāḷha, Kattika, and Phagguna—is called Pāṭihāriya-uposatha. Still other teachers say that while there are three ordinary Uposatha days in a fortnight—the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth—the Pāṭihāriya-uposatha is the observance that adds four extra days: the day preceding the eighth (the seventh), the day succeeding the eighth (the ninth), the day preceding the fourteenth (the thirteenth), and the day succeeding the fifteenth (the first day of the waxing moon). This is explained so that sons and daughters of good family who desire merit may observe it according to their wishes.

Among these three views in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, the first view—that observing the Uposatha for five months is Pāṭihāriya-uposatha—is similar in essence to the Aṅguttara Commentary. The only difference is that the Aṅguttara Commentary mentions three consecutive months, while the Sutta Nipāta Commentary mentions five consecutive months.

The third view in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is consistent with the Nemi Jātaka Commentary, the commentary on the Uttara Vimāna in the Vimānavatthu Commentary, the Theragāthā Commentary, and the Suruci Jātaka Commentary in the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta.
328:
(Di)
In the commentary to the fifth sutta of the Indaka Vagga in the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta, it is explained that the Uposatha observed on the day preceding the eighth (the seventh), the day succeeding the eighth (the ninth), the day preceding the fourteenth and fifteenth (the thirteenth), and the day succeeding them (the first day of the waning or waxing moon) is called Pāṭihāriya-uposatha. Additionally, the observance for half a month from the first day after the full moon of Thadingyut until the new moon day, as a supplement following the three months of Vassa, is also called Pāṭihāriya-uposatha (Saṃyutta Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 281).

Here, a question arises: why do these commentaries differ from one another, even though the Aṅguttara Commentary, Sutta Nipāta Commentary, Jātaka Commentary, and Saṃyutta Commentary were all written by the same author, Venerable Mahā Buddhaghosa? When considering what is logical and reasonable:

In the Visākhuposatha Sutta, where the three types of Uposatha are taught, the teaching was not based on Visākhā's personal practice, but rather on the three different manners of those who observe the Uposatha. For Visākhā herself, it was only the Ariya-uposatha. It should be understood that the three types were taught based on the varying dispositions of the many people who observe the Uposatha. Therefore, it is clear that the three types of Uposatha in the Visākhuposatha Sutta are the Buddha's own teaching.

However, regarding the specific Uposatha days, there is no teaching by the Buddha that strictly mandates they must be three days or six days. Regarding the aforementioned fourteen-day Uposatha, fifteen-day Uposatha, eight-day Uposatha, and Pāṭihāriya-pakkha Uposatha, the Buddha did not command that one must observe Uposatha on these specific days. In fact, the Buddha was merely recounting what Sakka, the King of Devas, told the Tāvatiṃsa devas based on reports from the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) who travel the human world to record the deeds of the virtuous. Sakka said, "Humans observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days, and they also observe it on the days called Pāṭihāriya." Thus, the classification of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days as Uposatha days is based on the existing practices of the people. On these days,
329:
(Dī)
it should be understood that there is no specific instruction from the Buddha saying that one must observe the Uposatha only on these days and not on others.

In this way, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth Uposatha days are merely the days that people were accustomed to designating and observing. According to the ancient tradition of human practice, there were three ordinary Uposatha days. Later, when people also began to observe the Uposatha on the fifth day (Pañcamī), the commentaries included the Pañcamī-uposatha, stating that there are four Uposatha days in a fortnight. In the present era, however, only four sabbath days per month are designated and observed as Uposatha days.

Thus, the Buddha did not strictly define which specific days must be Uposatha days. This lack of strict definition is because one can observe the Uposatha on any day one wishes. Following this principle, the Paṭijāgara-uposatha and Pāṭihāriya-uposatha days should also be understood as arising from the specific customs and designations of the people. It should be noted that the commentators wrote various views based on these differing human customs.

Furthermore, the Aṅguttara Pāḷi, Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi, Saṃyutta Pāḷi, and Jātaka Pāḷi, where these virtues are taught, are Suttanta teachings. Suttanta teachings are described in the scriptures as Vohāra-desanā (Conventional Teaching). This means they are teachings delivered by the Buddha, who was matchlessly skilled in worldly conventions, in accordance with the designations and terminology of the world of beings. In the world, human designations can never be entirely uniform. Since the matter of Uposatha days, which vary in designation, is entirely about performing meritorious deeds, there is no need to investigate which view is right or wrong. The fact that the Sutta Nipāta Commentary presents three views and instructs one to take whichever one prefers does not mean it is instructing one to hold one's own preference as the truth and others as false; rather, it means that those who wish to observe the Uposatha should do so according to the view they prefer.
330:
(Du)
Lay devotees observe the Uposatha in various ways, designating days that they prefer or that are convenient for them. All such observances result in the growth of merit, and the commentators wrote according to these various and diverse ways of observance. In the context of Suttanta teachings, even the Buddha did not exceed the boundaries of worldly convention (vohāra) when teaching the Dhamma. He taught in this way with the intention that beings should not violate the traditional boundaries and rules of the world that are not unwholesome.

The Buddha's primary intention was to show the ultimate realities (paramattha) of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) to enable beings to easily reach the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. While teaching pure ultimate reality would be highly beneficial for those with wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra), it could lead to unwholesome conduct and rebirth in woeful states for those who do not know how to reflect properly. How so? Those who reflect incorrectly on mind and matter might think: "In the world, there is only mind and matter. There is no 'I', no 'other'. If there is no 'other', then there is no such thing as the evil deed of killing another's life (pāṇātipāta). Since there is no 'I' or 'other', there is no 'mine' or 'his', and thus no evil deed of taking what is not given (adinnādāna). Since there is no 'other', transgressing against another's spouse does not constitute sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra)." In this way, they would violate worldly boundaries and commit evil deeds extensively.

In truth, while there is no 'I', 'other', 'man', or 'woman' from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) when teaching the collection of mind and matter, from the perspective of conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) in the Suttanta method, worldly boundaries should still exist. Even though it is just a collection of mind and matter, one can distinguish this collection as 'I', others as 'another', and identify certain collections of mind and matter as benefactors such as 'mother' or 'father'. These must be maintained from the perspective of conventional truth. If these worldly conventions and rules are violated, people will commit evil deeds extensively as mentioned, and thus the Suttanta Dhamma must be taught according to worldly convention to protect them from the danger of becoming food for the four woeful states.

If only the Suttanta Dhamma were taught, people would only remember designations such as 'I', 'other', 'my son', 'my daughter', 'my wife', or 'my property' as conventional terms, but they might cling to them as being
331:
(Dū)
absolutely real from an ultimate perspective. Because of such strong personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), they would not be able to attain the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.

Therefore, to lead beings to the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, the Buddha also had to teach the collection of ultimate realities of mind and matter. (This means that while the Buddha taught the Paramattha-desanā to lead beings to Nibbāna, He also had to teach the Suttanta-desanā, which is based on not violating worldly conventions, to protect those who might reflect incorrectly from the danger of falling into the four woeful states.)

Since the teachings and scriptures related to the Uposatha precepts are also Suttanta teachings, they should not violate human designations. Because the commentator explained according to the various ways people designate and observe their preferred days and months, it should be understood that even though there is only one author, the views appear diverse.

Some teachers have written judgments such as: "In the Vinaya Pāḷi, there is a rule for monks that they must not perform the Uposatha if it is not an Uposatha day; if they do, they incur a Dukkaṭa offence. In the same way, laypeople must not observe the Uposatha if it is not an Uposatha day."

Writing such things only shows a lack of skill in the methods of the Dhamma. The Vinaya teachings are described in the scriptures as Āṇā-desanā (Teaching of Authority). This means it is a teaching where the Buddha laid down rules as commands. Therefore, in the Vinaya method, whether one's intention is good or bad, a monk who refrains from doing what is forbidden is free from offence.
