Even if one thinks, "I will do this with a good heart," if it is a forbidden act, one is not free from offence, because one has violated the Buddha's authority which says "do not do it." Based on this method of Āṇā-desanā, where monks incur an offence for performing Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day, they argue that in the Suttanta-related observance of laypeople, "if it is not an Uposatha day, one must not observe it; if one does..."
332:
The view that 'it is blameworthy' is rooted in a lack of understanding of the method of the Teaching (desanā). In brief, the Uposatha is a pure and noble thing; it should be understood that it can be observed on any day, and the benefit is as great as the extent to which it is observed.

Therefore:
'Uposathaṃ vuccati aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ sabbadivasesu gahaṭṭhehi rakkhitabbhasīlaṃ = Uposatha is indeed the virtue endowed with eight factors that laypeople can observe on any day they wish to observe it,' as stated in the Commentary to the Mahāsudassana Sutta of the Mahāvagga. (This commentary is a work written by Venerable Dhammapāla, who also wrote the Anuṭīka, which is an explanation of the Mūlaṭīka, the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīka, the Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā, and other commentaries and sub-commentaries.)

## The explanation of the four types of virtue: Bhikkhu-sīla, Bhikkhunī-sīla, Anupasampanna-sīla, and Gahaṭṭha-sīla is finished.
**********
Alternatively, there are four types:
(1) Pakati-sīla (Natural virtue),
(2) Ācāra-sīla (Virtue of conduct),
(3) Dhammatā-sīla (Virtue of nature),
(4) Pubbahetu-sīla (Virtue of prior causes).

Among these four:
(1) The non-transgression of the five precepts, such as refraining from killing (pāṇātipāta), by the inhabitants of the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) is called Pakati-sīla. (All those born in the Northern Continent, without having formally undertaken the precepts, do not naturally transgress misdeeds such as killing. This refers to virtue that is complete by natural disposition.) This non-transgression of the five actions by the inhabitants of the Northern Continent is...
333: ...although it is not 'abstinence by undertaking' (samādāna-virati), the nature of 'abstinence by encounter' (sampatta-virati)—refraining when faced with a situation—is indeed attainable. (2) Ācāra-sīla refers to practicing according to the boundaries and rules established by one's ancestors, whether by lineage, region, or the belief system known as pāsaṇḍa. (Refraining from evil because it has been avoided by one's lineage is called kula-ācāra-sīla. Refraining because it is avoided by the majority in one's region is called desa-ācāra-sīla. Refraining according to a pāsaṇḍa belief is called pāsaṇḍa-sīla. In the word pāsaṇḍa, 'pāsa' and 'ḍa' are combined; 'pāsa' means a snare, referring to craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). 'Ḍa' means to cause or produce. Thus, pāsaṇḍa means a belief that produces the snares of craving and views.) (3) Dhammatā-sīla refers to the virtue where, from the moment the Bodhisatta is conceived, the mother has no desire for sensual pleasure with men. (The Bodhisatta’s mother is naturally endowed with the five precepts. Not to mention other men, she has no sensual desire even for her own husband from the time of conception. This is because the most noble Bodhisatta is dwelling in her womb. Since this virtue is naturally present in every [Bodhisatta's] mother, it is called dhammatā-sīla.) (4) Pubbahetu-sīla refers to the spontaneous wholesome desire to observe virtue and the subsequent practice of it without being taught by anyone, as seen in pure individuals like the youth Pippali (who would become Venerable Mahākassapa) and great Bodhisattas like King Mahāsīlava. (It means virtue that arises and is observed automatically in the present life due to the causal influence of virtue practiced in previous lives, without needing instruction from others.)
334:
Alternatively, there are four types:
(1) Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (Virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha),
(2) Indriya-saṃvara-sīla (Virtue of restraint of the sense faculties),
(3) Ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla (Virtue of purity of livelihood),
(4) Paccayasannissita-sīla (Virtue concerning the use of requisites).

These four are virtues specifically related to monks. When the Bodhisatta, the hermit Sumedha, reflected on the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī), he intended these four virtues when he uttered: 'Tatheva tvaṃ catūsu bhūmīsu, sīlāni paripūraya' (In the same way, you should fulfill the virtues in the four planes). Among those four:

## (1) Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla
The virtue that causes the one who guards it to be liberated from sufferings such as the lower realms is called Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla. (Pāti = one who guards; mokkha = causes to be liberated.)

A person who guards this virtue must: (a) be endowed with noble conduct (ācāra), (b) be endowed with noble—blameless—resorts (gocara). (c) Even for small faults as tiny as a 'paramāṇu-dust' particle, they must habitually view them as a great danger and a great fault as fearsome as Mount Meru, which is 168,000 yojanas deep above and below the water, and (d) they must well undertake and practice the training rules (sikkhāpada). To expand on that statement:

(a) In the world, there is proper conduct (ācāra) that should be practiced, and there is improper conduct (anācāra) that should not be practiced. Transgressing the three bodily misdeeds such as killing (pāṇātipāta), stealing, and sexual misconduct; transgressing the four verbal misdeeds such as lying (musāvāda), divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter—transgressing these seven misdeeds through the respective doors of body and speech; and any other bad actions that cause the destruction of virtue, which are not included among these seven bodily and verbal misdeeds, are called improper conduct (anācāra) that should not be practiced.
335: To mention some of the bad actions that cause the destruction of virtue: in this world, some monks live by a wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) loathed by the Buddha, such as giving bamboo, leaves, flowers, fruits, soap powder, or tooth-sticks to laymen and laywomen; humbling themselves and affirming even the incorrect words of laypeople to gain their affection; speaking with more falsehood than truth, like a mixture of cooked and uncooked beans in a soup; carrying or decorating the children of laypeople like nannies; running errands for laypeople until their calves are weary; practicing medicine, looking after property, or exchanging food and gifts. Such ways of living are called misconduct (anācāra). For monks, even if laypeople request bamboo, leaves, and such items for their use—let alone giving them unasked—it is not proper to give them. Giving such things is not the work of a monk. If one performs these improper acts, it is called 'corrupting families' (kula-dūsana) according to the Vinaya teachings. (It means the act of destroying the faith of laymen and laywomen.) Here, one might ask: 'If I have the item and do not give it to the requester, only then will their faith be destroyed. If I give it, will they not have more faith and devotion, thinking, "This monk gives me what I want"?' In this case, the devotion laypeople had for that monk as a disciple of the Buddha before he gave the item is true faith. When he gives bamboo and such, they think, 'The monk who gave me bamboo, the monk who gave me vegetables,' and develop a personal attachment. Therefore, the devotion arising from receiving gifts is not true, pure faith. True faith...
336: ...has been destroyed. With the intention of showing how true faith is destroyed, the Buddha taught this as 'kula-dūsana'—the act that destroys the genuine faith of laypeople. Regarding 'ācāra' (good conduct) which should be practiced: if one takes everything shown under 'anācāra' (misconduct) and reverses it, that constitutes the collection of good conduct. Reversing it means, for example, not transgressing the three bodily misdeeds such as killing, and so on. (b) Regarding the 'resort' (gocara), there are two types: blameless resort and blameworthy resort. Among these: Blameworthy resort means: in this Dispensation, some monks might frequent the company of prostitutes. (This refers to entering and leaving a prostitute's house familiarly.) They might frequent the company of widows, old maids, eunuchs, nuns, or taverns (liquor shops). They might associate with kings, great ministers, heretics (titthiya), and their disciples in a way that is improper for monks to mix with laypeople. They might visit houses where people have no faith or devotion toward the Buddha's disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and who speak abusively or threateningly, wishing for their harm, lack of benefit, and lack of happiness. All these—prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, nuns, taverns, kings, ministers, heretics, their disciples, and the houses of those faithless to the fourfold assembly—are called blameworthy resorts. The frequenting of such places by a monk is called blameworthy and faulty resort. 'Frequenting' (gocara) here refers to associating and making friends in an ignoble manner. Even in the case of a prostitute, if she invites a monk for an offering, he may go to receive the alms without losing mindfulness. Here, the five places—prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, and nuns—are mentioned in the context of the five cords of sensual pleasure...
337:
(Dā)
Because it is a place of dependence, it becomes an improper resort. Taverns and liquor shops are improper resorts because they cause danger to the holy life. Kings and their great ministers are improper resorts because they do not provide much benefit to the monk's practice and can destroy it with the thunderbolt of gain, honor, and fame. Houses of those without faith, houses of those without devotion, and houses where one is reviled and threatened are improper resorts because they cause the decline of faith and the agitation of the mind.

Having shown the improper resorts, the proper resorts should be understood by way of the opposite. By 'opposite', it means: those men and women who have faith, who believe in the Triple Gem and the law of kamma and its results. They are like inexhaustible wells and lakes for the monks. Their houses shine with the radiance of monks' robes (meaning monks constantly enter and leave). They are always brushed by the wind caused by the movement of the monks' robes and limbs. They desire the welfare and happiness of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. The homes of such men and women are called proper resorts for the monks.

Alternatively, the meaning of conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara) should also be understood in the following way. How should it be understood?

Improper conduct (anācāra) which should not be practiced is of two kinds: bodily misconduct (kāyika-anācāra) and verbal misconduct (vācasika-anācāra). Bodily misconduct means: being a monk, yet when arriving in the midst of the Saṅgha, not showing signs of respect; standing or sitting by brushing against or jostling the elder monks; standing or sitting in front of the elder monks; sitting in a place higher than the elder monks; sitting with the head covered; speaking while standing; speaking while waving, swinging, or raising the hands; walking on the cloister path with sandals while the elder monks are walking without sandals; walking on a higher cloister path while the elder monks are walking on a lower one; walking on a cloister path while the elder monks are walking on the ground; or walking—
338:
(Dha)
—on the cloister path while jostling the elder monks; sitting or standing by jostling them; obstructing junior monks from their seats (not giving them a seat); putting wood into the fire-shed or closing the door without asking permission from the elder monks; descending to the water-landing by jostling the elder monks or descending before them; bathing by jostling them or bathing before them; ascending to the bank by jostling them or ascending before them; when entering the village, walking by jostling the elder monks or walking before them; overtaking the elder monks who are walking ahead and walking in front of them; when arriving inside a town or village, hastily entering the private rooms of lay devotees or the rooms where women reside; stroking or touching the heads of children in that house (showing signs of affection). All this is called bodily misconduct (kāyika-anācāra).

Verbal misconduct (vācasika-anācāra) means: being a monk, yet when arriving in the midst of the Saṅgha, not showing signs of respect and preaching the Dhamma without asking permission from the elder monks; answering others' questions; reciting the Pātimokkha; speaking while standing; speaking while stretching or swinging the arms; when arriving in a town or village, addressing older women or young women by saying, "Woman named so-and-so (Sumanā, etc.), woman of such-and-such a clan (Gotamī, etc.), what is there? Is there gruel? Is there rice? Is there food? What is there to drink? What is there to chew? What is there to eat? What will you give to me?" and so forth, speaking without restraint of the senses. All this is called verbal misconduct (vācasika-anācāra).

Good conduct (ācāra) should be understood by way of the opposite of the aforementioned improper conduct (anācāra). Alternatively, it is called good conduct (ācāra) when one is endowed with respect, humility, shame (hiri), and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa); wearing the under-robe properly; covering oneself with the upper-robe properly; moving forward and backward gracefully; looking straight ahead and looking aside gracefully; bending and stretching gracefully; being endowed with the posture of downcast eyes; guarding the sense faculties; knowing the measure in food; and practicing wakefulness.
339:
(Dhā)
Being unforgetful; maintaining clear comprehension (sampajañña) in all things; having few desires; being easily satisfied; possessing effort and energy in wholesome states; and respectfully practicing the duties of the Ābhisamācārika-sīla mentioned earlier. This collection of qualities is called good conduct (ācāra).

Resort (gocara) is of three kinds: (1) Upanissaya-gocara = the resort that is a powerful cause for virtues such as morality; (2) Ārakkha-gocara = the resort that guards the mind; (3) Upanibandha-gocara = the resort that serves as the place for binding the mind. Among these three:

(1) A noble friend (kalyāṇamitta) who is endowed with the quality of speaking only the ten kinds of talk that lead to liberation from the round of suffering is called Upanissaya-gocara. By depending on such a noble friend, one can hear what has not been heard, purify what has been heard, dispel doubts, straighten one's view, and gain clarity of mind. Furthermore, by following the example of such a noble friend, one can increase in faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Therefore, that noble friend is called Upanissaya-gocara, being a powerful cause for the increase of virtues such as morality.

The ten kinds of talk that lead to liberation from the round of suffering are:
(1) Appicchakathā = talk on having few desires,
(2) Santuṭṭhikathā = talk on contentment with what one has,
(3) Pavivekakathā = talk on the suitability of living in seclusion,
(4) Asaṃsaggakathā = talk on not associating with those one should not associate with,
(5) Vīriyārambhakathā = talk on exerting effort in what should be practiced,
(6) Sīlakathā = talk concerning noble morality,
340:
(Dhi)
(7) Samādhikathā = talk concerning concentration,
(8) Paññākathā = talk concerning insight-knowledge and path-knowledge,
(9) Vimuttikathā = talk concerning the fruit of liberation (or talk concerning the five kinds of liberation),
(10) Vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā = talk concerning the knowledge and vision of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) that reflects on the path and fruit.
These are the ten.

In brief, those persons who habitually speak only these ten kinds of talk that lead to liberation, thereby enabling one to obtain the five benefits such as hearing what has not been heard, and those noble friends who cause the five qualities of faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom to increase—these persons are called Upanissaya-gocara, the resort that is a powerful cause for the increase of virtues such as morality.

(2) Mindfulness (sati) that guards the mind is called Ārakkha-gocara. Ārakkha = guarding the mind; gocara = the resort of mindfulness. A monk who resorts to this resort of mindfulness, when entering a town for alms, walks with downcast eyes, looking only a plow's length ahead, and with restrained senses. He walks without looking at the elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, infantry, or at women and men. He does not look up, nor does he look down, nor does he look at the eight directions. He walks only in this way. A monk who does not resort to the Ārakkha-gocara of mindfulness, when entering a town or village for alms, walks looking here and there like a confused crow. Therefore, mindfulness is called Ārakkha-gocara, the resort that guards the monk's mind so that unwholesome states do not enter.

(3) The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) are called Upanibandha-gocara because they are the great pastures where the mind is bound. (Upanibandha = where the mind is bound; gocara = great pastures.)
341:
(Dhī)
A monk who wishes to fulfill the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla to complete purity must be endowed with the aforementioned good conduct (ācāra) and proper resort (gocara). Furthermore, even in the case of very small faults the size of an atom, he should habitually see them as a great danger and a great fault, and thus properly undertake and practice the training rules.

## The Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla is completed.
**********
## (2) Indriya-saṃvara-sīla
Guarding the sense faculties is called Indriya-saṃvara-sīla. (The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six are called indriya (faculties). 'Indriya' means 'dominion' or 'governance'. In the act of seeing a visual form, only the eye (cakkhu-pasāda) has dominion; if the eye is defective, one cannot see (eye-consciousness cannot arise). Therefore, the Buddha taught the eye as the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya). In the same way, in hearing various sounds, the ear (sota-pasāda) has dominion; if the ear is defective, one cannot hear (ear-consciousness cannot arise). Therefore, the Buddha taught it as the ear-faculty (sotindriya). In smelling various odors, the nose (ghāna-pasāda) has dominion; if the nose is defective, one cannot smell (nose-consciousness cannot arise). Therefore, the Buddha taught it as the nose-faculty (ghānindriya). In tasting or eating various flavors, the tongue (jivhā-pasāda) has dominion; if the tongue is defective, one cannot taste or eat (tongue-consciousness cannot arise). Therefore, the Buddha taught it as the tongue-faculty (jivhindriya). In touching various tangibles, the body (kāya-pasāda) has dominion; if the body is damaged or defective, one cannot touch various tangibles (body-consciousness cannot arise). Therefore, the Buddha taught it as the body-faculty (kāyindriya). In knowing various cognizable objects, the mind (mano) has dominion; without the mind, one cannot know. Therefore, the Buddha taught the mind as the mind-faculty (manindriya). Restraining these six sense faculties is what is meant by Indriya-saṃvara-sīla.)
342:
The way to guard the sense faculties is... when seeing a form with the eye, one should let it remain in the mind exactly as it is seen (merely as a visual object). One must not grasp at the sign, such as 'this is a woman' or 'this is a man' or 'this is beautiful,' which causes the arising of defilements. One must not attend to the secondary characteristics (anubyañjana) such as the hands, feet, smiles, laughter, speech, or side-glances, which tend to manifest for the repeated arising of defilements within that very sign of a woman or man.
## The Story of Mahātissa Thera
In guarding this eye-faculty, one should take Mahātissa Thera, who resided on the summit of Cetiya Mountain, as an example. While Mahātissa Thera was walking from Cetiya Mountain into the city of Anurādhapura for alms, a certain woman in Anurādhapura, having quarreled with her husband and being beautifully adorned, was leaving for her parents' home. Upon seeing Mahātissa Thera walking with his eye-faculty restrained, she laughed loudly with the intention of attracting him to look at her. When Mahātissa Thera looked to see what it was, he perceived the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) in her teeth, continued to develop his monastic practice, and attained Arahantship.
Her husband, following her to bring her back, met the Thera and asked, 'Venerable sir, did you see a woman on the path you came by?' The Thera replied to that man:
Nābhijānāmi itthī vā, puriso vā ito gato.
Apica aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo, gacchatēsa mahāpathe.
'Layman, I did not know whether the one who went from here was a man or a woman. In truth, a collection of bones is traveling along this great road.' Thus he replied.
One should take this noble Thera as a good example, who, though seeing the form of a woman, saw it only as a sight and did not even keep in mind that it was a woman, but only developed his meditation and attained Arahantship.
343:
Because of the lack of restraint of the eye-faculty, unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā)—if the seen object is pleasant—and displeasure (domanassa)—if it is repulsive—would arise in that unrestrained monk. One should practice to guard and prevent those unwholesome states from arising through mindfulness.
Similarly, when hearing various sounds with the ear, smelling various odors with the nose, tasting various flavors with the tongue, touching various tangibles with the body, and cognizing various mental phenomena with the mind, one should practice to guard and prevent [defilements] through mindfulness, without grasping at the signs that cause defilements or the details and characteristics associated with those signs.
The Virtue of Restraint of the Sense Faculties (Indriya-saṃvara-sīla) is completed.
**********
## (3) Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla
Abstaining from livelihood based on requisites obtained through the power of the six training rules prescribed in the Vinaya teachings regarding livelihood, or through the power of other evil states, is called Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla (Virtue of Livelihood Purification).
The six training rules prescribed on account of livelihood are:
(1) If one, having evil desires and being overwhelmed by them, boastfully claims to have attained jhāna, path, or fruition which is not present or has never occurred in oneself, the training rule prescribes the offense of Pārājika (Defeat).
(2) If one acts as a matchmaker for men and women on account of livelihood, the training rule prescribes the offense of Saṅghādisesa (Formal Meeting of the Order).
344:
(3) If one, on account of livelihood, does not directly say 'I am an Arahant' but says, 'The monk who lives in your monastery is an Arahant,' and if the donor understands the speech, the training rule prescribes the offense of Thullaccaya (Grave Offense).
(4) If one, on account of livelihood, requests superior food for oneself while healthy and eats it, the training rule prescribes the offense of Pācittiya (Expiation).
(5) If a Bhikkhunī, on account of livelihood, requests superior food for herself while healthy and eats it, the training rule prescribes the offense of Pāṭidesanī (Confession). (The 'superior food' mentioned in these points 4 and 5 refers to food mixed with ghee, butter, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, or curd.)
(6) If a monk, on account of livelihood, requests curry or alms-food for himself while healthy and eats it, the training rule prescribes the offense of Dukkaṭa (Wrong-doing).
These are the six.
Regarding 'other evil states,' it refers to wrong livelihoods such as (a) Kuhana, (b) Lapana, (c) Nemittikatā, (d) Nippesikatā, and (e) Lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā. Among them:
(a) Making oneself an object of wonder through pretense is called Kuhana. This Kuhana is of three types:
(1) Kuhana through the use of requisites,
(2) Kuhana through talk related to the vicinity of jhāna, path, and fruition,
(3) Kuhana through various adjustments of postures to impress others.
Among these three:
(1) Having evil desires to show qualities that are not present in oneself, when lay donors offer requisites such as robes, though desiring them in his heart, he says to make them offer more: 'What is the use of expensive robes for a monk?'
345:
'It is only proper for a monk to wear rag-robes (pāṃsukūla).' (Regarding alms-food:) 'What is the use of expensive alms-food for a monk? It is only proper for a monk to use only the food obtained by begging.' (Regarding dwellings:) 'What is the use of an expensive monastery for a monk? It is only proper for a monk to live at the root of a tree or in the open air.' (Regarding medicine:) 'What is the use of expensive medicine for a monk? It is only proper for a monk to fulfill his medicinal needs with cow-urine or pieces of yellow or chebulic myrobalan.' To match such speech, that monk uses coarse and harsh robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicine. Donors, being impressed, think, 'This venerable one has few desires, is easily satisfied, is secluded from objective and subjective sensuality, does not socialize with laypeople, and possesses exerted energy,' and they invite him with more and more of the four requisites. Then, that monk with evil desires says boastfully, 'Laypeople, when these three—faith, the object to be given, and the recipient—meet, merit can greatly increase for a noble person of faith. You clearly have faith, and the object to be given is also present. I am indeed a recipient. If I do not accept, your merit will decrease and decline; therefore, though I have no desire, I must accept out of compassion for you.' After saying this, he accepts many robes, much alms-food, many dwellings, and many medicinal requisites, transporting them by the cartload. Thus, though being one with great desires, pretending to be one with few desires and acting to impress others by pretending to use coarse and harsh requisites is called Kuhana-vatthu through the use of requisites (paccaya-paṭisevana).
(2) Without directly saying 'I have attained jhāna, path, or fruition,' saying various things to make others believe he is a person who has attained them, such as: 'A monk who wears a robe of this nature is a monk of great power. A monk who carries a bowl of this nature, a monk who carries a water-strainer, a monk who carries a filter, a monk who wears a waist-band of this nature, or a monk who wears sandals of this nature is a monk of great power.'
346:
This and other various ways of speaking to make others think of oneself as a person who has attained jhāna, path, and fruition is called Kuhana-vatthu through talk in the vicinity of jhāna, path, and fruition (sāmanta-jappana).
(3) Desiring the praise and admiration of lay donors, thinking 'If I walk this way, they will praise and admire me,' and deliberately adjusting and pretending one's postures through walking, standing, sitting, or lying down as if one were a great Noble One (Ariya) to impress others is called Kuhana-vatthu through various adjustments of postures (iriyāpatha-saṇṭhapana).
(b) Lapana, which is included among evil natures, is... when seeing people coming to the monastery, saying proactively, 'Laypeople, for what purpose have you come? Have you come to invite monks? If you have come to invite, go ahead; I will follow carrying the bowl.' Or saying, 'I am the one called Tissa Thera; the King has devotion to me; the great ministers and officials have devotion to me,' and so on. In speaking with people, speaking in a way that follows their desires, giving them opportunities so as not to conflict or be tedious, and flattering them by calling them 'great wealthy man' or 'factory owner'—thus speaking in various ways to make them want to give even if they did not—is called the evil nature of Lapana.
(c) Nemittikatā, which is included among evil natures, is giving signs or hints so that they cannot help but give. The way of giving signs is... upon seeing someone carrying food, saying, 'Have you obtained food? Where did you get it? How did you manage to get it?' thus showing a sign of one's own desire. When seeing cowherds, pointing to the calves and asking, 'Do these calves grow by drinking milk, or do they grow only by drinking water?' and when the cowherds [reply], 'They grow by drinking milk...'
347:
"(The calves) are young cows, Venerable Sir," she replied. "I do not think so; if the calves were to drink milk, the monks would also receive milk (surely they would)." Such instances, where one informs the parents through the cowherd boys to prompt a donation of milk, or speaking even more directly (sāmantajappa), are the evil nature called lapana (scheming/hinting).

## The Story of the Family-Visiting Monk (Kulūpaka Bhikkhu)
Regarding this sāmantajappa—speaking so closely that it is impossible to avoid—the Visuddhimagga Commentary provides the story of a certain family-visiting monk. This monk, being very hungry, entered a house and sat down insistently. Seeing him, the housewife, who did not wish to give, complained, "There is no rice yet," and went to a nearby house as if searching for rice. The monk entered the inner room and looked here and there, seeing sugarcane leaning in the corner of the door, palm sugar in a jar, dried fish in a basket, rice in another jar, and ghee in yet another. He then returned to his seat and sat with a composed manner.

The housewife returned, complaining, "I could not find any rice." The monk said, "Laywoman, I saw an omen early on that today's alms would not be sufficient." When asked, "What kind of omen did you see, Bhante?", the monk replied, "On my way here for alms, I saw a snake as thick as the sugarcane leaning in the corner of your door. When I looked around for something to strike it with, I saw a stone the size of the palm sugar kept in your jar. When I threw the stone, the snake raised a hood as large as the dried fish in your basket. When the snake opened its mouth to bite the stone, I saw its fangs which were like the rice...
348:
...kept in your jar. Then, from the mouth of that angry snake, I saw foam and saliva mixed with venom, which looked like the ghee kept in your jar." Having been spoken to so closely that there was no way to hide or escape, the housewife said, "I can no longer deceive this shaven-headed monk." Giving up, she offered the sugarcane, cooked the rice, and offered everything along with the ghee, palm sugar, and dried fish.

(d) Nippesikatā, which is included in the evil natures, means 'wiping out' the virtues of a donor; (alternatively) it is seeking gain by 'grinding down' the virtues of others (donors), just as one grinds perfumes to extract the scent. The method of seeking is: speaking abusive words so that they dare not refrain from giving; speaking disparagingly, such as calling them 'creatures unlike humans' or 'creatures with no faith at all'; or speaking ironically to a non-giving donor, "Oh, what a great donor! Oh, what a magnificent donor!"; or mocking a non-giving donor in the midst of a crowd, saying, "Why do you say this person does not give? This person is always giving the word 'there is none' to all who come to receive alms." Seeking to obtain gains by thus grinding down the donor's reputation is called nippesikatā.

(e) Lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā, included in the evil natures, means seeking gain with gain. The method of seeking is: when food or drink is offered from one donor's house, upon reaching another house, one gives those items to the children of that house. This giving is done with the intent of making them happy and grateful so that they will give back much more in return. The obtained item is called 'lābha' in Pali and 'lābh' in Burmese. To remember it briefly, seeking to obtain many items from another house by using a small amount of items obtained from one house is called lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā, or seeking gain with gain.
349:
These five evil natures, such as kuhana (scheming), differ only in their specific modes of speech and action. In essence, they are all attempts to pull and manipulate donors so that they feel they cannot avoid giving, rather than the donors giving out of their own faith and devotion.

Livelihood based on items obtained by transgressing the six training rules laid down regarding the means of livelihood, or items sought through kuhana, lapana, nemittikatā, nippesikatā, and lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā, is called micchājīva (wrong livelihood). Abstaining from all such wrong livelihoods and remaining pure is called ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla (virtue of purification of livelihood).

Here ends Ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla.
**********
## (4) Paccayasannissita-sīla
Virtue that is fulfilled by depending on the four requisites is called paccayasannissita-sīla.
The four requisites are robes, alms food, lodging, and medicine. One cannot exist without using these four requisites; they must be used. It means that when using them, one must reflect on the nature of those requisites to prevent unwholesome states like greed and hatred from entering.

The manner of reflection is as follows: When using robes—
Without unwholesome intentions such as wanting to be beautiful or elegant, one should reflect on the appropriate reasons for the robe and use it, thinking: "I use this robe to ward off cold. I use this robe to ward off heat. I use this robe to ward off the touch of mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, lice, etc. I use this robe for the purpose of covering the body parts that cause shame."
350:
This reflection while using is to prevent the arising of unwholesome states like greed.

Regarding the requisite of alms food, one should reflect on its proper nature:
"I do not consume this alms food for the purpose of playing or carousing like children. I do not consume this alms food for the purpose of pride in my masculinity. I do not consume this alms food for the purpose of making the limbs plump and beautiful. I do not consume this alms food for the purpose of a beautiful complexion. I consume this alms food only for the purpose of maintaining and sustaining this body, for ending the affliction of hunger, and for assisting in the practice of the holy life. Thus, I shall eliminate the old feeling of hunger and not allow new feelings (such as indigestion or bloating from overeating) to arise. By eating moderately and appropriately, the maintenance of my body will continue without the old feeling of hunger or the new feeling of indigestion. In seeking and consuming this food, there will be blamelessness through righteousness and living in comfort by eating just enough."

One should consume it while reflecting in this way.
Regarding living by consuming moderately:

"Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;
Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno."

The Buddha taught: When a monk consuming alms food reaches the point where he would be full in four or five more mouthfuls, he should stop eating and drink water instead. For a monk whose mind is set solely on striving in meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), this is sufficient for living in comfort.
351:
In this regard, although the Buddha originally taught this for those practicing meditation, even those not practicing meditation can live comfortably regarding their stomach if they follow this. Therefore, it is a teaching that many should follow when eating.

Regarding the requisite of lodging, one should reflect on its proper nature without unwholesome intentions:
"I make use of this lodging to ward off cold. I make use of this lodging to ward off heat. I make use of this lodging to ward off the touch of mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, lice, etc. I make use of this lodging for the purpose of warding off the dangers of opposing cold and hot seasons and for the benefit of dwelling in comfort and seclusion."

One should use it while reflecting in this way.
Regarding the requisite of medicine, one should reflect on its proper nature:
"I make use of medicine, which is the opposite of disease and a protector of life, for the purpose of warding off painful feelings that have arisen or are arising due to the disturbance of the elements, and for the noble benefit of being free from affliction."

One should use it while reflecting in this way.

## (Robes)
To destroy cold and heat, to avoid mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, scorpions, and snakes; not with the mind of beautifying or decorating the body, but for the purpose of covering the limbs that would cause the loss of the virtue of modesty, I use this robe.

## (Alms Food)
I do not use these various kinds of food for play, pride, beauty, or plumpness. I use and depend on this food so that this body, which carries the four elements, may endure long, sustain life, be free from exhaustion, and be able to practice the twofold training of the Buddha's Dispensation...
352:
...so that old and new painful feelings do not arise, and so that I may live in comfort and be free from all faults, I consume and make use of this food.

## (Lodging)
To destroy cold and heat, to keep away mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, scorpions, and snakes, to be free from the dangers of the seasons, and for the sake of mental clarity, I dwell in and depend on this lodging.

## (Medicine)
To abandon and remove painful feelings that have arisen or will arise, which are oppressive and difficult to bear, and to be free from suffering so that I may clearly and joyfully fulfill the practice of the Dispensation of the Great Noble King of Humans (the Buddha), I use this medicine with this aim.
(Mnemonic by Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw)

Here ends Paccayasannissita-sīla.
**********
## The Procedure for Fulfilling These Four Virtues
Among these four virtues, Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha) should be fulfilled through faith (saddhā). Faith means: believing in the Buddha—that the Buddha, who taught the training rules, is truly the Buddha who can see all things correctly without exception (maintaining a clear mind toward the Buddha); believing in the training rules—that this collection of training rules I must now practice is truly the training rules taught and laid down by the Buddha (maintaining a clear mind toward the Dhamma); and believing in the Saṅgha—that the Noble Saṅgha, the disciples of the Buddha, are indeed those who practice this collection of training rules well (maintaining a clear mind toward the Saṅgha).

It means that if there is such faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, one can practice this Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla to fulfillment.
353:
(Ni)
Therefore, one should fulfill the collection of training rules exactly as preached and prescribed by the Blessed One, without leaving any remainder, undertaking them with faith and observing them respectfully, even without regard for one's own life. Indeed—

(Kikīva aṇḍaṃ camarīva vāladhiṃ) and so forth: "Just as a hen protects her eggs by sacrificing her life; just as a yak protects its tail by sacrificing its life; just as a wealthy man protects his only son with great care; just as a person with only one good eye protects that eye with great care; likewise, you who protect your virtue (sīla), maintaining respect throughout the three stages of life, should be those who cherish virtue (those who love and value virtue greatly)."

Such words were preached by the Blessed One.

## Stories of Elders who Fulfilled Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla by Sacrificing Their Lives

In ancient times, in the great forest named Mahāvaṭṭani in the island of Sri Lanka, thieves captured an Elder, bound him with creepers, and left him lying flat on the ground. Although the Elder could have struggled to free himself if he wished, he feared that if he did so, the creepers would break and he would incur an offense (bhūtagāma-pācittiya). Therefore, he remained lying there as he was left, developed insight (vipassanā) for seven days, reached the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and after passing away in that very place, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

Another Elder was also bound by thieves in Sri Lanka with Sinthama creepers and left lying flat so that he could not rise. At that moment, when a forest fire approached, the Elder could have cut the creepers if he wished, but fearing he would incur an offense, he did not cut them. Instead, he meditated on insight and became an Arahant at the very moment life ended and defilements were exhausted (known as samasīsī), and attained Parinibbāna. At that time, the Elder Abhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, arrived at that place with five hundred monks, and seeing the Elder's body, performed the funeral rites properly and had a stupa built.
354:
(Nu)
Therefore, it is stated as an instruction in the Commentary (Atthakathā):

Pātimokkhaṃ visodhento, appeva jīvitaṃ jahe.
Paññattaṃ lokanāthena, na bhinde sīlasaṃvaraṃ.

"A person of good family who purifies the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha should sacrifice even life itself. One should not break the training rule prescribed by the Lord of the World."

**********

Just as the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is to be fulfilled through faith, likewise, the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla) is to be fulfilled through mindfulness (sati). Only when the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, guarded and maintained by mindfulness, is complete, can the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha endure for a long time. If the restraint of the sense faculties fails, the restraint by the Pātimokkha also tends to fail.

During the time of the Blessed One, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, shortly after becoming a monk, failed in his restraint of the sense faculties while wandering for alms. Upon seeing a woman, lustful thoughts arose in him, and he said to the Venerable Ānanda:

"O Venerable Ānanda of the Gotama lineage, I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by the fire of sensual lust. I entreat you, out of compassion, please preach the excellent Dhamma that can extinguish this heat."

Then the Venerable Ānanda said:

"Your mind is consumed by the fire of lust because of perverted perception. Cast away the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta) associated with lust, and develop the mind towards the perception of foulness (asubha)."

He preached the Dhamma in this manner and others, and when Vaṅgīsa applied his mind accordingly, the fire of lust was extinguished.
355:
(Nū)
In another way, a person who wishes to fulfill the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties should be like the Elder Cittagutta, who resided in the Kuraṇḍaka Cave in Sri Lanka, or like the Elder Mahāmitta, who resided in the Coraka Monastery.

## The Story of the Great Elder Cittagutta

In the great cave called Kuraṇḍaka, beautiful and wonderful paintings of the renunciation scenes of the seven Buddhas, beginning with Vipassī, were painted. When many visiting monks were touring the monasteries and saw the paintings of the renunciation scenes, they went to the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, the paintings of the Buddha's renunciation scenes in the cave where you reside are very delightful."

The Elder replied, "Friends, I have lived in this great cave for over sixty years, but I did not know whether there were paintings or not. Only today, through you friends who have very sharp eyesight, do I know that there are paintings."

(The Elder had resided there for over sixty years but had never once looked up at the cave. At the entrance of that cave, there was also a large Karaka tree; he never looked up at that Karaka tree either. He only knew that the great Karaka tree had bloomed when he saw the fallen pollen on the ground every year.)

The King heard the news of the Elder's possession of such virtues of sense restraint and wished to pay respects. Although he sent messengers to invite him three times, the Elder did not come. Then the King issued an order and placed a seal, declaring that in the village where the Elder went for alms, the breasts of women with nursing infants were to be bound with cloth so they could not nurse, and they would not be allowed to nurse until the Elder came. When the Elder learned that the infants were suffering and crying because they could not nurse, he went to the city of Mahāgāma out of compassion for the children.

The King, hearing the news that the Elder had arrived, said, "Friends, go now. Bring the Elder into the palace."
356:
(Ne)
"Bring him here; I wish to receive the precepts." He had the Elder invited to the palace, paid respects, and offered alms-food, saying, "Venerable Sir, today I am not free to receive the precepts; I will receive them tomorrow." He then carried the Elder's bowl, followed him for a short distance, paid respects along with the Queen, and returned.

Whether it was the King who paid respects or the Queen, the Elder only said, "May the King be happy." After seven days had passed in this manner, the monks said, "Venerable Sir, whether the King pays respects or the Queen pays respects, you only say, 'May the King be happy.'"

Then the Elder replied, "Friends, I do not make a distinction that 'this is the King' or 'this is the Queen'." After seven days, the King realized that it was difficult for the Elder to reside in the city and gave him leave to return. When the Elder returned to his cave, he went up to the ambulatory (caṅkama) at night and practiced walking meditation.

The deity guarding the Karaka tree came and stood holding a lamp. At that time, the Elder's meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) was very pure and became very clear. The Elder, with a mind full of joy, thinking, "Why is my meditation subject so clear today?", attained Arahantship after midnight, making the entire mountain echo. (The sense restraint—indriya-saṃvara—of this Elder is truly worthy of emulation.)

## The Story of the Elder Mahāmitta

Regarding the story of the Elder Mahāmitta: The Elder's mother had a poisonous abscess on her breast. Since her daughter was a nun (bhikkhunī), she called her and said, "Go to your brother, tell him that I have a painful abscess, and bring back some medicine."

The nun went to her brother, the Elder Mahāmitta, and explained the situation. The Elder said, "I do not know how to take medicinal roots and such to prepare medicine."
357:
(Nai)
"I do not know the way, but I will tell you a kind of medicine. From the time I became a monk until today, I have never once looked at the object of a woman, who is of a different gender, by breaking my sense restraint with a mind of lustful greed. By this word of truth, may my mother be well. When you return and reach our mother, recite this word of truth that I have just spoken and stroke her body."

That sister, the nun, went to her mother, told her all that her brother, the Elder Mahāmitta, had said, and while reciting the word of truth as instructed, she stroked her mother's body. At that very moment, the mother's poisonous abscess crumbled and disappeared like a mass of foam. The mother rose from her place and spoke words of joy: "If the Blessed One were still alive, why would He not stroke the head of a monk like my son with His golden hand, which is interlaced with a net of golden light?"

The manner in which this Elder Mahāmitta guarded his senses is slightly different from the manner of the great Elder Cittagutta mentioned before. Elder Cittagutta's way of guarding was to keep his eyes downcast so as not to see or look at any object he encountered. Elder Mahāmitta, however, did not keep his eyes downcast in that way; he looked at whatever was present. But when he looked, even if he saw the object of a woman of a different gender, he guarded himself by preventing the mind of greed and attachment from entering (from arising).

For example, Elder Cittagutta's way of guarding the eye faculty (cakkhundriya) is like keeping the door of a house closed so that bad people cannot enter. Elder Mahāmitta's way of guarding the eye faculty is like not keeping the door closed, but forcefully preventing bad people from ever entering. The ways in which these two Elders guarded their senses are both wonderful and truly worthy of emulation.

**********
358: Just as one should fulfill the virtue of sense-restraint (indriyasaṃvara-sīla) with mindfulness, so too should one fulfill the virtue of purification of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) with effort (vīriya). This is because only a person with well-exerted effort can abandon wrong livelihood. Therefore, one must abandon unsearchable and improper ways, and fulfill that virtue through proper searching, such as going for alms, only with effort. Among the four requisites of alms-food, robes, lodgings, and medicine, for the two types—alms-food and robes—the following four methods are improper: making a sign (nimitta) to make donors want to offer, speaking in a roundabout way (obhāsa), speaking with indirect hints (parikathā), and direct begging (viññatti). (This means these four should not be done to obtain alms-food and robes.) Regarding the lodging requisite, only direct begging is improper. The other three are permissible. Among those three: Making a sign (nimitta) means, for example, when a monk is preparing the ground as if to build a monastery, and a donor asks, "Venerable sir, what are you doing? Who is having this built?" the monk replies, "No one is having it built yet." (Meaning, he says there is no donor yet.) Besides this preparation of the ground, various other actions that make people know "this monk desires a monastery" are also called making a sign. Speaking in a roundabout way (obhāsa) means asking, "Lay disciples, what kind of house do you live in?" and when they reply, "We live in a palace," saying, "Lay disciples, is it not also proper for monks to live in a palace?" and such other roundabout talk that makes one's desire for a monastery known. Speaking with indirect hints (parikathā) means saying things like, "The living quarters for the Saṅgha are very cramped," and so on.
359:
Regarding medicinal requisites, all four methods, such as making a sign, are allowable. However, whether it is allowable to use medicinal requisites obtained through signs and so on for a specific illness after that illness has been cured is a matter for investigation.

In this matter, the Elders who are Vinaya-holders (Vinayadhara) say, 'The Buddha has opened the way for its use. Therefore, it is allowable.' However, the Elders who are Sutta-holders (Suttantadhara) say, 'Because the Buddha permitted it, no offense (āpatti) can be incurred. Nevertheless, because it ruins the purity of livelihood, it is not allowable.'

A person who wishes to be endowed with the noble practice, even though the Buddha has permitted it, should avoid requisites obtained through the four mentioned methods—making a sign, speaking in hints, speaking in roundabout ways, or making a direct request—and should instead rely only on qualities such as fewness of desires. Even if it means death, they should avoid requisites brought about by these four points and only then use the four requisites. Such a person is called 'one endowed with the most noble practice of scrupulousness,' like the Venerable Sāriputta Thera.

## The Story of Venerable Sāriputta
Once, Venerable Sāriputta Thera, wishing to develop the Dhamma in a secluded place, was residing in a forest together with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera. At that time, one day, Venerable Sāriputta suffered from a wind-ailment and was very distressed and exhausted. When Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went to attend to Venerable Sāriputta in the evening, he saw him lying down and asked about the cause. He asked, 'Friend, when you had wind-ailment in the past, what medicine brought you relief?' Then Venerable Sāriputta said, 'Friend, when I was a layman and such a wind-ailment arose, my mother used to cook and give me thick milk rice mixed with ghee, honey, and molasses without adding water. By that milk rice, my wind-ailment was relieved.' When he said this, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...
360: "Let it be, friend. If you and I have merit, we shall receive undiluted milk-rice even tomorrow." A tree deity (rukkha-devatā) guarding a tree at the edge of the cloister (caṅkama) heard the two Elders conversing and thought, "I will cause milk-rice to be provided for the Venerable one tomorrow." Immediately, the deity went to the house of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's supporter (dāyaka) and possessed the eldest son, causing him distress. When the relatives gathered to treat the son, the deity said, "If you prepare and offer such milk-rice to the Elder tomorrow, I will release him." The relatives replied, "Even if you do not say so, we always offer alms-food to the Elder," and the next day, they prepared undiluted milk-rice. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna came to Venerable Sāriputta early and said, "Friend, please stay right here until I return from alms-round," and then entered the village. The people came out to meet him, took the Elder's bowl, filled it with undiluted milk-rice, and offered it. When the Elder made a gesture to leave, the people said, "Venerable sir, please eat. We will also offer separate milk-rice," and after serving the Elder milk-rice, they filled his bowl again and offered it. The Elder returned and presented it, saying, "Friend Sāriputta, please eat now." When Venerable Sāriputta saw the milk-rice, he reflected, "This milk-rice is very delightful. How did it come to be?" Upon reflecting, he saw the source of how the milk-rice was obtained and said, "Friend Mahāmoggallāna, this alms-food is not suitable to be consumed." Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, without feeling any resentment like "How can he not eat food brought by someone like me?", at the single word of Venerable Sāriputta, took the bowl...
361:
Holding it by the rim, he turned it over and discarded it in a suitable place. (This was not out of anger.)

As soon as the thick milk rice fell to the ground, Venerable Sāriputta's illness disappeared. (From that time on, it did not recur for forty-five years.) After that, he said to Venerable Moggallāna, 'Friend, thick milk rice that is brought about by relying on verbal utterance, even if one is so hungry that the intestines come out in coils and fall to the ground, is of a nature that is not fit to be consumed.'

In this matter, it should be specially noted that the Buddha only prohibited making a request—verbal intimation (vaci-viññatti). Venerable Sāriputta did not speak words of verbal intimation to request the thick milk rice; he merely recounted a past event because Venerable Moggallāna asked out of a desire to know. However, it should be understood that because it had become a verbal utterance—a verbal intimation—he did not delight in it and thus did not accept the thick milk rice.

## The Story of Ambakhādaka Mahātissa Thera
In the time of the Buddha, not to mention a Great Elder like Venerable Sāriputta, the Elder Mahātissa, who resided in the Cīragumba region of the island of Sri Lanka, was traveling during a time of famine. Due to lack of food and exhaustion from the journey, his body was weak and his strength greatly diminished. He stayed at the foot of a mango tree laden with fruit. Many mangoes were falling here and there nearby. No matter how hungry the Elder was, he did not think of picking them up and consuming them himself.

At that time, an old man arrived near the Great Elder and, realizing the Elder's exhaustion, made a drink from the mangoes and offered it to him. Then, placing the Elder on his back, he carried him toward the place the Elder wished to go. The Elder reflected, 'This person is not your father, nor your mother, nor a relative, yet he performs this act of carrying you on his back. This is only because of your possession of virtue.' Admonishing himself not to let his virtue and concentration (samādhi) fail, he developed insight (vipassanā) while being carried on the back. Proceeding through the stages of the Path, he attained Arahantship right there on that back.
362:
nor your mother, nor a relative, yet he performs this act of carrying you on his back. This is only because of your possession of virtue.' Admonishing himself not to let his virtue and concentration fail, he developed insight while being carried on the back. Proceeding through the stages of the Path, he attained Arahantship right there on that back.

This Great Elder is also a noble person who should be taken as an example and model in the matter of not being greedy for requisites and food.
**********
Just as one should fulfill the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) through effort (vīriya), one should fulfill the virtue concerning the use of requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla) through wisdom (paññā). Indeed, since only a wise person can see the benefits and faults in the four requisites as they truly are, that virtue concerning the use of requisites is a virtue to be accomplished through wisdom. Therefore, removing attachment to the four requisites, one should fulfill and use the requisites obtained in accordance with the Dhamma only after reflecting with the wisdom of review (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) according to the procedure already mentioned.

## Two Types of Reflection (Paccavekkhaṇā)
Reflection on the four requisites is of two types: (1) reflection at the time of receiving, and (2) reflection at the time of use. To expand: not only when using the four requisites, but also when receiving them, one must store them after reflecting either by (a) Dhātu-paccavekkhaṇā = reflecting in terms of elements, or (b) Paṭikūla-paccavekkhaṇā = reflecting in terms of loathsomeness.

(a) Dhātu-paccavekkhaṇā means: 'This robe,' 'this almsfood,' 'this dwelling,' 'this medicine' is merely a collection of elements (dhātu) in the form of an octad of pure matter (aṭṭhakalāpa) arising from causes. It refers to attending to and reflecting in terms of elements that the person who will use 'that robe,' 'that almsfood,' 'that dwelling,' 'that medicine' is also merely a collection of elements.

(b) Paṭikūla-paccavekkhaṇā means: reflecting on almsfood according to the meditation on the loathsomeness of food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), and reflecting, 'All these robes and so on...'
363:
Although the requisites are not repulsive by their own original nature, this means to reflect and consider them as repulsive, thinking that they certainly become repulsive once they reach this putrid carcass of a body.

## (Robes)
These requisites called robes,
If they were to exist on their own,
They would not be of a repulsive kind;
Yet, by means of using them
With this putrid, foul-smelling carcass of a body,
Before long, their original nature
Quickly vanishes and disappears,
And they shall surely become loathsome.

## (Alms-food)
These requisites called alms-food,
If they were to exist on their own,
They would not be of a repulsive kind;
Yet, by means of using them
With this putrid, foul-smelling carcass of a body,
Before long, their original nature
Quickly vanishes and disappears,
And they shall surely become loathsome.

## (Lodging)
These requisites called lodging,
If they were to exist on their own,
They would not be of a repulsive kind;
Yet, by means of using them
With this putrid, foul-smelling carcass of a body,
Before long, their original nature
Quickly vanishes and disappears,
And they shall surely become loathsome.

## (Medicine)
These requisites called medicine,
If they were to exist on their own,
They would not be of a repulsive kind;
Yet, by means of using them
With this putrid, foul-smelling carcass of a body,
Before long, their original nature
Quickly vanishes and disappears,
And they shall surely become loathsome.

(The specific point to be noted is that there are three types of reflection regarding the four requisites: (1) Mahāpaccavekkhaṇā, which is reflection as previously explained in detail; (2) Dhātupaccavekkhaṇā, which is reflection by way of elements as just explained; and (3) Paṭikūlamanasikāra Paccavekkhaṇā, which is reflection by way of repulsiveness. These three should be specifically understood.)
364:
When a monk uses robes and other requisites that have been properly reflected upon, his usage is blameless from beginning to end.

Regarding reflection at the time of use, the following is the decision that removes doubt. To elaborate, the usage of the four requisites is of four kinds:
(a) Usage as a thief (theyyaparibhoga),
(b) Usage as a debtor (iṇaparibhoga),
(c) Usage as an heir (dāyajjaparibhoga),
(d) Usage as a master (sāmiparibhoga).

Among these four:
(a) The usage of the four requisites by one who lacks virtue is called 'usage as a thief' (theyyaparibhoga), even if he uses them while living in the midst of the Saṅgha.
(The Blessed One permitted the use of the four requisites only for those who possess virtue. Donors also give only to those with virtue, intending for their meritorious deeds to bear great fruit. Therefore, these four requisites have nothing to do with immoral (dussīla) persons; because they use them despite having no right to them, the usage by an immoral person should be regarded as 'usage as a thief' = theyyaparibhoga. — Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā.)

(b) The usage of the requisites by a virtuous person without reflection is called 'usage as a debtor' (iṇaparibhoga). Therefore, robes should be reflected upon every time they are put on. Alms-food should be reflected upon mouthful by mouthful. If this is not possible, it should be reflected upon during the morning, the evening, the first watch of the night, the middle watch, or the last watch before dawn.
365:
It should be reflected upon. If dawn breaks without such reflection, one stands in the position of 'usage as a debtor' (iṇaparibhoga). Lodging should be reflected upon every time one enters within the eaves, and after entering, every time one sits or lies down. Medicine should be reflected upon both when it is accepted and when it is used. However, if one reflects when accepting but fails to reflect when using, one commits an offense; if one fails to reflect when accepting but reflects when using, one is free from the offense.

## The Four Purities of Virtue
The purity of virtue is of four kinds:
(1) Purity through confession (desanāsuddhi),
(2) Purity through restraint (saṃvarasuddhi),
(3) Purity through search (pariyyeṭṭhisuddhi),
(4) Purity through reflection (paccavekkhaṇāsuddhi).

Among these four:
Virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is purified through confession (desanāsuddhi), that is, by clearly revealing any offense committed.

Virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla) is purified through restraint. It becomes pure virtue only through restraint by resolving, "I will not do this again." (saṃvarasuddhi.)

Virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla) is virtue purified through search. It is purified by abandoning improper searches and obtaining requisites only in accordance with the Dhamma. (pariyyeṭṭhisuddhi.)

Virtue dependent on requisites (paccaya-sannissita-sīla) is called virtue purified through reflection. This virtue can only be purified by reflecting in the manner already described. (paccavekkhaṇāsuddhi.) Therefore, it is said: (Even if one fails to reflect when accepting, if one reflects when using, one is free from the offense.)
366:
(c) The usage of the four requisites by the seven types of learners (sekha, the lower seven noble disciples) is called 'usage as an heir' (dāyajjaparibhoga). The seven types of learners are the sons of the Blessed One. Therefore, just as a son receives his father's inheritance, they use the four requisites permitted by the Blessed One as heirs. (Although the four requisites are donated by lay donors, they become the property of the Blessed One because He permitted them.)

(d) The usage by Arahants is called 'usage as a master' (sāmiparibhoga). Since worldlings (puthujjana) and learners (sekha) are not yet free from craving (taṇhā) and must follow its lead, they do not have mastery in using requisites. Arahants, however, are truly liberated from the slavery of craving and thus have mastery in using requisites. For this very reason, those Arahants can use a repulsive requisite in a non-repulsive manner, a non-repulsive requisite in a repulsive manner, or, setting aside both these manners, use it with equanimity.

Among these four types of usage, 'usage as a master' (sāmiparibhoga) and 'usage as an heir' (dāyajjaparibhoga) are allowable for all [noble] persons. In this context, although sāmiparibhoga specifically pertains to Arahants, it can be said that if learners and worldlings use requisites without being greedy for the taste, abandoning the craving for taste through the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhārepaṭikūlasaññā), they are like those liberated from the slavery of craving and are entitled to sāmiparibhoga. It can also be said that Arahants and worldlings [who are practitioners] are also the heir-sons of the Blessed One.

'Usage as a debtor' (iṇaparibhoga) is not allowable. As for 'usage as a thief' (theyyaparibhoga), it goes without saying that it is certainly not allowable. Specifically, for a virtuous person,
367:
Usage with reflection is the opposite of iṇaparibhoga and is thus called 'usage as one who is debt-free' (āṇaṇyaparibhoga). Alternatively, because a virtuous worldling is endowed with the training of virtue through using requisites with reflection, he can be counted among the noble learners (sekha); thus, the usage with reflection by such a virtuous worldling is indeed called 'usage as an heir' (dāyajjaparibhoga).

Among these four types of usage, since 'usage as a master' (sāmiparibhoga) is the most excellent, a monk who longs for and desires that sāmiparibhoga should fulfill the virtue dependent on requisites (paccaya-sannissita-sīla) by using the four requisites with reflection according to the method described.

Here ends the group of four virtues.
**********
## The Group of Five Virtues
Alternatively, there are five kinds:
(1) Virtue of limited purity (pariyantapārisuddhisīla),
(2) Virtue of unlimited purity (apariyantapārisuddhisīla),
(3) Virtue of fulfilled purity (paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīla),
(4) Virtue untouched [by craving and views] (aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīla),
(5) Virtue of tranquilized purity (paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla).

Among these five:
The virtue of laypeople and novices is called 'virtue of limited purity' (pariyantapārisuddhisīla) because it is a virtue to be purified within a limited number.

In the Visuddhimagga Commentary, the nature of the numerical limitation of this pariyantapārisuddhisīla is not explained in detail. However, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary, as previously shown, limitation (pariyanta) is...
368:
There are two kinds: (a) limitation by training rules (sikkhāpadapariyanta) and (b) limitation by time (kālapariyanta). Among them, (a) limitation by training rules means that laymen and laywomen observe one, two, three, four, five, eight, or ten training rules according to their desire and custom. (Meaning they undertake training rules by limiting them as much as they wish or are able.) Probationers (sikkhamānā), male novices, and female novices undertake and practice the ten training rules. This is limitation by training rules.

(b) Regarding limitation by time: laymen and laywomen undertake virtue by limiting it to the duration of their offering when they give alms. When they go to a monastery, they undertake virtue for the duration before they return from the monastery. They undertake it by limiting the days and nights to one day, two days, three days, or longer. This is explained as limitation by time.

For monks, the Blessed One taught the 227 training rules of the two codes (dve mātikā) summarized from the Ubhatovibhaṅga Pāḷi, and in detail, nine thousand one hundred and eighty crores, five million, thirty-six thousand Vinaya practices to be guarded. The Elders who conducted the Councils also presented them in summary. This collection of training rules and virtue is called 'virtue of unlimited purity' (apariyantapārisuddhisīla).

Although there is a numerical limit here, it is called 'virtue of unlimited purity' (apariyantapārisuddhisīla) because monks must undertake and practice them without leaving any remainder in the limitation, and because one does not see a limit where virtue would be broken for the sake of these five: gain, fame, relatives, limbs, or life. This virtue is of the kind possessed by the Elder Mahātissa who resided in Ciragumba, who became an Arahant while eating a mango. This Elder...
369:
Even while lying under a mango tree, though extremely hungry and thirsty, he disregarded the threat to his life and maintained his virtue (sīla) alone.

The virtue of noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) that is completely purified is called Paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīla. The virtue of such noble worldlings, from the time of their ordination, is like a brilliantly shining ruby that has been well-polished, or like pure gold that has been well-refined. Because it is so extremely pure, it is free from even the stains of defilements that are merely thoughts, and thus it becomes a proximate cause for the Fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, such fulfilled virtue of noble worldlings is called Paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīla, like the virtue of Mahāsaṅgharakkhita Thera and his nephew, Saṅgharakkhita Thera.

## The Story of Mahāsaṅgharakkhita Thera

When Mahāsaṅgharakkhita Thera had passed sixty vassa (eighty years of age) and was lying on his deathbed, the community of monks asked him, "Venerable Sir, have you attained any supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma)?" The Elder replied, "I have no supramundane states attained yet."

Then, the young monk who was his attendant said, "Venerable Sir, many people living within a radius of twelve yojanas have gathered here, thinking, 'The Venerable Sir is about to enter Parinibbāna.' If they learn that you have passed away as a worldling (puthujjana), many people will be distressed."

At that, the Elder said, "Friend, I remained without practicing insight meditation (vipassanā) because I thought, 'I shall behold the future Metteyya Buddha.' If people will be distressed in this way, please help me up and give me the opportunity to focus my mind on the Dhamma." The young monk helped the Elder up and went outside. As soon as the young monk stepped out, the Elder attained Arahantship and gave a signal by snapping his fingers. The young monk then returned and helped the Elder lie down as before. When the young monk informed the other monks of this matter, the Saṅgha gathered and...
370:
...addressed him, "Venerable Sir, you have accomplished a very difficult task by attaining supramundane states at a time so close to death."

The Elder replied, "Friends, attaining supramundane states just before death was not difficult for me. Indeed, friends, I shall tell you what is truly difficult. Friends, since the time I became a monk, I do not see any action I have performed without mindfulness and wisdom. It is the constant maintenance of mindfulness and wisdom in all such activities that is far more difficult."

His nephew, the Elder Bhāgineyya Saṅgharakkhita, also attained Arahantship like his uncle when he reached his fiftieth vassa.

The virtue of trainees (sekha-ariya) that is not misapprehended by wrong view (diṭṭhi), and the virtue of worldlings (puthujjana) that is not misapprehended by lust (rāga)—these are called Aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīla. This is the kind of virtue practiced by Tissa Thera, the son of a householder.

## The Story of Tissa Thera, the Son of a Householder

In Sri Lanka, a householder had two sons. When the parents passed away, the elder son, the youth Tissa, handed over the entire inheritance to his younger brother and, having ordained, lived and practiced the Dhamma in a forest monastery.

Then, the younger brother's wife (the sister-in-law) thought, "Now we possess all this inheritance only because the brother-in-law has ordained. If he were to disrobe, we would have to divide and give him half. It is uncertain whether he will disrobe or not; I will only be at peace if he is dead." Thinking thus, she gave wealth to bandits and ordered them to kill the Elder.

The bandits went to the forest monastery and surrounded and captured the Elder during the first watch of the night. When Tissa Thera said, "I have no possessions that you would desire," they replied, "We did not come because we want possessions. We have come to kill you (at the command of your sister-in-law)."
371:
When they said this, Tissa Thera replied, "I have pure virtue, but I have not yet attained the Fruit of Arahantship. As I wish to establish myself in the Fruit of Arahantship by relying on this virtue, please give me the opportunity to practice the Dhamma until dawn."

The bandits refused, saying, "We cannot grant this. If you escape during the night, it will be a burden for us to pursue and capture you again. Therefore, we cannot allow it."

The Elder then said, "I will make it clear to you that I cannot escape," and taking a large stone, he himself struck and broke both his kneecaps.

When both his knees were completely broken, he said, "Have you not seen? I cannot escape by any means. I would loathe and be ashamed to die as a worldling without being free from lust." Only after he said this did the bandits grant him permission. Relying on his virtue, which was not misapprehended by lust, he practiced the monk's Dhamma throughout the night and attained Arahantship at dawn.

## The Story of an Unnamed Great Elder

A certain unnamed Great Elder was severely ill and could no longer feed himself with his own hands, lying and rolling in his own excrement and urine. A young monk saw him and remarked, "Oh, how painful are the formations of life (jīvita-saṅkhāra)!"

The Great Elder replied, "Friend, if I die now, I shall attain the bliss of the celestial realm. I have no doubt whatsoever about attaining this celestial bliss. However, any bliss obtained by breaking this virtue (meaning dying without becoming an Arahant) is very much like disrobing and returning to lay life."

He then said, "I shall die with my virtue intact (I shall die only after becoming an Arahant)." Lying right there, taking his illness as the primary object, he contemplated and meditated on the five aggregates and the phenomena of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa), and thus attained Arahantship.

(The virtue of these Elders is Aparāmaṭṭhasīla.)
372:
The virtue of Arahants and others is called Paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla because of its purity through the tranquilization of all defilements and distress. Thus, virtue is of five kinds by way of Pariyantapārisuddhisīla and so forth.

Alternatively, it is of five kinds as:
(1) Pahāna-sīla (Virtue of Abandoning),
(2) Veramaṇī-sīla (Virtue of Abstinence),
(3) Cetanā-sīla (Virtue of Volition),
(4) Saṃvara-sīla (Virtue of Restraint),
(5) Avītikkama-sīla (Virtue of Non-transgression).

Among these five:
The abandoning of killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth is called Pahāna-sīla. (In this context, the phrase 'killing and so forth' does not only refer to misconduct such as stealing and sexual misconduct, but it should be understood in brief that the abandoning of everything that should be abandoned by successive wholesome states is Pahāna-sīla. In Pali, 'pahāna' means 'abandoning'; it is the collection of wholesome consciousness and mental factors that occur in the manner of abandoning the respective things to be abandoned.)

The abstinence from things to be avoided, such as killing, which is the collection of wholesome consciousness and mental factors dominated by the mental factor of abstinence (virati-cetasika), is called Veramaṇī-sīla.

The volition (cetanā) that joins and fixes the mind to the abandoning and abstaining from killing and so forth is called Cetanā-sīla.

The collection of wholesome consciousness and mental factors dominated by the mental factor of mindfulness (sati-cetasika), which occurs by way of preventing and blocking things like killing that should be abandoned and avoided from entering the mind, is called Saṃvara-sīla.

The collection of wholesome consciousness and mental factors that occurs by way of not transgressing those acts like killing that should be abandoned and avoided is called Avītikkama-sīla.
373:
(These five types of virtue, such as Pahāna-sīla, are not virtues that occur separately like other virtues; by merely abstaining from committing acts such as killing, all five types can occur and be included.)

The section on the group of five virtues is finished.
The explanation of the divisions of virtue is finished.
**********
## The Defilement and Purification of Virtue

(6) What is the cause of the defilement of virtue?
(7) What is the cause of the purification of virtue?

In these questions, the causes of defilement and purification of virtue are subjects that should be explained together.

The cause of defilement refers to the nature of virtue being broken, torn, and so forth. Conversely, the non-breaking and non-tearing of virtue are the causes of its purification.

The breaking and tearing of virtue occur through destruction rooted in gain, influence, fame, and so forth, as well as through the seven bonds of sexuality (methunasaṃyoga). To elaborate:

If a monk's virtue in any of the seven classes of offenses (āpatti) is destroyed in the first set of training rules or the last set of training rules because of a desire for gain, fame, or reputation, his virtue is said to be broken (khaṇḍa) or fractured, like a cloth torn at the edge.

If a monk's virtue is destroyed in the middle set of training rules, his virtue is said to be torn (chidda), like a cloth with a hole in the middle.

If a monk's virtue is destroyed in two or three training rules in succession, his virtue is said to be spotted (sabala), like a cow that has dark or red spots on its back or belly.
374:
If a monk's virtue is destroyed in every other training rule and so forth, his virtue is said to be mottled (pammāsa), like a cow with variegated spots of different colors here and there.

(In both the virtue of laypeople and monks, if one training rule is destroyed at the beginning or the end, it is called fractured or broken. If a training rule is destroyed in the middle, it is called torn. If two or three types of training rules are destroyed consecutively at the beginning, middle, or end, it is called spotted. If training rules are destroyed extensively at intervals, such as every other rule, it is called mottled.)

Thus, the breaking, tearing, spotting, and mottling of virtue through destruction rooted in gain and so forth are indeed the defilement of virtue.

Even if the aforementioned breaking, tearing, spotting, and mottling are absent, virtue can still be defiled because of the seven matters related to sexuality.

I shall briefly describe the nature of the seven matters related to sexuality as taught in detail by the Blessed One in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Sattaka Nipāta, 5-Mahāyañña Vagga, 7-Jāṇussoṇi Sutta:

(1) A monk or brahmin, while claiming to lead the holy life, does not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman, yet he enjoys it when a woman leans against his body, or when she massages, bathes, or rubs him. (He enjoys the physical contact and services of a woman.)

(2) He does not engage in sexual intercourse and does not enjoy physical contact, yet he enjoys laughing and joking loudly with a woman.
