(3) He does not do those things, yet he enjoys gazing into a woman's eyes.
375:
(4) Otherwise, listening attentively and taking delight in the sound of a woman's laughter, talking, singing, or weeping from behind a wall or a fence, etc.;
(5) Otherwise, repeatedly reminiscing and taking delight in how one used to laugh, talk, and play with a woman in the past;
(6) Otherwise, seeing a householder or a householder's son who is presently endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure and is being surrounded and served by attendants in all matters, and taking delight in and craving for that state;
(7) Otherwise, aspiring for an unspecified celestial rebirth and practicing the noble life (brahmacariya), thinking: "By this virtue, this practice, this exertion, or this noble life, may I become a great deity (deva) or some unspecified deity," and taking delight in and craving for such a celestial state.
These are the seven sexual fetters (methuna-saṃyoga). Among these seven:
(1) In the first, although one does not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman, one takes delight in physical contact such as a woman coming and leaning against one, which is a bodily action associated with sexual matters.
(2) In the second, one no longer engages in bodily contact but takes delight in verbal actions such as loud laughter.
(3) In the third, without bodily or verbal action, one takes delight in looking eye-to-eye.
(4) In the fourth, one takes delight in listening to a woman's voice.
(5) In the fifth, it is not about the immediate present, but taking delight in what was done or heard in the past.
(6) In the sixth, it is taking delight in observing householders or their sons.
(7) In the seventh, without bodily or verbal involvement, it is merely the mental aspiration and delight in celestial luxury. These latter six are also categories associated with sexual intercourse. Therefore, they are called the seven sexual fetters (methuna-saṃyoga). (They are also called the seven minor sexual acts.)
In this way, the breaking, breaching, spotting, or mottling of virtue due to reasons such as gain and honor, or through the seven sexual fetters, constitutes the defilement of virtue.
376:
The purity of virtue, such as its being unbroken and unbreached, is explained by not letting the precepts be destroyed at all, or by properly mending them if they are destroyed; by not engaging in the seven minor sexual acts; and furthermore, by the non-arising of evil states such as: anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), detraction (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya). It is also shown through the arising of qualities such as fewness of wishes, contentment, and the thinning out of defilements.
Those virtues that are unbroken, unsevered, unbreached, unspotted, and unmottled are called 'free virtues' (bhujissa-sīla) because they effect liberation from the slavery of craving. They are called 'virtues praised by the wise' (viññūpasattha-sīla) because they are commended by the learned. They are called 'unprofaned virtues' (aparāmaṭṭha-sīla) because they are not handled by craving—thinking, "My virtue is so pure that it will bring great wealth and happiness in the future"—or by the self-view of identity (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), thinking, "This virtue is mine; my virtue is extremely pure; no one else has virtue like mine." These kinds of virtues are called 'virtues conducive to concentration' (samādhi-saṃvattanika-sīla) because they can lead to concentration close to jhāna (upacāra-samādhi) or concentration associated with jhāna (appanā-samādhi) as one progresses further.
As previously shown, these seven factors—being unbroken, unsevered, unbreached, unspotted, being able to revolt against craving, being praised by the wise, and not being handled by craving and views—are the factors for the purity of virtue. Only virtue endowed with these seven factors can bring about the two higher types of concentration. Therefore, a noble person who desires to attain concentration should strive with diligence to make their virtue complete with these seven factors.
The Chapter on the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī) ends.
**********
377:
## (C) Nekkhamma-pāramī
## Nikkhama and Nekkhamma
(Nikkhama = one who escapes; Nekkhamma = the act of escaping/renunciation.) This third perfection is often easily referred to as Nikkhama-pāramī. As previously shown, Nikkhama refers to the person who goes forth, a human entity, and that entity cannot be a perfection. Since only the nature of escaping can be a perfection, the perfection should not be called Nikkhama, but only Nekkhamma.
Escaping is also of two kinds: escaping from the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) and escaping from sense-pleasures (kāma). Escaping from the round of rebirth is the effect, while escaping from sense-pleasures is the cause. It means that only when one can practice to escape from sense-pleasures does the escape from the round of rebirth occur. Regarding these two types of escaping, the Buddhavamsa Pali teaches with reference to the escape from rebirth (the effect), comparing the three realms of existence to a great prison (bhavato parimuttiyā = for the sake of escaping from the three realms of existence).
## The Ultimate Reality of Nekkhamma-pāramī
While Dana and Sila can be identified with their respective distinct ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma), a separate distinct ultimate reality cannot be found for Nekkhamma. Therefore, the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary explains that the collection of wholesome mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) that function by way of escaping from the two types of sense-pleasures and the three realms of existence is called Nekkhamma-pāramī.
The two types of sense-pleasures refer to the objective sense-pleasures (vatthu-kāma) and the subjective defilement of lust (kilesa-kāma) as mentioned in the Mahāniddesa Pali. The three realms of existence are the three planes of existence.
Regarding the meaning of kāma, since the defilement of greed (lobha) craves for desirable objects, it is called kilesa-kāma. (In this sense, the Pali word kāma should be translated into Burmese as the nature that craves or the nature of craving.) The various objects that are desired are called vatthu-kāma. (In this sense, the Pali word kāma should be translated into Burmese as the things that are desired.) In the context of Nekkhamma-pāramī, the phrase 'escaping from sense-pleasures' refers to escaping from both these types of kāma.
378:
## How to Reflect to Escape
Regarding how to reflect to escape from the subjective defilement of lust (kilesa-kāma) among those two types of kāma, the Mahāniddesa Pali states:
Addasaṃ kāma te mūlaṃ, saṅkappā kāma jāyasi.
Na taṃ saṅkappayissāmi, evaṃ kāma na hohisi.
O Kilesa-kāma, I have seen your root. You arise because of the cause known as sensual thought (kāma-vitakka)—the thinking and imagining of desirable objects as being desirable. I shall no longer think of those objects as being desirable. O Kilesa-kāma, if I do not think in this way, you will no longer exist.
According to this Pali, one must first understand the three types of wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) and the three types of right thoughts (sammā-vitakka). The three wrong thoughts are:
(1) Kāma-vitakka = thinking and imagining objective sense-pleasures with attachment and craving;
(2) Byāpāda-vitakka = thinking and imagining the oppression or killing of others;
(3) Vihiṃsā-vitakka = thinking and imagining the harassment of others (not necessarily killing).
These are the three.
The three right thoughts are:
(1) Nekkhamma-vitakka = thinking and imagining the escape from objective sense-pleasures;
(2) Abyāpāda-vitakka = thinking and imagining associated with loving-kindness (mettā);
(3) Avihiṃsā-vitakka = thinking and imagining associated with compassion (karuṇā).
These are the three.
If one investigates and contemplates the root cause of kilesa-kāma, one will find and know kāma-vitakka, which is included among the three wrong thoughts.
379:
As long as one continues to think and imagine with that sensual thought (kāma-vitakka), the defilement of lust (kilesa-kāma) will only increase, and one will not be able to escape from it. Only when one does not engage in sensual thought will kilesa-kāma not arise, thereby allowing one to escape from it. Therefore, one should reflect to escape from kilesa-kāma according to the method mentioned before. Just as striving to escape from sense-pleasures results in the benefit of escaping from rebirth, striving, exerting, and reflecting to escape from kilesa-kāma can result in the benefit of escaping from objective sense-pleasures (vatthu-kāma).
From this Nekkhamma-pāramī onwards, the characteristics (lakkhaṇa), functions (rasa), manifestations (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna) of the higher perfections will be explained in detail in the upcoming Miscellaneous Section (Pakiṇṇaka-khaṇḍa); therefore, these characteristics and so on will not be mentioned hereafter.
## The Causal Relationship between Going Forth and Monkhood
In the context of this Nekkhamma-pāramī, the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary explains: "Nekkhammaṃ pabbajjāmūlakaṃ." According to this commentary statement, two meanings can be derived: "Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī) has monkhood (pabbajjā) as its root (cause)," and "Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī) is the root (cause) of monkhood (pabbajjā)."
In the first meaning, monkhood is the cause and renunciation (going forth) is the effect. This meaning is consistent with the Mahājanaka Jātaka. Indeed, King Mahājanaka, without the knowledge of his queen and consorts, had a trusted servant buy robes and an alms-bowl, and he first became a monk on the golden palace before going forth to the forest. Thus, for the Bodhisatta King Mahājanaka, because he became a monk first and then went forth, it can be said that monkhood was the cause and going forth was the effect.
In the second meaning, going forth (Nekkhamma-pāramī) is the root (cause) and monkhood is the effect. This meaning is consistent with the cases of the wise Sumedha, the Hatthipāla brothers, and others. Indeed, the wise Sumedha first went forth to the forest, and upon reaching the slopes of Mount Dhammika, he became a hermit monk when he found the hermitages created by Sakka. The Hatthipāla brothers also went forth to the forest first in the same manner, and when their mother, father, and the entire kingdom followed them...
381: As previously explained, renunciation from the defilements of sensuality (kilesa-kāma), which is the Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma pāramī), does not need to be classified by location. Kilesa-kāma is the nature of being attached to and craving for pleasant objects, which can arise anywhere. When such kilesa-kāma arises, it should be abandoned right where it occurs; the liberation from that kilesa-kāma through such abandonment is the essence of nekkhamma. Regarding renunciation from the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma), the wise Sumedha, the Hatthipāla brothers, and others renounced and went as far as the Himalayas (Himavanta). Therefore, one might wonder, 'If one wishes to fulfill the Perfection of Renunciation by renouncing vatthu-kāma, must one go as far as the Himalayas?' If circumstances allow and one wishes to go, one should indeed go. In the Jātaka stories taught regarding renunciation, the majority of individuals renounced and reached the Himalayas. This was because circumstances were favorable for them to go. However, in the Makhādeva Jātaka of the Ekakanipāta and the Nimi Jātaka of the Mahānipāta, it is mentioned that eighty-four thousand kings, from King Makhādeva to King Nimi, renounced as soon as a single grey hair appeared on their heads. In doing so, none of these kings went as far as the Himalayas; they renounced only in the royal mango grove near their own city of Mithilā. There, they practiced and attained meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledges (abhiññā), and subsequently reached the Brahma realm. Considering the accounts of these kings, even if one does not go to the Himalayas, if one renounces so as to be free from the sphere where one's kilesa-kāma roams, it should be understood that the Perfection of Renunciation is successful. Indeed, for the eighty-four thousand kings such as Makhādeva, abandoning their royal luxury and palaces—where they used to enjoy themselves—without any lingering attachment (ālaya) and living in the mango grove was itself the fulfillment and success of their Perfection of Renunciation. Therefore, it should be understood that for anyone, abandoning the sphere where they roam with kilesa-kāma without lingering attachment, and living in a suitable place free from kilesa-kāma without establishing a new such sphere, is indeed the practice of the Perfection of Renunciation.
382: ## Two Kinds of Renunciation The renunciation of Bodhisattas is of two kinds: (1) Renunciation of the young (unmarried); (2) Renunciation of the old (those with families). Although it is clearly stated in the Jātakas that individuals like the wise Sumedha and the Hatthipāla brothers fulfilled the Perfection of Renunciation by renouncing the vatthu-kāma of royal or wealthy status they possessed, they were only young men who had not yet established a household. For young men, even if vatthu-kāma exists, it cannot be said that they are forcibly bound by those objects. Only for the 'old' (married) who have established a household and live with a wife and children are they forcibly bound by vatthu-kāma such as wife and children. Considering this, it could be said that the renunciation of the married is more difficult than the renunciation of the young. Although it might be said that the renunciation of Prince Temiya was extremely difficult because he had to endure great suffering by pretending to be a cripple, a mute, and deaf just to be able to renounce, his bond to vatthu-kāma was almost non-existent. Therefore, although he suffered greatly in planning his renunciation, it cannot be said to be extremely difficult at the moment of renouncing because the bonds of vatthu-kāma were few. For this reason, in the Atthasālinī Commentary, when describing the Perfections fulfilled by various Bodhisattas, the section on the Perfection of Renunciation states: 'He fulfilled the Perfection of Renunciation in countless lives, such as when he was Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, and Prince Ayoghara. Specifically, however, the renunciation when he was King Cūḷasutasoma was so extraordinary that it should be called the Ultimate Perfection (paramattha pāramī).'
383:
The reason why only the renunciation of King Cūḷasutasoma is described as the Paramattha Nekkhamma Pāramī (Ultimate Perfection of Renunciation) in the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary is likely because it refers to King Cūḷasutasoma's liberation from the great and forceful bonds of sensual objects, such as his throne and wealth, as well as his wife, children, and parents. Prince Somanassa, Prince Ayoghara, Prince Hatthipāla, and Prince Temiya were only youths. It should be said that the renunciation of King Mahājanaka, who was an older man, was more difficult than the renunciation of those youths. However, in his case, the queens and consorts only followed and forcefully tried to restrain him after he had already become a monk and departed for the forest without their knowledge; they were not able to pre-emptively restrain or prevent him from renouncing or becoming a monk.

Eighty-four thousand kings, starting with Maghadeva, clearly informed their wives and children before their renunciation. Although their wives and children pleaded and tried to bind them in various ways upon being told, they renounced without succumbing to those bonds. However, the forest was not very far; it was merely their own mango grove park. As for King Cūḷasutasoma, as soon as he saw a single grey hair on his head, he gained a sense of urgency (Dhamma) and announced his intention to renounce in the midst of the assembly. Although his wife, children, mother, father, and all the troops wept and pleaded extensively, he ignored those pleas and renounced, traveling far until he reached the Himavantā. Therefore, it can be said that King Cūḷasutasoma's renunciation was more intense than that of King Maghadeva and others. For these reasons, the commentator explained King Cūḷasutasoma's perfection as the Paramattha Pāramī in the context of Nekkhamma Pāramī.

## Renunciation and the 'Nge-pyu' (Ordained Young)
Thus, although the scriptures mention the renunciation of youths as the fulfillment of Nekkhamma Pāramī, it should be said that it is not as difficult or constrained as the renunciation of older people (those with families). Furthermore, in their final life before becoming a Buddha, Bodhisattas—
384:
—no Bodhisatta renounces as a youth; they only renounce after a son is born. For this reason, in the present day, monks who have been in the Order continuously from their time as Sāmaṇeras (novices) are called 'Nge-pyu' (meaning 'done since childhood'). On the other hand, when older men with families abandon their wives and children to become monks, they are commonly referred to in Pāḷi as 'Nikkhama' and in Burmese as 'Taw-twet Ko-daw-gyi' (Great Forest-departing Monk).

Here ends the chapter on Nekkhamma Pāramī.

## (D) Paññā Pāramī
## Three Types of Wisdom
Regarding wisdom (Paññā), it is taught in the Ñāṇavibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga Pāḷi that there are three types of wisdom:
(1) Cintāmaya-paññā (Wisdom based on reflection),
(2) Sutamaya-paññā (Wisdom based on learning),
(3) Bhāvanāmaya-paññā (Wisdom based on mental development).

Cintāmaya-paññā refers to the knowledge and wisdom that arises through one's own power of thought regarding the causes and effects of various low or high worldly affairs and various arts and sciences (without having asked others or heard from others). (Cintā = thinking/reflection; Maya = accomplished/arisen; it means wisdom accomplished through reflection.)

The things understood through reflection include not only worldly matters but also the nature of the Dhamma. Therefore, all wisdom that can reflect upon and understand everything from ordinary worldly matters like carpentry and farming to the collective nature of Dhamma known as Dāna (generosity), Sīla (morality), Samatha (tranquility), and Vipassanā Bhāvanā (insight meditation) is Cintāmaya-paññā. If one wishes to say so, even the Buddha's great Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa (Omniscience) can be classified as Cintāmaya-paññā.
385:
(Wisdom)
The reason is that the Bodhisatta, Prince Siddhattha, attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) by contemplating, penetrating, and practicing the noble path to that wisdom by himself, without hearing it from anyone else.

However, regarding the fourth Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī) sought by the Bodhisatta Sumedha, it should be understood as the collection of wisdom that serves as the foundation for attaining the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) and the Great Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). It is not necessary to include the wisdom of the final life (pacchima-bhava) in which Buddhahood is attained. In the process of fulfilling the Perfection of Wisdom before the final life, Bodhisattas practice up to the early stage of the ninth level of insight, which is the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa), and stop there. Since the highest stage of Saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa leads directly to the Knowledge of the Path (Magga-ñāṇa), they do not practice to that peak. If they were to do so, they would become Noble Ones (Ariyas) by attaining the Path and Fruit in that very life and would simply enter Nibbāna in due course; they would not become a Buddha. Therefore, it should be noted that during their lives as Bodhisattas, they fulfill the Perfection of Wisdom only up to the early stage of Saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa.

Any wisdom that arises from questioning wise men because one cannot contemplate and understand by oneself, or from listening to their spontaneous teachings, is called Wisdom based on Hearing (Sutamaya-paññā). (Suta = hearing; maya = wisdom accomplished or arisen; meaning wisdom that arises from hearing.) This Sutamaya-paññā is as broad in scope as Wisdom based on Reflection (Cintāmaya-paññā). The only difference is between understanding through one's own reflection and understanding through hearing from others.

Wisdom based on Mental Development (Bhāvanāmaya-paññā) refers to the wisdom that arises within the meditative attainments (samāpatti) of those who enter various Jhana-samāpatti or Phala-samāpatti.

In the Ñāṇa-vibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga Pali, the Buddha taught various types of wisdom, categorized from groups of one to groups of ten. (One should refer to the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.)
386:
(Wisdom continued)
If the entire collection of wisdom is categorized into the three types—Wisdom based on Reflection (Cintāmaya-paññā), Wisdom based on Hearing (Sutamaya-paññā), and Wisdom based on Mental Development (Bhāvanāmaya-paññā)—it is all encompassed within them. To give a few examples:

Following the three types of wisdom starting with Cintāmaya, the Buddha also taught another triad: Wisdom based on Giving (Dānamaya-paññā), Wisdom based on Virtue (Sīlamaya-paññā), and Wisdom based on Mental Development (Bhāvanāmaya-paññā). Wisdom that arises concerning giving is called Dānamaya-paññā. Since the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā) exists in three stages—before giving, while giving, and after giving—the three types of wisdom associated with these three volitions are all called Dānamaya-paññā. Similarly, in Sīlamaya-paññā, the wisdom that arises in the preliminary stage when planning to undertake and practice virtue, the wisdom during the actual practice, and the wisdom during the subsequent reflection are all called Sīlamaya-paññā.

If these types of wisdom, such as Dānamaya-paññā and Sīlamaya-paññā, are understood through one's own reflection, they are included in Cintāmaya-paññā. If they are understood by hearing from others, they are included in Sutamaya-paññā. In this way, when other forms of wisdom are categorized into the three types starting with Cintāmaya, they all fit appropriately.

In the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, it is stated: "Paripucchanto budhaṃ janaṃ, paññāpāramitaṃ gantvā," which means "By questioning wise people, one reaches the pinnacle of the Perfection of Wisdom." This shows that the teaching is based on Sutamaya-paññā. This is because a person in this world who lacks a foundation of wisdom cannot contemplate or understand anything by their own will. To gain foundational wisdom, one must first acquire it by listening to wise men. Therefore, it is taught that one who wishes to fulfill the Perfection of Wisdom must first acquire wisdom by listening to wise men before they have a foundation of wisdom.

Only when a foundation of wisdom is acquired through listening to wise men can one gain the ability to contemplate and understand through one's own personal intellect. (In brief, it means one must first seek Sutamaya-paññā before seeking Cintāmaya-paññā.)

Regarding the lives in which the Great Bodhisattas fulfilled the Perfection of Wisdom, the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary and others mention the lives as the wise Vidhura, the wise Mahāgovinda,
387:
(Wisdom continued)
the wise Kudāla, the wise Araka, the wise Bodhi the wandering ascetic, the wise Mahosadha, and so on; it is stated that the number of lives in which the Perfection of Wisdom was fulfilled is countless. Such mentions refer only to those Bodhisatta lives where there was already a foundation of wisdom and Cintāmaya-paññā was fully developed. In these lives, such as that of the wise Vidhura, the foundational wisdom was already so strong that there was no longer a need to focus primarily on acquiring Sutamaya-paññā.

## Four Types of Sages (Kavi)
Based on these types of wisdom like Cintāmaya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta, teaches that there are four types of sages (Kavi):
(1) Cintā-kavi
(2) Suta-kavi
(3) Attha-kavi
(4) Paṭibhāna-kavi
(The word 'Kavi' is derived from the root 'ku', which means to praise. Therefore, a person who speaks in praise of what is praiseworthy is called a Kavi, meaning a wise person.) Among these four types of sages:

(1) A person who can contemplate and understand a matter by their own will is called a Cintā-kavi. (The act of praising those who deserve praise is the property of sages and is called poetry/kāvya.) One who can perform this poetic task through contemplation with their own intellect is called a Cintā-kavi.

(2) A person who can understand after hearing from someone else, and who performs the poetic task by taking methods heard from others, is called a Suta-kavi.

(3) A person who does not understand through their own reflection nor through hearing from others, but who can understand other similar meanings based on a difficult meaning they already know, is called an Attha-kavi. This refers to one who performs the poetic task based on a specific subject matter.
388:
(Wisdom continued)
(4) A person who has intuitive wisdom (paṭibhāna) and can penetrate and understand suddenly, without having to reflect, without hearing from others, and without having a prior meaning to use as a basis, is called a Paṭibhāna-kavi. (Like the Elder Vaṅgīsa during the time of the Buddha.)

## The Nature of Wisdom
Wisdom (Paññā) is a distinct ultimate reality known as a mental factor (cetasika). In the Dhamma-saṅgaṇī Pali, this mental factor of wisdom is taught under various names such as the Faculty of Wisdom (Paññindriya), Wisdom (Paññā), and Full Understanding (Pajānanā). Expressing a single reality through various names is the inherent nature of the Abhidhamma, which aims to fully explain all aspects that should be taught regarding a single phenomenon. The primary name is Paññindriya, a compound of the words 'Paññā' and 'Indriya'.

It is called Paññā because it knows the Four Noble Truths in their various aspects. Alternatively, it is called Paññā because it knows and makes known the three characteristics—impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta)—in their various aspects. It is called Indriya because it can overcome the ignorance (avijjā) and delusion (moha) of not knowing and not seeing. Alternatively, it is called Indriya because it exercises dominance in the characteristic of knowing. (Indriya = ability to overcome, or dominance.) By combining the two words, it is called Paññindriya. It is the nature of knowing the Four Noble Truths and the nature of knowing and making known the three characteristics of anicca, dukkha, and anatta in their various aspects.

That wisdom has the characteristic of producing light. Just as darkness disappears and light arrives when a lamp is lit inside a pitch-black room, when wisdom enters a matter that cannot be known or seen because it is covered by delusion (moha), the not-knowing (moha) disappears and one reaches a state of clear understanding. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Paññāsamā ābhā natthi," meaning "There is no light equal to wisdom."

Alternatively, it has the characteristic of discrimination. Just as a very skillful physician in the world discriminates for his patients, saying "this food is suitable, this food is unsuitable," etc., when this wisdom arises, it can discriminate and analyze, saying "this group of things is wholesome (kusala), this group of things is unwholesome (akusala)," and so on.
389:
(Wisdom continued)
Alternatively, wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of things. Or, like an arrow shot by a very skillful archer, it has the characteristic of penetrating without missing, deviating, or failing.

Regarding this characteristic, it is particularly important to note that seeing anything exactly as it truly is constitutes genuine wisdom and is blameless. For this reason, in the Compendium of Philosophy (Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha), this mental factor of wisdom is included and described among the beautiful mental factors (sobhana-cetasika). However, a question may arise:

In the Sulasa Jātaka (No. 419) of the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta in the Jātaka stories, there was a courtesan named Sulasa in the city of Bārāṇasī. She saved a thief named Sattuka from imminent death and lived with him as her husband. The thief, however, plotted against her. He made her wear ornaments worth a hundred thousand, took her to a mountain top, and upon reaching the summit, ordered her to remove the ornaments and prepared to kill her. At that time, Sulasa thought, "He is certainly going to kill me. I must get the better of him first through trickery." She then pleaded, "My dear, even though you are going to kill me, my love for you remains unchanged. Before I die, let me satisfy myself by paying respects to you from the four directions—front, back, left, and right."

The thief Sattuka, believing her, allowed her to pay respects. While the thief was standing at the edge of a steep precipice, she first gained his trust by paying respects from the front and sides. When she reached his back, she pushed him with all her might. When the thief fell and died, the Bodhisatta deity dwelling on the mountain top praised Sulasa, saying:

"Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, puriso hoti paṇḍito.
Ittīpi paṇḍitā hoti, tattha tattha vicakkhaṇā."

"It is not only men who are wise in every situation. A woman, too, is a wise person who is discerning and prudent in various circumstances."
This and other verses were spoken in praise of Sulasa.
390:
According to this Jātaka, some ask how the deity, the Bodhisatta, could praise Sulasa as wise, given that her plot to kill the thief was an act of killing (pāṇātipāta), a demeritorious deed where the mental factor of wisdom (paññā-cetasika) cannot arise or be associated.

Those who answer say that Sulasa's knowledge was not true wisdom (paññā). Among the three types of knowing—knowing through perception (saññā), knowing through consciousness (viññāṇa), and knowing through wisdom (paññā)—it was merely knowing through consciousness (viññāṇa), i.e., an intellectual thought. They explain that this consciousness itself is what was referred to as being 'wise'.

Others answer incorrectly and erroneously, saying that views are called diṭṭhi; right views are called sammā-diṭṭhi, and wrong views are called micchā-diṭṭhi. Since Sulasa's view was a wrong view, the mountain deity praised her as wise based on her having micchā-diṭṭhi. They claim this does not contradict Abhidhamma principles because the praise was not based on the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya).

Both the first and second answers greatly contradict Abhidhamma principles because they attempt to define consciousness (viññāṇa) and wrong view (diṭṭhi), which are not wisdom, as wisdom.

In truth, Sulasa's realization that 'If I speak this stratagem and plot in this way, I will win' is a correct understanding, and thus it is indeed knowing through wisdom (paññā). One should not doubt whether true wisdom can arise in the context of a demeritorious act. For example, simply knowing the various types of intoxicants—which are unsuitable to drink and causes of demerit—their properties, their value, and the effects of drinking them, is not an offense. An unwholesome state (akusala) only arises from the moment one intends to drink them.

To give another example, there are various doctrines in the world. Simply knowing and analyzing every single one of those doctrines without exception is not an offense. Among those various doctrines, knowing which doctrine...
391:
...is correct in cause and effect and which doctrine is wrong—knowing the truth as truth and the false as false—is not an offense. An offense only occurs from the moment one perceives a wrong doctrine as true and good.

Therefore, knowing correctly that 'I will win if I plot with such a stratagem' is not an offense; it is indeed knowing through wisdom (paññā). The demeritorious act (dusacarita) occurs from the moment one decides to act according to the plot and kill through stratagem. It should be certainly and definitely understood that the Bodhisatta mountain deity praised her as wise only in reference to the initial intelligence that arose before Sulasa committed the act of killing (pāṇātipāta).

As stated, one should distinguish between the sphere of intelligence and the sphere of the demeritorious act of killing. If one stubbornly maintains that Sulasa's knowledge cannot be true wisdom because it pertains to an evil act, it would lead to the point of finding fault even in the Buddha's Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). This is because the Buddha's great knowledge is called Omniscience because it can perceive all things, both good and bad. If true wisdom could not know evil things, then the Buddha's knowledge would not know evil things; if it did not know them, it could not be called Omniscience. In fact, it is called Omniscience precisely because it can perceive all things, both good and bad.

In summary, the Buddha knows all things, both faulty and faultless. However, regarding the performance of faulty acts, He has already abandoned them along with their latent tendencies (anusaya) and roots, so He never has the desire to do them, let alone actually doing them. Having thus perceived all faultless things, one should increase and develop faith (saddhā) by reflecting on His virtue of abandoning what should be abandoned and never performing such acts.
392:
Furthermore, in the Mahosadha Jātaka, which was taught regarding the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī), the wise Mahosadha (the Bodhisatta) devised various strategies while remaining within the city walls to make King Cūḷanī Brahmadatta fearful when he and his subordinate kings surrounded and attacked the kingdom of Videha. He also planned for King Cūḷanī Brahmadatta's great army to be defeated and flee in disarray. If one were to say that wisdom could not arise in these actions because they were not matters of merit (kusala), then there would be no instance of fulfilling the Perfection of Wisdom in the life of Mahosadha. In fact, the collection of events in the Mahosadha Jātaka consists of matters managed solely by the power of the Bodhisatta's wisdom, and the Buddha taught that it was a life in which he fulfilled the Perfection of Wisdom.

Considering such a collection of reasons, it should be analytically understood that in the Sulasa Jātaka, the mountain deity's praise of Sulasa as a wise woman was because she was indeed wise.

(This is the explanation regarding points that may cause doubt concerning the nature and characteristics of wisdom.)

## Types of Wisdom

As previously shown, the explanation in commentaries such as the Atthasālinī that wisdom is so called because it mostly knows and makes known the Four Noble Truths and the Three Characteristics is given according to the 'Exalted Method' (ukkaṭṭha-naya), referring to high-level wisdom. There is also a collection of lower-level wisdom that does not reach this standard. The existence of such wisdom is shown in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, in the Ñāṇa-vibhaṅga, where wisdom born of reflection (cintāmaya-paññā) and wisdom born of hearing (sutamaya-paññā) are taught (stating: 'Tattha katamā cintāmayā paññā, yogavihitesu vā kammāyatanesu yogavihitesu vā sippāyatanesu...' and so on). In teaching the spheres of work (kammāyatana) which are causes of livelihood, and the spheres of arts (sippāyatana) which are causes of livelihood, the commentary explains that various works managed by wisdom are called kammāyatana, and various arts managed by wisdom are called sippāyatana.
393:
Regarding the spheres of work (kammāyatana), there are two types: inferior and superior. Work such as carpentry is called inferior work. Farming, trade, and the like are called superior work. Regarding the spheres of arts (sippāyatana), arts such as wall-weaving and cloth-weaving are called inferior arts. Arithmetic, writing, and the like are called superior arts; these are explained in detail.

In this context, the distinction between work (kammāyatana) and art (sippāyatana) is that activities that can be performed without special training are called kammāyatana. Arts that are understood and mastered only through training are called sippāyatana. (Alternatively) In brief, a distinction should be made between matters performed without special training and manual skills mastered through special training. Oral knowledge mastered through training is called vijjā-ṭṭhāna (branches of knowledge).

In this matter, just as fire that burns inferior fuel and fire that burns noble fuel should not be distinguished as 'inferior fire' or 'noble fire' based on the quality of the fuel—but rather should only be called a weak fire if the fuel is weak and a strong fire if the fuel is strong—similarly, in the case of wisdom, it should not be distinguished as 'inferior wisdom' because the object known is inferior, or 'noble wisdom' because the object known is noble. It should only be called weak wisdom or strong wisdom, or (alternatively) easy wisdom or difficult wisdom. Just as the Atthasālinī commentary shows the characteristics of wisdom, one should not regard only high-level great wisdom as wisdom, but should also regard lower-level wisdom as wisdom.

Therefore, one who wishes to cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī) should, without choosing between high or low levels, inquire from the wise and cultivate it if it is something they do not yet know. For this reason, it is taught in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi: 'Paripucchanto budhaṃ janaṃ, paññāpāramitaṃ gantvā' (Inquiring from wise people, one reaches the Perfection of Wisdom).
394:
## Seven Causes for the Growth of Wisdom

Furthermore, in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibhaṅga Commentary), in the explanation of the Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga, seven causes for the growth of wisdom are explained. The seven are:

(1) Paripucchakatā: Repeatedly inquiring from the wise. (This first factor is the one described according to the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi verse: 'Paripucchanto budhaṃ janaṃ'.)

(2) Vatthu-visada-kiriyā: Making the internal and external bases clean. (One must not have internal impurity such as long hair, long toe-nails or finger-nails, long beard or mustache, physical stiffness, or heavy sweat and grime. There must also be no external impurity such as old, foul-smelling clothes or cluttered, dusty bedding. When internal and external bases are impure, the wisdom that arises is unclear and impure, just as a flame from a lamp with a dirty bowl, wick, and oil is not bright. To ensure the arising of clear, pure, and radiant wisdom, one must cleanse the internal and external bases, just as a flame from a clean lamp, wick, and oil is clear and pure.)

(3) Indriya-samatta-paṭipādanā: Balancing the faculties such as faith (saddhā). (Among the five faculties that govern the mind and mental factors in beings, if the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is too strong, the other four faculties become weak. Consequently, the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) cannot perform its duty of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) cannot perform its duty of establishing the object, the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) cannot perform its duty of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) cannot perform its duty of knowing. Therefore, if faith is excessive, one should strive to reduce and balance it by reflecting on the nature of reality that must be balanced, or by not attending to methods that increase faith. If the faculty of energy is too strong, then the faculty of faith [cannot perform] its duty of placing faith in the objects of devotion...)
395: (...cannot perform their respective functions; other faculties also cannot perform their own tasks. Therefore, one should diminish that excessive faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) by clearly developing the state of tranquility of both body and mind. In this same way, it should be understood that if any other faculty is too strong, the remaining faculties cannot perform their respective functions.) In balancing these faculties, the wise and virtuous especially praise the balancing of faith (saddhā) with wisdom (paññā), and concentration (samādhi) with energy (vīriya). One who is strong in faith but weak in wisdom tends to have devotion through empty clarity. (This means that because the wisdom to discern whether an object is worthy of devotion is weak, one tends to be devoted to what is not worthy of devotion. Believing things that are not the true Buddha, Dhamma, or Saṅgha to be the true Buddha, Dhamma, or Saṅgha is merely empty faith that does not lead to benefit because it is not true to reality.) Those with wrong views are devoted to what they perceive as Buddha or Dhamma according to their false beliefs. It should be well noted that their devotion is not true faith (saddhā), but merely wrong conviction (micchā-adhimokkha). One who is strong in wisdom but weak in faith cannot reach the straight and true path, but tends to stray into the path of craftiness and deceit. Just as in the world it is difficult to cure a disease caused by the wrong intake of medicine, it is very difficult to reform and cure a person who, having little faith and much wisdom, has strayed into the path of craftiness and deceit. Thinking craftily, 'Since there are two kinds of dāna—volitional dāna (cetanā-dāna) and material dāna (vatthu-dāna)—only volition can truly give good results in the next life. Material objects cannot give any good results. Therefore, there is no need to offer material objects; if one just maintains good volition, the necessary good results can be obtained,' such a person refrains from performing meritorious deeds like dāna and may fall into hell upon death. Only when both faith and wisdom are balanced can great benefits arise through devotion only to what is worthy of devotion and through the absence of craftiness.
396: Energy (vīriya) and concentration (samādhi) must also be balanced. If energy is weak and concentration is excessive, one may be overwhelmed by laziness called kosajja, appearing to be peaceful to achieve concentration but without any active effort. If energy is excessive and concentration is weak, one lacks stability and, being constantly active, may be overwhelmed by restlessness (uddhacca), thinking, 'If this work does not yield results as intended, it is not a productive task; therefore, it would be better to abandon this work and do something else.' If one strives to balance energy and concentration, laziness (kosajja) finds no entry, and restlessness (uddhacca) also finds no entry. Because both are balanced, one can quickly attain the meditative concentration called appanā. As for the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), there is no such thing as it being in excess; there is only the possibility of it being deficient. Therefore, it is stated in the scriptures that 'Mindfulness is like salt, which must be included in all edible dishes; and it is like the chief minister, who must be involved in all the king's affairs.' Thus, one should apply mindfulness to the utmost and develop faith and wisdom, energy and concentration in equal measure. If any one of them is in excess, there is a fault. Regarding this, Sayadaw U Budh wrote in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta Nissaya: If faith is in excess, it wanders. If wisdom is in excess, it is crippled. If energy is in excess, it scatters. If concentration is in excess, it shrinks. As for mindfulness, there is no excess. (4) Duppaññapuggala-parivajjana = Avoiding unwise persons. (A group of persons who lack the wisdom to penetrate the nature of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), etc., are called unwise (duppañña-puggala). This means one must avoid such persons from afar.)
397: (5) Paññavantapuggala-sevana = Associating with wise persons. (A wise person refers to one endowed with the fifty aspects of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). These fifty aspects of udayabbaya-ñāṇa should be looked up in the Burmese translation of the Paṭisambhidāmagga.) In both points (4) and (5), the explanation of the Commentator (Aṭṭhakathā-cariya) is given according to the highest standard (ukkaṭṭha-naya). The high standard is seen in point (4), where an unwise person is defined as one whose wisdom cannot penetrate the groups of phenomena such as the aggregates and bases. A person whose wisdom can penetrate the aggregates and bases is indeed a high-level wise person. Even if one cannot perceive such subtle and profound natures of the aggregates and bases, a person who knows generally, 'This is how one should give, this is how one should not; this is how virtue should be guarded, this is how it should not,' etc., regarding the Dhamma, or 'This practice leads to long life, this practice leads to short life,' etc., would seem as if they are not wise. In reality, one must also associate with such persons. Regarding the wise person mentioned in point (5), the definition 'one endowed with the fifty aspects of udayabbaya-ñāṇa' also refers only to high-level Vipassanā practitioners according to the highest standard. Regarding the pursuit of wisdom, according to the Buddhavamsa Pali, it is taught: 'Like a monk who goes on alms round from house to house without discriminating between the low, middle, or high, one should inquire and learn from any person who can understand, regardless of whether they are low, middle, or high.' Therefore, the unwise person to be avoided should be only one who knows nothing at all. The wise person to be associated with should be anyone who can properly answer and explain what one wishes to know. In brief, it means one should avoid the kind of person from whom nothing can be asked and learned, and associate with and serve the group of persons who can answer, more or less, what one does not yet know.
398: In the pursuit of wisdom, according to the Buddhavamsa Pali, one should first listen to and inquire from the wise to acquire wisdom based on learning (suta-maya-paññā). Only when unclear points arise within that acquired suta-maya-paññā should one develop and cultivate wisdom based on reflection (cintā-maya-paññā), which is the act of contemplating and reasoning. Regarding this matter, in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Tika Nipāta, Dutiya Paṇṇāsaka, 2-Mahāvagga, 5-Kālāma Sutta, many Kālāma princes reported to the Buddha: 'Many Dhamma preachers come to our region, and every group that comes only praises their own doctrine and rejects and attacks other doctrines. We are in doubt, unable to know exactly which doctrine to accept.' The essence of the Buddha's teaching to them was: 'One should consider and reflect with one's own wisdom and accept only the doctrine that is faultless.' According to this teaching, after performing the task of suta-maya-paññā by listening to the preachers' discourses, one should use the wisdom of reflection (cintā-maya-ñāṇa) to consider with one's own wisdom which doctrine alone is faultless. Furthermore, in the Pātha Jātaka, Dasaka Nipāta, 9-Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, when the Great Teacher of Takkasila himself came to inquire why children in Dhammapāla village do not die before their full lifespan, the Bodhisatta [who was to be] King Suddhodana, the Great Dhammapāla (the village headman), replied in the section: 'We listen to the Dhamma of all persons who come to our village. After listening, we reflect and consider; we do not like or accept the Dhamma of the unvirtuous, and we reject those people. We only like and accept the Dhamma of the virtuous, and we do not abandon those virtuous ones. Therefore, in our (Dhammapāla) village, children do not die before their full lifespan.' According to this Mahādhammapāla Jātaka as well, it is evident that one should first listen with suta-maya-ñāṇa and then reflect with cintā-maya-ñāṇa to accept and confirm the truth.
399: ## Associating with the Wise. In connection with the phrase 'associating with wise persons,' the question arises: 'What is the nature of association?' Simply going to a wise person and staying with them day and night does not mean one is associating with the wise. Only when one acts to gain some knowledge from the wise person is it called associating with the wise. In the world, according to the Maṅgala Dhamma 'not to associate with fools,' simply going to where a fool is does not mean one is associating with the fool. If one goes to the fool because of a desire to approach, entice, and admonish them, the Maṅgala Dhamma is not destroyed. It is like the Buddha going to stay with the ascetics of wrong view in the Uruvela forest. Only when one accepts any practice or doctrine of fools is it said that one associates with them. In the context of the Maṅgala Dhamma to associate with the wise, simply going to and living with a wise person is not called associating with the wise; only when one takes the path of Dhamma from the wise is it called associating with the wise. Therefore, in the phrase 'associating with wise persons,' merely living together with wise persons is not enough; it should be well understood that association occurs only when one gains and notes some amount of wisdom from those wise persons. (6) Gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariya-paccavekkhaṇā = Reflecting on the phenomena that are the domain of profound wisdom. (In this context, wisdom is like fire. Fire burns small and insignificant things if they are fuel; it also burns very large masses. In this way, while burning whatever is fuel without exception, if it is a fire that burns small and insignificant things, it is a small fire; if it is a fire that burns very large masses, it becomes a great fire. Similarly, wisdom knows everything that should be known. If it knows small things, it is small wisdom; if it knows obvious things, it is obvious wisdom; if it knows profound things, it is profound wisdom. Thus, it is called by various names based on the nature of what is known. The profound objects that are the domain of wisdom are...)
400:
(It refers to the groups of phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana). The knowledge that arises within these groups is called profound wisdom. This profound wisdom is as vast as the profound nature of the phenomena themselves. This means that the analytical investigation and reflection upon these numerous profound phenomena as they are known is the cause for the growth of wisdom.)

(7) Tadadhimuttatā = Having a mind inclined towards the development of that wisdom. (In all four postures—lying, sitting, standing, and walking—one must have a mind that desires and is inclined only towards the arising of wisdom. Having such a mind is another cause for the growth of wisdom.)

Frequent questioning,
Cleanliness of things,
Balancing the faculties,
Avoiding the foolish,
Associating with the wise,
Deep reflection,
And liberation (vimutta);
These are the seven causes for the growth of knowledge. (Sayadaw U Budh)

**********
## Qualities of Wisdom
This wisdom (paññā)—
(1) When it acts as the leader and chief in various matters, it is included as one of the four predominants (adhipati) known as vīmaṃsādhipati (predominance of investigation).

(2) Among the 22 faculties (indriya) that govern their associated mental states, it is included in four ways: as paññindriya, anaññātaññassāmītindriya, aññindriya, and aññātāvindriya. Specifically, the wisdom present in the 39 mundane types of consciousness associated with knowledge (lokiya ñāṇasampayutta citta) is paññindriya; the wisdom in the path-consciousness of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga citta) is anaññātaññassāmītindriya; the wisdom in the fruition of arahatship (arahattaphala) is aññātāvindriya; and the wisdom in the six intermediate supramundane types of consciousness is aññindriya.
401:
Regarding this Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā Pāramī) that is fulfilled, only the wisdom present in the 13 types of wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge (kusala ñāṇasampayutta citta) out of the 39 mundane types should be taken. (The functional (kiriya) group of consciousness pertains only to Arahats and not to worldling Bodhisattas. Furthermore, the resultant (vipāka) types of consciousness associated with knowledge are not states that one specially strives to arouse, but arise according to previous kamma. Therefore, the wisdom contained in those functional and resultant types of consciousness is not taken as the Perfection of Wisdom.) Great Bodhisattas must fulfill only the mundane wholesome Perfection of Wisdom until it is complete.

Among the five faculties included in the Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma (Factors of Enlightenment), paññindriya is also present. Under that paññindriya, there are both mundane and supramundane types. The paññindriya present in the supramundane paths and fruits cannot be included in the Perfection of Wisdom practiced by Bodhisattas. However, the paññindriya that arises in association with the great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala ñāṇasampayutta citta) while practicing mundane purifications (lokiya visuddhi) such as purification of virtue and purification of mind prior to the paths and fruits, is indeed included in the Perfection of Wisdom fulfilled by Great Bodhisattas.

(3) Similarly, among the five powers (bala) which are like the strength of associated states, it is included as the power of wisdom (paññā-bala). Among the four bases of power (iddhipāda), it is vīmaṃsiddhipāda; among the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), it is dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga; and among the eight path factors (maggaṅga), it is sammādiṭṭhi-maggaṅga. While there are powers, bases of power, factors of enlightenment, and path factors related to wisdom, the supramundane wisdom belonging to these categories is not included in the Perfection of Wisdom fulfilled by Great Bodhisattas. It should be understood without doubt that only the wisdom corresponding to paññā-bala, vīmaṃsiddhipāda, dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga, and sammādiṭṭhi-maggaṅga that arises in association with mahākusala ñāṇasampayutta citta during the practice of mundane purifications prior to the paths and fruits is included in the Perfection of Wisdom fulfilled by Great Bodhisattas.

Reflecting upon these extraordinary qualities of wisdom, may you be able to practice and fulfill the Perfection of Wisdom to its highest peak.

The Chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom ends.
**********
402:
## (E) Viriya Pāramī: The Perfection of Energy
## The Energy of the Bodhisatta
In the context of the Perfection of Energy (Viriya Pāramī), the Kesara Lion King is given as a simile. The nature of Kesara lions is that they never slacken their energy; they always exert effort. When catching a small rabbit, they do not slacken their energy or catch it carelessly just because it is a small creature. When catching a great elephant, they do not increase their effort thinking, "This elephant is very large; I must catch it with all my might." The effort and energy exerted when catching a small rabbit and when catching a great elephant are exactly the same.

A Bodhisatta who fulfills the Perfection of Energy must follow this example of the Kesara Lion King. In ordinary tasks that should be undertaken, one must not slacken energy or perform them carelessly. Only when a great and difficult matter arises should one not suddenly exert extreme effort. This means that one must exert effort according to one's natural capacity, whether in ordinary tasks or in great and difficult matters.

## The Habit of Energy from the Bodhisatta Lives
Because of the momentum of the Perfection of Energy fulfilled consistently in various matters, both great and small, during the lives as a Bodhisatta, even after becoming a Buddha, the Blessed One does not slacken His energy or preach with a careless, ordinary voice when teaching a single being, thinking, "It is only one being." Nor does He specially strain His energy to preach with an exceptionally loud voice in large assemblies like the first sermon of the Dhammacakka, thinking, "So that those at the very edge may hear." He preaches with the same effort and the same voice when teaching one person as He does when teaching many.
403:
The great distinction is that the Blessed One, being the Lord of inconceivable glory and power, possesses a natural and true voice that spreads exactly as far as there are listeners, without any fluctuation. If there is one listener, only that one person hears it (there is no sound that escapes outside the audience). If the audience is large, there is no instance where those in distant places cannot hear because of the crowd; those in the distance hear as clearly as those nearby. (Even the Venerable Sāriputta, when preaching the Samacitta Sutta, could not make the entire vast assembly hear with his natural voice and had to use his supernormal powers (iddhividha-abhiññā) to make everyone hear. He had to install an 'abhiññā loudspeaker'. The Buddha, however, could make the entire assembly hear with His natural voice alone. He did not need to specially arrange or create it through abhiññā.) This is a special attribute of the Buddha's glory.

All Buddhas do not exert energy only during their lives as Bodhisattas while fulfilling the perfections. In their final life before becoming a Buddha, when the time for enlightenment arrives, they must renounce the world and exert energy in the practice of austerities (dukkharacariyā) for at least seven days. Having practiced such austerities, as the time of enlightenment draws near, when He is about to sit upon the grass mat spread at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree, He resolves with the four-fold energy: "Let only my skin remain, let only my sinews remain, let only my bones remain, let all my flesh and blood dry up; I shall not rise from this seat until I attain Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." Thus, by establishing the four-fold energy and contemplating the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self of mental and physical phenomena, beginning with Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) through the Great Diamond Insight (Mahāvajira-vipassanā), He attained Buddhahood.

The four-fold energy (caturanga-viriya) consists of:
(1) Let only the skin remain,
(2) Let only the sinews remain,
(3) Let only the bones remain,
(4) Let all the flesh and blood dry up—
404:
—these are the four factors. (It means: "Even if all flesh and blood dry up because of not eating, I will not slacken my effort as long as these three—skin, sinews, and bones—which do not easily dry up, still remain.")

Energy (viriya), like wisdom, is a mental factor (cetasika). However, as shown before, wisdom is exclusively a wholesome state. Energy, on the other hand, is a miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) mental factor; it can be associated with the wholesome side and also with the unwholesome side. It can also be associated with the indeterminate (abyākata) side, namely resultants and functionals. Therefore, energy can be a noble wholesome state, a base unwholesome state, or an indeterminate state free from both wholesome and unwholesome. Noble and right energy is called Sammā-vāyāma (Right Effort). Base energy is called Micchā-vāyāma (Wrong Effort). In the context of this Perfection of Energy, only the state of Sammā-vāyāma must be cultivated and developed. One must fulfill only that energy which is Sammā-vāyāma until it is complete.

## Sammappadhāna Viriya
That Sammā-vāyāma is also called Sammappadhāna (Right Exertion). The meaning is the same. The Blessed One taught in the Sammappadhāna Vibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga Pali that this Sammappadhāna energy is of four types.

The four Right Exertions are:
(1) The effort to prevent the arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen in one's continuity in this life (or those that one does not remember ever arising in any place or regarding any object) at any time, in any place, or regarding any object.
(2) The effort to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen in one's continuity in this life.
(In this context, it is not actually possible to abandon past unwholesome states that have already occurred or have arisen and ceased. Those unwholesome states that occurred in the past [sentence ends abruptly]
405:
...has ceased; it no longer exists. It is impossible to abandon what does not exist. Therefore, the effort to prevent the arising of new unwholesome states similar to those that occurred in the past is what is called "the effort to abandon unwholesome states that have arisen in one's own continuum in this life.")

(3) Another is the effort to bring about wholesome states that have not yet arisen in one's own continuum in this life (or wholesome states that one does not remember or recall ever having arisen in one's continuum at any time, in any place, or regarding any object).

(4) Another is the effort to maintain and increase wholesome states that have already arisen or are currently arising in one's own continuum in this life. (In this context, it also means making an effort to repeatedly bring about wholesome states similar to those that have already arisen.)

In this way, it should be understood that there are four types of Right Effort (Sammappadhāna-vīriya).

## 11 Causes for the Arising of Energy
In the Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga Commentary, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta Commentary, and other texts, it is explained that there are 11 causes for the arising of energy (vīriya). These 11 are:

(1) Apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇatā = Reflection on the danger of the lower realms.

"If I am lax in energy and live heedlessly, I might fall into the lower realms after death. Among the four lower realms, if I fall into hell (niraya), I will suffer great pain through various terrifying forms of torture. If I reach the animal realm (tiracchāna), I will be caught in nets and traps and endure whatever humans do to me. If I reach the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), I will suffer from hunger and other miseries for a long time, even for the interval between the appearance of two Buddhas. If I reach the realm of asuras (asurakāya), I will endure suffering such as wind and heat with a body sixty or eighty cubits long, consisting of only skin and bones. At such times, the four Right Efforts mentioned above..."
406:
...will not have the opportunity to practice the good Dhamma. Only in this life is there the opportunity to practice." For one who reflects in this way, energy can arise.

(2) Ānisaṃsadassāvitā = Habitually seeing the benefits of energy.

"A lazy person can by no means be liberated from the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) and attain the supramundane Paths and Fruits (Lokuttara Magga-Phala). Only one who habitually exerts effort can attain these supramundane Paths and Fruits. Therefore, energy has the benefit of attaining the supramundane Paths and Fruits, which are very difficult to achieve." Only when one habitually sees and reflects on the benefits of energy in this way can energy arise.

(3) Gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā = Properly reflecting on the path to be traveled.

"All Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (Ariyasāvakas) reached the state of a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a Noble Disciple only through the path of energy. Therefore, energy is the straight path traveled by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples. Lazy people cannot follow this path; only those with good energy can follow it." For one who reflects in this way, energy can arise.

(4) Piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā = Respecting the alms-food donated by donors.

This point is particularly relevant to monks. When donors offer excellent alms-food, a monk should reflect: "These donors of alms-food are not your relatives. They do not offer this food because they wish to live depending on you. In truth, they donate only because they desire the great benefits of merit. Furthermore, the Buddha did not permit the consumption of alms-food donated by donors for the purpose of living carelessly and lightly. He permitted it only with the intention that you should practice the Dhamma of a monk and be liberated from the round of rebirths. A person who is lazy and lacks energy is not worthy of eating such food. Only one who..."
407:
...strives with effort is worthy of eating it." For one who thus respects and pays heed to the alms-food he receives, energy can arise.

(5) Dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā = Reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance to be received.

The inheritance that disciples are to receive from the Buddha consists of the seven treasures of the noble (saddhamma-dhana): faith (saddhā), virtue (sīla), learning (suta), generosity (cāga), wisdom (paññā), moral shame (hirī), and moral dread (ottappa). A lazy person cannot receive this sevenfold inheritance of the Buddha. Just as in the world, bad sons and daughters are disowned by their parents saying, "They are not our children," and thus do not receive the inheritance when the parents pass away, so too a lazy person cannot receive this inheritance of the Buddha, the seven treasures of the noble. Only one with effort can receive it. For one who reflects on the greatness of the inheritance to be received in this way, energy can arise.

(6) Satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇatā = Reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, the Buddha.

"My Teacher, the Buddha, is truly noble. At the time of His conception, His renunciation, His enlightenment, His preaching of the first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), His performance of the Twin Miracle of water and fire to subdue the heretics at Sāvatthī, His descent from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the city of Saṅkassa, His relinquishing of the life-force, and His final passing (Parinibbāna), the ten thousand world systems trembled. While you are truly a son or daughter of such a noble Buddha, is it fitting for you to live lazily and carelessly without practicing the noble Dhamma related to the Dispensation (Sāsana)?" For one who reflects and applies the mind in this way, energy can arise.

(7) Jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā = Reflecting on the greatness of one's own lineage.

"My lineage is not low. You are a descendant of King Mahāsammata, pure and free from any intermixture of castes, and a descendant of the lineage of King Okkāka..."
408:
...the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Rāhula. Rāhula is the true son of the Buddha's own breast, and I also bear the name of a Sakyan prince, a son of the Buddha. Rāhula and I are indeed brothers. It is not fitting for one of such a noble lineage to live heedlessly; one should indeed practice the excellent Dhamma." For one who reflects in this way, energy can arise.

(8) Sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā = Reflecting on the greatness of one's fellow practitioners.

"Your fellow practitioners, the Venerable Sāriputtra and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, as well as the eighty Great Disciples (Mahāsāvakas), practiced the excellent Dhamma and realized the supramundane Paths and Fruits. You should follow the path of practice of those noble fellow practitioners." For one who reflects on the greatness of fellow practitioners in this way, energy can arise.

(9) Kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā = Avoiding lazy persons from afar.

This means that energy can arise for one who avoids those who live lazily, like a python that has eaten its fill, abandoning all physical and mental duties and spending time in constant sleep and wandering.

(10) Āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā = Associating with persons who exert energy.

This means that energy can arise for one who associates with persons who possess exerted energy and who have dedicated both body and mind solely to their work.

(In Pali) Pahitatta = (In Myanmar) Dedicating both body and mind to the work. This means making a resolution: "As long as the task I have undertaken is not completed or successful, I will not stop my effort. I will stop only when it is successful (or, if not successful, only when the body perishes and I die)." Those who lack this quality of *pahitatta*...
409:
...tend to have thoughts of hesitation even before starting the work, such as, "Will this work really succeed? It might just fail." Even while working, if they do not easily reach the state they aimed for, they tend to lose their energy, retreating and giving up, thinking, "Even if I continue, it will not succeed.")

(11) Tadadhimuttatā = Having a mind inclined toward energy in all four postures.

This means that energy can arise for one whose mind is inclined only toward exerting energy in all four postures: lying, sitting, standing, and walking. These are the 11 causes for the arising of energy.

Reflecting on the lower realms,
Seeing the benefits,
Following the traditional path,
Respecting alms-food,
Inheritance,
Greatness of the Teacher,
Greatness of lineage,
Fellow practitioners,
Avoiding the lazy,
Associating with the energetic,
Inclination (adhimutta)—these are the eleven causes for the increase of effort. (Sayadaw U Budh)

**********
## The Fundamental Cause of Energy
The fundamental cause of energy is spiritual urgency or dread (saṃvega). That saṃvega is of three types:

(1) Cittutrāsa-saṃvega,
(2) Ottappa-saṃvega,
(3) Ñāṇa-saṃvega.

Among these three:
410:
(1) The trembling and fear of the mind due to the danger of elephants, tigers, swords, spears, etc., is called Cittutrāsa-saṃvega. In terms of ultimate reality (paramattha), it is the mental factor of hatred (dosa-cetasika). (Fear is due to weak dosa; ferocity is due to strong dosa.)

(2) The fear and trembling to perform evil deeds is called Ottappa-saṃvega. This Ottappa-saṃvega is a faultless, beautiful mental factor (sobhaṇa-cetasika).

(3) The fear and foresight gained by properly reflecting on cause and effect is called Ñāṇa-saṃvega. This is the kind of fear that virtuous people have toward the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). In the scriptures, the meaning of this Ñāṇa-saṃvega is also explained as wisdom (ñāṇa) accompanied by moral dread (ottappa).

If one also includes "Dhamma-saṃvega," which is the wisdom of the Arahants accompanied by moral dread that occurs in the mode of being terrified by all conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), as mentioned in the scriptures, there should be four types of saṃvega.

Saṃvega, which is the fundamental cause of energy, should be Ñāṇa-saṃvega alone. Indeed, if one foresees, reflects on, understands, and fears the suffering of saṃsāra through wisdom, one will properly strive for the practices that lead to liberation from that suffering. If there is no understanding and fear, one will not strive. Not only in the great and profound paths of practice, but even in ordinary worldly matters, a student who has Ñāṇa-saṃvega—foreseeing and fearing the suffering of being uneducated when reaching adulthood—will strive to learn. A student who lacks such foresight and fear (Ñāṇa-saṃvega) will not strive to learn. Similarly, among workers, a worker who reflects on and fears the hardship of food, clothing, and shelter will work hard. One who does not reflect or fear and lives aimlessly will not work hard. Based on these facts, it should be well understood that energy can arise only when there is Ñāṇa-saṃvega—the trembling of foresight and fear.
411: The reason for stating that "the fundamental cause of energy (vīriya) should only be intellectual urgency (ñāṇa-saṃvega)" is specifically for the noble Perfection of Energy (vīriya-pāramī) practiced by the Bodhisattas. As previously mentioned, there is energy for exerting oneself in good deeds as well as energy for exerting oneself in evil deeds. This energy related to evil also has agitation (saṃvega) as its cause. However, it is not related to intellectual urgency (ñāṇa-saṃvega); because it pertains to evil, it is only related to the agitation of mental terror (cittuttrāsa-saṃvega). If a person lacks wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and runs out of wealth for personal use, they will exert effort to steal the property of others. This is how wrong energy arises from unwholesome mental terror. One who lacks wise attention will exert effort in wicked deeds to protect themselves from impending dangers. One who possesses wise attention, however, will not exert effort in wicked deeds but will only exert effort in a collection of blameless actions. Thus, when it is said that effort (vīriya) arises due to agitation (saṃvega), the distinction between blameless effort and blameworthy effort is again fundamentally caused by the presence or absence of wise attention. In the context of the Perfection of Energy, one should not take wrong efforts; only wholesome efforts and blameless efforts should be taken. Considering the factors of Right Exertion (sammappadhāna) mentioned before, it might seem that only wholesome energy which causes the growth of merit should be taken. However, even if it does not cause the growth of merit, as long as it is not a wrong effort or an effort that increases evil, it should be included in the Perfection of Energy. The evidence to consider is as follows: In the Mahājanaka Jātaka, which is cited in the Commentaries as an example of fulfilling the Perfection of Energy to the utmost, the Bodhisatta Prince Janaka exerted himself by swimming in the ocean for seven full days. This very exertion is described in the scriptures as the supreme practice of the Perfection of Energy. Of that Prince Janaka...
412: The strenuous swimming was not intended for the cultivation of merit (kusala), nor was it a matter of generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), or meditation (bhāvanā). Just as it does not particularly produce merit, it is also not a matter that produces unwholesome states (akusala) such as greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), or delusion (moha). If unwholesome states do not arise, it should be regarded as a blameless (anavajja) matter. The energy of Prince Janaka's exertion was a type of energy free from unwholesome states and blameless, and thus it was indeed the Perfection of Energy. Although the swimming energy of the Bodhisatta Mahājanaka was not primarily a great work of generosity, virtue, or meditation, his mental attitude during the exertion was identical to the mental attitude of previous great Bodhisattas, and therefore it should be regarded only as noble energy. Indeed, when the ship Mahājanaka was on was about to be destroyed, the other seven hundred sailors, fearing the imminent death they could not avoid, only wept and lamented. They did not make the slightest effort to escape. Mahājanaka, however, thought that when encountering danger in the world, weeping and lamenting is not the work of wise men; a wise and good man must only strive to protect himself from the encountered danger. With the intention, "As a wise and good man, I will strive to swim to escape the danger of water," he swam boldly without the slightest fear or dread of death. Because his mental attitude was so noble, the Bodhisatta's swimming is also called noble swimming, and his energy was indeed noble energy. Bodhisattas courageously carry out and exert themselves in matters they encounter in every life they are born into, without retreating in any way. Not to mention human life, in the Kaṇha Jātaka (Ekanipāta, 3-Kuru-vagga, Jātaka No. 29), when the Bodhisatta was a young bull named Kaṇha, wishing to repay the old woman who had raised him, he tirelessly exerted himself to pull five hundred carts one by one out of the deep mud, which the other oxen could not move.
413:
In this way, the Vīriya Pāramī (Perfection of Energy) of the Bodhisattas did not diminish even in animal births; thus, when they became human, they never abandoned their inherent foundation of energy in whatever they did. It should be noted that in the life of King Kusa, his leaving the throne and enduring various hardships to strive until he was near Pabhāvatī was like a madness of defilements, driven by his underlying energy that refused to lose or surrender.

## The Life of Mahosadha
The Mahosadha Jātaka is also presented in the scriptures as the fulfillment of Paññā Pāramī (Perfection of Wisdom). In that life, the Bodhisatta also specially cultivated Vīriya Pāramī. Looking at the Mahosadha Jātaka as a whole, one can clearly see through the eye of wisdom how he tirelessly strove to make things right according to his understanding, with Paññā Pāramī—the true understanding of cause and effect in all things—as the leader. The efforts of Mahosadha in that Jātaka were not acts of Dāna, Sīla, or Bhāvanā, but were efforts made for the welfare of the people; thus, those efforts should be called and understood as Vīriya Pāramī. A question may arise again:

## The Energy of Mahosadha
"Did Mahosadha not also strive to make others unhappy? For example, when the city of Mithilā was surrounded by King Cūḷanī Brahmadatta's great army of eighteen Akkhobhaṇīs, Mahosadha arranged a battle of wits with King Cūḷanī Brahmadatta's teacher, the great Brahmin Kevaṭṭa. He lured him with a great ruby that had descended from the time of King Kusa, grabbed the Brahmin's loincloth, and threw him down, causing King Cūḷanī Brahmadatta's great army to flee in disarray. In doing so, did he not cause distress to King Cūḷanī Brahmadatta and his followers? Is Mahosadha, who strove to make the other side suffer, not someone who deserves blame?"

The answer is: For example, if a snake is biting a frog, one should not scare it away. People often think that if you scare it away, although the frog is saved, it is not without fault because the snake will suffer the distress of hunger.
414: The Buddha, however, taught by taking intention (cetanā) as the foundation. If the person who scares the snake has the underlying intention of wanting the snake to starve, there would be fault. However, if they do not focus on or attend to the snake's hunger but only have the intention for the frog's safety, there can be no fault. Similarly, in this matter performed by Mahosadha, although King Cūḷani-Brahmadatta and others became unhappy, Mahosadha had no evil intention to cause them unhappiness. It was an exertion intended for the citizens of Mithilā to be free from the danger of death, and thus Mahosadha should not be blamed in any way. Alternatively, King Milinda asked the Elder Nāgasena: "Venerable Sir, did the Buddha not know that if he ordained Devadatta, he would later cause a schism in the Saṅgha? If he knew, why did he ordain him? If he had not ordained him, would the schism not have been impossible?" To this, the Elder Nāgasena replied: "Great King, the Buddha saw that Devadatta would later cause a schism in the Saṅgha. Even though he saw this, he knew that if he did not ordain him, Devadatta would certainly commit even more wicked and violent deeds, such as fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi), which are worse than the act of causing a schism (saṅghabhedaka). Although the act of causing a schism leads to rebirth in the states of loss, it still has a limited duration. The Buddha, seeing that if he did not ordain him, Devadatta would commit deeds like fixed wrong view and suffer the pains of hell for an indefinite period, felt compassion, thinking, 'If he is ordained in my Dispensation, the suffering Devadatta must undergo will have a limit.' Thus, the Buddha ordained Devadatta to lighten his heavy suffering." He answered with various such analogies. (From Milindapañhā, 4-Meṇḍaka-vagga, 3-Devadattapabbajja-pañhā, page 113). Likewise, if Mahosadha had not caused King Cūḷani-Brahmadatta's army to be frightened, the entire city of Mithilā would have been utterly destroyed. By making them flee in fear, Mithilā was not destroyed, and King Cūḷani-Brahmadatta's kingdom also suffered no significant loss. In this way, it was only an exertion of protection with the wish for both sides to be happy, and thus there is nothing to blame in Mahosadha.
415:
## Qualities of Vīriya
This Dhamma of Vīriya (Energy) has the following qualities:
