(1) When it acts as the leader and chief in various matters, it is included as one of the four Predominances (Adhipati) called Vīriyādhipati.
(2) It is included as one of the 22 Faculties (Indriya) that govern co-arising mental states, called Vīriyindriya. However, only the Vīriyindriya associated with mundane wholesome consciousness (lokiya kusala citta) is to be taken as Vīriya Pāramī. Among the five Faculties included in the Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma, just as with Paññindriya, only the Vīriyindriya included in mundane purifications (lokiya visuddhi) is counted within Vīriya Pāramī. Similarly, the Vīriya of Right Effort (Sammappadhāna) included in mundane purifications is counted within Vīriya Pāramī.
(3) Likewise, it is included as Vīriya-bala (Power of Energy) among the five Powers (Bala) which are the strengths of associated states; as Vīriyiddhipāda (Base of Power of Energy) among the four Bases of Power (Iddhipāda); as Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga (Energy Factor of Enlightenment) among the seven Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅga); and as Sammā-vāyāma (Right Effort) among the eight Path Factors (Maggaṅga). It should be understood without doubt that the Vīriya which qualifies as Vīriya-bala, Vīriyiddhipāda, Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga, and Sammā-vāyāma, arising in association with Mahākusala Citta while the Great Beings (Bodhisattas) were practicing mundane purifications, is included in this Vīriya Pāramī.

Reflecting on these extraordinary qualities of Vīriya, may you be able to practice and cultivate Vīriya Pāramī to its highest peak.

Here ends the chapter on Vīriya Pāramī.
**********
## (F) Khantī Pāramī
## Explanation of Khantī
Regarding this Khantī Pāramī, it is stated in the Pāḷi (sammānāvamānakkhamo) to 'endure both honor and contempt.' The direct meaning of the Pāḷi is that one must be able to endure without the mind being elated when encountering good things, and without the mind being depressed when encountering bad things. The main point is: if greed (lobha) arises upon encountering a favorable worldly condition—
416:
If one becomes angry when encountering bad worldly conditions (lokadhamma), it cannot be said that one is enduring those good or bad objects. The intended meaning of patience (khanti) is not becoming greedy when encountering good worldly conditions and not becoming angry when encountering bad worldly conditions.

However, regarding the Perfection of Patience (khanti pāramī), the commentators (Aṭṭhakathā teachers) mostly explain and provide various illustrative stories focusing only on the patient endurance of physical or verbal transgressions by others without getting angry. Their explanation is as follows: "Khantīpāramitā is the collection of mental states (cittuppāda) dominated by non-hatred (adosa), which occurs in the manner of enduring the faults of beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra), and is embraced by great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and skillful means (upāyakosalla)." This is explained in the Pakiṇṇakakathā section of the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary.

Furthermore, in the explanation of the five types of restraint (saṃvara) in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa of the Atthasālinī Commentary, Khanti-saṃvara is explained as: "Khanti means endurance (adhivāsanā). That endurance is the four mental aggregates (nāma-khandhā) occurring in that manner. Some teachers (eke) say it is wisdom (paññā). Alternatively, khanti is simply the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa-cetasika)." This is also explained in the Mūlaṭīkā.

Some wise teachers also state:
In the Pali texts, it is mentioned as 'sammānāvamānakkhamo,' meaning 'endure both honor and contempt.' This suggests that one must endure when others treat one with honor and also when they treat one with contempt. However, people generally do not want to tolerate contempt or insults and tend to get angry. As for being treated with honor and respect, no one finds it intolerable, and no one gets angry. Only when one can remain without anger in situations where most would find it intolerable and become angry can it be truly called patience.
417:
It is argued that if one takes both honor and contempt as directly stated in the Pali, then the Perfection of Patience (khanti pāramī) would be indistinguishable from the Perfection of Equanimity (upekkhā pāramī). Since these wise teachers rely on the aforementioned Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary and Mūlaṭီkā, their words cannot be dismissed.

However, the distinction between Khanti and Upekkhā should be noted as follows: enduring the actions committed by beings and formations is Khanti. Being indifferent, without hatred or love, towards beings and formations is Upekkhā.

The Most Venerable Ledi Sayadaw, in his Maṅgala Sutta Nissaya, translated it as: "Khanti ca: enduring without being elated when encountering happiness (sukha) and without being despondent or furious when encountering suffering (dukkha)." This is very much in line with the Pali phrase 'sammānāvamānakkhamo.'

If we reconcile the Commentary's explanation with the Pali text: Great Bodhisattas, by their very nature, possess a profound disposition. Therefore, when they encounter happiness (or good worldly conditions), they do not become elated or restless with greed; they are naturally able to endure it. There is no need for them to specially discipline their minds to endure it. It is when they encounter suffering that they must specially discipline their minds to endure it so that it reaches the level of Khanti Pāramī. Alternatively, a Bodhisatta practicing Khanti Pāramī must endure both happiness and suffering so that neither greed nor anger arises. With this in mind, the Pali states 'sammānāvamānakkhamo'—meaning one must be able to endure honor without greed and endure contempt or insults without anger. However, since Great Bodhisattas naturally have a profound disposition, their endurance of happiness without greed or agitation is not seen as extraordinary; it is already accomplished by their nature. Therefore, the Commentaries focus on the endurance of suffering, which is difficult for ordinary people to endure, as Khanti Pāramī. If taken this way, there is no conflict between the Commentary's explanation and the Pali teaching.
418:
## The Ultimate Reality of Khanti
This Perfection of Patience (khanti pāramī) is not a single, distinct ultimate reality (paramattha) like the Perfection of Wisdom (paññā pāramī) or the Perfection of Energy (viriya pāramī); it is a group of wholesome mental factors led by the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa-cetasika), which has the characteristic of not being furious. (Alternatively) Like the Perfections of Wisdom and Energy, it is the distinct ultimate reality of the non-hatred mental factor (adosa-cetasika).

Although Khanti is the adosa-cetasika, not all instances of adosa-cetasika should be called Khanti. The reason is that adosa-cetasika is present whenever beautiful consciousness (sobhana-citta) arises (except in unwholesome and rootless consciousness). Only the adosa that occurs in the manner of preventing anger when others do or say things that would normally provoke anger is called Khanti or patience. The adosa-cetasika present in beautiful consciousness occurring in other manners is not called Khanti or patience.

## The Patience of Venerable Puṇṇa
I shall briefly describe the reflection of Venerable Puṇṇa, which is a wonderful example to follow regarding the practice of patience. During the time of the Buddha, Venerable Puṇṇa requested the Buddha's permission to go and reside in the Sunāparanta region. The Buddha asked, "Dear Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta are fierce and rough. If the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile you, what will you think?"

Venerable Puṇṇa replied, "Venerable Sir, if the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, I will think: 'These people of Sunāparanta are truly good. They are exceptionally good people because they only abuse and revile me, but they do not strike me with their fists or elbows.' Thinking of them as good people, I will restrain my anger and endure it."
419:
The Buddha asked again and again, "Dear Puṇṇa, if the people of Sunāparanta strike you with their fists or elbows, what will you think?" Venerable Puṇṇa replied, "Venerable Sir, if the people of Sunāparanta strike me with their fists or elbows, I will think: 'These people of Sunāparanta are truly good. They are exceptionally good people because they only strike me with their fists and elbows, but they do not pelt me with stones.' Thinking of them as good people, I will restrain my anger and endure it."

He continued in this manner, even if they were to kill him, saying, "I am fortunate. Some, like Venerable Gomika and Venerable Channa, had to perform the act of taking their own lives with a weapon (satthāhāraka-kamma). I have gained this without having to do it myself. Thinking thus, I will restrain my anger and endure it." The Buddha then praised him, saying "Sādhu" (Well done). (From the Puṇṇovāda Sutta, Saḷāyatana Vagga, Uparipaṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya).

Furthermore, in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka of the Cattālīsa Nipāta, Sakka, the King of Devas, asked the hermit Sarabhaṅga:
"O hermit born of the Koṇḍañña clan, what must one kill in this world so as not to sorrow even for a moment? What abandonment do the virtuous praise? Whose harsh words should one endure in this world? Please answer this for me."

The Bodhisatta hermit Sarabhaṅga replied:
"If one kills anger in this world, one will never have to sorrow. If one does not disparage the virtues of others (ingratitude), the virtuous will praise him. One should endure the harsh words spoken by all—those superior to oneself, those equal to oneself, and those inferior to oneself. The virtuous say that such endurance is the highest."
420:
Sakka, the King of Devas, asked again:
"Venerable hermit, it is understandable to endure the harsh words (abuse) of one who is equal to oneself or one who is superior to oneself. But how can one endure the harsh words (abuse) of one who is inferior to oneself?"

The Bodhisatta hermit Sarabhaṅga replied:
"One might endure the harsh words of a superior out of fear, because they are superior. One might endure the harsh words of an equal out of the foresight that if one does not endure, the other might strive to cause even greater harm. (These two types of endurance are not the highest form of patience.) Enduring the harsh words of one who is inferior in status, birth, etc., when there is no special reason to endure, is what the virtuous call the highest patience."

## The Patience of Sakka
Once, when Sakka was at war with the Asuras, the Devas of Tāvatiṃsa were victorious and captured Vepacitti, the King of the Asuras. They brought him to Sakka. Every time Vepacitti entered or left the Sudhamma Assembly Hall, he abused Sakka with harsh words. However, Sakka did not show any anger and remained patient. When the young deva Mātali asked, "Why do you not get angry when Vepacitti abuses you so harshly?", Sakka's reply included these words:

"One's own goal is supreme; there is nothing higher than patience. Truly, when a strong person endures a weak person, that is what they call the highest patience."
421:
The meaning is: O Mātali, among all benefits, one's own welfare is the highest; and among those personal benefits, there is no benefit greater than patience. One who, though truly possessing strength, endures the harsh words of the weak—the virtuous call such endurance the highest patience.

## Explanation for the Pali Texts
According to the previously mentioned Sagāthāvagga Sakkasaṃyutta Pali and the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka Pali, being able to remain without anger despite the verbal transgressions of others is defined as patience (khanti). However, it should not be understood that remaining without anger towards the physical transgressions of others is not patience. In the world, because verbal transgressions occur more frequently than physical ones, the Pali texts mentioned above state that "not being angry at the verbal transgressions of others who insult harshly is patience (khanti)," following the majority of cases. It should be understood without doubt that not being angry when physical transgressions are committed is also indeed patience (khanti).

The reason it should be so understood is that in the Khantivādī Jātaka, King Kalābu committed offenses against the ascetic Khantivādī not only through verbal transgression but also through physical transgression until the end of his life, yet the ascetic Khantivādī practiced patience. Furthermore, in the statement of the Elder Puṇṇa in the previously mentioned Puṇṇovāda Sutta, it should be noted that not only verbal transgressions but also successive levels of physical transgressions are included.

## Akkodha which is not Patience
As shown, only the restraint of anger regarding the physical and verbal transgressions committed by others against oneself is true patience (khanti). There is also anger that can arise without being connected to the physical or verbal transgressions of others. To give a brief example: in the world, when someone is assigned a task to perform, even if the person assigned manages and performs it to the best of their ability, the person who gave the order...
422:
...might still become angry and dissatisfied if it is not as they intended when they come to see it. Restraining this kind of anger is not patience (khanti); in truth, it is only called non-anger (akkodha).

## Akkodha and Khanti as Royal Virtues
Therefore, in the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka of the Asītinipāta (Jātaka No. 534), when the Ten Royal Virtues (rājadhamma) were taught, both the qualities of non-anger (akkodha) and patience (khanti) were included. The reason these two qualities are included is that not every restraint of anger qualifies as khanti; only some instances qualify as khanti.

As previously explained, patience (khanti) is the restraint of anger regarding the physical and verbal transgressions of others. Restraining the anger that arises from dissatisfaction when one's orders are not followed as desired does not qualify as patience (khanti) because it is not related to the physical or verbal transgressions of others; it only qualifies as non-anger (akkodha).

Kings, when issuing various commands, may feel dissatisfied even if those who obey the commands perform them well with good intentions. For such situations, one royal virtue called akkodha was taught, stating that they must not get angry. Separately, another royal virtue called patience (khanti) was taught, stating that they must also restrain anger and not be angry at the physical and verbal transgressions of others.

## Nine Causes of Malice
Regarding the arising of anger, the nine causes of malice (āghātavatthu) should also be noted. It should be noted that one does not get angry only for oneself; one also gets angry on behalf of those one loves and against those who are one's enemies. (This means one gets angry for oneself, for one's loved ones, and because of one's enemies.) In the arising of anger, one gets angry regarding the past that has gone by, the future that is to come, and the immediate present. Thus, as there are three types of persons—oneself, one's friend, and one's enemy—
423:
when counted together with the three periods of time—past, present, and future—for each person, they become nine. The enumeration of these nine is as follows:

(1) One gets angry thinking, "This person has done me harm in the past."
(2) One gets angry thinking, "This person is doing me harm now."
(3) One gets angry thinking, "This person will do me harm in the future." (These three are for oneself.)
(4) One gets angry thinking, "This person has done harm to my friend in the past."
(5) One gets angry thinking, "This person is doing harm to my friend now."
(6) One gets angry in anticipation, thinking, "This person will do harm to my friend in the future." (These three are for one's friend.)
(7) One gets angry thinking, "This person has done good to my enemy in the past."
(8) One gets angry thinking, "This person is doing good to my enemy now."
(9) One gets angry in anticipation, thinking, "This person will do good to my enemy in the future." (These three are for one's enemy.)
(From the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Navakanipāta, 1-Paṇṇāsaka, Chapter 3, Sutta 9.)

## Aṭṭhānakopa
Although the nine causes of malice (āghātavatthu) appear in the Pali texts as shown, there is also the quality of aṭṭhānakopa, which is getting angry at what is not a cause for anger in the world.
424:
When it rains, one thinks it rains too much. When it is fair weather, one thinks it is too fair. One gets angry at the wind for blowing, or at the sun for being hot, and so on; this is the mental factor of anger (dosa cetasika) arising at things that are not causes for anger. Restraining this anger called aṭṭhānakopa should be termed non-anger (akkodha). This aṭṭhānakopa occurs frequently in the nature of those who lack reflection.

## Eight Kinds of Strength
The Buddha taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhakanipāta, 1-Paṇṇāsaka, 3-Gahapativagga, Sutta 7, that this quality of patience is a strength of the virtuous in the world. The eight kinds of strength taught in that sutta are:

1. Crying is the strength of children (their means of reliance).
2. Anger is the strength of women.
3. Various weapons are the strength of thieves and dacoits.
4. Sovereignty over a vast territory is the strength of kings.
5. Arbitrarily censuring others is the strength of fools.
6. Careful and focused reflection is the strength of the wise.
7. Repeated consideration and reflection is the strength of the learned (those of great hearing).
8. Patience (khanti) in not being angry at the transgressions of others is the strength of recluses and brahmins.
These are the eight.

## Recluses and Brahmins
In this eighth point regarding the strength of patience, recluses and brahmins are mentioned together. One might wonder and ask whether these recluses and brahmins are of the same status.
425:
Regarding the term 'recluse' (samaṇa), it refers to recluses (ascetics) outside the Dispensation, and within the Dispensation, it refers to the disciples of the Buddha; since this is well-known to many, it needs no special explanation.

Only the person called 'brahmin' (brāhmaṇa in Pali) needs to be examined. Upon examination, in the Aggañña Sutta of the Pāthikavagga, Dīgha Nikāya, it is said that in the beginning of the world, when people's conduct became corrupt and King Mahāsammata was elected to rule, some people thought: "Evil things have overwhelmed the world; we do not wish to live mixed with those who are so full of evil that a king must be appointed to rule. We shall go to the forest, and keeping evil away from ourselves, we shall expel and cast it out." They went to the forest and lived developing meditative absorptions (jhāna). Because they lived in this way, those persons were called 'Brahmins'.

The Pali word 'Brāhmaṇa' means one who has put away evil. Those persons did not cook and eat food themselves; they ate fruits that fell naturally or food received as alms from towns and villages. Calling those persons 'Brahmins' is because their practice, virtue, and dignity were consistent with the meaning derived from the Pali word 'Brāhmaṇa'; thus they are called 'Brahmins by virtue' (guṇabrāhmaṇa). It means they are called Brahmins by reason of their virtuous qualities.

Later, after a long time, some among those 'Brahmins by virtue' were unable to maintain the practice and the exertion for meditative absorption of the virtuous Brahmins. They approached the vicinity of towns and villages, lived at the outskirts, and wrote Vedic texts. They also taught those who wished to learn. Those persons no longer exerted themselves in meditation to put away evil. However, they continued to adopt the name 'Brahmin'. The name 'Brahmin' they adopted, although they were not 'Brahmins by virtue' because they lacked the qualities deserving of being a Brahmin, they were called 'Brahmins by birth' (jātibrāhmaṇa) because they were descendants of the true 'Brahmins by virtue'. Because those 'Brahmins by birth' could not exert themselves to attain meditative absorption, they were recognized at that time as the inferior ones.
426:
Later, after a long period had passed, even though they were no longer able to strive for jhāna, they were regarded as noble because they based their lives on writing and teaching the Vedas, and the public designated them as 'noble' (brahmin). These jati-brahmana—those who are called brahmins based merely on their birth and lineage—even though they could not truly expel or wash away defilements through jhāna, they wished to show the people that they were still performing the act of 'washing away.' Thus, they would go down into rivers, soak in the water, and claim to be washing away impurities.

In the Bhūridatta Jātaka, when the Naga King Bhūridatta did not return to the Naga realm at his usual time after observing the Uposatha precepts, his younger and older brothers went out to search for him. During this search, the Nesāda Brahmin, who had shown disrespect and committed an offense against the Naga King Bhūridatta by handing him over to the snake charmer (Alampāyana), was soaking in the Yamunā River, thinking he would wash away the impurities of his offense. The younger brother, Subhoga Naga, while searching along the Yamunā River, found the Nesāda Brahmin, captured and punished him, and took him to the Naga realm.

Since there are these two types of brahmins, when it is taught that 'patience is the strength of recluses and brahmins,' the Buddha was referring to the guna-brahmana (brahmins by quality). According to the Aggañña Sutta, in times outside the Buddha's dispensation, those who wore white clothes and strove with the intention of abandoning evil defilements were called 'brahmana' in Pali, and 'ponna' in Burmese. When the Buddha's dispensation arrived, the Buddha described the noble qualities that merit the title 'brahmana' and taught a whole section called the 'Brahmanavagga' in the Dhammapada, consisting of forty-two verses. The brahmins described in these teachings are exclusively guna-brahmana. These guna-brahmana do not have further subdivisions; it is only the jati-brahmana who have various divisions.

## The Term 'Ponna'
Calling a brahmana 'ponna' in Burmese is not based on the Pali linguistic sense, but is merely a result of successive changes in Burmese vocabulary. Indeed, looking at historical records, in the era of Sri Ksetra (Pyay)...
427:
...during its prosperous times, brahmins were called 'Gavampati.' (Since brahmins mostly earned their living by raising cows, they were called 'Gavampati' in Pali; 'gavaṃ' means 'of cows,' 'pati' means 'lord,' so 'Gavampati' means 'owner of cows.')

Although this word 'Gavampati' is a Pali word, the Magadha dictionary (Abhidhāna) lists only six Pali terms that convey the meaning of brahmin: brahmabandhu, dvija, vippa, brahma, bhovādī, and brāhmaṇa. The word 'Gavampati' is not included. This term 'Gavampati' is merely a Pali word coined by the Burmese based on observable circumstances.

After the Sri Ksetra era, when the Bagan era arrived, they were no longer called 'Gavampati' but were changed to 'Hūryā-thamā.' 'Hūryā' is the name given to the texts of astronomy and astrology. Those who were proficient in these Vedic texts were called 'Hūryā-thamā.' Brahmins proficient in astrology were called 'White Hūryā,' while non-brahmins proficient in astrology were called 'Brown Hūryā.'

After the Bagan era, when the Pinya era arrived, they were no longer called 'Hūryā' but were commonly referred to as 'Ponnā' until the present day. Investigating the origin of this term, it is understood that those Hindus proficient in astrology mostly came to Pinya from the city of Punā (Pune) in India. Thus, they were called 'Punā' after their city of origin, and from that, the word shifted to 'Ponnā.'

The section on the Perfection of Patience (Khantī Pāramī) is finished.
**********
## (7) The Perfection of Truth (Saccā Pāramī)
Among the eight perfections—Dāna, Sīla, Nekkhamma, Paññā, Vīriya, Adhiṭṭhāna, Mettā, and Upekkhā—the original Pali forms are used: Dāna Pāramī, Sīla Pāramī, Nekkhamma Pāramī, Paññā Pāramī, Vīriya Pāramī, Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī, Mettā Pāramī, and Upekkhā Pāramī. However, for Khanti and Sacca, instead of using the original Pali forms (Khanti Pāramī, Sacca Pāramī), they are called Khantī Pāramī and Saccā Pāramī with long vowels in Burmese usage for ease of pronunciation and recitation.
428:
In such usage, there is no fault because the intellectual vision can still reach and focus on the original meanings of 'patience' and 'truthfulness.' When saying Khantī Pāramī and Saccā Pāramī, it is easy to recite and the intended meaning is understood.

## The Movement of the Morning Star (Venus)
In this section on Saccā Pāramī, regarding the meaning of the statement 'The Morning Star (Venus) does not deviate from its regular path,' the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary explains: 'Venus travels to the East for six months and to the West for six months.' This commentary statement should not be taken literally. The reason is that if Venus travels like other stars and constellations, it must travel only towards the West. Traveling towards the East is impossible. Because it seems impossible, one might feel inclined to reject the commentary's words. However, the ancients devised a fitting explanation: Venus is seen in the East near dawn, and after sunset at night, it is seen only in the West. Referring to this meaning, the Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa composed in verse 128 of the Pāramī-taw-khan Pyo:

'Using a simile to match the fame of Truth,
In the quest for fulfillment, the peerless one thought:
As the constellations revolve to the right,
Circling the peak of Mount Meru,
The Morning Star, the leader of the host,
With a brilliance exceeding others, like the moon,
Across the sky's expanse at sunset and sunrise,
In the East and the West, as the year turns,
Through the three seasons of rain, cold, and heat,
Fittingly follows its course without deviation,
Always constant in its path.
This radiant king of stars,
Is like a great scale for gods and men.'

Even when the Lord prayed for the supreme prize,
To his kin, to strangers, and to all people,
With noble words that bring peace,
Without excess or deficiency, firm and true,
His speech and his actions were as one.
With no one to disturb his uprightness,
Even when it was difficult to speak, avoiding the double-tongue,
He conquered through the power of Truth alone,
Digging out the root of the tongue of the Great Sage—
429:
Astrologers, however, according to the Sannittha method of calculation, say that for six months it travels ahead of the Sun, and for six months it follows behind the Sun. To align the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary with this astrological text, the interpretation should be: 'Chamāse, for six months; pacchimaṃ disaṃ, to the region behind the Sun; gacchati, it goes. Chamāse, for six months; purimaṃ disaṃ, to the region ahead of the Sun; gacchati, it goes.'

The summary to be noted is: as stated in the Pali texts, just as Venus never deviates from its regular path at any time but travels straight and true, one must speak only with honesty. Only such speech is to be regarded as Truth (Sacca). Therefore, the teacher Venerable Buddhaghosa explained in the Pāṭha Jātaka Commentary: 'The Morning Star, in all seasons, does not abandon its regular path to travel by another, but travels only by its regular path.'

## Two Kinds of Truth
Truth (Sacca) is not a separate ultimate reality (paramattha) like the factors of wisdom (paññā) or energy (vīriya). It is merely the nature of being unerring and correct (specifically, the mental factors of abstinence (virati), volition (cetanā), etc., are the actual states). Since the nature of correctness varies according to the context, the doctrine of Truth is also divided. The division is as follows:
(1) Sammuti-sacca (Conventional Truth),
(2) Paramattha-sacca (Ultimate Truth).
These are the two fundamental truths. (The Buddha taught that there are two truths: Sammuti-sacca and Paramattha-sacca. A third truth cannot be found; it does not exist in the world. This is stated in the Kathāvatthu Commentary, etc.)

Among these two: (1) Sammuti-sacca is the truth as designated and conventionally accepted by the people in the world. Most people designate and name things based on their shape and form. The way they designate is: 'An object with this shape and form is called a human.' 'An object with this shape and form is called an ox.'
430:
'An object with this shape and form is called a horse,' and so on. Among humans as well, they designate: 'An object with this kind of shape and form is a man,' 'An object with this kind of shape and form is a woman,' and so forth. One should understand this extensively for as many types of objects as there are.

If one refers to an object designated as a 'human' as a 'human,' it is Conventional Truth; in other words, it is true according to the designation. If one calls it an 'ox,' it cannot be Conventional Truth; it is not true according to the designation. If one refers to an object designated as a 'woman' as a 'man,' it is not Conventional Truth; it is not true according to the designation. In this way, one should distinguish and understand what is and what is not Conventional Truth.

## Paramattha-sacca (Ultimate Truth)
That which is not merely a designation by the people, but is a reality that truly and definitely exists, is called Ultimate Truth. For example, when it is said, 'The nature of knowing various objects is called Citta (Mind),' the nature of knowing the object according to that word 'Citta' truly exists as an ultimate reality; because it is true, it is called Ultimate Truth. When it is said, 'The collection of phenomena that change due to opposing causes such as cold and heat is Rūpa (Matter),' that nature of Rūpa truly exists in the ultimate sense; because it is true, it is called Ultimate Truth. In this way, the realities of Citta (Mind), Cetasika (Mental Factors), Rūpa (Matter), and Nibbāna are called Ultimate Truth because they truly exist and are true in the ultimate sense.

## Perception (Saññā) and Wisdom (Paññā)
Between these two truths, Conventional Truth is the object of perception (saññā); in other words, it can be known through perception. Marking and remembering based on form from childhood—such as 'this shape is a human,' 'this shape is a man,' 'this shape is a woman,' 'this shape is an ox,' 'this shape is a horse'—is the function of perception. If one looks through the markings of perception, the human figure clearly exists; the forms of man, woman, etc., all appear to exist clearly.
431:
Ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) is the object of wisdom (paññā). (Alternatively) it can only be clearly realized through wisdom. The sharper the wisdom, the more one can observe and see the ultimate truth. Wisdom is the act of analyzing anything to investigate and realize its fundamental nature. When it is said, "The nature of knowing various objects is called consciousness (citta)," if one investigates with wisdom whether this nature of knowing various objects truly exists or not, one clearly sees that it does exist. The way of seeing is this: if the phenomenon of knowing did not exist in the world, there would be no such thing as a "being," and there would only be clusters of material phenomena (rūpa) like stones, pebbles, logs, or posts. Those material things do not have the nature of knowing. Now, beings are indeed knowing and perceiving various objects. If one analyzes and contemplates in this way, the reality of knowing the object (citta) clearly appears.

Therefore, if it is said that the thing called "knowing" (or "citta" in Pali-derived Burmese) truly exists in the ultimate sense, it becomes clearer and clearer the more a person who habitually contemplates with wisdom considers it. For a person who looks with perception (saññā), however, it cannot be clear. It will only disappear. The reason is that perception, as previously shown, is the mental factor that marks shapes and forms. If it is said, "The reality of consciousness exists," perception will only scrutinize and ask about its shape and form: is it round, flat, square, powder, liquid, or vapor? If such questions are asked, there is no possibility of answering that consciousness is round, flat, square, powder, liquid, or vapor. If it cannot be so described, the person of perception might say that consciousness does not exist; for if it truly existed, it must be round, or flat, and so on. Thus, the person of perception is obsessed only with substance and form, and because no substance can be found, they would say that consciousness does not exist.

Just as ultimate truth disappears (i.e., no substance can be found) when viewed through the eyes of a person of perception, conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) also disappears when viewed through the eyes of a person of wisdom. The way it disappears is this: when the conventional truth called a "person" is analyzed by the nature of wisdom into hair, body hair, nails, teeth...
432:
...and so on, into the thirty-two parts, if one asks, "Is hair called a person?" one cannot answer that it is. If one asks, "Is body hair called a person?" one cannot answer that it is. In this manner, if one takes out each of the thirty-two parts one by one and asks if it is called a person, one must answer that it cannot be so called. When the whole person is thus divided into thirty-two parts and questioned, if no single part can be called a person, the person of wisdom would say that a "person" does not exist.

In this way, conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) or concepts (paññatti) are clear only when viewed with the corresponding perception (saññā), but they disappear when viewed with wisdom (paññā). Similarly, ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) is clear only when viewed with wisdom, but it disappears when viewed with perception.

A point particularly worthy of note here is the great ultimate reality of "Nibbāna." This ultimate reality of Nibbāna is the great nature of peace, free from all anxiety and suffering. This kind of peace can only be clearly realized and seen if one can contemplate it with sharp wisdom. If viewed with perception, it will only disappear.

## The View of One Who Relies on Perception
Nowadays, some people ask, "Is Nibbāna a great palace or celestial mansion? In what state do those who have entered Nibbāna dwell?" and so on. Such questioning should be understood as asking about Nibbāna—which is purely ultimate reality and the domain of wisdom—using only perception.

In truth, it should be understood that in Nibbāna, there are no palaces or celestial mansions, nor are there persons who enter and dwell there. (For those individuals who have realized and experienced the peace of Nibbāna through the Path and Fruition of Arahatship, after the moment of the final decease-consciousness (parinibbāna-cuti) of that last life, no new aggregates of mind and matter arise in any future existence; it is the peaceful cessation like the extinguishing of a great flame—this is what is called "attaining Parinibbāna." It is not that one dwells in Nibbāna as a substantial person.)
433:
If it is said in this way, it might seem that Nibbāna does not even exist clearly. Because it does not appear clearly in this way, those who rely on perception tend to think of it as a useless doctrine that is not worth desiring. To encourage such people of perception, some say, "Nibbāna is a great palace or celestial mansion that cannot perish, where one enjoys incomparable worldly-like bliss with special forms of mind and matter that are not subject to death or destruction." When this is said, the people of perception are often very satisfied and heartened because it mentions the shapes and forms they are accustomed to clinging to.

In reality, if a substantial form or shape is clearly found by looking with the nature of perception, it is not a true ultimate reality (paramattha); it is only a concept (paññatti). Likewise, if a substantial form disappears when looking with wisdom, it is pure concept. If it does not disappear, but rather its intrinsic nature (sabhāva-satti) becomes clearer the more one looks, it should be understood as a true ultimate reality. Therefore, one should not search for Nibbāna—which is merely peace, most noble, and a true ultimate reality—with perception that habitually grasps at shapes, forms, and substances. Instead, one should strive to contemplate and consider so that the reality of peace called Nibbāna appears through wisdom, which habitually discards substance and searches only for the true fundamental nature.

These two, conventional truth and ultimate truth, are both true according to their respective natures as shown. In the world, if one person, referring to the conventional sense, says, "Persons, men, and women clearly exist; if my words are not true, may I be struck by the scriptures (an oath)," and another person, referring to the ultimate sense, says, "Persons, men, and women do not clearly exist; if my words are not true, may I be struck by the scriptures," both of them will not be struck by the scriptures. This is because, although their words are contradictory, their underlying intentions are different, and each is true according to their own basis and intention. The words of the one who says persons, men, and women exist are true in terms of conventional concept (sammuti-paññatti), and thus are understood as conventional truth (sammuti-sacca).
434:
The words of the one who says persons, men, and women do not exist are also true in terms of the ultimate sense, and thus are understood as ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca).

Therefore, although the Buddhas primarily intend to teach the ultimate nature which truly exists, they do not teach by completely bypassing or discarding concepts; they teach by combining them with concepts. Even in the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, although the primary intent was to teach the two extremes and the Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā), He taught by combining them with the concept of a "monk" (bhikkhu), saying, "These two extremes should not be followed by one who is a monk," and so on.

## The Importance of Concepts
(In another way) when the Buddha teaches ultimate reality, He does not combine it with conventional concepts merely for the sake of clarity. Conventional truth and concepts are as important for beings as ultimate reality is. The importance is this: if the Buddha had taught only the collection of ultimate realities, for those who attend to the teaching wisely and correctly, they would contemplate according to the ultimate nature—"Everything in the world is only impermanent (anicca), only suffering (dukkha), and only non-self (anatta) which does not follow one's will and is not substantial"—and by practicing insight (vipassanā), they would go straight to the path of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.

However, for those who attend to it unwisely, they would think, "It is said there are only groups of mind and matter in the world which are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. There is no 'I,' no 'other.' If there is no 'I' or 'other,' there is no 'my property,' 'my son,' or 'my wife.' There is no 'other's property,' 'other's son,' or 'other's wife.' Any property can be used as desired. Since there is no 'other,' there can be no misconduct of killing (pāṇātipāta); there can be no theft. Since there is no 'other,' there is no 'other's wife,' and thus there can be no sexual misconduct (kāmesu micchācāra)." Thus, they would act recklessly and commit all kinds of misconduct. If they do so, immediately after death, they will only go to the four woeful planes (apāya). To protect and save them from such dangers of the woeful planes, the conventional truth of the Suttanta discourses was taught.
435:
Therefore, the Suttanta teaching is a teaching that greatly protects and supports beings so that they do not fall into the four woeful planes.

It is not only for protecting against the danger of woeful planes; it can also lead to good destinations (sugati) such as the human realm, deva realms, and brahma realms. This is because the Suttanta discourses mostly teach acts of merit such as generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), and tranquility meditation (samatha-bhāvanā), which lead to those good destinations. For an act of generosity to be accomplished, there must be the fulfillment of these factors: intention (cetanā), the recipient, the donor, and the object to be given. Among these, only the intention is an ultimate reality; the other three are entirely concepts. If concepts were completely discarded, the act of generosity itself could not occur. (The same applies to virtue and tranquility.) Therefore, it should be understood without doubt that conventional truth and concepts can lead to good destinations as mentioned. At the very least, if conventional truth were completely discarded, even the perfections (pāramī) which are the causes for becoming a Buddha could not be practiced and accumulated.

If only the Suttanta discourses were taught, it is true that people would not commit misconduct as mentioned. However, they would think, "Since the Buddha Himself taught that there is 'I,' 'other,' 'my property,' 'other's property,' 'my son and wife,' 'other's son and wife,' etc., then 'I,' 'my property,' 'my son and wife,' etc., truly exist." With such great clinging, the prospect of reaching the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna would gradually become distant. Therefore, to lead and save beings so they reach the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, the ultimate truth of the Abhidhamma teaching had to be taught again.

## The Reason for Teaching the Two Truths
Through the Abhidhamma teaching, although it is taught in the Suttas that "I," "my property," "my son and wife," etc., exist in the world, this is merely teaching in accordance with what is true in the sense of worldly convention. In reality, there is no "I," "other," "man," or "woman." Therefore, one should not remain clinging to "I," "other," "man," "woman," etc., which are only designated by way of convention, as things that truly exist. The Buddha had to teach again to remove the misconceptions of "I," "other," "man," "woman," etc., by showing that everything is indeed only impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
436:
In this way, following conventional truth (Sammuti-sacca), the Buddha had to teach both truths so that people would practice according to the two truths: that in the world, 'I,' 'others,' 'man,' 'woman,' etc., exist in terms of concepts (or exist in terms of conventional truth), but in reality, 'I,' 'others,' 'man,' 'woman,' etc., do not exist as ultimate realities (Paramattha).

## Natural Truth and Noble Truth
Within those two truths, Ultimate Truth (Paramattha-sacca) is further divided into two: (a) Sabhāva-sacca (Natural Truth) and (b) Ariya-sacca (Noble Truth). All ultimate realities—Citta (consciousness), Cetasika (mental factors), Rūpa (matter), and Nibbāna—are Sabhāva-sacca. This is because all of them are true in terms of their ultimate nature.

According to this Sabhāva-sacca, within mundane phenomena, there clearly exist Sukha (bodily pleasure) and Somanassa (mental pleasantness). If one is in contact with a pleasant touch, bodily pleasure (Sukha) arises due to that contact. (In common parlance, one is satisfied.) In saying this, it cannot be untrue; no one can deny that being in contact with a pleasant touch is good. This inability to deny it is because bodily pleasure (Sukha) truly arises when encountering a pleasant touch (iṭṭha-phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa).

In the same way, if the mind encounters a pleasant object or cause, that person's mind will certainly be happy; in Pāḷi, Somanassa-vedanā arises. No one can deny that this is possible, because the state of mental happiness (Somanassa) truly exists. Thus, one should know that according to the method of Sabhāva-sacca, the two states of bodily pleasure (Sukha) and mental pleasantness (Somanassa) clearly exist within mundane phenomena.

## Section on Ariya-sacca
## Dukkha Ariya-sacca
When reaching the method of Ariya-sacca (Noble Truth), Sukha (bodily pleasure) and Somanassa (mental pleasantness) can no longer be said to exist within mundane phenomena. It is only according to the method of Sabhāva-sacca that such Sukha and Somanassa are said to exist.
437: one will not be able to abandon mundane things. If one cannot abandon them, one cannot attain the state of an Ariya (Noble One). Therefore, a person who wishes to become an Ariya should contemplate the group of things called happiness and pleasure under Natural Truth, seeing them only as suffering (dukkha). The group of phenomena called happiness and pleasure according to Natural Truth is not an unchanging, permanent group; it is a group of phenomena that will change within a moment. In the world, most worldlings (puthujjana) mistakenly perceive and crave human and celestial riches as being solely pleasant and joyful. This craving exists because they do not know the nature of those riches, which is to be impermanent and subject to change. This failure to see is due to a lack of wisdom and foresight, and the strength of craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha). Those with wisdom and foresight, however, see that although these things appear pleasant and delightful before they change, they will certainly change and perish before long. Although there may be joy when obtaining these impermanent riches, when they are about to perish or have perished, the intense grief and suffering will be so great that it outweighs the previous joy. For example, if a poor man wins a hundred thousand in the lottery, he will be extremely delighted as soon as he hears the news. While being joyful, he might think, 'I will spend it grandly. I will enjoy myself to make up for all my past poverty.' If, before he can even spend it, the entire hundred thousand is lost due to some danger, one should reflect and consider how much his mind would suffer. It can be understood that the anxiety and grief at the time of loss would be far more overwhelming and unbearable than the joy felt at the time of gain. In mundane matters, any object is associated with both pleasant and unpleasant natures. Sensual pleasures (kāmaguṇa) of the five senses are pleasant and delightful according to the desires of worldlings. However, the Buddha taught: 'Appassādā bhikkhave kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā'—'Monks, sensual pleasures provide little gratification but much suffering and much despair.' Not to mention the Buddha, even his disciples, the Noble Ones (Ariyas), do not find delight in those mundane
438: sensual pleasures like worldlings do. However, the Buddha did not teach that there is absolutely no gratification in sensual pleasures. He taught that there is little gratification and much suffering, like saying 'a small measure of happiness and a great weight of suffering.' The nature of wise and virtuous people is that, regarding any matter, they do not first consider whether there is gratification (assāda), but first consider whether there is danger or fault (ādīnava) that causes mental distress. If they find danger (ādīnava), they no longer care even if there is gratification (assāda). They decide it is something undesirable. If there is no danger, they regard it as a good thing even if there is no gratification. For example, suppose someone is offered the position of a world-ruling king for just one day, with the condition that they will be executed the following day. If they are asked to accept this kingship, no one would dare or want to do it. In truth, the status of a world-ruling king for one day—something never before attained or possessed—is full of gratification from the perspective of a worldling. However, because the great danger of perishing and dying the next day is evident, no one would be able to enjoy the gratification of being a world-ruling king for that single day. In the same way, the Noble Ones see the danger of future change and destruction in everything, and thus they can no longer perceive the temporary, fleeting gratification before the change as something truly pleasant. Without such perception, only one who reflects and internalizes that 'In this world, there truly can be no such thing as happiness; there are only impermanent (anicca) things; because they are not permanent, they cannot be called happiness; they are truly only a mass of suffering' can attain the state of an Ariya. Thus, only by contemplating that there is only suffering within mundane phenomena can one become an Ariya. Therefore, this group of phenomena to be so contemplated is the truth that can truly lead to the state of an Ariya, and thus
439:
It is called the Noble Truth (Ariya Sacca). In another sense, because Noble Ones (Ariyas) always contemplate this collection of mundane phenomena as suffering in accordance with reality, it is called the Noble Truth.

Thus, according to the right knowledge and right vision of those striving to become Noble Ones and those who have already become Noble Ones, within the great cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) known as the three realms, there is no happiness, only suffering. Contemplating in this way is correct, and thus it is called the Noble Truth of Suffering (Dukkha Ariya Sacca).

In brief, the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā), known as the mundane phenomena of the three realms (tebhūmaka), are truly nothing but suffering. They are the absolute truth of suffering. The five aggregates of clinging are the five groups of phenomena: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, which are the bases of clinging as "my body," and so on. These five aggregates are called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

## The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Dukkha Samudaya Ariya Sacca)

This great mass of suffering, this truth of suffering known as the five aggregates of clinging, does not arise spontaneously without a cause. Among the many relevant causes, the most fundamental, primary, and significant cause is craving (taṇhā-lobha), which delights in and clings to various sense objects.

In this world, all sentient beings must suffer through planning, seeking, and working day and night for their comfortable living, food, and clothing; this suffering exists only because of craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha), such as the desire to live well and eat and dress well. If one could abandon and remove craving as much as possible—thinking, "I do not wish to eat well, I will eat whatever food is available just to survive; I do not wish to dress well, I will simply cover myself with easily obtainable leaves just to hide my shame"—then the suffering of striving and planning day and night like this would no longer exist. Therefore, it is clearly evident that craving, which perceives suffering as good and clings to it, is the cause of its arising.
440:
Not only for the present life, but also for the new lives to come, because of the desire to obtain only a good new life, one performs and accumulates various types of kamma. Due to these performed kammas, when a new life arises in the future, it is brought about by the kamma directed by the craving and greed of the present life. Therefore, when searching for the root cause of the arising of that new life, craving (taṇhā-lobha) is indeed the root cause.

In this way, because craving is the certain and true root cause that can produce suffering, known as the aggregates of clinging in a new life, this craving is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Dukkha Samudaya Ariya Sacca). It means the true cause that produces the collection of aggregates which is suffering. This Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering is also called the Truth of Origin (Samudaya Sacca) for short.

## The Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Dukkha Nirodha Ariya Sacca)

Although craving (taṇhā-lobha), known as the Truth of Origin, clings to and delights in various mundane sense objects like birdlime, it cannot cling to the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) called peace (santi)—which is the peaceful bliss that exists eternally without being conditioned by causes—just as a fly cannot land on a red-hot iron ball.

When searching for the reason why craving cannot cling to this unconditioned element, the ultimate reality of Nibbāna, it is because, from the nature of craving, the unconditioned element of Nibbāna is not something to be craved. To make this reason clearer: in the teaching of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), the Buddha taught, "vedanā-paccayā taṇhā" (with feeling as condition, craving arises). According to this, craving can only arise when there is the bliss of feeling (vedayita-sukha). The Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the unconditioned element, is not the kind of bliss that is felt (vedayita-sukha); it is only the bliss of peace (santi-sukha).

One might ask: "Can the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which has no feeling at all, be something desirable or something to be delighted in?"

Such a question arises because the mind of the questioner perceives only the feeling of sensation (vedanā) as true happiness, or (in another sense) because they have not contemplated the bliss of peace as true happiness. The answer is—
441:
There are two kinds of happiness: the happiness of feeling (vedayita-sukha) and the happiness of peace (santi-sukha). To provide a clear worldly analogy: in this world, there might be a wealthy man who is very fond of food and nourishment. This wealthy man lives by purchasing and consuming extremely expensive food. On the other hand, there is a great Vijjādhara (one accomplished in knowledge) who, having attained the perfection of nourishment (āhāra-siddhi), is far from wanting to eat the expensive food the wealthy man eats; indeed, he would even find it loathsome.

If one were to ask these two, "Who is happier regarding food?"

A person driven by craving (taṇhā) would say that only the wealthy man is happy, as only he gets to enjoy the best and most expensive things as he pleases. They would say the wealthy man is superior because the Vijjādhara does not get to enjoy any food at all. Such a statement is made because their mind is overwhelmed by craving, causing them to regard only the feeling (vedanā) that encourages craving as supreme.

However, the wise would say that only the Vijjādhara is happy regarding food. The wealthy man is surrounded by the suffering of maintenance (paṭisaṅkharaṇa-dukkha)—having to search for various flavors by any means and arrange them properly once obtained—and the suffering of expectation (āsā-dukkha), which is the desire to constantly change for something new. Vedayita-sukha can never be free from these two types of suffering. The Vijjādhara, because he lacks the vedayita-sukha of consuming food, is free from any suffering such as the suffering of maintenance or the suffering of expectation. He can live in great peace and happiness regarding food. Since the Vijjādhara's peaceful happiness is entirely unmixed with suffering and is pure bliss, the wise would answer that only the Vijjādhara is happier than the wealthy man regarding food.

In this matter, those driven by craving who say the wealthy man is happier speak only by looking at the pleasant feeling of eating to one's heart's content without seeing any fault. They cannot perceive as good or noble the Vijjādhara's peaceful and happy way of living without eating any food.
442:
Just as those overwhelmed by craving desire only to be a wealthy man, thinking it is the best, the nature of craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) is such that it does not perceive, desire, or long for the happiness of peace (santi-sukha), which is the absolute peace of the Unconditioned Nibbāna (asaṅkhata-nibbāna) without the presence of felt experience (vedanā).

In this regard, in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Navaka Nipāta, Mahāvagga, the third Sutta [Nibbānasukha Sutta]:

On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying among the monks and addressed them: "Friends, this Nibbāna is happiness. This Nibbāna is happiness." When he said this, the Venerable Udāyī asked the Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, how can there be happiness in Nibbāna where there is no feeling (vedanā)?" Then the Venerable Sāriputta preached: "Friend Udāyī, the very absence of feeling in Nibbāna is itself true happiness."

In this matter, in the view of unwise worldlings (puthujjana), only the occurrence of the five aggregates, which are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), is regarded as happiness. However, wise worldlings and the Noble Ones (Ariyas) regard only the cessation of those five aggregates of the Truth of Suffering—a cessation that does not arise again, like the extinguishing of a great fire—as happiness.

An example to practically consider and note regarding how the happiness of non-arising and peace is noble for worldlings with little wisdom is as follows: Suppose a person has suffered severely from a chronic wind-ailment (vāta-roga) for many years. Upon meeting a good physician and taking a dose of excellent medicine, that wind-ailment is completely cured at its root. When the wind-ailment is thus extinguished, how happy will that patient be? (Here, the extinguishing of the wind-ailment refers to the non-occurrence of that ailment.) He will be greatly happy and joyful. In reality, at that time, he is not consuming or enjoying any pleasant object; there is only the evident fact that the suffering of the wind-ailment has been extinguished and does not occur. Because of the cessation and non-occurrence of the wind-ailment without any felt experience, he will certainly be very glad and joyful, thinking, "A great suffering has been extinguished for me."

If one can be so joyful at the cessation of a minor wind-ailment, which is negligible compared to the great suffering of saṃsāra,
443:
if one can be so joyful at the cessation of a minor wind-ailment, why should one not be joyful when the great danger and suffering of saṃsāra is pacified? It should be well noted that one must truly be joyful and glad.

## Nibbāna
If one asks, "What reality is this Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering?" it should be answered and noted thus: "When that special ultimate reality (paramattha), the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) characterized by peace (santi-lakkhaṇa), is realized through the four path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa), all 1,500 defilements (kilesa) are extinguished at their root in a manner that they can never arise again. In the life where it is realized up to the Path of Arahantship, immediately after the final death (cuti) of that life, the suffering of the five aggregates is extinguished and does not arise anew, just as a great fire is extinguished. It does not arise again in any existence or destination (gati). That special ultimate unconditioned element, endowed with the aforementioned special qualities and characterized by peace, is called Nibbāna."

Worldlings cannot fully know the nature of Nibbāna like the Noble Ones. If one speaks or writes to make it seem as though one has the same insight as the Noble Ones without actually knowing it, there is a chance of error. Let alone Nibbāna, even regarding a worldly object that one has only read about but never seen or encountered personally, if one speaks as if one has seen it, one is prone to error. Since we worldlings cannot see and know Nibbāna completely like the Noble Ones, we should answer as previously stated to avoid error.

That special ultimate unconditioned reality characterized by peace is called Nibbāna. Derived from the Pali word 'Nibbāna,' it is called 'Nibbān' in the Burmese vernacular. When considering what kind of reality Nibbāna is, those who have not yet considered the nature of Nibbāna as described before may not know it correctly and might think of Nibbāna as a kind of indestructible country or a great city. The use of Nibbāna as a 'City of Safety' in water-pouring ceremonies or sermons is merely metaphorical (upacāra). In reality, Nibbāna is not a country
444:
or a great city. Some also think and say that within the great city of Nibbāna, the Noble Ones who have entered Parinibbāna live joyfully and happily with special forms of mind and matter that are free from aging, sickness, and death.

In truth, the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas, Arahants, and Paccekabuddhas does not mean they have gone into a great city of Nibbāna as those people imagine; such a city does not exist. As stated, Parinibbāna is the name for the cessation and non-arising of the five aggregates of mind and matter in any existence or destination after the moment of the final death (cuti) of the last life as an Arahant. (One should note the distinction between Nibbāna and Parinibbāna: Nibbāna is the special ultimate reality that is the object of the Paths and Fruits. Parinibbāna is the extinguishing of the aggregates of mind and matter so they do not arise anew.)

Because the word 'Nibbān' is a Burmese word partially derived from Pali, and because teachers instruct us to "aspire only for Nibbāna" when performing meritorious deeds, people do pray for Nibbāna. However, since most do not well understand the nature of Nibbāna, they may not feel a deep sense of satisfaction or earnestness in their hearts. If teachers were to instruct, "May you aspire for the cooling and pacification of all suffering and anxiety," people would understand it clearly in pure Burmese and would pray with deep satisfaction and earnestness.

## Two Types of Nibbāna
Suppose there is a very fine and valuable garment. While the owner who uses the garment is still present, it is called a fine garment with a user. When the owner passes away, it is called a fine garment without a user. (Here, the same single garment is called by two names depending on whether there is a user or not.) Similarly, the great ultimate Nibbāna, the unconditioned element characterized by peace which was the object of the Venerable Sāriputta's Path and Fruit, is called Sa-upādisesa-nibbāna during the period before the Venerable Sāriputta's Parinibbāna (because the five aggregates, the upādisesa, which can take that Nibbāna as an object, still exist).
445:
When the Venerable Sāriputta attains Parinibbāna, it is called Anupādisesa-nibbāna because the five aggregates (upādisesa) that can take that Nibbāna as an object no longer exist.

Only when one can suppress craving with wisdom and reflect properly can one desire the Nibbāna of peace. If one considers things by giving priority to craving without suppressing it with wisdom, one cannot clearly see Nibbāna as a reality that should truly be desired.

## Three Types of Nibbāna
Nibbāna is not only divided into two types as mentioned; it is further divided into three types according to the qualities and modes evident in that Nibbāna: (1) Suññata-nibbāna, (2) Animitta-nibbāna, and (3) Appaṇihita-nibbāna.

(1) (Suññata = void/empty): It is called Suññata-nibbāna based on the quality of being entirely void of all burdens and impediments (palibodha).

(2) (Nimitta = cause/sign): Conditioned things (saṅkhata) such as consciousness (citta), mental factors (cetasika), and matter (rūpa) are the causes of defilements. The way they occur is that conditioned things, whether mental or material, do not have the nature of being able to arise alone without being associated with other phenomena. Material phenomena arise in clusters of at least eight (called aṭṭhakalāpa rūpa). Mental phenomena also must arise in clusters of at least eight types of nature (referring to the five-sense consciousness). When a group of phenomena arises together in association, defilements such as attachment occur by perceiving them as a 'being,' a 'self,' or a 'substance.' Therefore, because conditioned consciousness, mental factors, and matter arise in clusters of similar types, they become the cause for the arising of defilements like craving and attachment through the perception of a 'being' or 'person,' and thus they receive the name 'nimitta.' Specifically, mundane consciousness, mental factors, and matter receive the name 'nimitta.' This nature of being perceivable as a 'being,' 'self,' or 'substance,' which is the sign (nimitta) for the arising of defilements, is entirely absent in Nibbāna. Therefore, it is also called Animitta-nibbāna.
446:
(la)
(3) (Paṇihita = longing). Longing is indeed craving (taṇhā). As previously explained, Nibbāna has absolutely no nature of being an object of longing through craving. When viewed through craving, it is not something desirable or to be longed for. Therefore, it is also called Appaṇihita Nibbāna. Thus, one should understand that there are three aspects of Nibbāna by distinguishing its qualities and attributes.
This Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is also briefly called Nirodha-sacca. This Nirodha-sacca is indeed the Asaṅkhata-dhātu (the unconditioned element, a nature that is not produced by any cause). Therefore, this Nirodha-sacca, the Asaṅkhata-dhātu, the ultimate reality of Nibbāna, is taught in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali as Appaccaya-dhamma (the causeless phenomenon) and Asaṅkhata-dhamma (the unconditioned phenomenon).
## Magga-ariya-sacca
Although Nibbāna is a reality that is causeless, unconditioned by any cause, and eternally manifest, reaching that state of peace and coolness called Nibbāna cannot happen without a cause. It can only be reached if there is a cause. The cause that enables one to reach it is none other than the Noble Practice. Therefore, the teaching that leads to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering, is called Dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā (the practice leading to the cessation of suffering).
## Majjhima-paṭipadā
In this world, living comfortably and following the whims of craving while enjoying sensual pleasures is not the way to reach Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering; it is merely the base practice called Kāmasukhallikānuyoga. Devoting oneself to causing pain and striving for suffering, such as burning oneself with fire, basking in the sun, or keeping one's arms constantly raised with the intention of preventing defilements from arising, is also not the way to reach Nibbāna; it is merely the base practice called Attakilamathānuyoga. Indeed, it is neither the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by following the whims of craving, nor is it the kind of practice that involves severe self-torture and hardship like burning oneself or basking in the sun.
447:
(lā)
According to the saying, 'Like a lute string, neither too loose nor too tight,' the practice that is neither too lax and comfortable nor too tight and painful—the middle way—is the true path to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. This practice is called Majjhima-paṭipadā (the middle way, neither lax nor tight).
This Majjhima-paṭipadā practice itself is called Magga. It means the path leading to Nibbāna. The group of factors such as wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) included in unwholesome states are called Duggati-magga (or Micchā-magga) because they lead to the four woeful planes. The group of factors such as right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) included in mundane wholesome states are called Sugati-magga (or Sammā-magga) because they lead to happy realms. The group of factors such as right view included in the supramundane path-consciousness are called Sugati-magga (or Sammā-magga) because they lead to Nibbāna. In the Saccavibhaṅga Commentary, it is explained as 'Magga' because these factors like right view present in the path-consciousness are sought by those desiring Nibbāna, because the group of factors itself seeks Nibbāna, and because it leads to Nibbāna by destroying defilements.
The reality denoted by 'Magga' is not a single factor; because there are eight factors as will be described, it is called Aṭṭhaṅgika-magga (the Eightfold Path). Each individual component is called a Maggaṅga (path-factor), while the collection of all eight is called Magga (the Path). The eight components are:
(1) Sammā-diṭṭhi = Right View (knowing the truth of suffering, knowing the true cause of suffering, knowing the true cessation of suffering, and knowing the true path leading to the cessation of suffering—these are the four types of knowledge).
(2) Sammā-saṅkappa = Right Intention (as shown in the perfection of renunciation, these are the three intentions: for liberation from sensual defilements and sensual objects, for non-destruction of others, and for non-harming of others).
(3) Sammā-vācā = Right Speech (abstaining from the four types of verbal misconduct).
448:
(li)
(4) Sammā-kammanta = Right Action (abstaining from the three types of bodily misconduct).
(5) Sammā-ājīva = Right Livelihood (abstaining from making a living through the seven types of misconduct).
(6) Sammā-vāyāma = Right Effort (striving to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to bring about unarisen wholesome states, and to continuously increase arisen wholesome states).
(7) Sammā-sati = Right Mindfulness (not forgetting to keep the mind established in the body, in feelings, in the mind, or in mental objects such as the hindrances).
(8) Sammā-samādhi = Right Concentration (this refers to the first jhāna, second jhāna, third jhāna, and fourth jhāna).
In the mundane sphere, these eight factors cannot all arise simultaneously at the same time; they arise together only as much as they can be associated individually. When reaching the supramundane level, all eight arise together simultaneously. Only these eight path-factors that arise simultaneously at the moment of the supramundane path are called Magga-ariya-sacca, the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus, Dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā Magga-ariya-sacca refers to the group of factors such as Sammā-diṭṭhi that arise together as a single unit at the same time. It should be understood that the word 'Magga' included in the group of supramundane states—Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna—also refers to these eight factors of the Magga-ariya-sacca.
The section explaining the Noble Truths is finished.

449:
(lī)
## Pariyatti-sacca and Paṭipatti-sacca
The collection of truths described so far are the Pariyatti-sacca (Truth of Learning) which are to be studied and understood. In the context of this Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca-pāramī), only the Paṭipatti-sacca (Truth of Practice) as practiced by great beings such as Bodhisattas is desired. That Paṭipatti-sacca is indeed Vaci-sacca (truthfulness in speech), which is the speaking of words that are true or the speaking of words accurately without deviation. Fulfilling this Vaci-sacca to completion within oneself is called "fulfilling the Perfection of Truthfulness." Great beings like the Bodhisatta especially fulfilled and cultivated this Vaci-sacca. This cultivated Vaci-sacca is again of three types:
(1) Saddahāpana-sacca,
(2) Icchāpūraṇa-sacca,
(3) Musāvira-maṇa-sacca.
(1) Vaci-sacca spoken truthfully to make others believe in oneself is called Saddahāpana-sacca.
(2) Vaci-sacca spoken truthfully to fulfill what one desires is called Icchāpūraṇa-sacca.
(3) Vaci-sacca spoken to abstain from telling lies is called Musāvira-maṇa-sacca.
## (1) Saddahāpana-sacca
Among these three, how the great Bodhisattas practiced to fulfill Saddahāpana-sacca can be known through the Bhisa Jātaka (No. 488) in the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta. The detailed story of that Bhisa Jātaka should be noted from the Jātaka stories. The summary of the account is as follows:
## Summary of Bhisa Jātaka
In the past, the young Mahākañcana, a Brahmin of Bārāṇasī, together with his six younger brothers, one younger sister, one male servant, one female servant, and one friend—
450:
(lu)
these ten people went forth into the forest together. They built a dwelling in a suitable place near a lotus pond and lived there, sustaining themselves by searching for fruits and such.
Initially, when they all went out to search for fruit, there were many people and much talk, making them like city dwellers. To prevent this, the eldest brother Mahākañcana gave an order, saying, "I alone will search for fruits; the rest of you must stay and practice the Dhamma peacefully." The younger brothers then said, "Our elder brother is the leader and teacher of us all. The teacher himself should not search for fruits. The younger sister and the female servant are also women and should not search. Only the remaining eight of us will take turns to search." Having agreed, the remaining eight took turns searching for fruits and lived on whatever they found.
After some time, because they were very content, they no longer searched for fruits but only searched for the lotus stalks (bhisa) in the nearby lotus pond, divided them into portions, and consumed them. The way they consumed them was: the person whose turn it was to search would collect the lotus stalks, divide them into eleven portions inside a leaf-hut, and after striking a stone gong in order of seniority, would take his own portion and return to his place to eat well and remain contemplating the Dhamma. The others, after hearing the sound of the stone gong, would each come, take their own portion, eat, and remain contemplating the Dhamma. They did not meet one another unless there was a special reason.
Because their practice of virtue was so intense, the celestial abode of Sakka, the King of Devas, trembled. Sakka reflected and, upon knowing the reason, became doubtful, wondering, "Do these people desire sensual pleasures or not?" Wanting to test their desire, he used his supernatural power to hide the eldest brother's portion for three consecutive days.
When the eldest brother came to take his portion on the first day and found no portion, he thought, "They must have forgotten to set aside a portion for me," and without saying anything at all, he simply returned to contemplate the Dhamma.
451:
He continued his practice with diligence. On the second day, thinking, "Perhaps they have not set aside my portion as a punishment for some fault of mine," he remained as before. When the third day arrived, he thought, "If I have a fault, I shall ask for forgiveness and pay respects," and in the evening, he had the stone gong struck to assemble everyone. He then spoke about not receiving his portion for three days, asking, "Why have you not set aside a portion for me? If I have a fault, please tell me; I shall apologize to you for that fault." Then, the eldest brother rose from his seat, paid respects to his elder brother, and asked, "Teacher, may I speak solely for myself, without involving others?" When the Bodhisatta gave him permission to speak...

"Venerable Sir, if I have stolen the lotus stalks that were your portion, may I obtain horses, cattle, silver, gold, and a lovely wife in this place, and may I live fully endowed with children and a wife."

Thus he uttered a curse. (The reason for uttering such a curse is that as long as there are beloved objects, one suffers grief and misery when separated from them; thus, wishing to disparage the pleasures of the senses, he uttered such a curse.)

Then the elder brother said, "You utter such a heavy curse; I believe that you did not eat them. Sit in your place." The others also said, "Friend, do not swear such an oath; your curse is very heavy," and they covered their ears. (They covered their ears because these individuals, having renounced the world to practice the Dhamma, greatly loathed the defilements and sensual pleasures; they were so terrified and shocked that they did not even wish to hear words related to sensuality.) Then the second brother said:

"Venerable Sir, if I have stolen the lotus stalks of your portion, may I be one who wears flowers and applies sandalwood from the Kāsī kingdom;
452:
may I have many children. May I have intense desire, longing, and attachment for sensual pleasures."

Thus he uttered a curse. (In this manner, all eight individuals uttered their respective curses.)

In this Jātaka, the leader, the venerable ascetic Mahākañcana, was the Bodhisatta, and the other ten were also future noble ones. Being individuals with mature dispositions who truly feared and loathed sensual pleasures, they boldly uttered the aforementioned curses to make others believe them. In this Bhisa Jātaka, it is not directly called "making an asseveration of truth" (sacca-kiriya), but only "uttering a curse." However, because the curses were uttered based on truthful words, they constitute the "Truthful Speech" (vacī-sacca) practiced by Bodhisattas. Among the various words spoken in these oaths, the core meaning is: "I did not steal the lotus stalks that were your portion." This core statement is a truthful declaration and thus constitutes vacī-sacca. The curses—such as "may I obtain such things" or "may such things happen"—were merely the inclusion of penalties to make others believe. Therefore, this kind of truth is called "Saddahāpana-sacca" (Truth to inspire faith/belief). It should be well noted that all oaths taken from the time of King Mahāsammata at the beginning of the world until the present governments are of this "Saddahāpana-sacca" type.

## Scriptural Oaths (Kyam-sacca)
In the world, before a specific text was written for taking oaths, people swore only by word of mouth as shown before; thus it was called "swearing an oath of truth." After a text was composed and written, people no longer swore by words alone but swore while holding the book in their hands (or placing it on their heads); hence the term "swearing a scriptural oath" (kyam-sacca) arose. In common parlance, this is called "holding the scripture," and being ordered to hold the scripture is called
453:
"administering the scripture" (kyam-taik). It should be understood that uttering a curse for the purpose of making others believe, such as "This is true; if it is not true, may such and such happen to me," is what is called a scriptural oath or Saddahāpana-vacī-sacca.

## Malediction (Kyin-se-gyin)
Uttering a curse intended for the harm of others without basing it on the truth is not an oath of truth, but merely "malediction" (kyin-se-gyin). An example of this malediction is found in...

## The Story of the Two Ascetics
In the past, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, an ascetic named Devala lived in the Himālaya. When he came to Bārāṇasī to seek salt and vinegar, he stayed temporarily in a potter's shed near the city gate with the potter's permission. Shortly after, an ascetic named Nārada also arrived and stayed in the same shed. When it was time to sleep, the ascetic Nārada carefully noted the position of Devala's bed and the entrance/exit door before sleeping. However, after lying down, the ascetic Devala did not sleep in his original place but went and slept across the middle of the entrance/exit door.

When the ascetic Nārada went down during the night, he accidentally stepped on Devala's matted hair. When Devala asked, "Who stepped on my hair?", Nārada replied gently, "Teacher, I stepped on it because I did not know you were there." Despite this, Devala said, "O wicked ascetic! Is it proper for you, coming from the forest, to step on my hair?" Nārada apologized, saying, "Teacher, I stepped on it because I did not know you were sleeping here. Please forgive me," and went outside while Devala continued to grumble.

Devala, fearing that Nārada would step on him again when he returned, swapped his head and feet positions and went back to sleep. When Nārada returned, he thought, "When I went down, I did not know where his head was and committed a fault by stepping on his hair; now I shall enter from the side of his feet."
454:
