Thinking thus, as he entered, he stepped on Devala's neck. When Devala asked, "Who is the one stepping on my neck?", Nārada replied, "Teacher, it is I." Devala then said, "O wicked ascetic! First you stepped on my hair, and now you step on my neck again. I shall curse you!" Nārada pleaded, "Teacher, I am not at fault. I committed the first error because I did not know you were sleeping like that. Now, to avoid another error, I entered thinking I was entering from the side of your feet. Please forgive me."

Devala said, "O wicked ascetic! I am going to curse you." Although Nārada pleaded, "Teacher, do not do this," Devala did not listen and cursed him: "Tomorrow morning, as soon as the sun rises, may your head split into seven pieces!" Then Nārada said, "Teacher, although I said I am not at fault and pleaded with you, you curse me. May only the head of the guilty one split into seven pieces!"

(Nārada's declaration was not born of a malicious intent to curse like Devala's, but was spoken as if cursing only to make the guilty Devala feel fear and remorse. Nārada was an ascetic of great power who could see eighty aeons—forty into the past and forty into the future.) Therefore, when he looked with his psychic power to see whether this curse would fall on the other or on himself, he saw it would fall on Devala. Out of compassion for Devala, he used his power to prevent the sun from rising.

When the sun did not rise at the proper time, the citizens went to the palace gate of the Great King and cried out in unison, "Great King, during your reign, the sun has failed to rise. Please act so that the sun may rise!" The King, reflecting on his own conduct and seeing no impropriety, thought there must be a special reason. Thinking, "It is likely due to a dispute among monks," he inquired if there were any ascetics in his kingdom. Upon hearing about the two ascetics, he went to them that very night with a large retinue. Following Nārada's instructions, he had Devala
455:
carry a lump of clay on his head and forced him to descend into a pond. Then, as soon as Nārada withdrew his power and the sun rose at dawn, the lump of clay split into seven pieces. Devala then dived into the water, moved to another place, and emerged from the water, thus finding safety. (Dhammapada Commentary, 1-Yamaka Vagga, 3-Tissa Vatthu)

In this story, Devala's curse, "May your head split into seven pieces as soon as the sun rises," was not for himself but was a word spoken with anger directed at Nārada; thus it should be known as a malediction, not a scriptural oath.

Similar to the malediction in this story, ancient stone inscriptions also recorded such things. For instance, at the end of the Naratungapaya inscription (dated 537 ME) located north of the Cūḷāmaṇi Temple in Bagan, it is inscribed: "May the one who destroys my merit be utterly ruined for seven generations. May he be cooked in Avīci Hell and become a 'hell-stump' who cannot be liberated even when successive Buddhas appear throughout the aeons."

Such maledictions are not the kind of things Bodhisattas usually do. In truth, they are a form of harsh speech (pharusa-vācā) or verbal misconduct; in another sense, they should be noted as the kind of words spoken by those with small minds to cause unbearable distress to one another.

This Saddahāpana-sacca is not only to be understood through the Bhisa Jātaka but also through the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka (Asīti Nipāta, 5). (The details of that Jātaka should be sought in the Birth Stories of the Five Hundred and Fifty.) The summary intended here is:

King Mahāsutasoma said to Porisāda, "I wish to return to my city for a short while. The reason is that while I was coming out to the Migājinna Garden, a Brahmin named Nanda requested to preach four verses of the Satāraha Dhamma (worth a hundred each). I promised to listen upon my return from the garden and told him to wait, thus leaving a 'word-debt.' I shall return to you after I have listened to this Dhamma and settled my word-debt." When he asked for permission, Porisāda...
456:
(Laṃ)
“You have escaped from the hands of death, yet you say you will return to death again. I cannot believe those words,” he rejected.

Then King Mahāsutasoma said, “Friend Porisāda... in this world, it is better to die with pure virtue; to live long with a wicked nature is only worthy of reproach by others. False words will not protect one from the dangers of the woeful states after death. Friend Porisāda... in this world, if someone were to say that a fierce wind blew the great rocky mountains on the earth up into the sky, or that the moon and sun fell to the ground, or that all rivers flowed upstream, you might believe those words. But if someone says, ‘King Mahāsutasoma spoke a lie,’ do not believe them. Friend Porisāda... if someone says the vast open sky has split in half, or the great ocean has dried up, or Mount Sineru has been uprooted along with its foundation, you might believe those words. But even if someone says, ‘King Mahāsutasoma spoke a lie,’ do not believe them.” Thus he spoke. Even after saying this, Porisāda did not fully believe him.

(These words currently spoken by King Mahāsutasoma are not yet a formal asseveration of truth; they are merely a foundation to make Porisāda believe that his words are true. Following this method, modern compositions called ‘vows of truth’ (thissa-hta) are written based on impossible things, such as ‘let water flow in the sky and the sun rise from the earth.’ Some people think and say these are intentionally devised by the wise for amusement. In truth, those compositions called ‘vows of truth’ are of the same nature as the words spoken by King Mahāsutasoma himself to Porisāda. This kind of speech...)
457:
(Lā)
...is named ‘Bhāva-alaṅkāra’ in treatises on rhetoric (alaṅkāra). (It means speech adorned by the wise to express their intent and make their words firm.)

Despite saying this, Porisāda could not believe him. King Mahāsutasoma thought, “This Porisāda does not believe me; I shall make him believe by swearing an oath.” He said, “Friend Porisāda... put me down from your shoulder for a moment; I will make you believe me by swearing an oath.” When he said this, Porisāda lowered the Great Being to the ground from his shoulder. The Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma said, “Friend Porisāda... if you wish it so, I shall stroke and rub this sword and spear with my hands, saying: ‘May I never again be born into a royal lineage well-guarded by such swords and spears.’ I will leave you for a short while, and after listening to the Dhamma to ensure no debt of words remains with the Brahmin Nanda as I promised in the capital, I will return to you by guarding the truth. If I have spoken falsely, may I never again be born into a royal lineage well-guarded by such swords and spears.” Thus he swore the oath to inspire belief.

Only then did Porisāda think, “This King Mahāsutasoma has sworn an oath that ordinary kings would hardly dare to swear. Whether he wishes to return or not, let it be. I too am a king; if he does not return, I will take blood from my own arm and offer it to the banyan tree deity.” Having thought thus, he released the Bodhisatta King Mahāsutasoma.

This verbal truth of King Mahāsutasoma is also a truth spoken to make Porisāda believe, and thus it is ‘Saddahāpana-sacca’ (Truth for inspiring faith). This kind of truth is the Perfection of Truth (Sacca-pāramī) that Bodhisattas must fulfill.

## (2) Icchāpūraṇa-sacca
(2) Regarding the verbal truth spoken to fulfill a desired object, one should look and learn from the third story of the Mahānipāta, the ‘Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka,’ and others.
458:
(Va)
In that Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, while the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇasāma was overwhelmed by the poison of the arrow and lay unconscious, the father and mother, brought by King Pīḷiyakkha, arrived at the place where Suvaṇṇasāma lay unconscious. The father, Dukūla, sat at the head and lifted his son's head, while the mother, Pārikā, sat at the feet, holding them and placing them on her lap. They wept, and being blind, they examined him only by touch. When the mother touched his chest, she found warmth and thought, “My son is not yet dead; he is merely unconscious due to the poison. I will dispel this poison by the power of my truth.” She then resolved:

(1) My son Sāma used to practice only the Dhamma in the past; if these words are true, may my son's poison be dispelled.
(2) (In the same way) My son Sāma used to practice only the holy life in the past.
(3) My son Sāma used to speak only the truth in the past.
(4) My son Sāma is one who cared for his parents.
(5) My son Sāma showed respect to the elders in the family.
(6) I love my son Sāma more than my own life.
(7) By all the merit performed by me and his father, may Sāma's poison be dispelled.

When these seven asseverations of truth were made, Suvaṇṇasāma (Suvaṇṇasyaṃ) turned and lay on his right side.

Then the father, thinking, “My son is alive; I too shall make an asseveration of truth,” made the seven asseverations of truth just as the mother had done. Then the Bodhisatta turned and lay on his other side.
459:
(Vā)
At that moment, a goddess named Bahusundarī, who had been Suvaṇṇasāma's mother in his seventh past life and now lived on Mount Gandhamādana in the Himālayas, came from Mount Gandhamādana. Arriving at Suvaṇṇasāma's place, she made an asseveration of truth: “I have lived on Mount Gandhamādana in the Himālayas for a long time. In all my time living there, there is no one I love more than Suvaṇṇasāma. If these words are true, may Sāma's poison be dispelled. Every tree on Mount Gandhamādana where I live is nothing but a sandalwood tree. If these words are true, may Sāma's poison be dispelled.” While the mother, father, and goddess were thus weeping and lamenting piteously, the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇasāma, youthful and inspiring in appearance, quickly stood up and sat down.

In this Jātaka, the words of truth uttered by the mother Pārikā, the father Dukūla, and the former mother, the goddess Bahusundarī, were spoken to fulfill the wish for Suvaṇṇasāma to be free from poison and reach well-being; therefore, it is called ‘Icchāpūraṇa-vacīsacca’ (Verbal Truth for the Fulfillment of a Wish).

## Suppāraka-vatthu
Furthermore, in the Suppāraka Jātaka of the Ekādasaka Nipāta, the account of Icchāpūraṇa-vacīsacca also appears. The summary of the account is as follows:

Long ago, a wise man named Suppāraka, the Bodhisatta, who lived in the seaport village of Kurukaccha (Bharukaccha) in the Kuru kingdom, worked as a ship's pilot (captain). After a long time, due to the sea spray, he lost his sight in both eyes and stopped working as a pilot. Later, at the request of merchants, he acted as the pilot and set sail. After seven days, due to an unseasonable wind, the ship could not follow the correct path and wandered on the surface of the ocean for four months, passing through:

(1) Khuramāli Sea,
(2) Aggimāli Sea,
(3) Dadhimāli Sea,
460:
(Vi)
(4) Kusamāli Sea,
(5) Naḷamāli Sea,

and arrived near the terrifying Balavāmukha Sea. The pilot Suppāraka said that once one reaches this sea, there is no one capable of turning back; they only sink and perish. Upon hearing this, all the merchants wept bitterly.

Then the Bodhisatta, the wise Suppāraka, thought, “I shall make an asseveration of truth to bring safety to all these people.” He then made the asseveration: “Since the time I have been conscious and wise, I have never intentionally harmed a single being. I have never stolen another's property, even as much as a blade of grass or a bamboo splinter. I have never even looked at another's wife with the power of greed. I have never spoken a lie. I have never drunk intoxicants, even as much as the tip of a blade of grass. By this word of truth, may this ship return safely to its original place.” The ship, which had been drifting for four months without stopping, turned back toward the village of Kurukaccha like a person with psychic power, and by the majesty of the truth, it reached the port of Kurukaccha in just one day.

This truthful verbal statement of the wise Suppāraka is also ‘Icchāpūraṇa-vacīsacca,’ as it was spoken to fulfill the wish for the safety of their group.

## Sivi-rāja-vatthu
In the Sivi Jātaka of the Vīsati Nipāta... in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the Sivi kingdom, the Bodhisatta King Sivi, although he gave and distributed 600,000 [kahāpaṇas] every single day, was not satisfied or content and had the thought to donate his own internal organs. To fulfill the Bodhisatta's wish and intention, Sakka, the King of Devas, disguised himself as a blind Brahmin and came to King Sivi, saying, “Great King... you have sight in both eyes. I cannot see with either. If you, Great King, would donate one of your eyes to me, you would still be able to see everything with the remaining one, and I too...”
461:
(Vi)
“With one eye given by the Great King, I shall be able to see everything. Therefore, please have compassion and grant me one of your eyes.” When the beggar made this request, King Sivi, who had already been contemplating such a gift, was greatly pleased and satisfied. He summoned the physician Sīvika and commanded, “You must surgically remove one of my eyes and give it to him.” Although the physician Sīvika, the ministers, the queen, and the royal attendants collectively pleaded with him to stop, he would not be deterred and insisted on the removal. When the physician removed the eye, the King looked at it with his remaining eye, and with great joy, he made an aspiration for Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) and handed the eye to the Brahmin.

The Brahmin was actually Sakka in disguise. As soon as he placed the eye into one of his own sockets, it became a perfectly normal eye. Seeing this, King Sivi was filled with immense clarity and joy. Despite the renewed pleas and protests from his ministers and the public, he insisted on having his remaining eye removed and donated it as well. As soon as Sakka placed the second eye into his other socket, it also became a perfectly normal eye. After speaking words of blessing, he disappeared in the manner of one departing.

Since King Sivi no longer had sight in either eye, he felt it was no longer appropriate to rule. He had a dwelling prepared near a pond within the royal auspicious garden. While he resided there, contemplating his gift of eyes, Sakka arrived and walked to and fro on the cloister path near the King to make his footsteps heard. When King Sivi asked who it was, Sakka replied, “I am Sakka. O Great King, ask for any boon you desire.” King Sivi replied, “I possess great wealth, treasures, gold, and silver. But now that both my eyes are destroyed, I desire only death.” Sakka then asked, “O Great King, when you say you desire death, is it because you truly wish to die, or is it because of your blindness?” When the King confirmed it was because of his blindness, Sakka said, “O Great King, I cannot simply create sight for these eyes. They will only see through the power of Truth. Please perform an Act of Truth.” Thereupon, King Sivi said—
462:
(Vu)
“I love the many beggars who come to my presence to ask for alms, and among those beggars, I love the one who asks for what he desires. By this declaration of truth, may my eye be restored.”

As soon as he made this Act of Truth, the first eye was perfectly restored. Then again—

“When the blind Brahmin came to me and asked for my eyes, I gave both eyes to that Brahmin. At the time of that giving, my mind was filled with great delight and satisfaction. By this declaration of truth, may the other eye be clearly restored.”

As soon as he made this Act of Truth, the second eye was restored exactly as declared. Those two eyes were not the original natural eyes from his mother’s womb, nor were they the divine eye of higher knowledge (dibba-cakkhu); rather, they were eyes that arose through the majestic power of the Perfection of Truth (Sacca-pāramī).

This Act of Truth by King Sivi, performed to restore his natural sight, is known as the Wish-fulfilling Verbal Truth (Icchāpūraṇa-vacī-sacca).

In the Maccha Jātaka (No. 75) of the Varuṇa Vagga in the Ekakanipāta, it is recorded that when the Bodhisatta was born as a fish, there was a severe drought and the water dried up. As crows were pecking at and eating the fish, the Bodhisatta, the King of Fish, made an Act of Truth: “Although I was born into a species that usually preys upon its own kind, I have never eaten a single fish, even one the size of a grain of rice. By this declaration of truth, let the great rain fall.” Immediately upon this declaration, a heavy rain fell.

Furthermore, in the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka (No. 35) of the Kulāvaka Vagga in the same Ekakanipāta, the Bodhisatta was born as a quail. At an age when he could not yet fly with his wings or walk with his feet, a great forest fire broke out and approached.
463:
(Vū)
As his parents had fled, he thought, “In this world, there exist the quality of pure morality, the principle of truth, and the quality of compassion. I must now perform an Act of Truth.” He then declared: “I have wings, but I cannot yet fly. I have feet, but I cannot yet walk. My parents have fled. O forest fire, turn back! Go away!” Upon saying this, the forest fire retreated to a distance of sixteen karīsas and was extinguished. There is a point here worthy of special consideration:

In the aforementioned Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka and others, when the Act of Truth was performed, it was based on wholesome deeds (kusala), so it is quite fitting that the desired result was achieved. However, in the quail king’s Act of Truth, the foundational words do not specifically mention wholesome deeds; they only state: “I have wings but cannot fly, I have feet but cannot walk, and my parents have fled.” One might wonder how an Act of Truth based on facts that are not related to merit can fulfill the desired result.

The nature of Truth (Sacca) is that the foundation is simply the *fact of being true*, whether the underlying cause is wholesome or not. Even if a statement concerns a wholesome matter, if it is spoken untruthfully, it does not constitute Verbal Truth (Vacī-sacca), nor can it have any beneficial power. Only through speaking truthfully can the desired result be fulfilled and power be manifest.

The words spoken by the Bodhisatta quail were a statement of fact, thus constituting Verbal Truth and enabling the fulfillment of the desired result. It should be noted that although the content of the quail king’s declaration was not a matter of merit, it was also not a matter of demerit. Even if a statement is related to unwholesome matters, if it is spoken truthfully, it can constitute Verbal Truth and achieve the desired result, as seen in the Kaṇha-dīpāyana Jātaka (No. 444) of the Dasakanipāta. (The details should be sought in that Jātaka story.) In that Kaṇha-dīpāyana Jātaka:

When the ascetic Kaṇha-dīpāyana returned from visiting the ascetic Maṇḍavya and reached his hermitage, the landowner Maṇḍavya, who was his supporter, arrived with—
464:
(Ve)
his wife and their young son, Yaññadatta. They came to the teacher-ascetic, offered drinks, and were discussing the affairs of the ascetic Maṇḍavya. Meanwhile, the son Yaññadatta was playing with a ball at the edge of the cloister path, and the ball rolled into a termite mound where a snake lived. When Yaññadatta reached his hand into the mound to retrieve the ball, he was bitten by the snake. The venom took effect immediately, and he collapsed on the spot.

Realizing it was a snakebite, the parents picked up their son, laid him at the feet of the ascetic Kaṇha-dīpāyana, and pleaded with him to treat the boy so he might recover. Kaṇha-dīpāyana replied, “I do not know a medicine that can overcome snake venom. I shall treat him by performing an Act of Truth.” Placing his hand on Yaññadatta’s head, he declared: “I became an ascetic because I was weary of the lay life, yet I was only able to live with a clear mind for seven days. After those seven days, for fifty years until today, my mind has not been clear or delighted. I have remained an ascetic only by endurance. By this declaration of truth, may the rising venom vanish and may the boy Yaññadatta live.” Upon this Act of Truth, the venom in the upper part of Yaññadatta’s chest subsided and entered the earth.

Yaññadatta opened his eyes, looked at his parents, called out “Mother, Father” just once, and then rolled over and fell back asleep. Then Kaṇha-dīpāyana said to the father, the landowner Maṇḍavya, “I have treated your son with my power; now you too treat your son with your power.” The father, Maṇḍavya, then declared: “Whenever monks, Brahmins, or guests arrived, I never once felt delight or faith in my heart. I never let anyone know that I lacked this faith and delight; I kept it hidden. Even when I gave alms, I did so only for the sake of appearance, without wanting to give. By this declaration of truth, may the rising venom vanish and may the young Yaññadatta live.” Upon this Act of Truth, the venom in Yaññadatta’s—
465:
(Vai)
upper body from the waist up subsided and entered the earth.

Yaññadatta stood up and sat down, but he could not yet stand upright. Then the father urged the mother to perform an Act of Truth. The mother said, “I do have a point for an Act of Truth, but I do not dare to perform it in your presence.” The father urged her, saying, “Perform it by any means.” With his permission, the mother declared: “I do not love the snake that bit my son; I hate it intensely. No different from my hatred for this snake, I hate the father of this child (Maṇḍavya) just as much. By this declaration of truth, may the rising venom vanish and may my son Yaññadatta live.” Upon this Act of Truth, all the venom from Yaññadatta’s body subsided and entered the earth, and Yaññadatta got up and began playing with his ball again.

(It should be noted that although the underlying facts of the Acts of Truth performed by these three—the ascetic, the teacher, and the supporter—were all negative things they had kept secret, their courageous and honest disclosure constituted genuine Truth. Therefore, the desired result was fulfilled through the power of that Truth.)

A question may arise: If, as stated, an honest disclosure of a fact—whether good or bad—constitutes Truth and can fulfill a desired result, then if people of the present day speak any truth, whether good or bad, will it constitute Verbal Truth and fulfill their desired wishes?

The answer is: Among the three types of Truth, the Truth of Abstaining from Falsehood (Musāvāda-viramaṇa-sacca)—which is the practice of avoiding lies and speaking only what is true—always dwells in the mouths of the virtuous. The mouths of the ancient Great Beings mentioned in the scriptures were the permanent dwelling places of this Truth, the great Realm of Truth. Since the Realm of Truth is exceedingly pure and noble, the Truth that arises in this Realm of Truth is capable of achieving the desired—
466: (Exposition) It can fulfill beneficial results. In the era of those ancient virtuous ones where this Dhamma of Truth (Sacca) flourished and shone, just as Truth could provide desired benefits, the evil of falsehood (musāvāda) could also swiftly bring about undesirable penalties and dangers. That the evil consequences and dangers of falsehood could be swiftly delivered in such an era of Truth is known through the Cetiya Jātaka (6) of the Aṭṭhakanipāta. (In this Cetiya Jātaka, King Cetiya was swallowed by the earth due to the lie of mistakenly calling the elder the younger and the younger the elder.) Nowadays, the mouths of most people frequently use the motto 'Without falsehood, the verse is not smooth,' and they mostly speak untruths. As these have become wicked and ruined nations of falsehood, it should be understood that the merit of Truth arising in such wicked and ruined nations cannot clearly provide beneficial results, nor can the demerit of falsehood clearly provide evil results. Thus, in the Naḷapāna Jātaka (10) of the Sīlavagga, Ekakanipāta (2), due to the power of Truth of the Bodhisatta monkey king, the reeds became hollow and open throughout their length. In the Sambulā Jātaka (9) of the Tiṃsanipāta, due to the truthful words of Princess Sambulā, Prince Sotthisena was cured of leprosy and found happiness. In the Temiya Jātaka of the Mahānipāta, Queen Candādevī observed virtue and made an act of truth, thereby giving birth to and obtaining the Bodhisatta Prince Temiya. In the Janaka Jātaka of the Mahānipāta, due to the truthful words of the sub-king Polajanaka, his shackles were released, the prison doors opened, and the sub-king Polajanaka was able to leave. In the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka (7) of the Apaṇṇakavagga, Ekakanipāta (1), the mother, a wood-gatherer, made an act of truth and threw the Bodhisatta youth into the sky...
467:
When he was thrown, the Bodhisatta prince remained sitting cross-legged in the sky...

In the Mahāmora Jātaka of the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta (8), the power of the Truth is well-noted from the accounts in the ancient Jātakas, such as how a hunter became a Paccekabuddha after listening to the Dhamma of the Bodhisatta peacock king, and how a flock of birds was released from their bonds by the hunter's act of truth (following the Bodhisatta's guidance): "Many birds that I previously kept caged in my house, as I am now free from the bonds of defilements, may they be free from their bonds just as I am free."

## The Power of Truth during the Buddha's Lifetime

During the Buddha's lifetime, when the three calamities of malignant disease, non-human beings (demons), and famine occurred in the city of Vesālī, the Buddha went there with a large company of monks. He taught and instructed the Venerable Ānanda to walk between the three layers of the city walls of Vesālī and recite words of prayer as an act of truth. The Venerable Ānanda walked around throughout the night reciting the words of truth, and the three calamities were appeased, as detailed in the Ratana Sutta and its commentary. This collection of verses for the act of truth is known as the Ratana Sutta Paritta. In this Ratana Sutta, it is taught that among the various treasures known in the human world, the deva world, and the worlds of Nāgas and Garuḷas, there is no treasure equal to the Buddha. By this truth, may there be freedom from the three calamities and may there be happiness. It is a discourse that declares various qualities of the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—containing twelve points of truth (or fifteen points, including the final three points recited by Sakka, the King of Devas). This Ratana Sutta is recorded as the first sutta of the Cūḷavagga in the Sutta Nipāta (2), and as the sixth sutta in the Khuddakapāṭha.

In the Aṅgulimāla Sutta of the Rājavagga (6), Majjhima Paṇṇāsa (4), while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla Thera reported to the Buddha about a woman in Sāvatthī who was unable to give birth.
468:
Following the method given by the Buddha, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla Thera went to that woman and made an act of truth: "Since I was born into the Noble birth, I do not recall intentionally killing any living being. By this truth, may there be well-being for you and your child." Upon making this act of truth, she gave birth easily, and both mother and child were well.

In this way, it should be understood that during the Buddha's lifetime, the recitation of words of truth fulfilled the desired benefits.

## The Power of Truth during the Era of the Sīhala Sāsana

After the Buddha's Parinibbāna, when the Sāsana reached the island of Sri Lanka (Sīhala-dīpa), the Elder Mahāmitta, who resided at the Coraka Monastery, was asked by his mother through her daughter (a bhikkhunī) for medicine for a malignant abscess on her breast. He replied, "I do not know of ordinary medicine. However, I will give you a special kind of medicine. Since I was ordained as a monk until today, I have never looked at a woman of a different nature with a lustful mind that breaks the restraint of the senses. By this truth, may my mother be well." He then instructed, "Go back, and when you reach our mother, recite this act of truth as I have said and stroke her body." As soon as the bhikkhunī went to her mother and did as the Elder Mahāmitta had instructed, the mother's malignant abscess dissolved like a clump of foam, and she recovered, as described in the Sīlaniddesa section of the Visuddhimagga Commentary.

Furthermore, in the opening of the section on abstinence as the occasion arises (sampatta-virati) in the Dvārakathā of the Cittuppādakaṇḍa in the Atthasālinī Commentary, it is mentioned that a woman living in Sri Lanka became ill. The doctor said, "She will recover if she gets fresh hare meat." The elder brother sent his younger brother (Jaggana) to the field to find a hare. When the younger brother Jaggana reached the field, a hare saw him and ran away in fear, but it got caught in a creeper and cried out in a terrified voice.
469:
Jaggana ran and caught the hare, but then he reflected, "If I kill this young hare to save my mother's life, it would not be in accordance with the Dhamma." Having considered this, he released it, saying, "Go and live in peace," and returned home. When he arrived, his elder brother met him and asked, "Did you get a hare?" When he told the truth about releasing it, the elder brother threatened and scolded him. Then, the younger brother Jaggana approached his mother and stood there, saying, "Since I was born, I do not know of ever killing a living being with the intention to kill. By this truth, may my mother be healthy and well." At that very moment, it is said that the mother became healthy and well.

In this way, it should be well-noted that even after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, various individuals performed the Truth that fulfills wishes (Icchāpūraṇa-sacca).

The section on the Truth that fulfills wishes is finished.
**********
## (3) The Truth of Abstaining from Falsehood (Musāvādamani Sacca)

The background story regarding the verbal truth of abstaining from falsehood can be known through the Vidhura Jātaka of the Mahā Nipāta and others. The summary of the relevant main point from the long story in that Jātaka is as follows:

When King Koravya and the yakkha Puṇṇaka were about to play dice, they made a pact: "If King Koravya loses, Puṇṇaka may take whatever he desires from the King's possessions, excluding (1) the King's person, (2) the Chief Queen, and (3) the White Umbrella. If Puṇṇaka loses, King Koravya may take Puṇṇaka's mind-made jewel and his noble steed." When they played, King Koravya lost, and Puṇṇaka demanded, "Great King, I have won. Give me the stakes according to the original pact."

At that time, because King Koravya had truly lost, he could not deny it and gave permission, saying, "Take whatever you desire." Puṇṇaka then said he would take the great minister Vidhura. Then, King Koravya thought, "If the great minister is said to be my own self, it is true; he is also my refuge and reliance. Therefore—"
470: the great minister should not be compared with other possessions I own, such as gold and silver; he should be compared only with my life. Therefore, I do not own the great minister.' Then Puṇṇaka said, 'O King, our mere arguing over whether the great minister Vidhura is your property or not will not settle the matter. Let us go and ask the great minister Vidhura himself and abide by his decision.' King Koravya joyfully agreed and they went to the minister. When they reached the minister, Puṇṇaka said, 'O Minister, even the devas praise the great minister Vidhura of the Kuru people, saying he is established in the Dhamma. Is that word truly true? Are you indeed a slave of King Koravya, or are you a relative of equal status, or a relative of superior status? Please tell us. Between the two types of names in the world, Anvattha (meaningful) and Ruḷhī (conventional), which type is your name "Vidhura"?' (The meaning of the question 'Which type of name is the name Vidhura?' is: In the world, there are two kinds of names: Ruḷhī names, which are given arbitrarily as one sees fit without being consistent with the underlying meaning, and Anvattha names, which are given in accordance with the underlying meaning. (For example) calling an ugly person 'Maung Hla' (Mr. Beautiful) is a Ruḷhī name because it is given arbitrarily without being consistent with the underlying meaning. (Inconsistent means the name is 'Beautiful' but the person is ugly). If, however, a truly beautiful and graceful person is named 'Maung Hla', that name is an Anvattha name because it is given in accordance with the underlying meaning. Now, when Puṇṇaka the Yakkha asks the great minister Vidhura, 'Which type of name is the name Vidhura?', he means: Is it a Ruḷhī name or an Anvattha name? If the minister is not established in the Dhamma, your name will be a Ruḷhī name. Only if you are established in the Dhamma will it be an Anvattha name. The name Vidhura means [abstaining from] evil...)
471:
(The term 'Sādhū' means a virtuous person who oppresses and eliminates unwholesome states. One becomes a true virtuous person only by standing firm in the Dhamma. Thus, the name Vidura would be an 'anvatttha' name (a name consistent with its meaning). If one does not stand firm in the Dhamma, it would be a 'rūḷhī' name, a mere conventional name given arbitrarily. This was the intended meaning of the question.)

At that time, the great minister Vidura thought: "I could say that I am a relative of the King, or that I am superior to the King, or that I have no relation to the King at all. However, since there is no refuge in the world equal to Truth, I should speak only the truth." Having thus reflected, he replied truthfully: "Dear friend, in this world, there are four types of slaves:
(1) One born of a slave mother,
(2) One bought with wealth,
(3) One who becomes a slave voluntarily,
(4) One captured in war.
Among these four, I am a slave who came voluntarily to serve King Koravya."

Because the great minister Vidura voluntarily came to serve King Koravya, he identified himself as the third type among the four kinds of slaves. This truthful speech (vacī-sacca), spoken honestly as it should be, was not spoken with the intent of making others believe him (saddahāpana), nor was it spoken with the intent of fulfilling a personal desire (icchāpūraṇa). Indeed, it was spoken out of a desire to abstain from false speech; therefore, it is called 'musāvāda-viramaṇa-vacīsacca' (the verbal truth of abstaining from lying).

Similarly, in the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, when King Pīḷiyakkha asked Suvaṇṇasāma, "What is your lineage? Whose son are you? Tell me your and your father's lineage," Suvaṇṇasāma thought: "If I were to say I am a deva, a naga, a kinnara, or of the royal caste, this person would surely believe me."
472:
"However, I should speak only what is true." Having thus reflected, he replied only with the truth, saying, "I am the son of a fisherman," and so on. This truthful speech of Suvaṇṇasāma, like that of the great minister Vidura, was not for the purpose of making others believe him, nor for the fulfillment of any personal desire. In truth, it was spoken to abstain from false speech; thus, it is called 'musāvāda-viramaṇa-vacīsacca'.

In the Bhūridatta Jātaka, when the Brahmin Nesāda came to the place where the Bodhisatta was observing the Uposatha precepts and asked, "Who are you? Are you a powerful deva king, or a naga of great majesty?", the Naga King Bhūridatta thought: "If I were to say I am one of the Sakka devas or similar beings, this Brahmin would surely believe me. But now, I should speak only what is true." Having thus reflected, he spoke only the truth, stating that he was a naga of great power. This speaking of only the truth by the Naga King Bhūridatta, like that of the great minister Vidura, was not to make others believe him, nor for the fulfillment of any personal desire. In truth, it was spoken to abstain from false speech; thus, it is called 'musāvāda-viramaṇa-vacīsacca'.

Among the Ten Perfections, the truth required for the sixth perfection, the Perfection of Truth (Sacca Pāramī), is precisely this 'musāvāda-viramaṇa-sacca'. The Bodhisattas of the past always exerted effort in this 'musāvāda-viramaṇa-sacca', which is the abstinence from false speech. In every successive life, they fulfilled the Perfection of Truth by speaking the truth. Occasionally, when an opportunity to speak arose where speaking would necessitate lying, if they remained silent out of a desire to protect the nature of truth, it cannot be called 'vacī-sacca' (verbal truth) in the strict sense because no words were uttered. It is then only 'virati-sacca' (the truth of abstinence) from false speech. This 'virati-sacca' is also included and counted within 'vacī-sacca'.
473:
## How Great Bodhisattas Use the Three Types of Truth
Great Bodhisattas employ (1) 'Saddahāpana-sacca' (truth for gaining trust) only when they encounter a situation where they fear others might distrust them; otherwise, they do not usually employ it. Similarly, when a specific necessary matter arises, they employ (2) 'Icchāpūraṇa-vacīsacca' (verbal truth for fulfilling a wish) to fulfill that desire. If there is no such necessary matter, there is no need to perform this truth. However, they constantly hold and fulfill (3) 'Musāvāda-viramaṇa-vacīsacca' (verbal truth of abstaining from lying). Reflecting on the practice of these Bodhisattas, virtuous people should especially strive to protect and fulfill 'musāvāda-viramaṇa-vacīsacca', which is the abstinence from false speech.

The classification of the three types of truth is finished.
**********
## Classification into Two Types of Truth
When the aforementioned truths are summarized and re-classified briefly, there are only two:
(1) Vacībheda-siddhi-sacca (Truth accomplished upon utterance)
(2) Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca (Truth that must be protected and performed after utterance)

The 'Saddahāpana-sacca' found in the Bhiṣa Jātaka mentioned earlier, and the 'Icchāpūraṇa-vacīsacca' found in the Suvaṇṇasāma, Suppāraka, Sivi, Maccha, Vaṭṭaka, Kaṇhadīpāyana, Naḷapāna, Sambulā, Temiya, Janaka, Kaṭṭhavāhana, and Mahāmora Jātakas, as well as the 'Musāvāda-viramaṇa-vacīsacca' found in the Vidura, Suvaṇṇasāma, and Bhūridatta Jātakas—all these are to be understood as 'Vacībheda-siddhi-sacca'. This is because the purpose of the truth is accomplished simultaneously with the respective utterance. There remains no further task to manage or protect to make the truth effective.
474:
As shown previously, the truth performed by the Bodhisatta King Sutasoma towards Porisāda in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka was indeed 'Saddahāpana-sacca', performed so that Porisāda would believe his promise: "I will return; if I do not, let such-and-such happen." However, it cannot be said that the purpose of the truth was accomplished merely by the utterance of the words. The true nature of the truth would only be fulfilled upon his actual return. Since he had to specifically arrange to return after making the vow to ensure the truth was realized, this truth of King Sutasoma is to be understood as 'Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca'.

In the same way, the truth performed by King Jayadissa in the Jayadissa Jātaka (Timsanipāta, 3) and the truth performed by Prince Rama in the Dasaratha Jātaka (Ekādasanipāta, 7) are both 'Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca'.

A summary of the truth performed by King Jayadissa is as follows: King Jayadissa of Uttara-pañcāla in the Kingdom of Kapila went hunting in the forest accompanied by his army. On the way, he met a Brahmin named Nanda from Takkasila who wished to preach the Dhamma. The King made an appointment to listen to the sermon upon his return and then proceeded to the forest.

Upon reaching the forest, he divided the hunting tasks with his ministers. When a deer escaped through the King's sector, he pursued it relentlessly, caught it after a long distance, cut it into two pieces, and carried it on a shoulder pole. While returning, he stopped to rest under a banyan tree. When he rose to leave, a man-ogre (manussa-barūsa) residing at that tree stopped him, saying, "You have become my food; you shall not leave." (The term 'man-ogre' here means he was not actually an ogre; he was King Jayadissa's own elder brother who had been snatched by an ogress at birth to be eaten, but she raised him as her son instead. Thus, he lived with the mind, diet, and habits of an ogre. After the ogress mother died, he, a true human, lived alone like an ogre.)

Then King Jayadissa said, "I have an appointment to hear the Dhamma from a Brahmin who came from Takkasila. Please let me return to hear that Dhamma. After hearing it, I will return in order to protect the truth of my word." Upon this promise, the man-ogre...
475:
...released him. (It should be understood that although it was not mentioned that they were brothers, the man-ogre released him easily because of a sense of compassion, as the saying goes, 'blood speaks'.) King Jayadissa returned, heard the Dhamma from the Brahmin, and was about to return to the forest to be eaten by the ogre when his son, Prince Alīnasattu (the Bodhisatta), offered various reasons and pleaded, "I will go in your place, father." The King granted permission and sent his son. This truthful word of King Jayadissa, "I will return," is 'Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca' because it had to be protected and fulfilled after being spoken.

A summary of Prince Rama's truth is as follows: King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī had a son, Prince Rama, a younger son, Prince Lakkhaṇa, and a daughter, Sītā Devī, by his chief queen. After the queen passed away, he appointed a new queen, who gave birth to a son named Bharata. Because the new queen repeatedly pleaded with King Dasaratha to hand over the throne to her son Bharata, King Dasaratha called his two elder sons and said, "I fear for the safety of my eldest sons because of the new queen and her son Bharata. Astrologers have predicted that I have twelve more years to live. Therefore, my sons, go and hide in the forest now, and return after twelve years to take over the throne and the kingdom."

Prince Rama promised to follow the command, and as the two brothers were leaving for the forest, their sister Sītā Devī also followed them, saying she did not wish to be separated from her brothers. Although the astrologers predicted King Dasaratha would live twelve more years, he passed away after nine years due to the grief over his children. When the ministers did not wish to crown Prince Bharata and followed the news to where Prince Rama was, they reached him and pleaded with him to return to the city and rule the kingdom since the father had passed away. Prince Rama replied, "I promised my father that I would return to the city and rule only after twelve years according to his command. If I return now, the words I spoke will not be true. I do not wish to break my word. Therefore..."
476:
"Take only your younger brother Prince Lakkhaṇa and younger sister Sītādevī, appoint them as heirs, and let you ministers rule the country," he commanded. Here, King Rāma had to delay and protect the truth of the promise he made to his father. This is indeed Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca (the truth of subsequent protection).

## Truth Related to Time
To easily distinguish between Vacībheda-siddhi-sacca and Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca, the summary should be noted as follows:

Truth is of four types:
(1) Truth related only to the past,
(2) Truth related to both the past and the present,
(3) Truth related only to the future,
(4) Truth not specifically marked by time.

Among these four types, only the truth related to the future is Pacchānurakkhaṇa-sacca, while the remaining three types are all Vacībheda-siddhi-sacca.

How the four types occur respectively: Among the truths in the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, the collection of truths spoken by the mother and father, such as "Sāma practiced only the Dhamma in the past; he used to practice only noble conduct; he used to speak only truthful words; he served his parents; he respected his elders," are truths related only to the past.

The truth "We love Suvaṇṇasāma more than our own lives," the truth spoken by the goddess Bahusundarī "There is no one loved more than Sāma," and the truth "All trees on this Mount Gandhamādana are only fragrant trees"—this collection of truths are those not specifically marked by time.

The collection of Icchāpūraṇa-sacca (truth of fulfilling wishes) found in the Suppāraka Jātaka and Sivi Jātaka are truths related only to the past. Similarly, the collection of Icchāpūraṇa-sacca in the Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka and Naḷapāna Jātaka are also truths related only to the past.
477:
In the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the statement "I have wings but cannot fly, I have feet but cannot walk" relates to both the past and the present. As for the future, since he will be able to fly with wings and walk with feet, it does not relate to the future.

In the Sambulā Jātaka, the truth "There is no other loved more than my lord," and the truths of Queen Candādevī in the Temiya Jātaka are truths not specifically marked by time.

In this manner, one should consider, reflect upon, and note the relevance of various truths to their respective times.

## Paramattha-sacca-pāramī
Regarding the Perfection of Truth, the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary explain that the Perfection of Truth of King Mahāsutasoma—who sacrificed his life to protect the truth of his word, as he had promised the man-eater Porisāda that he would return—is the Ultimate Perfection (Paramattha-pāramī). In the story of King Mahāsutasoma, the making of the truth-vow occurred with Porisāda, but the matter of truth was not yet completed by merely saying so; it had to be protected further to reach completion. As he had said he would return, he had to return after reaching the city of Indapatta. Therefore, when he first said to Porisāda, "I will return," the sacrifice of his life was not yet evident. Only when he returned from the city of Indapatta to protect his truth did the sacrifice of his life become evident. For this reason, the Commentaries state only "jīvitaṃ cajitvā saccamanurakkhantassa" (of the king who protected the truth by sacrificing his life); they do not explain it as "jīvitaṃ cajitvā saccaṃ bhaṇantassa" (of the king who spoke the truth by sacrificing his life).

## Two Truths to be Considered
In this matter, it is appropriate to compare and reflect upon the two truths: the truth of King Mahāsutasoma and the truth of the Great Minister Vidhura. The truth of the Great Minister Vidhura, as preached in verse 102 of the Vidhura Jātaka already mentioned, is the speaking of the truth that "I am indeed a slave." As soon as he spoke thus, the matter of truth was accomplished. However, regarding the Great Minister's speaking of the truth about being a slave,
478:
there was no reason to be concerned about his death, nor could he die merely by being a slave. Therefore, if one were to say that the truth of the Great Minister Vidhura does not reach the level of King Mahāsutasoma's truth, it would be a point for discussion.

In reality, one can reflect and consider that the Great Minister Vidhura included the nature of sacrificing his life with the intention: "After this young man takes me away, if he wishes to kill me, he will; if he kills me, I will accept death." The reason is that the Great Minister, as a wise man, would have reflected that this young man did not win him because he wished to revere or honor him. If he had wished to revere or honor him, he would have spoken clearly, requested, and invited him. Now, however, since there was no such request or invitation, and he won him through a game of dice to take absolute possession, he would not grant him freedom. Furthermore, although he was called a young man, he was actually the ogre Puṇṇaka, and just by seeing his behavior, the Great Minister would have known that this person was harsh and fierce. Moreover, when the Great Minister Vidhura gave advice and admonition to the King and his household and said, "My task is finished," the ogre-youth Puṇṇaka replied (verse 196): "Do not be afraid or tremble; just hold firmly to the tail of my noble horse. Your seeing of this world alive now is your last sight of it." At that time, the Great Minister Vidhura replied, "I have no evil deeds that lead to the lower realms; why should I be afraid?" Based on these words of the Great Minister, the sacrifice of his life is evident.

Considering these circumstances, the truth of the Great Minister Vidhura also involves the nature of sacrificing his life, and thus it would not be lower than the truth of King Mahāsutasoma. Although one might not say it is superior, it should be considered that the levels are equal.

## Instruction
In this Perfection of Truth, the quality of being able to obtain and fulfill what is needed by making a truth-vow as a basis is more extraordinary than the previous Perfections. In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka
479:
(verse 62), it is also preached: "Ye keci me atthi rasā pathabyā, saccaṃ tesaṃ sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ = Whatever tastes there are throughout the earth, among those tastes, truth alone is the sweetest taste." Therefore, one should strive fervently and exert effort to enjoy the very sweet taste of truth.

The Section on the Perfection of Truth ends.
**********
## (h) Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī
## Resolution (Undertaking)
The Pali word Adhiṭṭhāna was translated by ancient scholars into Burmese as "sauk-ti-gyin" (undertaking/resolution). It is necessary to reflect and consider clearly what the meaning of this Burmese word "sauk-ti-gyin" should be. Upon reflection...

In the context of virtue (sīla), scholars also translated the Pali word samādāna as "sauk-ti-gyin." The word samādāna is formed by combining the prefixes (saṃ), (ā), the root (dā), and the suffix (yu) (or anu). It is a word that must be translated as "taking well." Therefore, saying "undertaking virtue" (sīla sauk-ti-the) in the context of virtue carries the literal meaning of "receiving virtue."

Based on this literal meaning, ancient scholars made it known that "virtue must be given by the monks, and the lay devotees must receive it from the monks." Then, they clearly established the Pali sequence for requesting virtue, such as "Ahaṃ bhante tisaraṇena saha... sīlaṃ detha me bhante," for those who wish to receive virtue to approach any monk. To this day, those who wish to undertake virtue must recite and request according to that sequence. It is indeed a very refined and noble procedure.

(In this regard, based on the final words "sīlaṃ detha me bhante," which mean "Venerable Sir, please give me the precepts,"
480:
some people nowadays tend to complain, "I wish to receive virtue, but I cannot because I do not meet a monk." Even if those who know the true nature say, "If you do not meet a monk, you can also receive it at a pagoda or before a Buddha image," they may remain unsatisfied because the Buddha image does not know how to 'give' virtue. In fact, one should not note that virtue can only be obtained if requested from and given by monks. It can certainly be obtained by undertaking it in the presence of a pagoda or a Buddha image.)

In this matter, one should understand the brief meaning of the Pali sequence to be recited when undertaking and receiving virtue.

First, when the lay devotees recite the sequence of words for paying homage to the Triple Gem and teachers, starting with "Okāsa, Okāsa," along with the words of aspiration, the teacher monk recites a sequence of words for making aspirations and giving blessings, topped with the appropriate liberating Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. After that—

When the lay devotees recite the sequence of words for requesting virtue according to the five or eight precepts, starting with "Ahaṃ bhante tisaraṇena saha," the teacher monk (without any word meaning "I will give virtue") speaks the encouraging words of introduction: "Yamahaṃ vadāmi, taṃ vadetha." (The meaning of these words is: "Whatever sequence of words I speak, follow and speak that sequence which I speak." This is the meaning. Since those requesting virtue do not know how to speak to obtain virtue, it is an encouragement saying, "I will arrange and speak the words first so that you may know; follow and speak whatever I say.") Furthermore, in the sequence of words spoken by the teacher monk, one should carefully note that it consists of: (First) the homage to the Buddha starting with "Namo Tassa," (Second) the Pali for taking refuge starting with "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi," (Third) the collection of Pali for undertaking and receiving the training rules, and (Fourth) the encouragement to fulfill this collection of refuge and virtue by maintaining the practice of heedfulness (appamāda).

In this way, because the general public wishes to practice virtue but does not know how to speak, the teacher monk provides the sequence of words to be spoken.
481:
(Son)
Leading the way by reciting first, and the lay devotees following and reciting after, is what is commonly referred to in worldly usage as "receiving the precepts from a monk" or "the monk giving the precepts."

In this way, although the Pali word *samādāna* literally means "taking well," this is merely the grammatical meaning. To make the intended profound meaning clear, ancient scholars established and taught the translation as "undertaking" (*sauk-ti*). The meaning explained here regarding *sīla* (virtue) should be understood in the same way when undertaking the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), such as "*Paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmi*" (I undertake the refuse-rag-robe wearer's practice) or "*Tecīvarikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmi*" (I undertake the triple-robe wearer's practice). This word "undertaking" (*sauk-ti*) is not only used in the context of *sīla* and *dhutaṅga*; it is also used in the context of *adhiṭṭhāna* (determination).

The Pali word *adhiṭṭhāna* is composed of the prefix *adhi-*, the root *ṭhā-*, and the suffix *-ana*. Although its grammatical meaning is "establishing particularly or excessively," ancient scholars translated it into Burmese simply as "*adhiṭṭhāna* = undertaking/determination" (*sauk-ti*) according to its essential meaning. This word "*sauk-ti*" is not Pali; it is an archaic Burmese word. If one reflects on what its nature should be in modern usage, it is a very remarkable Burmese word. The remarkable nature is as follows:

If the word "*sauk*" is used alone, in ancient usage (*porāṇa*), it means "to erect" or "to plant." Even today, what is called "planting a banner" was referred to in ancient times as "erecting a banner" (*ta-khon sauk*). In ancient times, a flower pinned straight and upright on a woman's hair-knot was called *vaṭaṃsakā* in Pali and *u-sauk-pan* in Burmese. (Meaning a flower placed or erected on the top of the head.)

The meaning of the single word "*ti*" (to stay/place) implies bringing an object from elsewhere and setting it down. From ancient times until now, there has been a custom of calling the construction of a Sīmā hall or a monastery "erecting a Sīmā" (*thein sauk*) or "erecting a monastery" (*kyaung sauk*), because the pillars must be erected first. In the case of establishing a pagoda (*zedi*), it cannot be erected all at once.
482:
(Ha)
Because bricks must be taken and laid down slowly one by one, the custom is to call it "establishing a pagoda" (*zedi ti*). In using these two terms together, there is a traditional saying: "Establish a Buddha [statue/pagoda], erect a monastery" (*Phayā ti, kyaung sauk*).

Thus, although these two words have different individual meanings, when combined as "*sauk-ti*" (undertaking/determination), they carry a deeper meaning than their original sense: "keeping the mind firm, immovable, and unshakeable," or in another way, "making it established." Therefore, the ancient term "*sauk-ti*" means in modern terms "keeping the mind firm, immovable, and unshakeable; making it established." Thus, when saying "undertaking *sīla*" (*sīla sauk-ti*), it means "keeping the *sīla* firm, immovable, and unshakeable in the mind; making it established."

In Pali: *Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi*.
In ancient Burmese: I undertake (*sauk-ti*) the precept which is the refraining from taking the life of living beings.
In modern usage: I keep the set of practices for refraining from taking the life of living beings "firmly, without deviation, and unshakeably in my mind; I make it established."
These Pali, ancient Burmese, and modern expressions all share the same meaning. (The same should be understood for the *adinnādāna* precept and others.)

In the phrase "keeping *sīla* firm, immovable, and unshakeable in the mind," *sīla* refers to the proper restraint of body and speech. "Keeping it unshakeably and firmly in the mind" means keeping that restraint of *sīla* without deviation or shaking within the time period one has determined, making it firmly established. In this context of *adhiṭṭhāna*, the undertaking or keeping in mind that constitutes a *pāramī* (perfection) requires a much more intense degree of mental focus and firm establishment than in the ordinary case of *sīla*. Therefore, when the Bodhisatta Sumedha reflected on the *Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī*, he considered it using the simile of a great rock mountain: just as a great rock mountain stands firm, immovable, and unwavering despite fierce winds, so too must one practice. Thus, he reflected on the *Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī* with the simile of a great rock mountain.

Considering this reflection using the simile of a great rock mountain, it is clear that "*adhiṭṭhāna*" (undertaking/determination) means keeping (establishing) the intended task or work in the mind so that it stands firm, immovable, and unshakeable.
483:
(Hā)
This means that if one desires the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and the knowledge of Omniscience (i.e., if one wishes to become a Buddha), one must have a mental firmness as solid as a great rock mountain in practicing the noble Dhamma that leads to Buddhahood.

## Various Kinds of Adhiṭṭhāna

Thus, *adhiṭṭhāna* or undertaking is the act of making the mind as firm and unshakeable as a great rock mountain. To present the various types of such firm establishment or determination as found in the scriptures:

## Uposatha Adhiṭṭhāna

In the *Uposathakkhandhaka* of the *Vinaya Mahāvagga*, it is mentioned that there are three types of Uposatha: *Saṅgha-uposatha*, *Gaṇa-uposatha*, and *Puggala-uposatha*. Among these, *Saṅgha-uposatha* is the Uposatha performed when at least four monks assemble in a Sīmā hall to observe the Uposatha on the full-moon or new-moon days. When performing this *Saṅgha-uposatha*, one monk recites the *Pātimokkha* text while the other monks listen respectfully. This *Saṅgha-uposatha* is also called *Suttuddesa-uposatha* according to the manner of its performance. (*Sutta* = the Pali text of the Vinaya rules; *uddesa* = an Uposatha characterized by summary recitation; it means an Uposatha where the Pali text of the Vinaya rules is recited in summary.)

If there are only two or three monks, not reaching the full count of four, they must perform *Gaṇa-uposatha*. In performing Uposatha, only when there are at least four monks is it called a *Saṅgha* (Community); if there are only two or three, it is not called a *Saṅgha*, but a *Gaṇa* (group or collection of individuals). In performing this *Gaṇa-uposatha*, if there are three monks, it is done after performing a *ñatti* (formal motion); if there are only two, no *ñatti* is performed, and the two or three monks each recite their declaration of purity from offenses (*āpatti*). Therefore, this *Gaṇa-uposatha* is also called *Pārisuddhi-uposatha*, meaning an Uposatha where one's purity must be declared.

If there is only one monk, he must perform *Puggala-uposatha*. The manner of performing *Puggala-uposatha* is that if there is still time, he should wait in expectation that other monks might arrive.
484:
(Hi)
After waiting and hoping, if no other monk arrives and the time expires, the Blessed One taught that he should resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*): "Today is my Uposatha day." The meaning is that he must make the thought "Today is my Uposatha day" firm and established in his mind. This Uposatha is called *Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*. (Meaning an Uposatha that must be kept firmly in the mind.) This is the nature of *adhiṭṭhāna* as it appears in the context of Uposatha.

## Cīvara Adhiṭṭhāna (Determination of Robes)

Monks, after receiving a robe, must determine (*adhiṭṭhāna*) that robe within ten days, or else perform *vikappanā* (assignment). If one heedlessly keeps it beyond ten days without determining it or performing *vikappanā*, that robe must be forfeited according to Vinaya procedures. It also constitutes a *pācittiya* offense. Therefore, when a robe is obtained, within ten days, one must determine it by saying, "I determine this robe." If it is determined in this way, the robe does not need to be forfeited according to Vinaya procedures, and no *pācittiya* offense is incurred. In this *cīvara-adhiṭṭhāna*, the intended meaning is: "I keep firmly in my mind that this robe is an inner robe (or an upper robe, or an outer robe, or an accessory cloth)." (From the *Vinaya Pārājika-pāḷi, Nissaggiya, Cīvara-vagga*, first training rule.)

## Patta Adhiṭṭhāna (Determination of the Alms-bowl)

In the same way, when monks obtain an alms-bowl, they must determine it within ten days by saying, "*Imaṃ pattaṃ adhiṭṭhāmi* = I determine this bowl." If ten days pass without determination, the bowl must be forfeited according to Vinaya procedures, and a *pācittiya* offense is incurred, as taught in the *Vinaya Pārājika, Nissaggiya, Patta-vagga*, first training rule. In this *patta-adhiṭṭhāna*, keeping firmly in the mind that "This vessel is my alms-bowl" is what is called "determining the bowl."

It should be noted that these *Uposatha-adhiṭṭhāna*, *Cīvara-adhiṭṭhāna*, and *Patta-adhiṭṭhāna* are technical Vinaya usages and terms, and they cannot be included in the three types of *adhiṭṭhāna* that will be distinguished later. (The reason why they cannot be included will become clear later.)
485:
(Hī)
## Jhāna Adhiṭṭhāna (Determination of Absorption)

In the context of *jhāna*, if one attains, for example, the first *jhāna*, the method of developing and practicing it through the five kinds of mastery (*vasībhāva*) is explained in the *Visuddhimagga* Commentary, *Pathavīkasiṇa-niddesa*, and other sections. The word *vasībhāva* comes from the Pali and means "mastery" or "dominion." Therefore, "five kinds of *vasībhāva*" means five kinds of mastery. When the first *jhāna* is attained, one must practice and develop mastery over that attained first *jhāna* in five aspects.

The first aspect or type is called *āvajjana-vasī*, which is mastery in reflection. When the first *jhāna* is attained, one must reflect on which factors are included in one's *jhāna* and what the characteristics of those factors are. At the beginning of reflection, it does not appear easily and remains slow; this is because there is not yet mastery in reflection. When mastery in reflection is achieved, it appears easily and clearly; at that time, *āvajjana-vasī* is perfected.

After that, one must practice with the second mastery called *samāpajjana*. *Samāpajjana* = attainment = the occurrence of *jhāna* thoughts within one's mental continuum. (The continuous occurrence of *jhāna* thoughts in one's mental continuum is called "attaining *jhāna*.") After mastering reflection (*āvajjana-vasī*), one must practice to achieve mastery in attainment. (Just as one becomes proficient in learned scriptures by repeated recitation), one can achieve mastery in *samāpajjana* by repeatedly entering the attained *jhāna*. Before mastery, even if one enters it, the *jhāna* thoughts cannot yet occur easily in the mental continuum. When mastery is achieved through frequent attainment, the *jhāna* thoughts occur easily in the mental continuum every time one enters it. At that time, *samāpajjana-vasī* is perfected.

After that, one must practice with the third mastery called *adhiṭṭhāna*. *Adhiṭṭhāna* here means, when attaining, resolving or undertaking to keep the *jhāna* established in one's mental continuum for a specific duration. Before mastery, the *jhāna* thoughts may last longer than the intended time or shorter than the intended time. (For example) resolving, "May the *jhāna* factors continue to occur in my mental continuum for about one hour."
486:
Even if one makes a resolution, the sequence of jhāna consciousness might break before an hour is up, or it might break after an hour has passed. This happens because the mastery of resolution, the act of determination, and the firm establishment of the mind are not yet proficient. When one becomes proficient, the jhāna consciousness occurs and remains exactly according to the intended time. When one can resolve and maintain the jhāna consciousness to coincide with the intended time, the mastery of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī) is fulfilled.

Next, one must practice with the fourth mastery called vuṭṭhāna. Vuṭṭhāna means emerging from the jhāna one has entered. (Emerging from jhāna means the transition from the sequence of jhāna consciousness to the occurrence of life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness, which is different from jhāna consciousness.) The sovereignty and mastery over emerging from jhāna at the intended time is called vuṭṭhāna-vasī.

Next, one must develop proficiency in contemplating the factors involved in jhāna through the fifth mastery, paccavekkhaṇa-vasī. In such contemplation, as shown in the first mastery of adverting (āvajjana-vasī), it does not appear easily before one is proficient; it appears easily only when one becomes proficient. (Adverting refers to the āvajjana in the reviewing process (paccavekkhaṇa-vīthi), and reviewing refers to the reviewing impulsions (paccavekkhaṇa-javana) that occur immediately after that adverting. If one can practice to make the adverting occur quickly, the reviewing impulsions will also occur quickly. Therefore, it is explained in the scriptures that when the mastery of adverting is fulfilled, the mastery of reviewing is also fulfilled.)

In summary, regarding the instruction to practice the attained jhāna through the five masteries, the mastery of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī) should be understood as the sovereignty and mastery in being able to place and maintain the jhāna consciousness in one's mental continuum exactly according to the intended time without any deficiency or excess.

## Resolution of Psychic Power

Furthermore, in the Iddhividha-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga Commentary...
(1) Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi,
(2) Vikubbana-iddhi,
487:
(3) Manomaya-iddhi,
(4) Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi,
(5) Samādhivipphāra-iddhi,
(6) Ariya-iddhi,
(7) Kammavipākaja-iddhi,
(8) Puññavanta-iddhi,
(9) Vijjāmaya-iddhi,
(10) Sammāpayoga-iddhi—
Thus, it is stated that there are ten types of iddhi. (Iddhi = accomplishment or fulfillment; the ability to accomplish or fulfill what is desired is called iddhi in Pali, and tan-kho [power] in Burmese.)

(1) Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi means resolving with knowledge: "Let me, who am one, become many, a hundred or a thousand." One resolves, determines, and firmly establishes the mind. The successful production of as many created forms (nimmitarūpa) as desired, in an amazing manner, is called adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi. (This adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi is the psychic power concerned only with creating various forms, similar or dissimilar to oneself, externally, while the original physical body of the possessor of the power remains unchanged.)

(2) Transforming one's body from its original state into the form of a great dragon (nāga), a great garuda, etc., is called vikubbana-iddhi. (Vi = various; kubbana = creating/transforming. It means transforming one's original appearance and creating various desired forms.)

(3) Creating a small body similar to oneself from within one's own body, without changing one's own body and not purely externally, is called manomaya-iddhi. Manomaya = accomplished by the mind. (In this manomaya-iddhi, it is not creating various things outside the body like adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi, nor is it transforming one's own appearance like vikubbana-iddhi; it is the act of keeping the original body as it is and producing/extracting a small mind-made body from within that primary body as desired by the mind.)
488:
(4) The special amazing fulfillment that occurs through the pervasion of the power of knowledge is called ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi. The cause of this ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi should be understood through the cases of Venerable Bākula and others.

## The Story of Venerable Bākula

I shall extract the essential summary of the story of Venerable Bākula, which is detailed in the Commentary to the Etadagga-vagga of the Ekaka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. Venerable Bākula was the son of a wealthy man in the city of Kosambī. Shortly after his birth, on the day of his naming ceremony, while the baby was being bathed in the Yamunā River, a fish came and swallowed him. As soon as it swallowed him, the fish felt an intense heat in its belly and, unable to stay still, swam away and reached the city of Vārāṇasī. It was caught by fishermen and sold throughout Vārāṇasī. The wife of a wealthy man in Vārāṇasī bought it herself, and when she cut open the fish's belly, she found a beautiful baby. Since she had no children and longed for a son, she was overjoyed, saying, "I have gained a son!" and raised him.

When the parents in Kosambī heard this news, they came to claim him, saying, "He is our son; you must return him." The wife of the wealthy man in Vārāṇasī refused, saying, "He came into our hands because of our merit; we cannot return him." When the case reached the court, the judges gave a decision in favor of both parties. Thus, because the boy had two mothers and two fathers, he was named "Bākula". (Bā = two; kula = family/clan. It means having two families, such as two mothers and two fathers.)

The fact that this young boy suffered no harm despite being swallowed by a fish is an amazing and extraordinary point. This extraordinary event was due to the pervasion of the power of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa) that he was certainly to attain in this very life. (It can also be said that it was due to the pervasion of the power of his brilliant pāramī knowledge, which would certainly lead him to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship in this life.) This kind of power is called ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi.
489:
## The Story of Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera

Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera was conceived in the womb of a daughter of a wealthy man in Sāvatthī. Just before he was to be born, his mother passed away. While the body was being cremated, people poked it with stakes to make it burn easily. The tip of a stake struck the corner of the baby's eye in the womb. When the baby cried, they realized he was not yet dead. They removed the body from the funeral pyre, cut open the womb, and took the baby out. This child became a novice at the age of seven and attained Arahatship.

The fact that this young boy, the future Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera, did not die during the cremation was due to the pervasion of the power of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship that he was certainly to attain in this very life. (It can also be said that it was due to the pervasion of the power of his brilliant pāramī knowledge, which would certainly lead him to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship in this life.)

(5) Samādhivipphāra-iddhi means... the amazing extraordinary occurrence that happens just before entering, during, or just after emerging from the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) called concentration (samādhi). It is the fulfillment (power) caused by the pervasion of the power of concentration. Regarding this power, many stories are presented in the Visuddhimagga Commentary, starting with the story of Venerable Sāriputta. I shall present just the story of Venerable Sāriputta...

## The Story of Venerable Sāriputta

Once, while Venerable Sāriputta was staying with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna at the Kapota Canyon, he was meditating in the open on a moonlit night, having just shaved his head. At that time, a wicked yakkha was traveling with a companion. Seeing Venerable Sāriputta's shaven head, he felt a strong urge to strike it. Despite his companion's warnings, he struck the Elder's head with all his might. The sound of the blow was as loud as a thunderclap. However, because of the blow from this wicked yakkha...
490:
...the Elder felt no pain at all. It should be understood that this was due to the pervasion of the power of the concentration he was dwelling in.

(6) Ariya-iddhi means... if Noble Ones (ariya) wish to view a repulsive object as non-repulsive, they can do so. If they wish to view a non-repulsive object as repulsive, they can perceive it as such. The ability to perceive any object according to how one wishes to attend to it is a power that only Noble Ones can achieve; this power is called ariya-iddhi (the power of the Noble Ones).

(7) Kammavipākaja-iddhi means... the ability of birds and such to fly in the sky. Birds do not have to make any specific effort in this life to be able to fly; it is a nature that comes as a result of past kamma. The ability of devas, brahmas, the first humans of the aeon, and certain vinipātika-asuras to travel in the sky is also kammavipākaja-iddhi.

(8) Puññavanta-iddhi means... the ability of Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) and others to travel in the sky. It means having powers such as traveling in the sky because they are persons of merit. All the soldiers and followers who follow a Universal Monarch through the sky are also said to possess power by depending on the Universal Monarch, who is the truly meritorious one. The wealth and prosperity of Jotika, Jaṭila, Ghosaka, Meṇډaka, and others are also puññavanta-iddhi.

(The difference between kammavipākaja-iddhi and puññavanta-iddhi is as follows: The power that is fulfilled from birth in this life, exactly as ordained by the kamma of a past life without any planning or effort in the current life, is called kammavipākaja-iddhi.

In puññavanta-iddhi, although puññā refers to wholesome kamma, that merit is not purely the merit brought from a past life; it also includes factors that must be exerted and performed as support in the current life. Thus, it is not something that comes solely from birth...)
491:
(Explanation)
The power that is fulfilled upon obtaining the necessary supports and conditions produced through effort in the present life is called Puññavanta-iddhi. To explain more clearly:
A Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) does not possess the Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) from the moment of birth; rather, the object known as the Wheel Treasure arrives only after he has practiced the duties of a Universal Monarch along with the observance of the Uposatha. Therefore, it should be understood that the cause of obtaining the Wheel Treasure is not solely due to past kamma, but also involves the supporting kamma of the present life.
(9) Vijjāmaya-iddhi refers to the ability of those possessed of science/knowledge (Vijjādhara) to travel through the sky, and so on. (It means the power accomplished through specially created mantras, medicinal arts, etc.)
(10) Sammapayoga-iddhi refers to various types of fulfillment obtained through the right exertion and performance of various tasks. (This Sammapayoga-iddhi has a very broad scope; in the highest sense, the paths and fruits (Magga-Phala) are also called Sammapayoga-iddhi because they are obtained through right exertion. To summarize and present it most concisely, all verbal arts, all manual crafts, the study of the three Vedas, the study of the three Piṭakas, and (at the lowest level) all fulfillments arising from plowing, planting, and so on, are to be understood as Sammapayoga-iddhi.)
Among these ten types of iddhi, the first, Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi, involves—as previously explained—resolving, undertaking, and firmly holding in the mind, such as the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka Thera did, to make a single body become a hundred or a thousand. Although ordinary people who do not possess iddhi also have such undertakings, they are not fulfilled according to their undertaking because they lack the foundation of meditative concentration (jhāna-samādhi). However, it should be noted without doubt that for those with iddhi, because their foundation of jhāna-samādhi is very strong, they achieve fulfillment according to their resolve.
## Resolve Preceding Cessation
When entering the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), if an Anāgāmī or an Arahant who has attained all eight meditative attainments is about to enter that nirodha-samāpatti, just before entering, they resolve: "During the days I am in this attainment,
492:
may my belongings that are separate from my body not be destroyed by any danger; if the Saṅgha should desire my presence, may I emerge from the attainment before the messenger monk arrives; if the Blessed One should call me, may I emerge from the attainment at the very moment he calls." Having made such a resolve, undertaken it, and held it firmly in the mind, they then enter the attainment.
When they enter in this way, during the time of the attainment, according to the resolve, the belongings of the person in attainment that are separate from the body cannot be destroyed by the five kinds of enemies. If the Saṅgha has a need during the time of attainment, they emerge from the attainment even before the messenger monk arrives. If the Blessed One calls, they emerge at the very moment of the call. As for the belongings in contact with the body of the person in attainment, such as the robes, they cannot be destroyed by the five kinds of enemies even without making a resolve, due to the power of the attainment.
## Three Types of Resolve
The nature of undertaking and holding firmly in the mind, which is called resolve (adhiṭṭhāna), is of three kinds according to the context:
(1) Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna (Resolving and holding firmly in the mind to show a sign in advance.)
(2) Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna (Resolving and holding firmly in the mind for a desired purpose or aspiration.)
(3) Vata-adhiṭṭhāna (Resolving and holding firmly in the mind to practice a duty or vow.)
## (1) Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna
Among these, the matter of Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna should be understood through the Campeyya Jātaka of the Vīsati Nipāta and others. The summary of the intended meaning according to the Campeyya Jātaka is: When the Naga King Campeyya announced that he would go to the human realm to observe the Uposatha, Queen Sumanā Naga said, "The human realm is full of many dangers.
493:
If any danger should occur, by what sign shall we know?" The Naga King then took her to the auspicious pond and said, "Look at the pond. If any enemy captures and mistreats me, this water will become turbid. If a Garuḍa captures me, this water will boil. If a snake charmer captures me, it will turn bright red like the color of blood." After announcing these signs, he made a resolve to observe the Cātuddasī (fourteenth day) Uposatha and went to the human realm.
While he was observing the Uposatha in the human realm, he was captured by a snake charmer and did not return to the Naga realm for about a month. The Queen, being anxious, looked at the pond and saw the surface of the water appearing bright red like the color of blood.
