(In this instance, although it is not directly stated that the Naga King resolved, "If enemies mistreat me, let this water be turbid; if a Garuḍa captures me, let it boil; if a snake charmer captures me, let it be red like blood," considering the context, the Naga King must have undertaken this and held it firmly in his mind before speaking to the Queen. Since it was an act of resolve by the Naga King, it should be considered that it happened exactly as he said.)
This resolving, undertaking, and firm holding in the mind by the Naga King Campeyya is called Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna because it was an undertaking to show a sign in advance.
In the same way, when the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha went forth into the homeless life, after cutting his hair on the banks of the Anomā River, he resolved: "If it is true that I shall become a Buddha, let it remain in the sky; if I cannot become a Buddha, let it fall to the ground." Having so resolved, he threw his hair into the sky, and it remained in the sky like a hanging garland, as stated in the Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā Nidāna. This instance is also Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna because it was a prior resolve by the Bodhisatta to know the sign of whether he would become a Buddha.
Furthermore, after Prince Siddhattha became a monk and practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for six years, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the merchant's daughter Sujātā on the banks of the Nerañjarā River and thought, "If I
494:
am to become a Buddha today, may this golden bowl float upstream; if not, may it float downstream." Having so resolved, he set the bowl adrift on the river current, and the golden bowl floated upstream and reached the abode of the Naga King Kāla, as recorded in the scriptures. In this case too, it is Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna because the Bodhisatta made a resolve to know the sign of whether he would become a Buddha by floating the golden bowl on the water's surface.
In this manner, any resolve made in the world to know in advance whether one's desired object will be fulfilled is called Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna.
This type of resolve is very prominent and frequently practiced in the world even up to the present time. At powerful Buddha statues or spirit shrines, people often perform the act of lifting stones. In doing so, they usually speak and resolve, "If my plan is to be fulfilled, let this stone be heavy; if it is not to be fulfilled, let it be light," or alternatively, "If it is to be fulfilled, let it be light; if it is not to be fulfilled, let it be heavy." When they lift it, they read the sign in advance as to whether their desired matter will be fulfilled or not based on the heaviness or lightness of the stone. These acts of stone-lifting are also Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna.
## (2) Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna
Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna is the act of resolving, undertaking, and holding firmly in the mind for the fulfillment of one's own aspiration or wish. This Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna should be understood through the words found in the Vidhura Jātaka.
In the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) on verse 197 of the Vidhura Jātaka, it is explained that the Bodhisatta Minister Vidhura proclaimed boldly, "I do not fear death," and having undertaken a resolve with a fearless demeanor like a maned lion, he reflected on the perfections (pāramīs) as his guide, dressed himself firmly in his garment, and followed while holding the horse's tail. This resolve of Minister Vidhura is called Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna because it was a resolve for the purpose of wanting the garment he was wearing to remain firm without coming loose.
495:
In the Naḷapāna Jātaka (No. 20) of the Sīla Vagga, Ekaka Nipāta, twenty thousand monkeys led by the Bodhisatta Monkey King wanted to drink water from a pond guarded by a fierce water-ogre without descending into the pond. They were made to take a reed from the reed-thicket growing around the pond. To ensure there were no nodes or joints inside the reed, the Bodhisatta Monkey King made an act of truth and blew into it, whereby the entire reed became hollow throughout. When it came time for them to drink, since there were many monkeys and he could not blow them one by one for each monkey, it is recorded that he gave a resolve: "Let all the reeds around this pond become hollow throughout." In this case, the resolve of the Bodhisatta Monkey King is also Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna because it was a resolve made out of a desire for the many monkeys to be able to suck up water individually.
In the Kukkura Jātaka (No. 22) of the Kuruṅga Vagga, Ekaka Nipāta, the palace dogs ate the leather of the state chariot of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī. Thinking that the dogs of the townspeople from outside the palace had entered and eaten it, the king's men hunted and killed the outside dogs. Many dogs, not daring to stay in the city, gathered at a cemetery. At that time, the Bodhisatta Dog inquired about the matter and realized that the leather of this royal chariot could not have been eaten by outside dogs, but only by the palace dogs. He instructed, "Wait patiently; I will enter the palace." Then, reflecting on the perfections and placing loving-kindness (mettā) at the forefront, he resolved, "May no person be able to throw even a stone or a stick at me," and entered the city alone. In this case, the resolve of the Bodhisatta Dog is Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna because it was a resolve to carry out a task with the desire to keep the outside dogs safe from danger.
In the Mātaṅga Jātaka of the Vīsati Nipāta, during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the low caste of the Caṇḍālas and was named Mātaṅga. The daughter of a merchant in Bārāṇasī, who held the view that seeing a pleasant object is auspicious, was named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. One day, while Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā was coming out to play in the park with a large retinue, the Bodhisatta Mātaṅga also—
496:
While entering the city, the Bodhisatta Mātaṅga, the outcaste, encountered the retinue of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. Being a person of humble status, he moved aside to avoid them. However, upon seeing him, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā exclaimed, "I have seen something loathsome; this is an inauspicious day!" Instead of proceeding to the park for recreation, she turned back and returned home from that very spot. Her followers and sycophants, complaining, "Because of you, we have been deprived of our enjoyment, food, and drink today," beat, kicked, and struck him until he was unconscious before they departed. When Mātaṅga regained consciousness after a while, he thought, "The people of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā have oppressed and tormented me, though I am innocent. I shall not rise until I obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā." The Commentary states that he went and lay down at the gate of the merchant, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s father, making this resolution. This resolution of the Bodhisatta Mātaṅga was an undertaking intended to humble the pride of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, and thus it is called Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna (Resolution of Aspiration).

In the Commentary to the Vinaya Mahāvagga, it is also mentioned that shortly after the Buddha’s enlightenment, after completing the seven weeks of stay, he was residing at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. When the two brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika, arrived to offer rice cakes (the bowl offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma had disappeared on the day he was to receive the thick milk-rice), the Buddha reflected on what vessel he should use to accept the offering. The Four Great Kings then offered four emerald bowls to the Buddha, but he did not accept them. Subsequently, the Four Great Kings offered four stone bowls the color of mung beans. To preserve the faith of the four Great Kings, the Buddha accepted them. He then placed the four bowls one on top of the other and resolved, "Let there be only one bowl." It is explained that they became a single bowl with four distinct rims. This instance should also be understood as the Buddha’s Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna.

## Distinction between Adhiṭṭhāna and Sacca
There is a tendency to regard Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna and Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna, mentioned in this chapter on Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī, as being the same as Icchāpūraṇa-sacca mentioned in the chapter on Sacca Pāramī, without making a distinction. This is because all three are related to the fulfillment of one's own desires.
497:
The connection is as follows: In the case of Icchāpūraṇa-sacca (Truth for the fulfillment of desire), when the mother and father of Suvaṇṇasāma and the deity Bahusundarī made an Act of Truth, they did so out of a desire for the poison of the arrow in Suvaṇṇasāma to be neutralized. In the case of Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna (Resolution for a portent), the Bodhisatta threw his hair into the air with the aspiration for his future Buddhahood, resolving that if he were truly to become a Buddha, the hair should not fall back to the ground. In the case of Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna, when the great minister Vidhura was about to follow by holding onto the horse's tail, he made a resolution, "May my lower garment not come loose," because he desired that his garment remain secure. Because the primary element of 'desire' is similar in these cases, people often mistake them as being of the same nature without distinction. For this reason, some people nowadays use the terms together, saying, "We perform Sacca-adhiṭṭhāna," and so on.

In reality, Sacca is a distinct perfection among the ten perfections, and Adhiṭṭhāna is also a distinct perfection among the ten perfections. Therefore, Sacca and Adhiṭṭhāna should be understood as different and distinct categories. The difference is this: Sacca, as previously explained, is the nature of truthfulness, whether the outcome is good or bad. Making an aspiration for a desired goal based on that nature of truth is called Icchāpūraṇa-sacca. Making a resolution or undertaking for a desired goal spontaneously, without basing it on any specific truth, is Adhiṭṭhāna.

To explain further: In the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, when the mother and father made the Act of Truth, they said, "Suvaṇṇasāma has always practiced only the Dhamma in the past." (This is the foundational truth.) "By this word of truth, may the poison in my son disappear." (This is the aspiration for the desired goal.) Thus, in Icchāpūraṇa-sacca, the aspiration for what is desired is based on the nature of truth.

When the Great Bodhisatta said, "If I am to become a Buddha, may this hair not fall to the ground," and threw his hair into the sky, it was done without basing it on a prior truth; thus, the foundation of truth is absent. It should be understood only as an Adhiṭṭhāna (undertaking) for a portent—the falling or not falling of the hair to the ground—to know in advance whether he would become a Buddha or not.
498:
When the great minister Vidhura, about to follow by holding the horse's tail, resolved, "May this garment of mine not come loose," it also had no foundation in any truth; therefore, it is not related to Sacca but is merely Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna.

In this way, one should carefully note that Sacca and Adhiṭṭhāna differ based on whether or not they are rooted in or founded upon a certain nature of truth.

## (3) Vata-adhiṭṭhāna
Regarding Vata-adhiṭṭhāna, it is necessary to analyze and understand the meaning of the term 'Vata'. 'Vata' refers to a special practice or vow. This special practice can be of two kinds: good or bad. In the Abhidhamma teachings, there is a type of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) designated as Sīlabbata-parāmāsa, which means the misapprehension of habits and vows.

Misapprehension means following the habits of cattle (go-sīla) or the practices of cattle (go-vata). It is the mistaken belief that if one behaves according to the habits of cattle—such as eating while standing, or voiding excrement and urine while standing—one will be purified from Saṃsāra (liberated from the round of rebirths). (In this context, it does not mean that the cattle themselves possess the wrong view of Sīlabbata-parāmāsa; it means that the person who imitates and practices those habits of cattle is the one who possesses that wrong view.) Therefore, it should be understood that even in unwholesome contexts, a special practice is called 'Vata'.

In the context of this Adhiṭṭhāna, however, since it pertains to the noble perfections (pāramī), those base 'Vata' practices cannot be included. It should be understood that only noble practices such as giving (dāna) and observing morality (sīla) are called 'Vata'. If one undertakes to practice these noble perfections and meritorious deeds, it can indeed be called Vata-adhiṭṭhāna. However, one cannot say that the Perfection of Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī) is accomplished merely by the act of undertaking it. This is because Adhiṭṭhāna does not concern the past that has already gone or the present that is currently occurring; it can only become a perfection if one actually practices in the future according to what has been undertaken and firmly held in the mind.
499:
No matter how fervently one makes a resolution or undertaking at the present moment, if one fails to practice it in the future, it becomes a useless and meaningless resolution.

Regarding this matter, the Kavi-lakkhaṇa orthography manual states: "Like the horn of a rhinoceros, let the resolution and the mode of practice be firm and certain." The meaning is: if one wishes to make a resolution, let it be like the horn of a rhinoceros. A rhinoceros has only one horn, not two. Therefore, a resolution must remain as it was resolved. It must not be broken; it must be practiced firmly and certainly. This statement from the Kavi-lakkhaṇa is very much in accord with the similes found in the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, such as "Yathāpi pabbato selo" (Just as a mountain of stone). The meaning of this simile has been explained previously.

Among the various types of Adhiṭṭhāna mentioned earlier, the resolution for the Uposatha, the resolution for robes, and the resolution for the bowl are Vinaya procedures that must be followed to remain free from ecclesiastical offenses (āpatti); they cannot be included in the three types: Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna, Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna, and Vata-adhiṭṭhāna. The resolutions included in the five masteries (vasībhāva), the resolutions included in the ten psychic powers (iddhi), and the resolution that precedes the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are all types of Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna.

## The Bodhisattas and the Three Types of Adhiṭṭhāna
Among these three types of Adhiṭṭhāna described, the Great Bodhisattas do not specifically fulfill Pubbanimitta-adhiṭṭhāna and Āsīsa-adhiṭṭhāna for the purpose of completing the Perfection of Resolution; they only perform them when the occasion arises. To fulfill the noble Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī, which is the cause for attaining the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), they primarily strive in Vata-adhiṭṭhāna.

To show a portion of how they strive, in the Sivirājacariya section of the Cariyāpiṭaka Pali, it is said:

Nisajja pāsādavare, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā.
Yaṃkiñci mānusaṃ dānaṃ, adinnaṃ me na vijjati.
Yo pi yāceyya maṃ cakkhuṃ, dadeyyaṃ avikampito.
500:
This means: "Dear Sāriputta, when I was King Sivi, sitting upon my noble palace, I thought: 'There is no kind of gift given by humans that I have not given. Should anyone come and ask for my eye, I would give it to them without wavering.'"

In this passage, King Sivi undertook and firmly held in his mind the resolution: "If anyone should come to me today and say they want my eye, I will give it to that solicitor without wavering or shrinking back." In accordance with his undertaking, when Sakka, disguised as a brahmin, came to ask for one eye, he sacrificed both eyes without wavering. This resolution of King Sivi was a resolution related to the act of giving (dāna).

Also, in the Bhūridattacariya section, it is said:

Caturo aṅge adhiṭṭhāya, semi vammikamuddhani.
Chaviyā cammena maṃsena, nahāru-aṭṭhikehi vā.
Yassa etena karaṇīyaṃ, dinnaṃyeva harāku so.

This describes how the Naga King Bhūridatta made a resolution while observing the Uposatha vows. The meaning is: "Having resolved upon these four factors—(1) the outer and inner skin, (2) the flesh and blood, (3) the sinews, and (4) the bones—should anyone have a need for any of these four parts, let them take whichever part they wish to use; it is already given by me." Having made this resolution, he lay coiled upon an anthill.

In this instance, the Naga King Bhūridatta made the resolution in connection with morality (sīla), with the thought: "I will endure the loss of these four parts of my body, but I will not let my morality be broken." Thus, it is a resolution related to morality.

In the Campeyya Jātaka of the Vīsati Nipāta (Jātaka No. 506), the Naga King Campeyya, after instructing his queen on the signs by which she might know if he were in danger, went to observe the Uposatha vows, as previously mentioned—
501:
(ḷai)
“Nimittāni ācikkhitvā cātuddasīuposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā tattha gantvā vammikamatthake nipajji” —
This is explained in the Commentary as follows: It means that after explaining the signs, he made a resolution to observe the Uposatha of the fourteenth day (the new moon), departed from the Naga realm, went to the human world, and lay down coiled on top of an anthill. This resolution of the Cāmpayya Naga King was a resolution made solely for the purpose of observing virtue (sīla).

In the case of King Sivi’s resolution to donate his eyes and the resolutions of the Bhūridatta Naga King and the Cāmpayya Naga King to observe virtue, the act of donation or observing virtue is one thing, while the act of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) is another; they are distinct mental states. King Sivi’s act of giving (dāna) his pair of eyes occurred at the moment he gave them to the Brahmin (Sakka), but the resolution had already occurred when he intended and firmly decided to give before the actual donation. Thus, the resolution comes first and the donation second. Similarly, in the case of the Naga kings' virtue, the resolution was made in advance, and the virtue followed. In the world, it is natural that for any task, people first resolve in their minds, “I will do it this way,” and only then perform those tasks.

## The Resolution of Prince Temiya
The Bodhisatta was the son of the King of Kāsi and was named Prince Temiya. (He was named Prince Temiya because on the day he was born, heavy rain fell throughout the kingdom of Kāsi, making everyone feel cool, peaceful, and refreshed.) When Prince Temiya was one month old, while he was sitting on his father's lap, four thieves were captured and brought before the King. Seeing the King pass various sentences on them, the Prince was greatly terrified and felt very distressed, thinking, “How shall I plan to escape from this royal palace?”

The next day, while sitting alone under the white parasol, he reflected on his father’s judicial decisions from the previous day. Fearing the prospect of having to rule as a king, the Bodhisatta sat fading like a lotus flower crushed by a hand.
502:
(ḷo)
A goddess who guarded the white parasol and had been his mother in a previous life said, “Dear son, do not worry. If you wish to escape from the royal palace, make a resolution: ‘I will act as if I am lame though I am not, as if I am deaf though I am not, and as if I am mute though I am not.’ If you carry out these three things, your wish will be fulfilled.” Hearing this, the Bodhisatta Prince Temiya resolved, “I will practice all three firmly,” and he practiced them without fail exactly as he had resolved.

For sixteen years, although he was tested (his desires were probed) in various ways, he continued to observe and practice the three points of his resolution without any failure. Then, his father the King issued an order, saying, “My son is indeed truly lame, deaf, and mute; take him to the cemetery and bury him alive.”

In this Jātaka, although they tested the Bodhisatta Prince Temiya with various methods to make it difficult for him to endure for sixteen years, his steadfastness in not breaking his resolution—like a great stone mountain as described in the Buddhavamsa Pali—was a great act of Adhiṭṭhāna. It should be noted that the Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī fulfilled by the Great Bodhisattas can only be accomplished when one can courageously and sacrificially fulfill a set of practices resolved with intense will, remaining firm and unwavering like Prince Temiya.

The Chapter on Adhiṭṭhāna Pāramī ends.
**********

## (9) Mettā Pāramī
## The Three Types of Pema (Affection)
In the term Mettā Pāramī, the Pali word 'Mettā' was translated by ancient teachers as “loving” (affection). The Pali word 'Pema' was also translated by ancient teachers as “loving.” The love expressed by the word Mettā is specific, while the love expressed by the word Pema is general. Therefore, affection according to Pema is—
503:
(ḷo) 
(1) Taṇhā-pema,
(2) Gehasita-pema,
(3) Mettā-pema—
Thus, it is divided into three types. Among these three:

(1) Taṇhā-pema refers to the mutual love and attraction between a woman and a man through the power of lustful craving (taṇhā-lobha). In treatises on rhetoric (Alaṅkāra), this Taṇhā-pema is called Siṅgāra.

(2) The mutual affection and attachment between parents and children, brothers and sisters, etc., is called Gehasita-pema; it means affection based on living in a home. In treatises on rhetoric, this affection is called Vacchala. Both Taṇhā-pema and Gehasita-pema are not wholesome states (kusala); Taṇhā-pema is lustful passion (taṇhā-rāga), and Gehasita-pema is simply greed (lobha).

(3) Desiring the welfare and prosperity of others is called Mettā-pema. This Mettā has no nature of wanting to be constantly attached or inseparable from others. Even if people are as far apart as separate universes, one is satisfied if one knows that the distant person is prosperous and happy; there is no difficulty or burden felt because of not living together. Therefore, Mettā is a pure and noble state and also receives the name Brahmavihāra (Sublime Abode). It means that dwelling in the constant development of this state is a noble way of living. Not only Mettā, but also Karuṇā (compassion), Muditā (appreciative joy), and Upekkhā (equanimity) receive the name Brahmavihāra.

Therefore, all four are collectively called the four Brahmavihāra dhammas. They are also called the four Brahmacariya dhammas. (Brahma = noble; Vihāra = dwelling. These four Brahmavihāra dhammas are also called the four Appamaññā dhammas. It means states that arise towards beings who are immeasurable in number.)

When it is said that one must develop loving-kindness (Mettā), it should be specially noted that it must not be the impure Taṇhā-pema or Gehasita-pema, but only this very pure and noble Mettā-pema. The method of developing this Mettā will be explained clearly later.
504:
(ḷaṃ)
## Mettā and Adosa
Mettā is a reality that clearly exists in the ultimate sense (paramattha). However, when listing ultimate realities one by one, Mettā is not shown separately; rather, by showing the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa-cetasika), Mettā is included as a part of adosa. This means that adosa-cetasika has a broad scope, and Mettā is included within that scope of adosa-cetasika as a specific portion.

To make it clearer: according to the Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha, adosa-cetasika is associated with all 59 beautiful consciousnesses (sobhana-citta). Whenever a sobhana-citta arises, adosa-cetasika is present. Adosa can take various objects, but Mettā can only take the concept of beings (satta-paññatti) as its object. In performing various acts of charity (dāna) or observing various precepts (sīla), adosa must be present; however, every time such adosa arises, it is not called Mettā. Only when adosa-cetasika arises with the mode of desiring the welfare and happiness of beings, taking the concept of beings as its object and wishing for them to be happy, etc., is that adosa-cetasika called Mettā.

In the previously explained Khantī Pāramī, although adosa-cetasika is taken as the reality for Khantī, not all adosa is taken as Khantī; only the adosa that prevents one from getting angry at all when others wrong one is taken. Similarly, not all adosa-cetasika is taken as Mettā; only the adosa-cetasika that arises with the mode of desiring the benefit of beings is taken as Mettā.

## The 528 Ways of Mettā
Regarding this Mettā, many people speak of and know that there are 528 types of Mettā. In reality, it is not because the essence of Mettā itself has 528 varieties, but it should be noted that people say "528 Mettā" because there are 528 methods of developing Mettā as mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali.

The way it becomes 528 methods is that there are five kinds of unspecified (anodhisa) radiation, which do not set limits on individuals or beings. The five kinds are:
505:
(ḷās)
(1) Sabbe sattā = (All beings)
(2) Sabbe pāṇā = (All breathing things)
(3) Sabbe bhūtā = (All creatures/manifested things)
(4) Sabbe puggalā = (All individuals)
(5) Sabbe attabhāvapariyāpannā = (All those included in the individual personality)—
If one directs the mind using any one of these five categories towards all beings within the thirty-one planes of existence, all are included without exception. Since there are no beings not included in these five, these five are called the five Anodhisa (unspecified) categories. (They are also called the five kinds of Anodhisa individuals.) The word 'odhisa' in the Pali term 'anodhisa' means 'limit' or 'boundary'; by saying 'anodhisa', it means 'without limit' or 'unspecified'.

## The Usage of Satta and Puggala
In Pali, if one says 'Satta' (being), it refers to all beings in the thirty-one planes. If one says 'Puggala' (individual/person), it likewise refers to all those in the thirty-one planes. There is no difference in status or rank; if one is called 'Satta', one can also be called 'Puggala'. If one is called 'Puggala', one can also be called 'Satta'. In the Burmese vocabulary, however, a great distinction in status is made between 'Satta-wa' (being) and 'Puggala' (person). The terms 'foolish being' or 'lowly being' are used only for the inferior classes, while 'foolish person' or 'lowly person' are not used at all. In using the word 'Puggala', it is used as 'great noble persons', 'extraordinary persons', etc.; the terms 'great noble beings' or 'extraordinary beings' are never used. This means that inferior living things are called 'Satta-wa', while noble living things are called 'Puggala'. One should also be mindful of this difference where the Pali and Burmese usages diverge.
506:
(A)
In the practice of specified (odhisa) mettā:
(1) Sabbā itthiyo = (All women)
(2) Sabbe purisā = (All men)
(3) Sabbe ariyā = (All noble ones)
(4) Sabbe anariyā = (All non-noble ones)
(5) Sabbe devā = (All deities and Brahmas)
(6) Sabbe manussā = (All human beings)
(7) Sabbe vinipātikā = (All beings in states of deprivation)
Among these seven types, because each type is specifically defined, they are called the seven specified (odhisa) types. (They are also referred to as the seven types of specified persons.)

Thus, as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, one should first understand the twelve types of persons to whom mettā is to be directed: five types of unspecified (anodhisa) persons and seven types of specified (odhisa) persons.

Regarding the four modes of developing mettā towards these twelve types of persons:
(1) Averā hontu = (May they be free from enmity)
(2) Abyāpajjā hontu = (May they be free from mental suffering)
(3) Anīghā hontu = (May they be free from physical suffering)
(4) Sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu = (May they be able to maintain themselves happily in both body and mind)
These four modes were taught. Since there are four modes of directing mettā for each of the twelve types of persons, the total is twelve multiplied by four, which equals forty-eight.

Develop mettā for all twelve types of persons until complete, such as: "May all beings be free from enmity, may they be free from mental suffering, may they be free from physical suffering, may they be able to maintain themselves happily in both body and mind..." and so on. You will personally realize that there are forty-eight ways. These forty-eight are the mettā directed without specifically marking the directions.
507:
(Ā)
Furthermore, when one wishes to direct mettā by marking the directions, there are ten directions: East, West, North, South, Southeast, Northwest, Northeast, Southwest, Downward, and Upward. Since there are forty-eight ways for each direction, the total for the ten directions is four hundred and eighty. (Develop mettā for the twelve types of persons across the ten directions until complete, such as: "In the eastern direction, may all beings be free from enmity, may they be free from mental suffering, may they be free from physical suffering, may they be able to maintain themselves happily in both body and mind. In the eastern direction, may all breathing things be free from enmity..." and so on. You will personally realize that there are four hundred and eighty ways.)

When these four hundred and eighty ways of directional mettā are added to the previous forty-eight ways of non-directional mettā, it becomes the (528) ways of mettā.

Ancient teachers have traditionally established this method of 528 ways of mettā as a recitation procedure under the name "Mettā-po" (Directing Mettā). In truth, when one wishes to direct mettā, if one wishes to use the very first method among the 528, directing it by saying (in Pāḷi) "Sabbe sattā averā hontu," the first method of developing mettā is complete and correct. (If one wishes to develop it in Myanmar), saying "May all beings be free from danger and enmity" makes the first method complete and correct. Even by reciting and repeatedly developing this first method alone, it is called the development of mettā-bhāvanā. If one wishes to develop the second method instead of the first, saying (in Pāḷi) "Sabbe sattā abyāpajjā hontu," or (in Myanmar) "May all beings be free from mental suffering," it is called the development of mettā-bhāvanā. (In this manner, one should understand all five hundred and twenty-eight ways through wisdom.)

The 528 ways of developing mettā presented here is the method taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi and is a very well-known and widely used method. (In this Pāḷi text, at the end of the mettā development method, the methods for developing karuṇā, muditā, and upekkhā...
508:
(I)
...are not taught consecutively.) However, in current books titled 'Mettā-po', at the end of the four modes of mettā development from the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, the following are included together:
(a) Dukkhā muccantu = The method of developing karuṇā: "May they be released from suffering."
(b) Yathāladdhasampattito mā vigacchantu = The method of developing muditā: "May they not be parted from the prosperity they have attained."
(c) Kammassakā = The method of developing upekkhā: "They are the owners of their kamma; they fare according to their own kamma."
These were added by ancient teachers so that those who wish to develop karuṇā-bhāvanā, muditā-bhāvanā, and upekkhā-bhāvanā can do so by taking the method from the mettā-po.

As established, if one wishes to develop karuṇā, one should develop it as: "Sabbe sattā dukkhā muccantu" = May all beings be released from suffering. If one wishes to develop muditā: "Sabbe sattā yathāladdhasampattito mā vigacchantu" = May all beings not be parted from the prosperity they have already attained. If one wishes to develop upekkhā: "Sabbe sattā kammassakā" = All beings are the owners of their kamma.

One should not assume that mettā must only be directed exactly as it appears in the Pāḷi text, or that it is improper to direct mettā in ways not directly mentioned. This is because the Pāḷi words that can encompass all beings without distinction are not limited to five types like sattā, pāṇā, bhūtā, puggalā, and attabhāvapariyāpannā; there are also sarīrī, dehī, jīva, pajā, jantu, hinda-gu, etc. Therefore, if one contemplates, "Sabbe sarīrī averā hontu" = May all beings with bodies be free from enmity, it is indeed called directing mettā.

Regarding the modes of directing, although there are only four types in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, if one contemplates with modes such as "Sabbe sattā sukhino hontu" = May all beings be happy, or "Sabbe sattā khemino hontu" = May all beings be safe, it can truly become mettā. Thus, it should be understood based on the evidence of the Metta Sutta Pāḷi that true mettā can occur even if the group of beings to receive mettā is expressed with other names or Pāḷi synonyms, and even if the mode of directing is done through other modes.
509:
(Ī)
## The Method of Developing Mettā in the Metta Sutta
The Metta Sutta Pāḷi was taught by the Blessed One concerning the forest-dwelling monks who were meditation practitioners (kammaṭṭhāna-yogī). It is the Pāḷi text that the Noble Elders who conducted the Councils recorded in the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi and the Khuddakapāṭha Pāḷi. In this Pāḷi text, the Buddha first taught 15 qualities that a person who wishes to develop mettā must practice and fulfill even before developing it. These qualities are called in Pāḷi the 15 'Mettā-pubbabhāga' qualities, meaning the 15 qualities to be fulfilled in advance before directing mettā.

Those qualities are: A person who is skilled in seeking his own good, and who wishes to attain and dwell in the state of Nibbāna, which is extremely cool and peaceful, should act as follows:
1. He must be capable of practicing what is good.
2. He must be upright in his conduct.
3. He must be thoroughly upright, without even a single instance of crookedness.
4. He must be easy to be well-admonished by the wise.
5. He must be gentle in good matters.
6. He must not be arrogant.
7. He must be contented and satisfied only with the requisites he clearly receives.
8. He must be easy to support (not demanding) for others who look after him.
9. He must have few unnecessary duties that are not required for the practice.
10. He must have a light and easy livelihood. (This means not being someone who is cluttered with many possessions when about to travel, but being as light as a bird in flight with only the eight requisites.)
11. He must have calmed and composed faculties.
510:
(U)
12. He must have wisdom that is mature, well-discerning, and skilled in blameless matters.
13. He must not be coarse in body, speech, or mind.
14. He must not be attached to or cling to lay supporters.
(Since this point was taught as an instruction for monks, it is specifically relevant to monks; however, laypeople should also take it as a guideline and understand that they should not be overly attached or clinging to friends.)
15. He must not perform even the slightest action that the wise would blame.
These are the 15 qualities.

Only after first fulfilling these 15 qualities is the mode of directing mettā taught as: "Sukhino vā khemino hontu, sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā" and so on.

If the method of developing mettā-bhāvanā in this Metta Sutta is summarized, three types emerge:
(a) Sabba-saṅgāhika-mettā = Mettā that pervades all beings with a single phrase.
(b) Duka-bhāvanā-mettā = Mettā developed by grouping beings into two sets.
(c) Tika-bhāvanā-mettā = Mettā developed by grouping beings into three sets.

## (A) Sabba-saṅgāhika-mettā
Among these three, the method of developing Sabba-saṅgāhika-mettā is taught in the Pāḷi as: "Sukhino vā khemino hontu, sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā." According to this teaching, if one wishes to develop mettā clearly:
(1) Sabbe sattā sukhino hontu = May all beings be endowed with bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha).
(2) Sabbe sattā khemino hontu = May all beings be free from danger.
(3) Sabbe sattā sukhitattā hontu = May all beings be endowed with mental happiness (cetasika-sukha).
If one recites and develops mettā with such a mindset, it is called developing the Sabba-saṅgāhika-mettā of the Metta Sutta.
511:
(Ū)
## (B) Duka-bhāvanā-mettā
The methods for developing Duka-bhāvanā-mettā and Tika-bhāvanā-mettā can be confusing if one does not know how to extract them from the Pāḷi text. (I will not show how they are confusing, for fear of causing further confusion.) The Duka-bhāvanā-mettā method consists of four pairs:
(1) Tasa-thāvara-duka = A pair of beings who have fear and those who do not.
(2) Diṭṭha-adiṭṭha-duka = A pair of beings who are seen and those who are unseen.
(3) Dūra-santika-duka = A pair of beings who are far and those who are near.
(4) Bhūta-sambhavesī-duka = A pair of beings who are Arahants and those who are worldlings/trainees (sekkha).

Regarding these four:
(1) Tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = May all beings without exception—the 'tasa' (trembling) beings who are worldlings and trainees not yet free from craving and fear, and the 'thāvara' (stable) beings who are Arahants free from craving and fear—be happy in both body and mind. If one contemplates and develops mettā thus, it is true Tasa-thāvara-duka-bhāvanā mettā.
(2) Diṭṭhā vā adiṭṭhā vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = May all beings without exception—those who are seen and those who are unseen—be happy in both body and mind. If one contemplates and develops mettā thus, it is true Diṭṭha-adiṭṭha-duka-bhāvanā mettā.
(3) Dūrā vā avidūrā vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = May all beings without exception—those living in distant places and those living in nearby places—be happy in both body and mind. If one contemplates and develops mettā thus, it is true Dūra-santika-duka-bhāvanā mettā.
512:
(A)
(4) Bhūtā vā sambhavesī vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = If one contemplates and develops the thought, "May all beings without exception—whether they have already come into being (Arahants and those who have completed their existence) or are seeking birth (those in the process of rebirth)—be happy in mind and body," this is truly the development of loving-kindness in the dyad of Bhūta and Sambhavesī.

These four methods of developing loving-kindness mentioned above are called Duka-bhāvanā-mettā. This means developing loving-kindness by categorizing beings into two groups.

## (C) Tika-bhāvanā-mettā
The methods for developing this Tika-bhāvanā-mettā are:
(1) Dīgha-rassa-majjhima-tika = The triad of the long, the short, and the medium-sized.
(2) Mahantāṇuka-majjhima-tika = The triad of the large, the small, and the medium-sized.
(3) Thūlāṇuka-majjhima-tika = The triad of the stout, the lean, and the medium-sized.

Among these three:
(1) Dīghā vā rassā vā majjhimā vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = If one contemplates and develops the thought, "May all beings without exception—whether they have long bodies, short bodies, or medium-sized bodies—be happy in mind and body," this is truly the development of loving-kindness in the triad of Dīgha-rassa-majjhima.

(2) Mahantā vā aṇukā vā majjhimā vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = If one contemplates and develops the thought, "May all beings without exception—whether they have large bodies, small bodies, or medium-sized bodies—be happy in mind and body," this is truly the development of loving-kindness in the triad of Mahantāṇuka-majjhima.

(3) Thūlā vā aṇukā vā majjhimā vā anavasesā sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā = May all beings without exception—whether they have stout bodies, lean bodies, or medium-sized...
513:
(Ai)
...bodies—be happy in mind and body," if one contemplates and develops this thought, it is truly the development of loving-kindness in the triad of Thūlāṇuka-majjhima.

These three methods of developing loving-kindness mentioned above are called Tika-bhāvanā-mettā. This means developing loving-kindness by categorizing beings into three groups.

The aforementioned (A) Sabbasaṅgāhika-mettā, (B) Duka-bhāvanā-mettā, and (C) Tika-bhāvanā-mettā are forms of loving-kindness that aspire for the welfare and happiness of others, and thus they are called Hitasukhāgamapatthanā-mettā.

Just as the aspiration and desire for the welfare and happiness of others is called Hitasukhāgamapatthanā-mettā, the aspiration for others to be free from harm and suffering is called Ahita-dukkhānāgamapatthanā-mettā. The method for developing this Ahita-dukkhānāgamapatthanā-mettā is taught in the Pāḷi Canon as:

Na paro paraṃ nikubbetha,
nātimaññetha katthaci naṃ kañci.
byārosanā paṭighasaññā,
nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya.—

The meaning is: "Oh, may one being not deceive another; may one not despise another; may they not wish for each other's suffering through physical, verbal, or mental provocation or through resentment." If one contemplates and develops this thought, it becomes Ahita-dukkhānāgamapatthanā-mettā.

A question may arise: "Why are various methods from the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi and various methods from the Metta Sutta Pāḷi being presented, instead of showing only a single method for developing loving-kindness?"

The answer is: The minds of worldlings (puthujjanas) are accustomed to wandering restlessly among various objects. A mind that wanders restlessly among various objects cannot remain firmly established in the object of loving-kindness meditation through only one method.
514:
(Aw)
Only by changing the objects of focus and practicing repeatedly can concentration (samādhi) be gradually attained and the mind become firmly established. Therefore, the Buddha taught various methods of developing loving-kindness, and subsequent teachers have also presented them. (Alternatively), individuals who strive in the practice of loving-kindness meditation have different underlying temperaments (ajjhāsaya). For some, the method of developing unspecified loving-kindness (anodhisa-mettā) is clear to their wisdom. For others, the method of specified loving-kindness (odhisa-mettā) is clear. For some, the method of developing it by marking the directions is clear. For some, the method of all-inclusive loving-kindness (sabbasaṅgāhika-mettā) from the Metta Sutta is clear. For some, the dyad (duka) method, and for others, the triad (tika) method is clear. Thus, because those who practice loving-kindness meditation have various underlying temperaments, the Buddha taught various methods, and subsequent teachers have presented them in full so that each person can take the object that is clear to them and develop the Dhamma of loving-kindness.

## The Loving-kindness of Bodhisattas
Regarding the way the Bodhisattas developed loving-kindness (how they fulfilled the Perfection of Loving-kindness), the Pāḷi texts point to the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka. This account of Suvaṇṇasāma appears in two places: the Cariyāpiṭaka Pāḷi and the Mahānipāta. The brief summary in the Cariyāpiṭaka Pāḷi is as follows: "Dear Sāriputta, when I was Suvaṇṇasāma, living in the hermitage created by Sakka, I dwelt in the forest developing loving-kindness toward lions and tigers. I lived in the forest surrounded by lions, tigers, leopards, bears, buffaloes, spotted deer, and wild boars. Not a single animal was afraid of me, nor was I afraid of any animal. Being supported by the power of loving-kindness, I delighted in the forest at that time."

According to this Pāḷi text, nothing specific is known about Suvaṇṇasāma's lineage or birth; it is only known that he lived nobly and delightfully in the forest with wild animals, supported by the power of mutual loving-kindness without fear.
515:
(Awl)
In the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka of the Mahānipāta, after being struck by an arrow, the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇasāma asked, "Why did you shoot me with an arrow?" King Pīḷiyakka replied, "While I was lying in wait to shoot a deer, the deer coming toward the arrow's path saw you and fled in terror. Because of that, I became angry and shot you." In the words spoken in return by Suvaṇṇasāma:

Na maṃ migā uttasanti, araññe sāpadānipi = The deer are not frightened when they see me; (not only deer) even the beasts of prey in the forest are not frightened of me.

Bhīrū kimpurisā rāja, pabbate gandhamādane.
Sammodamānā gacchāma, pabbatāni vanāni ca.
O King, even the very timid Kinnaras living on Mount Gandhamādana come to me with joy, and we wander together through the mountains and forests.

Considering these Pāḷi passages, it is evident that because the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇasāma lived in the forest and developed loving-kindness toward all forest animals, including the Kinnaras, all creatures in the forest felt loving-kindness toward Suvaṇṇasāma.

Among the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, although it is directly stated that one is dear to humans and dear to devas, yakkhas, and petas, based on this Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, it should be noted that not only humans and devas but also animals feel affection through the power of loving-kindness. (The eleven benefits of loving-kindness were previously explained in the section on the Virtue of the Nine-factored Uposatha). Regarding the benefit 'amanussānaṃ piyo' (being dear to non-humans such as devas, yakkhas, and petas), the story of the Elder Visākha is presented in the Brahma-vihāra-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga Commentary. The presentation is as follows:

## The Story of the Elder Visākha
A householder named Visākha from the city of Pāṭaliputta, having heard reports about the island of Sri Lanka, wished to go there to practice the Dhamma. He handed over his wealth and possessions to his wife and children...
516:
(An)
...and after crossing over to the island of Sri Lanka, he reached the Mahāvihāra monastery and was ordained as a monk. After his ordination, he studied the Dve-mātikā (the two summaries of the Vinaya) for five months. He then left the Mahāvihāra and searched for a group of monasteries suitable for developing meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), usually staying for four months at each monastery.

While this Elder Visākha was traveling to the mountain monastery named Cittalapabbata, he encountered a fork in the road. As he was considering which path to take, a mountain deity pointed the way with a finger. He arrived at the Cittalapabbata monastery and stayed there for four months. When he planned to leave for another monastery the next day and lay down to rest, the deity guarding the Manosilā tree at the end of the ambulatory path sat on a plank at the head of the stairs and wept. The Elder asked, "Who is it that is weeping now?" The deity replied, "I am the deity of the Manosilā tree, venerable sir." When asked, "Why are you weeping?" the deity replied, "It is because you are going to depart, venerable sir." When asked again, "How has my staying here been of benefit to you?" the deity replied, "Venerable sir, while you stay here, the devas, yakkhas, and others in this place have loving-kindness for one another (they are affectionate toward each other). Now, if you depart, those devas, yakkhas, and others will engage in discord and strife, and will even speak harsh words to one another."

The Elder said, "If it is as you say, that you all live in peace because of my staying here, then very well, I will stay here for another four months." When those four months had passed and the Elder again planned to leave, the tree deity wept and stopped him as before. In this way, every time the four months were up and the Elder planned to leave, the deity would weep and stop him. Consequently, the Elder did not move to another place and attained Parinibbāna right there at the Cittalapabbata monastery.

Based on this story, the loving-kindness of the Elder Visākha did not only result in those who received his loving-kindness being affectionate toward the Elder himself, who was the sender of loving-kindness; those recipients also felt affection toward one another.
517:
It should be well noted that affection is gained based on the Elder's loving-kindness (mettā).

## The Loving-kindness of the Hunter
In the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka (2) of the Asītinipāta (Book of Eighties), the Bodhisatta, as the King of Swans, was caught in a snare and suffered greatly. Through the discourse of the General Swan, the hunter felt remorse and gently picked up the Bodhisatta. With a heart of great and intense loving-kindness (mettā) aimed at relieving the suffering, he tended to the swan. Due to the power of the hunter's mettā, not even a mark of the snare remained on the leg; the tendons, flesh, and skin were perfectly reconnected, and the leg returned to its original state.

This is only a summary of the essential points from the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka. The full details should be taken from the original Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka. The same is mentioned in the First Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka of the Asītinipāta, the Rohaṇamiga Jātaka (5) of the Vīsatinipāta (Book of Twenties), and the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka (6). Based on these Jātaka accounts, one should well understand the great power and influence of mettā.

## Lust Masquerading as Loving-kindness
It is noteworthy that, according to the Netti-aṭṭhakathā, "Lust (rāga) deceives by wearing the mask of loving-kindness (mettā)." Therefore, one who wishes to develop mettā towards beings should be especially careful not to develop lust that masquerades as mettā. In the Brahmavihāra-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga Commentary, it is also explained: "The subsiding of anger is the perfection of mettā, while the arising of lustful attachment is the failure of mettā."

The meaning is that if one develops mettā towards a person they hate, the angry mind of hatred disappears, and the mettā that desires their welfare enters. This disappearance of hatred is the perfection of mettā. However, if while genuine mettā is arising, a mind of attachment and lustful affection for that person arises, then genuine mettā is lost. This means one has been deceived by lust masquerading as mettā.
518:
This mettā is one of the ten perfections (pāramīs). Just as the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇasāma made every being he encountered feel affection for him, one should develop and practice the perfection of mettā. This practice is not only one of the ten perfections but also one of the forty Samatha meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) that lead to the attainment of jhāna and higher knowledge (abhiññā). Therefore, the noble Bodhisattas of the past developed mettā with sharp concentration and reached the state of jhāna and abhiññā (known in Pali as appanā). Examples of fulfilling the perfections while also attaining jhāna and abhiññā are found in the Seyya Jātaka (2) of the Abbhantara-vagga (4), Tikanipāta, and the Ekarāja Jātaka (3) of the Kāliṅga-vagga (1), Catukkanipāta.

## Seyya Jātaka
The brief summary of the Seyya Jātaka is as follows: King Brahmadatta of Benares ruled in accordance with the ten royal virtues, practiced charity (dāna), observed the five precepts, and kept the Uposatha. At that time, a minister committed an inappropriate offense in the palace and was expelled from the country by King Brahmadatta. He then served the nearby King of Kosala and urged him to attack and seize Benares, saying it would be easily taken. Consequently, the King of Kosala surrounded and attacked Benares. He captured King Brahmadatta, who offered no resistance, along with his ministers, bound them in chains, and imprisoned them.

While in prison, King Brahmadatta developed mettā towards the King of Kosala, who was a thief [of his kingdom], and attained mettā-jhāna. Due to the power of that mettā, the King of Kosala's body began to burn. It felt as if his entire body was being scorched by a pair of torches. Suffering greatly and in intense pain, the King of Kosala asked his ministers, "Why is this happening to me?" The ministers replied, "This great suffering has come upon you because you have imprisoned the virtuous King Brahmadatta." When he heard this, the King of Kosala went quickly to King Brahmadatta, asked for forgiveness, and returned the kingdom, saying, "Let your kingdom be..."
519:
...your kingdom indeed." In this Jātaka, it is clearly evident that King Brahmadatta attained jhāna through the power of mettā.

## Ekarāja Jātaka
The story of the Ekarāja Jātaka is similar to the Seyya Jātaka, involving a minister who committed an inappropriate offense while serving King Brahmadatta of Benares. Both the Seyya Jātaka and the Ekarāja Jātaka follow the same pattern as the Mahāsīlava Jātaka (1) of the Āsīsa-vagga (6), Ekakanipāta. The full details should be sought in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka.

In this Ekarāja Jātaka, specifically, King Dubbhisena of Kosala captured the King of Benares, who was sitting gracefully among his ministers in the palace courtyard. He had him bound, placed in a basket, and hung upside down above the palace gate. King Brahmadatta, focusing on King Dubbhisena the thief, developed mettā and attained jhāna and abhiññā. He then cut the ropes that bound him upside down and remained sitting cross-legged in the air. King Dubbhisena's body also suffered intense burning, and he groaned, "It's so hot, it's so hot!" while rolling back and forth on the ground. When he asked his ministers, "Why is this happening to me?", they replied, "Your Majesty, you have reached this great state of suffering because you unlawfully captured a righteous and innocent king and hung him upside down." He ordered, "If that is so, go quickly and release him." When the king's men went quickly and saw King Brahmadatta sitting cross-legged in the air, they returned and reported the matter to King Dubbhisena.

## The Loving-kindness of the Buddha
During the time of the Buddha, when the Buddha and the Saṅgha were traveling to the city of Kusinārā, the Malla princes made a pact: "If anyone does not go to welcome the Buddha and the Saṅgha, they shall be fined this much." A Malla prince named Roja, who had been a friend of Venerable Ānanda when he was a layman, also went to...
520:
...welcome and serve the Buddha and the Saṅgha along with the other Malla princes. At that time, Venerable Ānanda praised Roja the Malla, saying that it was a great gain for him to welcome and serve the Buddha and the Saṅgha in this way. Roja the Malla honestly replied that he did not welcome them out of devotion to the Triple Gem, but only because of the pact agreed upon by the Malla princes. Venerable Ānanda was not pleased and went to the Buddha to report the matter, requesting the Buddha to make Roja's heart tender. The Buddha then specifically focused on Roja and radiated mettā towards him. Consequently, Roja the Malla, like a young calf separated from its mother, could not stay still in his palace but went to the monastery where the Buddha was staying. With genuine faith arising, he paid homage to the Buddha, listened to the Dhamma, and attained the stage of a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer).

On another occasion, while the Buddha and the Saṅgha were on an alms round in Rājagaha, Devadatta conspired with King Ajātasattu and released the extremely intoxicated elephant Nālāgiri towards the Buddha. The Buddha triumphed over the elephant Nālāgiri by sprinkling the cool water of mettā. At that time, the people of Rājagaha joyfully recited this verse:

'Some tame with sticks, with hooks, and with whips.
The Great Sage tamed the elephant named Nālāgiri without a stick or a weapon, by sprinkling the cool water of mettā.'

The section on the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā Pāramī) is finished.
**********
521:
## (9) Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā Pāramī)
## Meaning of Upekkhā
The Pali word "Upekkhā" is translated into Burmese as "viewing appropriately." Viewing appropriately means, when faced with the distinction between suffering and happiness, not taking sides but viewing both suffering and happiness with balance. This kind of viewing was translated by ancient scholars as "looking on with equanimity."

If one does not carefully consider the meaning of these scholars' words, one might think and say, "Looking on with equanimity means discarding the object without paying attention or caring." This discarding without attention is not what is called upekkhā. Upekkhā must indeed take an object. However, there is no difference such as one way when meeting a painful object and another way when meeting a pleasant object; it is simply viewing and reflecting on them uniformly as a commonality.

## How to Develop Equanimity
The method for developing this equanimity (upekkhā) is the same as the method for developing loving-kindness (mettā) found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali. In the method for developing mettā, there are four modes of practice, resulting in five hundred and twenty-eight methods. However, in the method for developing upekkhā, there is only one mode of practice: "Kammassakā = they are the owners of their own kamma." Therefore, only one-fourth of five hundred and twenty-eight, which is one hundred and thirty-two (132) methods, can be obtained.

The way they are obtained is as follows: as shown in the method for developing mettā, there are twelve types of individuals: five unspecified (anodhisa) individuals and seven specified (odhisa) individuals. Since there is only one mode of practice, "Kammassakā," the number of methods does not increase. [The methods are:] All beings are owners of their kamma; all breathing things are owners of their kamma; all creatures are owners of their kamma; all persons are owners of their kamma; all those included in personality are owners of their kamma; all females are owners of their kamma; all males are owners of their kamma; all noble ones are owners of their kamma; all ordinary persons are owners of their kamma; all devas are owners of their kamma; all humans are owners of their kamma; all those in states of deprivation are owners of their kamma. Without being limited by directions like this...
522:
The twelve methods obtained. When these twelve are multiplied and divided by the ten directions, one gets one hundred and twenty; when added to the twelve methods obtained without dividing by directions, there are one hundred and thirty-two methods in total. Among these one hundred and thirty-two methods, one may develop equanimity (upekkhā) using any method one prefers. It should not be noted that it cannot be developed in other ways.

To clarify further... as shown in the method for developing loving-kindness (mettā), if one wishes to develop it by using other terms to refer to individuals, one can certainly do so. Regarding the mode of development, in the place of the phrase "kammassakā," one can also develop it using other Pali phrases that have the same meaning as this Pali. These Pali phrases, as taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Pañcaka Nipāta, (6) Nīvaraṇa Vagga, (7) Abhiṇha Sutta: "Sabbe sattā kammassakā kammadāyādā kammayonī kammabandhū kammappaṭisaraṇā"...

Kammassakā = they are the owners of their kamma,
Kammadāyādā = they are the heirs of their kamma,
Kammayonī = they have kamma as their origin (source),
Kammabandhū = they have kamma as their kinsman,
Kammappaṭisaraṇā = they have kamma as their refuge—

As translated in this way, since these five Pali terms have the same meaning, instead of developing with "Sabbe sattā kammassakā," one may use:

Sabbe sattā kammadāyādā,
Sabbe sattā kammayonī,
Sabbe sattā kammabandhū, or
Sabbe sattā kammappaṭisaraṇā—

It should be understood and noted that one can develop it using whichever Pali terms one prefers and which are clear to one's wisdom.
523:
## Points to Consider
In this matter, there is something to consider: Loving-kindness (mettā), which is one of the perfections (pāramī) to be fulfilled, is clearly a noble perfection because it involves maintaining a heart that wishes for the happiness of all beings. As for equanimity (upekkhā), although it is also a perfection to be fulfilled and practiced, it involves reflecting on all beings thus: "The happiness or suffering of beings occurs only according to their own kamma. If they have kamma deserving of happiness, they will be happy. If they have kamma deserving of suffering, they will suffer. There is no need for me to be concerned." Would it not be difficult to say that this kind of reflection is very noble? (To use common parlance) Would it be wrong to say that it is simply being indifferent and not caring about beings? Therefore, it is necessary to consider why equanimity can be a noble perfection.

Upon consideration... in both worldly and Dhamma matters, it is natural that things which are difficult to obtain or achieve are valuable, while things which are easy to obtain or achieve are not so valuable. In the world, pebbles, rubbish, and sand are not very valuable because they are so easy to find, whereas gold, silver, and precious gems are very valuable because they are difficult to obtain and achieve; this is clearly known and seen by most people.

Similarly, in the Dhamma, evil states such as greed (lobha) and hatred (dosa) are not valuable at all because they are very easy to obtain and arise; they do not require deliberate planning or effort to produce. They are difficult to prevent and tend to arise excessively; they are very much like worthless weeds. Meritorious states such as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla) cannot arise automatically without effort; they are a collection of states that emerge only when one can strive and practice. Among that collection of states, it is very difficult to obtain and produce genuine loving-kindness (mettā), which is part of the merit of mental development (bhāvanā) and is of a higher level than generosity and virtue.

The difficulty is as follows... among the three types of persons—the enemy (verī), the neutral person (majjhatta), and the dear person (piya)—to develop loving-kindness towards an enemy...
524:
...it is very difficult to produce. It is not as difficult towards a neutral person (majjhatta), who is neither a friend nor an enemy, as it is towards an enemy. It can be developed and produced easily and without difficulty only towards a dear friend (piya). However, if one does not develop loving-kindness towards the enemy (verī) and the neutral person (majjhatta), for whom it is difficult to maintain an object of loving-kindness, and instead follows the easy path by developing it only towards a dear friend, that loving-kindness is not valuable because it lacks difficulty. Furthermore, developing such loving-kindness does not amount to fulfilling the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī).

If one wishes to develop the perfection of loving-kindness properly to reach fulfillment, one must first develop loving-kindness towards oneself. Developing loving-kindness towards oneself in this way is a personal matter, and thus loving-kindness can arise fully and without exception quite easily. It is said that one must first develop loving-kindness towards oneself because one wants to use the loving-kindness that has arisen fully through developing it towards oneself as a benchmark.

Then, when developing it towards the enemy, the neutral person, and the friend, one must be able to develop it equally, without any distinction, just like the benchmark loving-kindness (developed towards oneself). Will it be easy to develop such equal loving-kindness towards all three types of persons, no different from oneself? It is not very easy. Setting aside the enemy and the neutral person, according to the teaching "Attasamaṃ pemaṃ natthi = There is no love equal to self-love," it will be difficult to produce and maintain loving-kindness towards even a dear person (piya) that is equal to oneself. Only the loving-kindness that can be sent equally—to the point where one cannot distinguish between not only a friend but also a neutral person and an enemy, treating them all as the same class and equal to oneself—is a true perfection (pāramī).

If one considers this reason, one will know how difficult it is for true mettā-pāramī to arise and how valuable it is. It is because of developing this difficult and highly valuable mettā-pāramī that even wild animals like tigers and lions...
525:
...felt affection for Suvaṇṇasāma, as shown previously. According to this principle of loving-kindness, in the case of equanimity (upekkhā), the equanimity that would qualify as a perfection is even more difficult than loving-kindness.

The difficulty is as follows... among the three types of persons mentioned, it is not very easy for the state of equanimity to arise even towards a neutral person (majjhatta). In the world, people say things like, "I am now indifferent to this person; I regard him as kammassakā in this business," etc. Because they speak only of the nature of not taking interest or not caring, it is as if such disregard (upekkhā) is of no consequence. In reality, to achieve equanimity, one must actually take the object and pay attention.

Just as it is easy to develop loving-kindness towards a friend, it is also relatively easy to develop equanimity towards a neutral person. The reason is that, by nature, since there is no love or hate towards a neutral person, it is easy to guard against the arising of a mind that wishes for that person's happiness or a mind that wishes for their destruction. It is more difficult to develop equanimity towards an enemy than towards a neutral person. The reason is that, because there is a natural feeling of hatred towards an enemy, if it is said that the enemy has met with ruin, a feeling of joy and delight tends to arise easily. If it is said that the enemy has become prosperous and happy, a feeling of envy and displeasure tends to arise easily. It is difficult to guard against and block both of those feelings from entering or arising. If even a small amount of such feelings enters, the nature of equanimity fails.

Even more difficult than developing equanimity towards an enemy is developing it towards a dear person (piya). The reason is that, because of natural affection and love for a dear person, if it is said that the dear person has attained happiness, the mind tends to become exceptionally joyful and delighted. If it is said that the dear person has met with ruin, extreme worry and grief tend to enter. It is very difficult to restrain and block those two types of feelings—joyful delight and the arrival of worry—from entering.

Without having the kinds of difficulties described, if one can remain indifferent with the same...
526:
...attitude, without any distinction, towards all three classes—the neutral person (majjhatta), the enemy (verī), and the dear person (piya), as well as oneself—only then does the nature of equanimity reach fulfillment and success. As long as there is any difference in attitude towards these three types of persons, the state of equanimity cannot properly reach fulfillment.

In equanimity, as previously shown, it is not a nature of not taking an object, not caring, or discarding it; rather, it is a nature where one must take the object and pay attention. In paying such attention, the genuine equanimity is the ability to clearly reflect, taking beings as the object, thus: "I cannot make any effort for the happiness or for the suffering of beings, including myself. Beings who have come with kamma deserving of happiness will surely be happy. Beings who have come with kamma deserving of suffering will surely suffer. Since the happiness and suffering of those beings are related only to their own kamma, one cannot be concerned in any way." Because one does not have to worry or be concerned for beings in this way, the state of equanimity is very subtle; it is very steady and peaceful. The further it reaches above loving-kindness, the higher its level becomes.

Regarding the high level... this equanimity, like loving-kindness, is one of the forty subjects of tranquility meditation (samatha-kammaṭṭhāna) and is also one of the ten perfections (pāramī). According to the method of tranquility, if one wishes to meditate on and develop the subject of equanimity, it must be developed only for the highest jhāna; it is not to be developed for the lower jhānas. To clarify further... for those with duller wisdom, the jhāna reaches the end of the jhāna stages only after five successful completions. For those individuals, the Buddha taught the five jhānas. This is called the fivefold method (pañcaka-naya). Therefore, for those with duller wisdom, the jhāna obtained the first time is the first jhāna, and the jhānas obtained the second, third, fourth, and fifth times are the fifth jhāna; thus, there are five jhānas for those with duller wisdom.

For individuals with sharp wisdom, they reach the end of the jhāna states in only four successful completions. For those individuals, the Buddha taught the four jhānas. This is called the fourfold method (catukka-naya). Therefore, for those with sharp wisdom, the jhāna obtained the first time is the first jhāna, and the jhānas obtained the second, third, and fourth times are the fourth jhāna; thus, there are four jhānas.
527:
(Continued)

There are two methods: the fivefold jhāna for persons of duller intellect and the fourfold jhāna for persons of sharp intellect. One who strives to attain jhāna before having attained any jhāna at all should not yet practice the meditation on equanimity (upekkhā-kammaṭṭhāna). According to the fivefold method, the meditation on equanimity is associated only with the fifth jhāna; according to the fourfold method, it is associated only with the fourth jhāna. Therefore, if one is a person of duller intellect, one can practice the meditation on equanimity only when one wishes to attain the final fifth jhāna after having successfully practiced other samatha-kammaṭṭhānas up to the fourth jhāna. If one is a person of sharp intellect, one can practice the meditation on equanimity only when one wishes to attain the final fourth jhāna after having successfully practiced other samatha-kammaṭṭhānas up to the third jhāna. The reason is that, as previously shown, equanimity is a state that is subtle, stable, and noble, and thus it pertains only to the higher jhānas. It does not pertain to the lower jhānas.

Loving-kindness (mettā) pertains only to the lower four or three jhānas. Considering this point, it is evident that the state of equanimity is more noble and superior to loving-kindness. If the intention is merely to fulfill the Perfection of Equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) and not to practice it as a samatha-kammaṭṭhāna, one can develop and practice equanimity at any time.

## Mahālomahaṃsacariya

Regarding this Perfection of Equanimity, I shall further present the manner in which the Bodhisatta fulfilled the intense Perfection of Equanimity, which was so profound it caused the hair to stand on end, as recorded in the Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā.

In the distant past, the Bodhisatta was born into a noble family of great wealth. When he reached the age for education, he mastered all branches of knowledge under a Disāpāmokkha teacher. Upon his return, he lived while properly looking after and serving his parents. When his parents passed away, his relatives told him to properly maintain and increase the wealth and property inherited from his parents.
528:
(Continued)

However, the Bodhisatta, based on the nature of the impermanence of conditioned things (saṅkhāra), developed an increasing and intense sense of dread and fear toward all realms of existence. Having attained the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) regarding the body, he had no desire whatsoever to descend into the entanglement of the thicket of defilements (kilesa) which is overwhelmed by the burdensome affairs of household life. For a long time, his desire to escape from the realm of sense-pleasures (kāma) had been constantly increasing. Although he wished to renounce his vast wealth and become a monk in accordance with this increasing desire, he reflected: "If I become a monk, I will still become prominent through people praising my virtues." Loathing such fame, gain, and respect, he did not become a monk but instead thought: "Will I be able to remain unshaken by worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain and loss?" Thinking thus, he resolved to bring the Perfection of Equanimity to its pinnacle by fulfilling practices such as enduring the oppression of others and maintaining neutrality toward them. He left home in his ordinary clothes, leading a life of extreme austerity. He appeared to others as if he were weak, dull, or someone without a mind (incapable of anger), becoming an object of disrespect and harassment for many. He wandered through villages and market towns, staying only one night in each place. In places where he was treated with great disrespect, he stayed for a long time. When the clothes he wore became worn out and decayed, he made do with whatever small pieces of cloth remained. When those pieces decayed further, he did not accept clothes offered by anyone but wandered about covering his body with whatever material he could find just to conceal his shame.

After living in this manner for a long time, he arrived at a certain market town. In that town, the children and youths were of a transgressive nature. Some of them, such as the sons, grandsons, and servants of hunters or those associated with the king, were flighty in mind, arrogant, frivolous, harsh-tongued, and spoke scattered, disorderly words. They constantly wandered about making fun of and mocking others. When they saw elderly people...
529:
(Continued)

...or men and women walking in poverty, they would follow them, put ash into a cone, and pour it over their backs. They would also place Pandanus leaves under their armpits (to cause unbearable irritation). When the elderly grandfathers and grandmothers turned back to look because of such perverse actions, the youths would mock them by imitating the hunched, bent, or crippled, and laugh intensely at them.

When the Bodhisatta saw these youths in that market town acting so improperly and transgressively, he thought: "Now I have found a good support and opportunity to fulfill the Perfection of Equanimity," and he stayed in that market town. When the transgressive youths saw the Bodhisatta, they began to perform their perverse actions. The Bodhisatta, pretending to be unable to endure their actions and pretending to be afraid, got up and ran away. The youths followed closely behind him.

When those foolish youths followed him without losing sight of him, the Bodhisatta reached the vicinity of a cemetery. He thought: "In this place, there is no one to forbid or speak to these foolish youths. I shall fulfill my Perfection of Equanimity beautifully." He entered the cemetery and lay down, using a human bone (skull) as a pillow. The foolish youths, seeing their chance, went to where the Bodhisatta was lying and committed various perverse offenses, such as spitting on him with phlegm and saliva, and then they left. In this manner, those foolish youths came and did this every single day.

Wise people, however, when they saw the foolish youths committing such offenses, forbade them. Recognizing that "This person is a great noble ascetic and yogi of great power and majesty," they performed extensive acts of worship, homage, and reverence.
530:
(Continued)

The Bodhisatta, however, felt no love for the wise who worshipped him, nor did he feel any hatred for the fools who offended him. He maintained a neutral and equal attitude toward both, thus fulfilling the Perfection of Equanimity.

(Although this collection of events is called the Mahālomahaṃsa Jātaka, the name Mahālomahaṃsa is not the name of the Bodhisatta. It is called Mahālomahaṃsa because everyone who saw the practice of this Bodhisatta experienced great horripilation, with their hair standing on end.)

## The Fulfillment of Equanimity

The subsiding of both hatred and love is the fulfillment of equanimity. (The Perfection of Equanimity is the very peace of both hatred and love; as long as they have not subsided, it is meant that the Perfection of Equanimity does not occur.)

Being in a daze or staring blankly without knowing or seeing anything regarding social affairs is the failure of equanimity. It is meant that such a state should not be called equanimity. Therefore, such staring in a daze is not equanimity; it is merely ignorance that is mistaken for equanimity. True equanimity should be understood as clearly perceiving the causes of happiness and suffering, and good and bad, yet reflecting with clear vision: "These matters do not concern me; they concern only the kamma of those beings."

In the Netti-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: "Intense delusion and staring in a daze can deceive by appearing as neutrality toward various good and bad objects. (Moha can deceive by pretending to be equanimity.) The lack of desire to strive in wholesome states can deceive by appearing as the divine abiding of equanimity. (The element of laziness, kosajja, can pretend to be equanimity.)" (Netti-aṭṭhakathā, page 90). As explained in the Netti-aṭṭhakathā, one should be especially mindful...
531:
(Continued)

...not to be deceived by delusion (moha) and laziness (kosajja) which masquerade as equanimity.

## The Definition of Equanimity

In terms of ultimate reality (paramattha), equanimity is a distinct mental factor that can be clearly identified; it is the mental factor called tatramajjhattatā. However, not all instances of the mental factor tatramajjhattatā can be called the Perfection of Equanimity. Since tatramajjhattatā is a mental factor associated with all beautiful consciousness (sobhana-citta), it arises in every beautiful consciousness. The tatramajjhattatā that can truly be the Perfection of Equanimity is the mental factor that takes beings as its object and reflects on the fact that beings are the owners of their own kamma (kamma-sakata), thinking: "The happiness and suffering of beings occur only according to their kamma; no one can intervene and take responsibility for it." The tatramajjhattatā that arises by taking the Triple Gem, dāna, or sīla as objects, without taking beings as objects, cannot be the Perfection of Equanimity.

Furthermore, when one looks on with neutrality by taking the happiness and suffering of beings as an object, the mental factor tatramajjhattatā does not arise alone; many associated mental factors and consciousness arise together. In such an occurrence, although the object of tatramajjhattatā and the object of the associated consciousness and mental factors are the same, the neutrality toward the happiness and suffering of beings is the inherent nature of tatramajjhattatā. Therefore, this tatramajjhattatā is specifically designated by the name "Perfection of Equanimity." When this occurs, the consciousness and mental factors associated with tatramajjhattatā also become included in the Perfection of Equanimity; the only distinction is that tatramajjhattatā acts as the leader and chief.

## The Ten Types of Equanimity

Thus, although it is a distinct mental factor in terms of ultimate reality, there are also types of equanimity that cannot be included in the Perfection of Equanimity. For this reason, in the Visuddhimagga-aṭṭhakathā and the Atthasālinī-aṭṭhakathā—
532:
(Chi)
It is stated that there are ten types of equanimity (upekkhā):
1. Saḷaṅgupekkhā (Six-limbed equanimity),
2. Brahmavihārupekkhā (Divine-abiding equanimity),
3. Bojjhaṅgupekkhā (Enlightenment-factor equanimity),
4. Vīriyupekkhā (Effort equanimity),
5. Saṅkhārupekkhā (Formations equanimity),
6. Vedanupekkhā (Feeling equanimity),
7. Vipassanupekkhā (Insight equanimity),
8. Tatramajjhattupekkhā (Equanimity as specific neutrality),
9. Jhānupekkhā (Jhāna equanimity),
10. Pārisuddhupekkhā (Purification equanimity).

(1) Among these ten, Saḷaṅgupekkhā refers to the state of Arahants who, when the six types of pleasant or unpleasant objects appear at the six sense doors, do not rejoice when a desirable (iṭṭha) object appears, nor are they displeased when an undesirable (aniṭṭha) object appears.
