They always maintain mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) and observe with equanimity. This equanimity, which does not abandon the pure original nature when the six types of pleasant or unpleasant objects appear at the six sense doors of an Arahant, is called Saḷaṅgupekkhā. (It means equanimity regarding the six limbs, where the six limbs refer to the six sense doors and the six sense objects.)

(2) Brahmavihārupekkhā is the neutrality observed by considering that the happiness or suffering of beings occurs only according to their own kamma. (It means equanimity through noble living. This Brahmavihārupekkhā itself is the Perfection of Equanimity, Upekkhā Pāramī.)

(3) Bojjhaṅgupekkhā refers to the equanimity called 'evenness among conascent states.' When striving to attain the Path and Fruition (magga-phala), if some factors are weak and others are excessive, one must normally uplift the weak and restrain the excessive. However, upon reaching the state of the Enlightenment Factors (bojjhaṅga), which are the constituent parts of the Path, the associated mental factors become balanced without excess or deficiency.
533:
(Chī)
(4) Vīriyupekkhā is the effort that occurs in a balanced manner, neither lacking nor excessive, while striving to attain the Path and Fruition.

(5) Saṅkhārupekkhā is the nature of equanimity in taking as objects the formations (saṅkhāra) such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), which are respectively abandoned through the first jhāna and so on, while striving to attain concentration and the Path and Fruition. (This Saṅkhārupekkhā occurs when insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) matures. When insight knowledge is not yet mature, one must take care in abandoning formations like the hindrances. When it matures, one no longer needs to pay special attention to those formations but remains in a state of equanimity.)

(6) Vedanupekkhā is the feeling of experiencing the taste of an object neither as pleasant nor as painful, but only as a neutral experience.

(7) Vipassanupekkhā is the contemplation with a neutral stance when specifically investigating the nature of impermanence (anicca) and so on of the aggregates (khandha) and other phenomena. (In this context, the brief meaning of the word 'Vipassanā' should be understood as follows: 'Vi' = special, 'Passanā' = seeing. Seeing with special knowledge is called Vipassanā. The manner of special seeing is this: seeing that in the world there are entities such as 'I', 'others', 'man', 'woman', etc., is merely the basic perception known by everyone; it is only perception (saññā). It is not a special knowledge penetrating with wisdom. Seeing that 'In the ultimate sense of reality, there is no such thing as a self or another being; it is merely a collection of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) that is prone to disintegration and destruction; and those mind and matter are perishing incessantly moment by moment; it only appears as if they do not perish because new phenomena are constantly arising to replace them'—this is called Vipassanā. This is the summary of its meaning.)

(8) Tatramajjhattupekkhā is the state of occurring in a neutral manner without having to strive for harmony among the conascent (sahajāta) states that are already balanced in their respective functions.
534:
(Chu)
(9) Jhānupekkhā is the nature of being able to remain neutral even towards the sublime bliss (sukha) occurring in the third jhāna, without falling into or being involved in the aspect of that bliss. (It refers to the equanimity obtained specifically in the final jhāna.)

(10) Pārisuddhupekkhā is the nature of being purified from all opposing states and not having concern for the pacification of those opposing states. (It is the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, which is purified from all opposing states.)

Among these ten, six types—Saḷaṅgupekkhā, Brahmavihārupekkhā, Bojjhaṅgupekkhā, Tatramajjhattupekkhā, Jhānupekkhā, and Pārisuddhupekkhā—are identical in their ultimate essence (tathā-sabhāva). They are all the single mental factor of neutrality (tatramajjhattatā cetasika).

One might ask: "If they are the same ultimate essence, why are they divided into six types?" (The answer is:) Although they are the same ultimate essence, they are called by six different names according to their different occasions. For example, although it is the same single person, he is called 'kumāra' (child) when young, 'yuva' (youth) when grown, and as he ages further, 'vuḍḍha' (elder), 'senāpati' (general), 'rāja' (king), and so on, being distinguished by age and occasion. This is explained in the Visuddhimagga Commentary and the Atthasālinī Commentary.

To make it clearer: "They are distinguished into six types because of their different functions (kicca)." The differences in function are:
(1) As previously shown, the function of Saḷaṅgupekkhā is to be able to attend to all six types of pleasant and unpleasant objects with a neutral mind.
(2) The function of Brahmavihārupekkhā is to remain neutral regarding the happiness and suffering of beings by taking beings as the object.
(3) The function of Bojjhaṅgupekkhā is to remain neutral in attending to the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that must be abandoned while striving to attain jhāna, path, and fruition.
535:
(Chū)
(4) The function of Vīriyupekkhā is the nature of effort occurring evenly without deficiency or excess.
(5) The function of Saṅkhārupekkhā is to remain neutral without uplifting or restraining the conascent (sahajāta) states that are occurring evenly without deficiency or excess.
(6) The function of Vedanupekkhā is to remain neutral in the experience of an object.
(7) The function of Vipassanupekkhā is the nature of remaining neutral in the investigation and scrutiny of mind and matter through the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
(8) The function of Tatramajjhattupekkhā is the nature of remaining neutral towards associated states that are occurring evenly.
(9) The function of Jhānupekkhā is the nature of remaining neutral even towards the most sublime jhāna bliss.
(10) The function of Pārisuddhupekkhā is the nature of equanimity purified from all opposing states.

In this way, one should note that not only the functions but also the locations and objects are distinct. Since Vīriyupekkhā is the mental factor of effort (vīriya cetasika) and Vedanupekkhā is the mental factor of feeling (vedanā cetasika), these two types of equanimity do not mix in essence with the others. Saṅkhārupekkhā and Vipassanupekkhā are both only the mental factor of wisdom (paññā cetasika). Although these two are the same in essence, they are divided into two because of their distinct functions. The difference in function is:

Vipassanupekkhā is the nature of contemplating to see clearly the three characteristics of formations—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—without needing to pay special attention anymore. Saṅkhārupekkhā is the nature of remaining neutral without fear or trembling in taking formations as objects.

## Upekkhā Pāramī and the Ten Types of Equanimity
Among these ten types of equanimity presented by the Great Commentators, the 'Upekkhā Pāramī' (Perfection of Equanimity) does not appear directly. One might wonder whether it is absent because Upekkhā Pāramī is not included in any of the ten types, or if the presentation by the Great Commentators is incomplete. Upon reflection, it should not be said that the Great Commentators' presentation is incomplete or lacking; rather, it should be understood that Upekkhā Pāramī is included within Brahmavihārupekkhā among the ten types of equanimity already shown.
536:
(Che)
Is it not included, or is the presentation of the Great Commentators incomplete? Upon reflection, it should not be said that the presentation of the Great Commentators is incomplete or lacking. It should be understood that Upekkhā Pāramī is included within Brahmavihārupekkhā among the ten types of equanimity previously shown.

Some teachers, however, state: "Brahmavihārupekkhā and Upekkhā Pāramī are different. The way they differ is: being able to maintain a single, undifferentiated mind towards those who wrong or offend oneself and those who treat one with love and care is Upekkhā Pāramī. Maintaining a single state of mind regarding the happiness and suffering of beings, thinking that their happiness and suffering occur only according to their kamma, is Brahmavihārupekkhā."

According to these teachers, Upekkhā Pāramī focuses only on those who wrong or love oneself; it does not focus on the nature of happiness and suffering. If it focuses on the happiness and suffering of beings, it is not Upekkhā Pāramī but only Brahmavihārupekkhā. However, in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāli, the nature of Upekkhā Pāramī is taught as:

*Tatheva tvampi sukhadukkhe, tulābhūto sadā bhava.*
*Upekkhāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissati.*

In this Pāli passage, it is taught based on both happiness and suffering: "*Sukhadukkhe tulābhūto* = May you be like a balance scale in both happiness and suffering." Also, in the Mahālomahaṃsa-cariya section of the Cariyāpiṭaka Pāli:

*Ye me dukkhaṃ upadahanti, ye ca denti sukhaṃ mama.*
*Sabbesaṃ samako homi.-----*

Starting with these words, it is taught based on both suffering and happiness: "Those who bring me suffering and those who give me happiness, I am equal towards all of them." Furthermore, it is taught: "*Sukhadukkhe tulābhūto, yasesu ayasesu ca* = Being like a balance scale whether in happiness or suffering, or in fame or ill-repute."
537:
(Chai)
In the Atthasālinī Commentary and the Jātaka Commentaries, it is also explained based on both happiness and suffering: "In this way, although the village children caused happiness and suffering through spitting phlegm and such, or through worshipping with flowers and perfumes, the equanimity of the Bodhisatta, which did not overstep the nature of neutrality, is 'Paramattha Upekkhā Pāramī' (The Ultimate Perfection of Equanimity)."

Furthermore, in the Visuddhimagga Commentary and the Atthasālinī Commentary, when describing the characteristics of Brahmavihārupekkhā, they state: "*Sattesu majjhattākāralakkhaṇā upekkhā* = Equanimity has the characteristic of occurring as a neutral mode towards beings." Since it is stated generally as "towards beings," the term 'beings' can include both those who wrong oneself and those who love oneself, as well as happy beings and suffering beings. Therefore, the meaning that the mode of being able to maintain a neutral mind towards those who wrong or love oneself is also Brahmavihārupekkhā is clear. If that is so, the meaning that Upekkhā Pāramī is included in Brahmavihārupekkhā also becomes clear.

The section on Upekkhā Pāramī ends.

## The Chronicle of Dīpaṅkara Buddha
Regarding the statement in Page (287), Paragraph (A): "(Prince Dīpaṅkara reached maturity)", I shall present a point for reflection.

Prince Siddhattha, the Bodhisatta of our Gautama Buddha who appeared during a lifespan of one hundred years, reached maturity and took over the throne to rule at the age of sixteen. At what age should the maturity of Prince Dīpaṅkara, who appeared during a lifespan of one hundred thousand years, be defined? This point should be considered and reflected upon deeply.
538:
(Chau)
Just as the age of maturity for Prince Siddhattha, who was born during a hundred-year lifespan, is designated as sixteen years, it would not be appropriate to designate the age of maturity for the Bodhisatta Prince Dīpaṅkara, who was born during a hundred-thousand-year lifespan, as sixteen years. Furthermore, if one were to designate it according to the same ratio (sixteen percent) as in the hundred-year lifespan, it would be as if the age of maturity in a hundred-thousand-year lifespan should be designated as sixteen thousand (16,000) years. However, it would be difficult to assert or record that it must follow this exact proportion.

This is because, in the Cakkavatti Sutta, the third sutta of the Pāthikavagga of the Dīgha Nikāya, where the Buddha taught by distinguishing various lifespans:

For the ten-year lifespan:
"Dasa-vassāyukesu bhikkhave manussesu pañca-vassikā kumārikā alaṃpateyyā bhavissanti."
"Monks, among humans with a ten-year lifespan, five-year-old girls will be fit for marriage."

And for the eighty-thousand-year lifespan:
"Asīti-vassasahassāyukesu bhikkhave manussesu pañca-vassasatikā kumārikā alaṃpateyyā bhavissanti."
"Monks, among humans with an eighty-thousand-year lifespan, five-hundred-year-old girls will be fit for marriage."

In this Pali text, the Buddha only specifically taught the age of maturity for girls in the ten-year and eighty-thousand-year lifespans. For humans of other lifespans, He did not teach the age of maturity in this manner. Furthermore, in the ten-year and eighty-thousand-year lifespans, it was directly taught only for girls; although it was not directly taught for boys, if one wishes to assume, one should assume that it would be the same for boys as it is for girls.
539:
(Chaw)
Thus, just as the age of maturity differs between the ten-year and hundred-year lifespans, the age of maturity for humans will also certainly differ between the hundred-year and thousand-year lifespans, and between the thousand-year and ten-thousand-year lifespans, and so on.

According to the Cakkavatti Sutta Pali, it is clear that five hundred years is the age of maturity in an eighty-thousand-year lifespan. However, in the case of Prince Dīpaṅkara, it is a hundred-thousand-year lifespan, so it remains to be considered whether five hundred years should be designated as the age of maturity or not.

Considering the gradual increase from the ten-year lifespan onwards, the age of maturity should also differ between the eighty-thousand-year and hundred-thousand-year lifespans. Thus, it could be said that if it is five hundred years for eighty thousand, it should be six hundred years for a hundred thousand. Since there is no direct scriptural text, this should be understood through reasoning.

Alternatively, in the ascending cycle (vivaṭṭa-kappa) where lifespans increase, the age of maturity is designated as five hundred years. It could also be argued that even if the lifespan exceeds eighty thousand and reaches a hundred thousand, it should be designated as five hundred years, which is the most frequent number appearing in the Pali texts. Therefore, it should be said that the age of maturity for Prince Dīpaṅkara is either five hundred or six hundred years.

On page (288), in paragraph (b):
This describes how the Bodhisatta Prince Dīpaṅkara went out to the park and saw the omens, as stated in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary.

According to this account, it is mentioned that the Bodhisatta saw only the three great omens—the old man, the sick man, and the dead man—created by the devas; the fourth omen, the monk, was not mentioned. This implies that he renounced the world after seeing only the first three omens without seeing the monk omen.
540:
(Chan)
In the Pali text, however:
"Nimitte caturo disvā, hatthiyānena nikkhami."
"Having seen all four omens, he departed for the forest by elephant vehicle."

According to this Pali text, he must have seen all four omens before departing for the forest on an elephant vehicle.

In the section on the renunciation of Prince Siddhattha, which is explained in detail in texts such as the Jātaka Commentary, it is stated that he departed for the forest separately after seeing the four great omens in sequence, four months apart.

In the Mahāpadāna Sutta of the Mahāvagga Pali, in the section on the renunciation of the Bodhisatta Vipassī Buddha by chariot, it is taught that on his first trip to the park, he saw an old man on the way and returned to the palace from that very spot without reaching the park. Similarly, on the second trip he saw a sick man, and on the third trip he saw a dead man, returning to the palace each time. On the fourth trip, however, he saw a monk and was pleased; he ordered the chariot to be driven to where the monk was. Upon arrival, he sent the charioteer back with the chariot and did not return to the palace, but renounced the world immediately.

According to this Pali text, the Bodhisatta Vipassī Buddha went out to the park four times, saw the four great omens in sequence, and on the fourth time, he did not return to the palace but renounced immediately, so there was no separate departure for the forest. However, because the renunciation happened immediately after seeing the monk omen on the fourth trip, it is taught in the Vipassī Buddhavaṃsa Pali:

"Nimitte caturo disvā, rathayānena nikkhami."
"Having seen the four omens, he departed by chariot vehicle."
541:
(Chār)
Therefore, in this Dīpaṅkara Buddhavaṃsa as well:

"Nimitte caturo disvā, hatthiyānena nikkhami."

In order not to contradict this Buddhavaṃsa Pali text, and because in this very Buddhavaṃsa Commentary it will be explained later that the Bodhisattas of the twenty-four Buddhas renounced after seeing the four great omens—and since those explanations are based on the Pali text "Nimitte caturo disvā"—to ensure consistency within the Commentary:

"On the fourth occasion, the Bodhisatta Prince Dīpaṅkara, being adorned with ornaments provided by the deva Vissakamma, departed for the park riding a royal elephant, surrounded by eighty-four thousand (84,000) elephants. Upon seeing the monk omen, he was pleased and developed the desire to renounce. Surrounded by a great army, he entered the park, descended from the royal elephant, and wandered through the park. While sitting on a very cool and pleasant stone slab, at the moment he formed the intention to renounce, a Mahābrahmā from the Suddhāvāsa realm, who was an Arahant, brought the eight requisites and appeared clearly before the Bodhisatta to offer them."

This should be understood in this way.

Only by understanding it thus will it not contradict the natural law (dhammatā) included among the thirty natural laws of Bodhisattas: "Cattāri nimittāni disvā jātamattaputtānaṃ mahāsattānaṃ mahābhinikkhamanaṃ" = "Every Bodhisatta renounces the world after seeing the four great omens and immediately upon the birth of a son."

On page (289), in paragraph (c):
The statement by the commentator that ten million (one koṭi) people followed the Bodhisatta Prince Dīpaṅkara in renouncing the world seems like it might be too many.
542:
(Ja)
One might wonder and ask if it is not too many. It cannot be said to be too many. The reason is that it was a time of a hundred-thousand-year lifespan.

To elaborate further, in the Cakkavatti Sutta of the Pātheyya Pali:
"Among humans living in an eighty-thousand-year lifespan, there are only three types of illness:
(1) Hunger,
(2) Drowsiness and lethargy after eating,
(3) Aging."

It is taught that during this eighty-thousand-year lifespan, the great island of Jambudīpa is so prosperous and wealthy that villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals are only a 'cock's flight' apart. Just as the Avīci hell is crowded with hell-beings, Jambudīpa is crowded with people during the eighty-thousand-year lifespan.

If people were this crowded even during an eighty-thousand-year lifespan, it goes without saying that they would be even more crowded during a hundred-thousand-year lifespan.

Considering the reason for such density and abundance: in an era of extremely long lifespans, after beings are born, no various diseases arise (because there are no significant diseases, deaths are very few). While births might not be few, because those who perish are extremely few, the population becomes very large.

Therefore, it should be well noted that saying "about ten million people followed him in renouncing" should not be considered an exaggeration.

The condition of people with eighty-thousand or a hundred-thousand-year lifespans, who are virtuous beings with extremely pure minds,
543:
(Jā)
should not be compared or considered alongside the people of the current era who have very short lives. Indeed, the wholesome merit (kusalakamma) of modern humans is weak; therefore, diseases are prevalent, life is short, and food is scarce. Although they strive hard to produce and obtain plenty of clothing, paddy, and rice for human use, their efforts often do not go far and fail to yield results, mostly ending in ruin. In the era of the virtuous ones of old, because their wholesome merit was powerful, there were no diseases and life was long. Food was abundant. It should be believed and noted that due to the power of their merit, all their efforts for clothing did not go to waste, and even a small area could produce a great amount of clothing.

On page (300), in paragraph (d):
When it is said, "The lifespan of that Dīpaṅkara Buddha was a hundred thousand," it should not be understood to mean that the Buddha Dīpaṅkara remained for the full hundred thousand years. It should be understood that He taught only the hundred-thousand-year lifespan that humans lived at that time.

It is the nature of Buddhas to remain for only four-fifths of the lifespan in which they are born, and they invariably attain Parinibbāna when one part remains. Therefore, in the commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta of the Mahāvagga, in the explanation of the lifespan limit (āyupariccheda):
"Āyuppamāṇaṃ pañca koṭṭhāse katvā cattāri thatvā pañcame vijjamāneyo parinibbuto."
This explains that "having divided the lifespan into five parts, they remain for four parts and attain Parinibbāna while the fifth part still exists."

Therefore, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, who was born during a hundred-thousand-year lifespan, divided the hundred thousand years into five parts, remained for the four parts which equal eighty thousand years, and attained Parinibbāna when one part remained. Thus, it should be understood that the Buddha's lifespan was eighty thousand years.

The evidence from the Pali text is: in the section where the Buddha Koṇḍañña prophesied to the Bodhisatta King Vijitāvī that he would become a Buddha named Gotama in the future:
"Āyu vassasataṃ tassa, gotamassa yasassino."
Although it is taught that "The lifespan of that famous Gotama is a hundred years..."
544:
(Gyi)
That one hundred years refers only to the era in which He was born; as for the actual lifespan of Gotama Buddha, as previously stated, it should be considered that He lived for only eighty years, which is four-fifths of the one hundred years.

On page (301), paragraph (e):
Regarding the teaching, "That Buddha Dīpaṅkara, together with His community of disciples, has reached the state of peace (Parinibbāna)...", it should not be understood that the Buddha and His disciples attained Parinibbāna at the same time.

In the Verañja-kaṇḍa of the Pārājika Pāḷi, in the response given by the Buddha to the Venerable Sāriputta's inquiry regarding the long or short duration of the Sāsana (Dispensation), if one summarizes the detailed explanation of the commentator: "The Sāsana of the three Buddhas—Vipassī, Sikhī, and Vessabhū—who were long-lived, lasted for only two generations of disciples, whereas the Sāsana of later Buddhas such as Kakusandha lasted for many more generations than just two."

Since it is explained that the Sāsana of long-lived Buddhas lasts for two generations of disciples, it should be understood that the Sāsana of Buddha Dīpaṅkara, who appeared during the 100,000-year lifespan era, and Buddha Sumana, who appeared during the 90,000-year lifespan era, also lasted for two generations of disciples.

Regarding those two generations of disciples: for the first generation of disciples who met Buddha Dīpaṅkara, there were 100,000 years; for the second generation of disciples who were ordained under those first disciples, there were another 100,000 years. Thus, for 200,000 years after Buddha Dīpaṅkara attained Parinibbāna, the disciples continued to exist prominently. It should be understood that only after those 200,000 years did the Sāsana disappear along with the disciples.
545:
(Ghī)
In the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, however, at the beginning of the Koṇḍañña Buddhavaṃsa explanation, it is stated: "When Buddha Dīpaṅkara attained Parinibbāna, His Sāsana lasted for 100,000 years." According to this view, it is to be understood that the Sāsana lasted for only one generation of disciples.

The Chronicle of Buddha Dīpaṅkara ends.

## The Chronicle of Buddha Maṅgala
On page (317), paragraph (f):
Regarding the term "Vaṅkapab Mountain"... in the Pāḷi term Vaṅkapabbata (Vaṅka = crooked/winding; Pabbata = mountain; Vaṅkapabbata = crooked mountain). When ancient teachers translated Vaṅkapabbata into Burmese, they did not translate it literally as "crooked mountain" to fit Burmese speech; instead, they dropped the last two letters 'ba' (ဗ) and 'ta' (တ) from Pabbata and translated it only as "Vaṅkapab" in a corrupted Pāḷi form.

Nowadays, the word has shifted and is no longer called "Vaṅkapab" but is called "Vaṅkapā" (labyrinth). Thus, the intended meaning of the term "Vaṅkapā," which evolved from "Vaṅkapab," is "crooked mountain."

In present-day light festivals and similar events, structures made to be difficult for people to enter and exit (because they consist of winding paths) are called "Vaṅkapā," intending to compare them to the crooked mountain.

For example, among the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), the practice of taking cloth discarded on the dust/ground, sewing it into a robe, and wearing it is originally called "Paṃsukūlika-dhutaṅga" in Pāḷi. However, the last two letters 'li' (လိ) and 'ka' (က) were dropped from the word Paṃsukūlika, and it was called "Paṃsukū." From that "Paṃsukū," the word shifted to "Paṃthakū" and further changed to "Pintakū."

The original meaning of the word "Paṃsukū" is cloth that is mixed with dust because people have discarded it on the dust as they no longer wish to use it.
546:
(Ghu)
It refers to cloth mixed with dust. In ancient times, because holy men wished to abandon greed and attachment regarding clothing, they did not seek good, new cloth but instead searched for and collected discarded rags. Such collection is called "collecting Paṃthakū."

Furthermore, the practice of monks not keeping various dishes but putting both rice and curry into the alms-bowl and consuming them is called "Pattapiṇḍika-dhutaṅga" in Pāḷi. When ancient teachers translated this Pāḷi into Burmese vernacular derived from Pāḷi, they dropped the two letters 'ḍi' (ဍိ) and 'ka' (က) and translated it as "Pattapiṇ." From there, the word shifted to "Pattapaing" and then again to "Bat-la-baing." In the context of this Pattapiṇḍika-dhutaṅga or Pattapaing-dhutaṅga—although the intended meaning is to consume rice and curry together in a single bowl (or dish)—some people take the meaning to an extreme, believing one must mix them until the curry and rice are indistinguishable before eating. They then use the expression "like Bat-la-baing" to describe things that are so mixed that other edible items cannot be distinguished.

Furthermore, although the practice of living only at the foot of a tree appears in the scriptures as "Rukkhamūlika-dhutaṅga," in Burmese vernacular, the two letters 'li' (လိ) and 'ka' (က) are dropped, and it is called "Rukkhamū-dhutaṅga."

The word "Vaṅkapā" is similar to these aforementioned names of the dhutaṅga practices.

On page (325), paragraph (g):
In describing the qualities and attributes of Brahmins, the commentator explained the meaning of the two terms (Padako, Veyyākaraṇo) in the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga: "He is able to teach, perceive, and master various types of words (pada) and various grammatical methods remaining from words."

According to this view, being endowed with the wisdom and skill to master nouns (nāma-pada), verbs (ākhyāta-pada), prefixes (upasagga-pada), and particles (nipāta-pada) is called Padaka. Being endowed with the wisdom and skill to master various grammatical methods such as gender (liṅga), roots (dhātu), stems (pakati), suffixes (vibhatti), and affixes (paccaya) which remain from words is called Veyyākaraṇa.
547:
(Ghū)
According to this commentary's explanation, "words and the grammatical methods remaining from words" should already be included in the science of grammar called Akkhara-pabheda, which explains various linguistic methods along with names such as letters and consonants, as shown previously in the section on Sumedha the Brahmin.

For this reason, the author of the Sīlakkhandhavagga-abhinava-ṭīkā—after providing a formal introduction saying, "Ayaṃ aṭṭhakathāto aparo nayo" (This is another method from the Commentary)—explained that one is called a Padaka because one can recite even the Vedas in the form of verse (gāthā-pada) and prose (cuṇṇiya-pada). In this New Sub-commentary on the Sīlakkhandhavagga, only the meaning of Padaka was explained as another method, while the meaning of Veyyākaraṇa was not specifically explained as a separate method.

Therefore, it is very appropriate if one takes the meaning of Padaka to be verse compositions (gāthā-bandha) known as Pajja in the science of rhetoric, and takes the meaning of Veyyākaraṇa to be prose compositions (cuṇṇiya-bandha) known as Gajja. (In the nine divisions of the Buddha's teaching, Veyyākaraṇa is also prose.) Thus, it is translated as: "He is able to teach, perceive, and master various verse compositions called Pada and various prose compositions called Veyyākaraṇa."

By translating it this way, one can gain an additional quality: "not only understanding various grammatical methods called Akkhara-pabheda but also being skilled and proficient in the writing and recitation of verse (gāthā-bandha) and prose (cuṇṇiya)." Intending this very meaning, the Venerable Mahā Sīlavaṃsa composed in the Sutaung-khan Pyo (Sumedha Brāhmaṇa - Paññā-pala section):

"Distinctive poetry, for the sake of composition, in fixed verse forms and in prose; speaking and commanding, clearly and purely, without hesitation; within the verses themselves, the nuances are deep."

The Anudīpanī (Additional Explanation) ends.
